On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will forget her nursling, and every pregnant female will drop her load, and you will see people as intoxicated, though they are not intoxicated, but the punishment of God is severe.﴾ ﴿Among people is one who disputes about God without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil.﴾ ﴿It has been decreed for him that whoever allies with him, he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whom We will for a specified term, then We bring you out as infants, then that you may reach your maturity. Among you is one who is taken in death, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known. And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and grows every lovely kind of pair.﴾ ﴿That is because God is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things Powerful.﴾ ﴿And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that God will raise up those in the graves.﴾

The relation (munasabah) of the beginning of this surah to what precedes it is that Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the condition of the wretched and the blessed and mentioned the Greatest Terror, which is what is said on the Day of Resurrection. The polytheists of Makkah had denied the return (al-ma'ad) and denied it, because the punishment was delayed for them. This surah was revealed as a warning to them and a frightening, because of what it contains of the mention of the quake of the Hour and the severity of its terror, and the mention of what is prepared for those who deny it, and as an admonition to them concerning resurrection through their development in their creation, and through the stillness of the earth and its stirring after that with plants. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﹙O mankind﹚ is general. It has been said: the intended people are the people of Makkah. Allah, exalted is He, drew attention to the reason for taking heed, which is what the Hour leads to of its terrors. It is by omitting a modifier, meaning: ﴿Fear﴾ the punishment of ﴿your Lord﴾. The zalzalah (quake) is the disturbing movement, and it occurs at the first blast (of the Trumpet). It has been said: at the second. It has been said: at the saying of Allah, "O Adam, send forth the group for the Fire." The majority said: in this world, at the end of time, and it is followed by the rising of the sun from its west.

It is reported from al-Hasan: it is on the Day of Resurrection. It is reported from ʿAlqamah and al-Shaʿbi: at the rising of the sun from its west. It is attributed to the Hour because it is one of its portents. The verbal noun (al-masdar) is attributed to its subject, and the omitted object, which is the earth, is indicated by ﴿When the earth is shaken with its shaking﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1]. The attribution of the quake to "the Hour" is metaphorical (majaz). It is permissible to attribute it to the object, following the practice of extension in the adverbial complement (al-zarf), so that "the Hour" becomes the object. On these estimations there is a literal quake.

Al-Hasan said: the strongest quake is what occurs together with the establishment of the Hour. It has been said: the quake is a metaphor, and the intended meaning is the severity of the Hour and the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. The word "thing" (shay') here indicates its application to what does not exist, because the quake has not yet occurred. Whoever prohibits applying it to the non-existent says: He made the quake a "thing" because of the certainty of its occurrence and its coming into existence.

Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the most terrifying attributes in His saying ﴿you see it﴾ and the verse, so that they would look at that attribute with their insight and imagine it with their intellects, so that this would move them toward His piety, exalted is He, since there is no deliverance from those hardships except through piety. It is related that these two verses were revealed at night during the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited them, and he was not seen to weep more than on that night. When they woke in the morning, they did not remove the saddles from the animals, did not pitch the tents at the time of halting, and did not cook a pot; they were among the grieving weepers and the reflective.

The governing element (al-nasib) of ﴿the Day﴾ [in the verse] is ﴿will be forgetful﴾. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿you see it﴾ refers to the quake, because it is what is spoken of, and the existence of the nursing mother's forgetfulness and the pregnant woman's delivery indicates this. This is when the literal meaning is intended, which is the origin, and it would be in this world. It is reported from al-Hasan: ﴿every nursing mother will forget﴾ her nursling, not for weaning, ﴿and every pregnant one will deliver﴾ what is in her womb, not in completion.

A group said: the pronoun refers to (p. 350) the Hour, so the forgetting and the delivery are an expression of the severity of terror on that day, and there is no forgetting or delivery there, like their saying: "a day on which the youth grows gray." The word ﴿nursing mother﴾ (murdi'ah) is used instead of murdi' (nursing female, without the feminine ending) because it is intended as the act, not as a genealogical attribute, in the sense of "one who has the quality of nursing." As the poet said:

Like a nursing mother of other children, who has neglected her own children—this is the straying from the right course.

The apparent meaning is that what is in His saying ﴿of what she nursed﴾ means "that which" (alladhi), and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning "she nursed it." This is strengthened by the transitivity of "to lay down" (wada'a) to the object in His saying "her burden" and not to the verbal noun. It has been said: "ma" is a verbal noun, meaning "concerning her nursing."

Al-Zamakhshari said: the murdi'ah is the one who, at the time of nursing, puts her breast into the infant's mouth, while the murdi' is the one whose habit is to nurse even if she is not actually nursing at the time the description applies. So it is said "murdi'ah" to indicate that when this terror surprises her while she has put the suckling infant's breast in its mouth, she pulls it out of its mouth because of the consternation that overtakes her. Some Kufan grammarians restricted "murdi'ah" to the mother of the child and "murdi'" to the hired wet-nurse, and this is invalid by the poet's verse:

Like a nursing mother of other children, who has neglected
the house—so this is murdi'ah with the feminine ending, and she is not the mother of the one she nurses.

The saying of the Kufans that the description specific to the feminine does not need the feminine ending, because the ending is only introduced for distinction, is rejected by the Arabs' saying: murdi'ah, ha'idah (menstruating), and talaqah (divorced).

The majority read ﴿will be forgetful every﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and the ha', and raf' (nominative) on "every." Ibn Abi ʿAblah and al-Yamani read with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha', meaning ﴿causes to forget﴾ (tudhhilu): the quake or the Hour causes every [nursing mother] to forget, with the accusative. The word "hamal" with fatha means what is in a belly or on the top of a tree.

The majority read "and you see" (wa-tara) with an open ta' as the address to the singular. Zayd ibn ʿAli read with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ra', meaning "and the quake (or the Hour) makes you see." Al-Zaʿfarani and ʿAbbas in his choice read with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the ra', and raised "the people" and made the verb feminine according to the interpretation of the group. Abu Hurayrah, Abu Zurʿah ibn ʿAmr ibn Jarir, and Abu Nahik read likewise, except that they put "the people" in the accusative, so "see" (tara) took three objects. One of them is the concealed pronoun in "see," which is the second-person pronoun, the object that has not been named as subject. The second and third are ﴿the people drunk﴾: it affirmed that they are "drunk" by way of comparison, then it negated the reality of it, which is drunkenness from wine, because of the bewilderment they are in and the confusion of the intellect.

The majority read "drunk" (sukara) in both places on the pattern fu'ala, and the disagreement concerning fu'ala with a damma on the first letter was already mentioned: is it a plural or a collective noun? Abu Hurayrah, Abu Nahik, and ʿIsa read with a fatha on the sin in both places, and it is a broken plural whose singular is sakran. Abu Hatim said: this is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Akhawan, Ibn Saʿdan, and Masʿud ibn Salih read "sakra" in both places, and it was transmitted from the Messenger; ʿImran ibn Husayn and Abu Saʿid al-Khudri related it, and it is the reading of ʿAbd Allah and his companions and Hudhayfah. Sibawayh said: some people say sakra, making it like marda (sick), because they are two states that enter upon a person; then they made ruba (curdled milk drunk heavily) like sakra, and they are those who are stupefied with sleep from drinking the curdled milk. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: it is valid that it is a plural of sakir, like zamna and zamin, and Sibawayh has transmitted that "rajul sakir" means sakran, so sakra then is for the feminine form of the plural. Al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, Abu Zurʿah, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Aʿmash read "sukra" with a damma on the sin in both places. Abu al-Fath said: it is a singular noun like al-bushra, and Abu ʿAli gave me this ruling. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is strange. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: fu'la with a damma on the first letter is from the description of a single female, but when it was made a description of people, who are a group, the group was treated like the singular feminine. Also from Abu Zurʿah: sakra with a fatha on the sin, and "bi-sukra" with a damma. From Ibn Jubayr also: sakra with a fatha without an alif, and "bi-sukara" with a damma and alif. From al-Hasan also: "sukara" with "sukr," and [the verse] says "or do you not see it?" in the address of the plural: they are all made viewers of it. Then it says "and you see" in the address of the singular, because seeing is tied to the people being in the state of drunkenness, so each one is made a viewer of the others, overcome by fear of Allah's punishment, which took away their intellects and returned them to the state of one whom drunkenness takes away his mind and discernment. This exception (istidrak) came with the report that ﴿the punishment of Allah﴾ is ﴿severe﴾, because what preceded is, in relation to the punishment, like a gentle state: it is the forgetting, the delivery, and seeing people like drunkards. It is as if it were said: these are light conditions, ﴿but the punishment of Allah is severe﴾, neither light nor gentle, because "but" (lakin) must fall between two things that are opposed in some respect. Its discussion has already passed.

﴿And among the people is one who disputes about Allah﴾, that is, about His power and His attributes. It has been said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. It has been said: concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. It has been said: concerning al-Nadr, who was a contentious man, who would say: the angels are the daughters of Allah, the Qur'an is the fables of the ancients, and Allah is not able to revive one who has decayed and become dust. The verse applies to everyone who indulges in disputation concerning what is permissible for Allah and what is not permissible of attributes and acts, without referring to knowledge, evidence, or fairness. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿every rebellious devil﴾ is from the jinn, like His saying ﴿and they do not call upon other than a rebellious devil﴾ [al-Nisa: 117]. It has been said: it is possible that it is from mankind, like His saying ﴿devils of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 112].

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, He mentioned the one who was heedless of the recompense on that day and denied it. Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿and follows﴾ (wa-yattabiʿu) lightly. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿upon him﴾ refers to ﴿one﴾ (man), since it is what is being spoken of; and in ﴿that he﴾, ﴿takes him as a friend﴾, and ﴿for he﴾ it also refers to him. The doer, "takes him as a friend," is the pronoun of "one," and likewise the ha' in ﴿misguides him﴾. It is permissible that the ha' in this aspect (that) is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-shan). The meaning is that this disputant, because of his abundance of disputation in falsehood and his following of the devil, has become a leader in error for whoever takes him as a friend, so his condition is that he misguides whoever takes him as a friend. It has been said: the pronoun in "upon him" refers to ﴿every rebellious devil﴾; this was said by Qatadah, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned no other. Ibn ʿAtiyyah gave the first view as a possibility. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it appears to me that the pronoun in the first "that he" refers to the devil, and the second to "one who," who is the one who takes as a friend. Al-Zamakhshari said: "and the writing upon him" is like: "it [the decree] wrote the misguidance of whoever takes him as a friend upon him," and it inscribed it on him because that is evident in his condition.

The majority read "it was written" (kutiba) in the passive voice. It was also read "kataba" in the active voice, meaning "Allah wrote." The majority read "that he" with a fatha on the hamzah, in the position of the object that has not been named as subject; and "so that he" (fa-anna-hu) with fatha as well, and the fa' is the answer to "one who" (man) if it is conditional, or it is part of the predicate of "one who" if it is relative. And "so that he" is in the estimate of "so his condition is that he misguides him," that is, his misguidance, or "so he has the right to misguide him."

Al-Zamakhshari said: as for whoever reads with a fatha, it is because the first (anna-hu) is the subject of "wrote," meaning as an object that has not been named as subject, and the second is conjoined to it. This is not permissible, because if you make "so that he" a conjunction with "that he," it remains without the completion of a predicate, because "whoever takes him as a friend" has "whoever" as its subject; if you estimate it as relative there is no predicate for it to be a predicate, and if you make it conditional there is no answer for it, when you make "so that he" a conjunction with "that he." Like al-Zamakhshari's statement, Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "that he" is in the position of raf' as the object that has not been named as subject, and the second "that he" is a conjunction with the first, emphasizing it in the same way; this is an error for the reason we have explained. Al-Aʿmash and al-Juʿfi from Abu ʿAmr read "innahu" and "fa-innahu" with kasra on both hamzahs. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: Abu ʿAmr read "innahu man tawallahu fa-innahu yudilluhu" with kasra on both. Its discussion has ended.

It is not well known from Abu ʿAmr. The apparent meaning is that this is from attributing "wrote" to the sentence in a verbal way, meaning "wrote this statement upon him," as you say: "he wrote, indeed Allah commands justice." Al-Zamakhshari said: or by estimating "before," or the object that has not been named as subject is the book, and the clause "that he whoever takes him as a friend" is in the position of the object that has not been named as subject, as if the estimate were "qila" (it was said). This is not permissible according to the Basrans, because the subject for them cannot be a clause, so this cannot be an object that has not been named as subject. As for the second, it is also not permissible according to the Basran school, because "inna" is not broken after what has the meaning of saying; rather after the explicit "qala" (he said). The meaning of "and guides him" (wa-yahdihi) is "and drives him," and he expressed it with the word "guidance" by way of mockery.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 22, verse 1–7 (part 3 of 3):

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned those who dispute concerning the power of Allah without knowledge, and their disputation was about the Gathering (al-hashr) and the Return (al-ma'ad), He mentioned two clear proofs for that. The first is in the human being himself and the beginning of his creation, and his development through seven stages: the dust, the drop (nutfah), the clinging clot (alaqah), the lump of flesh (mudghah), his being brought forth as an infant (tifl), his reaching maturity (bulugh al-ashudd), and his being taken in death (tawaffi) or being returned to decrepitude (al-haram). The second is in the earth which you see changing from one state to another. When the intelligent person considers this, its possibility by reason is established for him; then, when the report of the Law (khabar al-shar') arrives concerning its occurrence, it becomes obligatory to affirm it, and that it will certainly occur.

Al-Hasan recited ﴿مِنَ البَعْثِ﴾ (min al-ba'th) with a fatha on the ayn ('ayn), and this is a dialect (lughah) of it, like al-halb and al-tard in al-halb and al-tard. The Kufans hold that sukun on the ayn is a lightening (takhfif), which they apply analogically to forms whose middle radical is a guttural letter (harf halq), such as al-nahr and al-nahar, and al-sha'r and al-sha'ar. The Basrans do not apply it analogically, and whatever comes of that kind is, in their view, among what has two dialects.

The meaning: if you doubt the Resurrection, then what removes your doubt is that you look at the beginning of your creation ﴿مِن تُرابٍ﴾ (from dust), that is, your origin Adam, and the verb is directed at them because they are his descendants, or in consideration of the intermediate means of generation, because the seed (al-mani) and the menstrual blood are generated from nourishment, and nourishment is animal and plant, the animal returns to plants, and plants come from earth and water, and the drop (nutfah) is the seed. It is said that ﴿نُطْفَةٌ﴾ refers to Adam; this is related by al-Naqqash. The alaqah is a solid piece of blood. The meaning of ﴿وغَيْرِ مُخَلَّقَةٍ﴾ (and not fully formed) is that it is not complete and not smooth; the lumps vary accordingly, and so they differ in length, shortness, completeness and deficiency. Mujahid said that ﴿غَيْرِ مُخَلَّقَةٍ﴾ is that which is miscarried (tastasqit). This was also said by Qatadah, al-Sha'bi and Abu al-'Aliyah. Since the human being has diverse limbs, and each of them is specialized in a creation, it is apt to intensify the verb, because in it there are many creations.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited ﴿مُخَلَّقَةً﴾ with the accusative, and ﴿غَيْرَ﴾ also in the accusative, as a circumstantial (hal) from the preceding indefinite noun; this is rare, and Sibawayh made it analogical. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ﴾ (so that We may make clear to you), by this gradation, Our power, and that He who is able to create mankind ﴿مِن تُرابٍ﴾ first, ﴿ثُمَّ مِن نُطْفَةٍ﴾ then (from a drop), there is no proportion between dust and water, and He is able to make the drop (alaqah), and between them there is clear difference; then He makes the alaqah a lump (mudghah), and the lump bones; He is able to re-create what He originated. Rather, this is more within power and easier in analogy. The verb occurring without an object for the clarified thing is an informing that through these acts of His there becomes manifest of His power and knowledge what thought cannot grasp and description cannot encompass. End.

﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ﴾ is connected to ﴿خَلَقْناكم﴾ (We created you). It is said that ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ﴾ refers to the matter of the Resurrection. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a parenthetical insertion between the two statements. Al-Kirmani said: it means your guidance and your misguidance. It is also said that ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ﴾ means that shaping (al-takhlīq) is a choice of the choosing Agent, and without Him part of it would not have become not fully formed. Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited ﴿لِيُبَيِّنَ لَكم وَيُقِرَّ﴾ with the ya'. Ya'qub and 'Asim in one narration recited ﴿ونُقِرَّ﴾ with the accusative, coordinated with ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ﴾.

Also from 'Asim, ﴿ثُمَّ يُخْرِجَكم﴾ with the jim in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿ونُقِرَّ﴾ when that is in the accusative. From Ya'qub, ﴿ونَقُرُّ﴾ with a fatha on the nun and a damma on the qaf and the ra', from qarra al-ma' (he poured the water). Abu Zayd al-Nahwi recited ﴿ويَقِرَّ﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and the ra' and a kasra on the qaf. In al-Kalam of Ibn Habbar: ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ﴾, ﴿ونُقِرَّ﴾, ﴿ونُخْرِجَكم﴾ with the accusative in them; al-Mufaddal with the ya' in them together with the accusative; Abu Hatim with the ya' and the raf'; 'Umar ibn Shabbah with the ya' and the raf'. End.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the recitation with the raf' is an information that He, exalted is He, establishes in the wombs whatever He wills to establish of that.

﴿إلى أجَلٍ مُسَمًّى﴾ (until an appointed term), which is the time of delivery; and whatever He does not will to establish, the wombs eject it or miscarry it. The recitation with the accusative is a causal clause coordinated with another causal clause, and the meaning is: We created you, arranging you in this gradation for two purposes: the first, that We make clear Our power; the second, that We establish in the wombs whomever We establish, until they are born, grow up, and reach the limit of obligation, so that I may impose obligation upon them. This recitation is supported by His saying ﴿ثُمَّ لِتَبْلُغُوا أشُدَّكُمْ﴾ (then that you may reach your maturity). End.

Yahya ibn Wthab recited ﴿ما نِشاءُ﴾ with a kasra on the nun. The appointed term differs according to each foetus: one falls away (miscarried), and one is complete, its matter emerging alive. He made ﴿طِفْلًا﴾ singular because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar), as said by al-Mubarrad and al-Tabari; or because the purpose is to indicate the category; or because the meaning of ﴿يُخْرِجُكم﴾ is each one, as when you say: "the men are satisfied by a loaf," meaning each one is satisfied. Al-Zamakhshari said: al-ashudd is the perfection of strength, intellect and discernment, and it is among the plural forms for which no singular has been used, like al-ashuddah and al-quyud and others; as if it were a strengthening in no single thing, so it was formed on the plural form for that reason. End.

(p-353) The discussion of al-ashudd and its duration in time has preceded. Some people said it is the plural of shiddah, as an-'um is the plural of ni'mah. As for al-quyud: from Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani, its singular is qayd. ﴿ومِنكم مَن يُتَوَفّى﴾ (and among you is he who is taken in death). It was also recited ﴿يُتَوَفّى﴾ with a fatha on the ya', meaning he fulfils his term. The majority recite it with a damma, meaning after reaching maturity and before decrepitude, and this is ﴿أرْذَلِ العُمْرِ﴾ (the most abject age) and senility (al-kharaf); he returns to the state of childhood, weak in constitution and feeble in intellect. There is no fixed limited time for that, but it depends on what occurs among people. We indeed see one whose age has advanced and who has approached a hundred or reached it, in extreme quality of mind and perception, with strength and vigour, and we see one who is in the age of middle years whose constitution has weakened. Allah, exalted is He, made clear that He is able to bring him to the state of senility, just as He was able to gradate him to the state of completeness; so likewise He is able to re-create the bodies which He graded through these stages and to bring them into the second creation.

﴿لِكَيْلا﴾ (so that) is connected to ﴿يُرَدُّ﴾ (is returned). Al-Kalbi said: so that he does not know anything after his first knowing. It was said: so that he does not acquire knowledge and forget what he knew. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, so that he becomes a forgetful one, such that when he acquires knowledge of something, he soon forgets it and his knowledge of it vanishes, until he is asked about it at that very moment; he says to you, "Who is this?" and you say, "So-and-so," and he does not linger for a moment before asking you about him again. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr and Nafi' that they pronounced the mim of ﴿العُمْرِ﴾ with sukun.

﴿وتَرى الأرْضَ هامِدَةً﴾ (And you see the earth lifeless). This is the second proof, which it includes; the first proof is the verse. Since the first proof is some stages of the creation not arranged in order, He said ﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ في رَيْبٍ مِنَ البَعْثِ فَإنّا خَلَقْناكُمْ﴾ and did not refer in all its stages to seeing. Since this second proof is observed by the eyes, He referred it to seeing and said "you see," O hearer or disputant, ﴿الأرْضَ هامِدَةً﴾. Because of its clarity this proof is repeated in the Qur'an. ﴿الماءَ﴾ (the water) is the water of rain, rivers, springs and wells; its ﴿اهْتِزازُها﴾ (its quivering) is its loosening and the agitation of some of its parts due to the emergence of plants; ﴿ورَبَتْ﴾ (and it swells) means it increases and expands. Abu Ja'far, 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far, Khalid ibn Ilyas and Abu 'Amr in one narration recited ﴿ورَبَأتْ﴾ with hamza here and in Fussilat, meaning it rose and became elevated; it is said: so-and-so raises himself above such a thing, that is, he elevates himself from it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its meaning is that it comes from raba'tu al-qawm, when I ascended a height of land as a sentinel, so the earth by the water extends and rises. End.

It is said: rabi' and rabi'ah. The poet said:
"We sent a sentinel before that, laden, like the wolf of al-Ghada which walks in harm and guards itself."

That which we have mentioned of the creation of the children of Adam and their development through those stages, and of the revival of the earth accomplished by this, is the reality (haqiqah) of Allah, exalted is He; He is the Established, the Existent, the Capable of reviving the dead and of every thing that is within power. He has promised the Resurrection, and He is capable of it, so it must come to be. His saying ﴿وأنَّ السّاعَةَ﴾ (and that the Hour) to its end is an emphasis of His saying ﴿وأنَّهُ يُحْيِي المَوْتى﴾ (and that He revives the dead). The apparent reading is that His saying ﴿وأنَّ السّاعَةَ آتِيَةٌ﴾ (and that the Hour is coming) is not included in the cause of what was mentioned before, so it is not coordinated with the "that" which immediately precedes it; it is therefore on an implied basis, the matter being "that the Hour..." and that is the subject, with the predicate being "bi-anna" (that). It was also said that this is in the accusative by a hidden verb, meaning "We did that."

**Surah al-Hajj is Madani.**

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing. On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will forget her nursling, and every pregnant female will drop her load, and you will see people as intoxicated, though they are not intoxicated, but the punishment of God is severe.﴾ ﴿Among people is one who disputes about God without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil.﴾ ﴿It has been decreed for him that whoever allies with him, he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whom We will for a specified term, then We bring you out as infants, then that you may reach your maturity. Among you is one who is taken in death, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known. And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and grows every lovely kind of pair.﴾ ﴿That is because God is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things Powerful.﴾ ﴿And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that God will raise up those in the graves.﴾

(p. 349) This surah is Makki (revealed in Mecca) except for (﴿These two adversaries﴾ [al-Hajj: 19] up to the completion of three verses), as stated by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that they are four verses, up to His saying ﴿the punishment of the burning﴾ [al-Hajj: 22]. Al-Dahhak said: it is Madani (revealed in Medina). Qatadah said: except from His saying ﴿We did not send before you any messenger﴾ [al-Hajj: 52] to ﴿a lasting punishment﴾. The majority said: some of it is Makki and some of it is Madani.

(p. 346) *Dhahila 'an al-shay'* (ذَهَلَ عَنِ الشَّيْءِ) means to be preoccupied with something, so that one is distracted from it. Qutrub said this, and others said: it means to be heedless because of an occupying concern, such as grief, pain, or something else. It is also said: it means with bewilderment. *Al-mudghah* (المُضْغَةُ, a lump of flesh) is a small piece of flesh the size of what can be chewed. *Al-mukhallaqah* (المُخَلَّقَةُ) is that which is shaped, smooth, without deficiency or defect. It is said: *khalaqa al-siwak wal-'ud* (خَلَقَ السِّواكَ والعُودَ), meaning he made it even and smooth, from their saying: *sakhra khalqa'* (صَخْرَةٌ خَلْقاءُ), that is, a smooth rock. *Al-tifl* (الطِّفْلُ, child) is used from the time of a child's separation from the womb until puberty. It is also used for the young of a wild animal. It is applied to the singular, dual, plural, masculine, and feminine with one form. It is also said *tifl*, *tiflan*, *atfal* (plural). A woman *atfalat* means she became one with a child. *Al-tafl* with a fatha on the ta' means tender, delicate; a girl is *tafla* (tender), and tender fingers are *banan tafl*. *Qad tafala al-layl* means the night's darkness came on. *Al-tafal*, with a fatha on the fa' and a vowel on the ta', is the time after the afternoon prayer when the sun begins to set. *Al-tafal* also means rain. Al-Mubarrad said: it is a noun used as a verbal noun, like *al-rida* and *al-'adl*, applying to the singular and plural. *Hamadat al-ard* (هَمَدَتِ الأرْضُ) means the earth dried up and became effaced. *Al-thawb* (the garment) wore out. End of quote. Al-A'sha said:

She said, "Why is your body pale, and I see your garments worn and faded?"

*Al-bahij* (البَهِيجُ) means beautiful, pleasing to the beholder. It is said: "So-and-so has *bahja*," meaning beauty. He became *bahuja*, with a damma, *bahajatan* and *bahjatan*, so he is *bahij*. *Abhajani* means he pleased me with its beauty. *Al-'atf* (العَطْفُ) means side. The two *'itfa* (عِطْفا) of a man are his right and left sides. Its root is from *al-'atf*, which means softness. The cloak is called *al-'itaf*. *Al-Majus* (المَجُوسُ) are a people who worship fire, the sun, and the moon. It is also said they worship fire. It is also said they are a people who separated from the Christians and wore wool garments. It is also said they are a people who took something from the religion of the Christians and something from the religion of the Jews, and they are those who say the world has two principles: light and darkness. It is also said that the *mim* in *Majus* replaces a *nun*, because of their use of impurities. *Sahharat al-shahm bil-nar* (صَهَرْتُ الشَّحْمَ بِالنّارِ) means I melted the fat with fire, and *al-suhara* is the melted buttock. It is also said: it becomes ripe. The poet said:

The sun melts it, but it does not melt.

*Al-miqma'ah* (المِقْمَعَةُ), with a kasra on the mim, is the whip with which the one being beaten is struck. *Al-lu'lu'* (اللُّؤْلُؤُ) is the pearl. It is said: its small and large ones. *Al-damir* (الضّامِرُ) is the emaciated. *Al-'amiq* (العَمِيقُ) means distant. Its root meaning is distance downward. It is said: *bi'r 'amiq*, meaning a well of deep bottom. The verb is *'amuqa* and *'ammaqa*. The poet said:

When horses come from deep mountain paths, along which goes a dusty, pale rider.

It is said *ghamiq* with a ghayn. Al-Layth said: *'amiq* and *mu'iq* are used by the tribe of Tamim. *A'maqtu al-bi'r* and *am'aqtuha*, and it has become deep, *'amuqat* and *ma'uqat*, *'amaqatan* and *mu'aqatan*. It is far in depth. *Al-ma'q*, *al-am'aq*, and *al-a'maq* are the far edges of the desert. He said:

And the standing one of the far edges, the emptied of the hollow.

*Al-tafath* (التَّفَثُ) originally means filth and dirt. It is said to someone who is disgusting: "What is your *tafath*?" From Qutrub: *tafitha al-rajul*, the man's filth increased on his journey. Abu Muhammad al-Basri said: *al-tafath* is from *al-tuffa*, which is the dirt under the nails, and the *fa'* was changed into a *tha'* like *maghthur*. *Al-sahiq* (السَّحِيقُ) means far away. *Wajaba al-shay'* means it fell. *Wajabat al-shams jibatan* means the sun set. Aws ibn Hajar said:

Did not the sun of the day eclipse, and the full moon, for the setting mountain?

*Al-qani'* (القانِعُ) is the one who asks. *Qani'a qanu'an* means he asked. *Qani'a qana'atan* means he refrained and was content with his modest means. Al-Shammakh said:

His person is more chaste than the one who begs; a man's wealth improves him and makes him rich.

*Al-wathan* (الوَثَنُ): Shimr said: every image made of wood, stone, gold, silver, copper, or the like. The Arabs used to set them up and worship them. It is also applied to the cross. Al-A'sha said:

The needy circle around his doors, like the circling of the Christians around the door of the idol.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Adi ibn Hatim when he saw a cross around his neck: "Cast the idol from you." Its derivation is from *wathana al-shay'*, meaning he set it in its place and it became firm. *Al-wathin* is the one who stays, firmly fixed in its place. Ru'ba said:

Over the faithful friends of pure loyalty, the idol.

He means constancy upon the covenant. *Al-budn* (البُدْنُ) is the plural of *badanah*, like *thumr* is the plural of *thamarah*, as said by al-Zajjaj. It was named so because it grows fat (*tabdunu*). Al-Layth said: *al-badanah*, with the ta' marbuta, applies to the she-camel, the cow, and the camel, which are permissible for sacrifice and offerings, and it does not apply to a sheep. It was called *badanah* because of its size. It is also said it is specific to camels. It is also said it is what is marked (*ash'ara*) from a she-camel or cow, said by 'Ata' and others. It is also said *al-badan* is a singular noun of a collective kind, meaning the large fat one from the camels and cows, and it is said of a fat man. *Al-mu'tarr* (المُعْتَرُّ) is the one who approaches without asking. Ibn Qutaybah said: *gharrahu* and *ightarrahu*, *'arrahu* and *i'tarahu*: he came to him seeking his kindness. The poet said:

Ask the nighttime visitor who approaches, O mother of Malik, when he comes to me between my destiny and my slaughter.

Another said:

By your life, the one who approaches does not come to our lands that we would deny him with the lost, the ruined.

* *

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing. On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will forget her nursling, and every pregnant female will drop her load, and you will see people as intoxicated, though they are not intoxicated, but the punishment of God is severe.﴾ ﴿Among people is one who disputes about God without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil.﴾ ﴿It has been decreed for him that whoever allies with him, he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whom We will for a specified term, then We bring you out as infants, then that you may reach your maturity. Among you is one who is taken in death, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known. And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and grows every lovely kind of pair.﴾ ﴿That is because God is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things Powerful.﴾ ﴿And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that God will raise up those in the graves.﴾

The relation (munasabah) of the beginning of this surah to what precedes it is that Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the condition of the wretched and the blessed and mentioned the Greatest Terror, which is what is said on the Day of Resurrection. The polytheists of Makkah had denied the return (al-ma'ad) and denied it, because the punishment was delayed for them. This surah was revealed as a warning to them and a frightening, because of what it contains of the mention of the quake of the Hour and the severity of its terror, and the mention of what is prepared for those who deny it, and as an admonition to them concerning resurrection through their development in their creation, and through the stillness of the earth and its stirring after that with plants. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﹙O mankind﹚ is general. It has been said: the intended people are the people of Makkah. Allah, exalted is He, drew attention to the reason for taking heed, which is what the Hour leads to of its terrors. It is by omitting a modifier, meaning: ﴿Fear﴾ the punishment of ﴿your Lord﴾. The zalzalah (quake) is the disturbing movement, and it occurs at the first blast (of the Trumpet). It has been said: at the second. It has been said: at the saying of Allah, "O Adam, send forth the group for the Fire." The majority said: in this world, at the end of time, and it is followed by the rising of the sun from its west.

It is reported from al-Hasan: it is on the Day of Resurrection. It is reported from ʿAlqamah and al-Shaʿbi: at the rising of the sun from its west. It is attributed to the Hour because it is one of its portents. The verbal noun (al-masdar) is attributed to its subject, and the omitted object, which is the earth, is indicated by ﴿When the earth is shaken with its shaking﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1]. The attribution of the quake to "the Hour" is metaphorical (majaz). It is permissible to attribute it to the object, following the practice of extension in the adverbial complement (al-zarf), so that "the Hour" becomes the object. On these estimations there is a literal quake.

Al-Hasan said: the strongest quake is what occurs together with the establishment of the Hour. It has been said: the quake is a metaphor, and the intended meaning is the severity of the Hour and the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. The word "thing" (shay') here indicates its application to what does not exist, because the quake has not yet occurred. Whoever prohibits applying it to the non-existent says: He made the quake a "thing" because of the certainty of its occurrence and its coming into existence.

Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the most terrifying attributes in His saying ﴿you see it﴾ and the verse, so that they would look at that attribute with their insight and imagine it with their intellects, so that this would move them toward His piety, exalted is He, since there is no deliverance from those hardships except through piety. It is related that these two verses were revealed at night during the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited them, and he was not seen to weep more than on that night. When they woke in the morning, they did not remove the saddles from the animals, did not pitch the tents at the time of halting, and did not cook a pot; they were among the grieving weepers and the reflective.

The governing element (al-nasib) of ﴿the Day﴾ [in the verse] is ﴿will be forgetful﴾. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿you see it﴾ refers to the quake, because it is what is spoken of, and the existence of the nursing mother's forgetfulness and the pregnant woman's delivery indicates this. This is when the literal meaning is intended, which is the origin, and it would be in this world. It is reported from al-Hasan: ﴿every nursing mother will forget﴾ her nursling, not for weaning, ﴿and every pregnant one will deliver﴾ what is in her womb, not in completion.

A group said: the pronoun refers to (p. 350) the Hour, so the forgetting and the delivery are an expression of the severity of terror on that day, and there is no forgetting or delivery there, like their saying: "a day on which the youth grows gray." The word ﴿nursing mother﴾ (murdi'ah) is used instead of murdi' (nursing female, without the feminine ending) because it is intended as the act, not as a genealogical attribute, in the sense of "one who has the quality of nursing." As the poet said:

Like a nursing mother of other children, who has neglected her own children—this is the straying from the right course.

The apparent meaning is that what is in His saying ﴿of what she nursed﴾ means "that which" (alladhi), and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning "she nursed it." This is strengthened by the transitivity of "to lay down" (wada'a) to the object in His saying "her burden" and not to the verbal noun. It has been said: "ma" is a verbal noun, meaning "concerning her nursing."

Al-Zamakhshari said: the murdi'ah is the one who, at the time of nursing, puts her breast into the infant's mouth, while the murdi' is the one whose habit is to nurse even if she is not actually nursing at the time the description applies. So it is said "murdi'ah" to indicate that when this terror surprises her while she has put the suckling infant's breast in its mouth, she pulls it out of its mouth because of the consternation that overtakes her. Some Kufan grammarians restricted "murdi'ah" to the mother of the child and "murdi'" to the hired wet-nurse, and this is invalid by the poet's verse:

Like a nursing mother of other children, who has neglected
the house—so this is murdi'ah with the feminine ending, and she is not the mother of the one she nurses.

The saying of the Kufans that the description specific to the feminine does not need the feminine ending, because the ending is only introduced for distinction, is rejected by the Arabs' saying: murdi'ah, ha'idah (menstruating), and talaqah (divorced).

The majority read ﴿will be forgetful every﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and the ha', and raf' (nominative) on "every." Ibn Abi ʿAblah and al-Yamani read with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha', meaning ﴿causes to forget﴾ (tudhhilu): the quake or the Hour causes every [nursing mother] to forget, with the accusative. The word "hamal" with fatha means what is in a belly or on the top of a tree.

The majority read "and you see" (wa-tara) with an open ta' as the address to the singular. Zayd ibn ʿAli read with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ra', meaning "and the quake (or the Hour) makes you see." Al-Zaʿfarani and ʿAbbas in his choice read with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the ra', and raised "the people" and made the verb feminine according to the interpretation of the group. Abu Hurayrah, Abu Zurʿah ibn ʿAmr ibn Jarir, and Abu Nahik read likewise, except that they put "the people" in the accusative, so "see" (tara) took three objects. One of them is the concealed pronoun in "see," which is the second-person pronoun, the object that has not been named as subject. The second and third are ﴿the people drunk﴾: it affirmed that they are "drunk" by way of comparison, then it negated the reality of it, which is drunkenness from wine, because of the bewilderment they are in and the confusion of the intellect.

The majority read "drunk" (sukara) in both places on the pattern fu'ala, and the disagreement concerning fu'ala with a damma on the first letter was already mentioned: is it a plural or a collective noun? Abu Hurayrah, Abu Nahik, and ʿIsa read with a fatha on the sin in both places, and it is a broken plural whose singular is sakran. Abu Hatim said: this is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Akhawan, Ibn Saʿdan, and Masʿud ibn Salih read "sakra" in both places, and it was transmitted from the Messenger; ʿImran ibn Husayn and Abu Saʿid al-Khudri related it, and it is the reading of ʿAbd Allah and his companions and Hudhayfah. Sibawayh said: some people say sakra, making it like marda (sick), because they are two states that enter upon a person; then they made ruba (curdled milk drunk heavily) like sakra, and they are those who are stupefied with sleep from drinking the curdled milk. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: it is valid that it is a plural of sakir, like zamna and zamin, and Sibawayh has transmitted that "rajul sakir" means sakran, so sakra then is for the feminine form of the plural. Al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, Abu Zurʿah, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Aʿmash read "sukra" with a damma on the sin in both places. Abu al-Fath said: it is a singular noun like al-bushra, and Abu ʿAli gave me this ruling. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is strange. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: fu'la with a damma on the first letter is from the description of a single female, but when it was made a description of people, who are a group, the group was treated like the singular feminine. Also from Abu Zurʿah: sakra with a fatha on the sin, and "bi-sukra" with a damma. From Ibn Jubayr also: sakra with a fatha without an alif, and "bi-sukara" with a damma and alif. From al-Hasan also: "sukara" with "sukr," and [the verse] says "or do you not see it?" in the address of the plural: they are all made viewers of it. Then it says "and you see" in the address of the singular, because seeing is tied to the people being in the state of drunkenness, so each one is made a viewer of the others, overcome by fear of Allah's punishment, which took away their intellects and returned them to the state of one whom drunkenness takes away his mind and discernment. This exception (istidrak) came with the report that ﴿the punishment of Allah﴾ is ﴿severe﴾, because what preceded is, in relation to the punishment, like a gentle state: it is the forgetting, the delivery, and seeing people like drunkards. It is as if it were said: these are light conditions, ﴿but the punishment of Allah is severe﴾, neither light nor gentle, because "but" (lakin) must fall between two things that are opposed in some respect. Its discussion has already passed.

﴿And among the people is one who disputes about Allah﴾, that is, about His power and His attributes. It has been said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. It has been said: concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. It has been said: concerning al-Nadr, who was a contentious man, who would say: the angels are the daughters of Allah, the Qur'an is the fables of the ancients, and Allah is not able to revive one who has decayed and become dust. The verse applies to everyone who indulges in disputation concerning what is permissible for Allah and what is not permissible of attributes and acts, without referring to knowledge, evidence, or fairness. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿every rebellious devil﴾ is from the jinn, like His saying ﴿and they do not call upon other than a rebellious devil﴾ [al-Nisa: 117]. It has been said: it is possible that it is from mankind, like His saying ﴿devils of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 112].

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, He mentioned the one who was heedless of the recompense on that day and denied it. Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿and follows﴾ (wa-yattabiʿu) lightly. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿upon him﴾ refers to ﴿one﴾ (man), since it is what is being spoken of; and in ﴿that he﴾, ﴿takes him as a friend﴾, and ﴿for he﴾ it also refers to him. The doer, "takes him as a friend," is the pronoun of "one," and likewise the ha' in ﴿misguides him﴾. It is permissible that the ha' in this aspect (that) is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-shan). The meaning is that this disputant, because of his abundance of disputation in falsehood and his following of the devil, has become a leader in error for whoever takes him as a friend, so his condition is that he misguides whoever takes him as a friend. It has been said: the pronoun in "upon him" refers to ﴿every rebellious devil﴾; this was said by Qatadah, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned no other. Ibn ʿAtiyyah gave the first view as a possibility. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it appears to me that the pronoun in the first "that he" refers to the devil, and the second to "one who," who is the one who takes as a friend. Al-Zamakhshari said: "and the writing upon him" is like: "it [the decree] wrote the misguidance of whoever takes him as a friend upon him," and it inscribed it on him because that is evident in his condition.

The majority read "it was written" (kutiba) in the passive voice. It was also read "kataba" in the active voice, meaning "Allah wrote." The majority read "that he" with a fatha on the hamzah, in the position of the object that has not been named as subject; and "so that he" (fa-anna-hu) with fatha as well, and the fa' is the answer to "one who" (man) if it is conditional, or it is part of the predicate of "one who" if it is relative. And "so that he" is in the estimate of "so his condition is that he misguides him," that is, his misguidance, or "so he has the right to misguide him."

Al-Zamakhshari said: as for whoever reads with a fatha, it is because the first (anna-hu) is the subject of "wrote," meaning as an object that has not been named as subject, and the second is conjoined to it. This is not permissible, because if you make "so that he" a conjunction with "that he," it remains without the completion of a predicate, because "whoever takes him as a friend" has "whoever" as its subject; if you estimate it as relative there is no predicate for it to be a predicate, and if you make it conditional there is no answer for it, when you make "so that he" a conjunction with "that he." Like al-Zamakhshari's statement, Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "that he" is in the position of raf' as the object that has not been named as subject, and the second "that he" is a conjunction with the first, emphasizing it in the same way; this is an error for the reason we have explained. Al-Aʿmash and al-Juʿfi from Abu ʿAmr read "innahu" and "fa-innahu" with kasra on both hamzahs. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: Abu ʿAmr read "innahu man tawallahu fa-innahu yudilluhu" with kasra on both. Its discussion has ended.

It is not well known from Abu ʿAmr. The apparent meaning is that this is from attributing "wrote" to the sentence in a verbal way, meaning "wrote this statement upon him," as you say: "he wrote, indeed Allah commands justice." Al-Zamakhshari said: or by estimating "before," or the object that has not been named as subject is the book, and the clause "that he whoever takes him as a friend" is in the position of the object that has not been named as subject, as if the estimate were "qila" (it was said). This is not permissible according to the Basrans, because the subject for them cannot be a clause, so this cannot be an object that has not been named as subject. As for the second, it is also not permissible according to the Basran school, because "inna" is not broken after what has the meaning of saying; rather after the explicit "qala" (he said). The meaning of "and guides him" (wa-yahdihi) is "and drives him," and he expressed it with the word "guidance" by way of mockery.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 22, verse 1–7 (part 3 of 3):

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned those who dispute concerning the power of Allah without knowledge, and their disputation was about the Gathering (al-hashr) and the Return (al-ma'ad), He mentioned two clear proofs for that. The first is in the human being himself and the beginning of his creation, and his development through seven stages: the dust, the drop (nutfah), the clinging clot (alaqah), the lump of flesh (mudghah), his being brought forth as an infant (tifl), his reaching maturity (bulugh al-ashudd), and his being taken in death (tawaffi) or being returned to decrepitude (al-haram). The second is in the earth which you see changing from one state to another. When the intelligent person considers this, its possibility by reason is established for him; then, when the report of the Law (khabar al-shar') arrives concerning its occurrence, it becomes obligatory to affirm it, and that it will certainly occur.

Al-Hasan recited ﴿مِنَ البَعْثِ﴾ (min al-ba'th) with a fatha on the ayn ('ayn), and this is a dialect (lughah) of it, like al-halb and al-tard in al-halb and al-tard. The Kufans hold that sukun on the ayn is a lightening (takhfif), which they apply analogically to forms whose middle radical is a guttural letter (harf halq), such as al-nahr and al-nahar, and al-sha'r and al-sha'ar. The Basrans do not apply it analogically, and whatever comes of that kind is, in their view, among what has two dialects.

The meaning: if you doubt the Resurrection, then what removes your doubt is that you look at the beginning of your creation ﴿مِن تُرابٍ﴾ (from dust), that is, your origin Adam, and the verb is directed at them because they are his descendants, or in consideration of the intermediate means of generation, because the seed (al-mani) and the menstrual blood are generated from nourishment, and nourishment is animal and plant, the animal returns to plants, and plants come from earth and water, and the drop (nutfah) is the seed. It is said that ﴿نُطْفَةٌ﴾ refers to Adam; this is related by al-Naqqash. The alaqah is a solid piece of blood. The meaning of ﴿وغَيْرِ مُخَلَّقَةٍ﴾ (and not fully formed) is that it is not complete and not smooth; the lumps vary accordingly, and so they differ in length, shortness, completeness and deficiency. Mujahid said that ﴿غَيْرِ مُخَلَّقَةٍ﴾ is that which is miscarried (tastasqit). This was also said by Qatadah, al-Sha'bi and Abu al-'Aliyah. Since the human being has diverse limbs, and each of them is specialized in a creation, it is apt to intensify the verb, because in it there are many creations.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited ﴿مُخَلَّقَةً﴾ with the accusative, and ﴿غَيْرَ﴾ also in the accusative, as a circumstantial (hal) from the preceding indefinite noun; this is rare, and Sibawayh made it analogical. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ﴾ (so that We may make clear to you), by this gradation, Our power, and that He who is able to create mankind ﴿مِن تُرابٍ﴾ first, ﴿ثُمَّ مِن نُطْفَةٍ﴾ then (from a drop), there is no proportion between dust and water, and He is able to make the drop (alaqah), and between them there is clear difference; then He makes the alaqah a lump (mudghah), and the lump bones; He is able to re-create what He originated. Rather, this is more within power and easier in analogy. The verb occurring without an object for the clarified thing is an informing that through these acts of His there becomes manifest of His power and knowledge what thought cannot grasp and description cannot encompass. End.

﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ﴾ is connected to ﴿خَلَقْناكم﴾ (We created you). It is said that ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ﴾ refers to the matter of the Resurrection. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a parenthetical insertion between the two statements. Al-Kirmani said: it means your guidance and your misguidance. It is also said that ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ﴾ means that shaping (al-takhlīq) is a choice of the choosing Agent, and without Him part of it would not have become not fully formed. Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited ﴿لِيُبَيِّنَ لَكم وَيُقِرَّ﴾ with the ya'. Ya'qub and 'Asim in one narration recited ﴿ونُقِرَّ﴾ with the accusative, coordinated with ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ﴾.

Also from 'Asim, ﴿ثُمَّ يُخْرِجَكم﴾ with the jim in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿ونُقِرَّ﴾ when that is in the accusative. From Ya'qub, ﴿ونَقُرُّ﴾ with a fatha on the nun and a damma on the qaf and the ra', from qarra al-ma' (he poured the water). Abu Zayd al-Nahwi recited ﴿ويَقِرَّ﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and the ra' and a kasra on the qaf. In al-Kalam of Ibn Habbar: ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ﴾, ﴿ونُقِرَّ﴾, ﴿ونُخْرِجَكم﴾ with the accusative in them; al-Mufaddal with the ya' in them together with the accusative; Abu Hatim with the ya' and the raf'; 'Umar ibn Shabbah with the ya' and the raf'. End.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the recitation with the raf' is an information that He, exalted is He, establishes in the wombs whatever He wills to establish of that.

﴿إلى أجَلٍ مُسَمًّى﴾ (until an appointed term), which is the time of delivery; and whatever He does not will to establish, the wombs eject it or miscarry it. The recitation with the accusative is a causal clause coordinated with another causal clause, and the meaning is: We created you, arranging you in this gradation for two purposes: the first, that We make clear Our power; the second, that We establish in the wombs whomever We establish, until they are born, grow up, and reach the limit of obligation, so that I may impose obligation upon them. This recitation is supported by His saying ﴿ثُمَّ لِتَبْلُغُوا أشُدَّكُمْ﴾ (then that you may reach your maturity). End.

Yahya ibn Wthab recited ﴿ما نِشاءُ﴾ with a kasra on the nun. The appointed term differs according to each foetus: one falls away (miscarried), and one is complete, its matter emerging alive. He made ﴿طِفْلًا﴾ singular because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar), as said by al-Mubarrad and al-Tabari; or because the purpose is to indicate the category; or because the meaning of ﴿يُخْرِجُكم﴾ is each one, as when you say: "the men are satisfied by a loaf," meaning each one is satisfied. Al-Zamakhshari said: al-ashudd is the perfection of strength, intellect and discernment, and it is among the plural forms for which no singular has been used, like al-ashuddah and al-quyud and others; as if it were a strengthening in no single thing, so it was formed on the plural form for that reason. End.

(p-353) The discussion of al-ashudd and its duration in time has preceded. Some people said it is the plural of shiddah, as an-'um is the plural of ni'mah. As for al-quyud: from Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani, its singular is qayd. ﴿ومِنكم مَن يُتَوَفّى﴾ (and among you is he who is taken in death). It was also recited ﴿يُتَوَفّى﴾ with a fatha on the ya', meaning he fulfils his term. The majority recite it with a damma, meaning after reaching maturity and before decrepitude, and this is ﴿أرْذَلِ العُمْرِ﴾ (the most abject age) and senility (al-kharaf); he returns to the state of childhood, weak in constitution and feeble in intellect. There is no fixed limited time for that, but it depends on what occurs among people. We indeed see one whose age has advanced and who has approached a hundred or reached it, in extreme quality of mind and perception, with strength and vigour, and we see one who is in the age of middle years whose constitution has weakened. Allah, exalted is He, made clear that He is able to bring him to the state of senility, just as He was able to gradate him to the state of completeness; so likewise He is able to re-create the bodies which He graded through these stages and to bring them into the second creation.

﴿لِكَيْلا﴾ (so that) is connected to ﴿يُرَدُّ﴾ (is returned). Al-Kalbi said: so that he does not know anything after his first knowing. It was said: so that he does not acquire knowledge and forget what he knew. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, so that he becomes a forgetful one, such that when he acquires knowledge of something, he soon forgets it and his knowledge of it vanishes, until he is asked about it at that very moment; he says to you, "Who is this?" and you say, "So-and-so," and he does not linger for a moment before asking you about him again. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr and Nafi' that they pronounced the mim of ﴿العُمْرِ﴾ with sukun.

﴿وتَرى الأرْضَ هامِدَةً﴾ (And you see the earth lifeless). This is the second proof, which it includes; the first proof is the verse. Since the first proof is some stages of the creation not arranged in order, He said ﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ في رَيْبٍ مِنَ البَعْثِ فَإنّا خَلَقْناكُمْ﴾ and did not refer in all its stages to seeing. Since this second proof is observed by the eyes, He referred it to seeing and said "you see," O hearer or disputant, ﴿الأرْضَ هامِدَةً﴾. Because of its clarity this proof is repeated in the Qur'an. ﴿الماءَ﴾ (the water) is the water of rain, rivers, springs and wells; its ﴿اهْتِزازُها﴾ (its quivering) is its loosening and the agitation of some of its parts due to the emergence of plants; ﴿ورَبَتْ﴾ (and it swells) means it increases and expands. Abu Ja'far, 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far, Khalid ibn Ilyas and Abu 'Amr in one narration recited ﴿ورَبَأتْ﴾ with hamza here and in Fussilat, meaning it rose and became elevated; it is said: so-and-so raises himself above such a thing, that is, he elevates himself from it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its meaning is that it comes from raba'tu al-qawm, when I ascended a height of land as a sentinel, so the earth by the water extends and rises. End.

It is said: rabi' and rabi'ah. The poet said:
"We sent a sentinel before that, laden, like the wolf of al-Ghada which walks in harm and guards itself."

That which we have mentioned of the creation of the children of Adam and their development through those stages, and of the revival of the earth accomplished by this, is the reality (haqiqah) of Allah, exalted is He; He is the Established, the Existent, the Capable of reviving the dead and of every thing that is within power. He has promised the Resurrection, and He is capable of it, so it must come to be. His saying ﴿وأنَّ السّاعَةَ﴾ (and that the Hour) to its end is an emphasis of His saying ﴿وأنَّهُ يُحْيِي المَوْتى﴾ (and that He revives the dead). The apparent reading is that His saying ﴿وأنَّ السّاعَةَ آتِيَةٌ﴾ (and that the Hour is coming) is not included in the cause of what was mentioned before, so it is not coordinated with the "that" which immediately precedes it; it is therefore on an implied basis, the matter being "that the Hour..." and that is the subject, with the predicate being "bi-anna" (that). It was also said that this is in the accusative by a hidden verb, meaning "We did that."

**Surah al-Hajj is Madani.**

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing. On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will forget her nursling, and every pregnant female will drop her load, and you will see people as intoxicated, though they are not intoxicated, but the punishment of God is severe.﴾ ﴿Among people is one who disputes about God without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil.﴾ ﴿It has been decreed for him that whoever allies with him, he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whom We will for a specified term, then We bring you out as infants, then that you may reach your maturity. Among you is one who is taken in death, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known. And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and grows every lovely kind of pair.﴾ ﴿That is because God is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things Powerful.﴾ ﴿And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that God will raise up those in the graves.﴾

(p. 349) This surah is Makki (revealed in Mecca) except for (﴿These two adversaries﴾ [al-Hajj: 19] up to the completion of three verses), as stated by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that they are four verses, up to His saying ﴿the punishment of the burning﴾ [al-Hajj: 22]. Al-Dahhak said: it is Madani (revealed in Medina). Qatadah said: except from His saying ﴿We did not send before you any messenger﴾ [al-Hajj: 52] to ﴿a lasting punishment﴾. The majority said: some of it is Makki and some of it is Madani.

(p. 346) *Dhahila 'an al-shay'* (ذَهَلَ عَنِ الشَّيْءِ) means to be preoccupied with something, so that one is distracted from it. Qutrub said this, and others said: it means to be heedless because of an occupying concern, such as grief, pain, or something else. It is also said: it means with bewilderment. *Al-mudghah* (المُضْغَةُ, a lump of flesh) is a small piece of flesh the size of what can be chewed. *Al-mukhallaqah* (المُخَلَّقَةُ) is that which is shaped, smooth, without deficiency or defect. It is said: *khalaqa al-siwak wal-'ud* (خَلَقَ السِّواكَ والعُودَ), meaning he made it even and smooth, from their saying: *sakhra khalqa'* (صَخْرَةٌ خَلْقاءُ), that is, a smooth rock. *Al-tifl* (الطِّفْلُ, child) is used from the time of a child's separation from the womb until puberty. It is also used for the young of a wild animal. It is applied to the singular, dual, plural, masculine, and feminine with one form. It is also said *tifl*, *tiflan*, *atfal* (plural). A woman *atfalat* means she became one with a child. *Al-tafl* with a fatha on the ta' means tender, delicate; a girl is *tafla* (tender), and tender fingers are *banan tafl*. *Qad tafala al-layl* means the night's darkness came on. *Al-tafal*, with a fatha on the fa' and a vowel on the ta', is the time after the afternoon prayer when the sun begins to set. *Al-tafal* also means rain. Al-Mubarrad said: it is a noun used as a verbal noun, like *al-rida* and *al-'adl*, applying to the singular and plural. *Hamadat al-ard* (هَمَدَتِ الأرْضُ) means the earth dried up and became effaced. *Al-thawb* (the garment) wore out. End of quote. Al-A'sha said:

She said, "Why is your body pale, and I see your garments worn and faded?"

*Al-bahij* (البَهِيجُ) means beautiful, pleasing to the beholder. It is said: "So-and-so has *bahja*," meaning beauty. He became *bahuja*, with a damma, *bahajatan* and *bahjatan*, so he is *bahij*. *Abhajani* means he pleased me with its beauty. *Al-'atf* (العَطْفُ) means side. The two *'itfa* (عِطْفا) of a man are his right and left sides. Its root is from *al-'atf*, which means softness. The cloak is called *al-'itaf*. *Al-Majus* (المَجُوسُ) are a people who worship fire, the sun, and the moon. It is also said they worship fire. It is also said they are a people who separated from the Christians and wore wool garments. It is also said they are a people who took something from the religion of the Christians and something from the religion of the Jews, and they are those who say the world has two principles: light and darkness. It is also said that the *mim* in *Majus* replaces a *nun*, because of their use of impurities. *Sahharat al-shahm bil-nar* (صَهَرْتُ الشَّحْمَ بِالنّارِ) means I melted the fat with fire, and *al-suhara* is the melted buttock. It is also said: it becomes ripe. The poet said:

The sun melts it, but it does not melt.

*Al-miqma'ah* (المِقْمَعَةُ), with a kasra on the mim, is the whip with which the one being beaten is struck. *Al-lu'lu'* (اللُّؤْلُؤُ) is the pearl. It is said: its small and large ones. *Al-damir* (الضّامِرُ) is the emaciated. *Al-'amiq* (العَمِيقُ) means distant. Its root meaning is distance downward. It is said: *bi'r 'amiq*, meaning a well of deep bottom. The verb is *'amuqa* and *'ammaqa*. The poet said:

When horses come from deep mountain paths, along which goes a dusty, pale rider.

It is said *ghamiq* with a ghayn. Al-Layth said: *'amiq* and *mu'iq* are used by the tribe of Tamim. *A'maqtu al-bi'r* and *am'aqtuha*, and it has become deep, *'amuqat* and *ma'uqat*, *'amaqatan* and *mu'aqatan*. It is far in depth. *Al-ma'q*, *al-am'aq*, and *al-a'maq* are the far edges of the desert. He said:

And the standing one of the far edges, the emptied of the hollow.

*Al-tafath* (التَّفَثُ) originally means filth and dirt. It is said to someone who is disgusting: "What is your *tafath*?" From Qutrub: *tafitha al-rajul*, the man's filth increased on his journey. Abu Muhammad al-Basri said: *al-tafath* is from *al-tuffa*, which is the dirt under the nails, and the *fa'* was changed into a *tha'* like *maghthur*. *Al-sahiq* (السَّحِيقُ) means far away. *Wajaba al-shay'* means it fell. *Wajabat al-shams jibatan* means the sun set. Aws ibn Hajar said:

Did not the sun of the day eclipse, and the full moon, for the setting mountain?

*Al-qani'* (القانِعُ) is the one who asks. *Qani'a qanu'an* means he asked. *Qani'a qana'atan* means he refrained and was content with his modest means. Al-Shammakh said:

His person is more chaste than the one who begs; a man's wealth improves him and makes him rich.

*Al-wathan* (الوَثَنُ): Shimr said: every image made of wood, stone, gold, silver, copper, or the like. The Arabs used to set them up and worship them. It is also applied to the cross. Al-A'sha said:

The needy circle around his doors, like the circling of the Christians around the door of the idol.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Adi ibn Hatim when he saw a cross around his neck: "Cast the idol from you." Its derivation is from *wathana al-shay'*, meaning he set it in its place and it became firm. *Al-wathin* is the one who stays, firmly fixed in its place. Ru'ba said:

Over the faithful friends of pure loyalty, the idol.

He means constancy upon the covenant. *Al-budn* (البُدْنُ) is the plural of *badanah*, like *thumr* is the plural of *thamarah*, as said by al-Zajjaj. It was named so because it grows fat (*tabdunu*). Al-Layth said: *al-badanah*, with the ta' marbuta, applies to the she-camel, the cow, and the camel, which are permissible for sacrifice and offerings, and it does not apply to a sheep. It was called *badanah* because of its size. It is also said it is specific to camels. It is also said it is what is marked (*ash'ara*) from a she-camel or cow, said by 'Ata' and others. It is also said *al-badan* is a singular noun of a collective kind, meaning the large fat one from the camels and cows, and it is said of a fat man. *Al-mu'tarr* (المُعْتَرُّ) is the one who approaches without asking. Ibn Qutaybah said: *gharrahu* and *ightarrahu*, *'arrahu* and *i'tarahu*: he came to him seeking his kindness. The poet said:

Ask the nighttime visitor who approaches, O mother of Malik, when he comes to me between my destiny and my slaughter.

Another said:

By your life, the one who approaches does not come to our lands that we would deny him with the lost, the ruined.

* *

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing. On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will forget her nursling, and every pregnant female will drop her load, and you will see people as intoxicated, though they are not intoxicated, but the punishment of God is severe.﴾ ﴿Among people is one who disputes about God without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil.﴾ ﴿It has been decreed for him that whoever allies with him, he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whom We will for a specified term, then We bring you out as infants, then that you may reach your maturity. Among you is one who is taken in death, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known. And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and grows every lovely kind of pair.﴾ ﴿That is because God is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things Powerful.﴾ ﴿And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that God will raise up those in the graves.﴾

The relation (munasabah) of the beginning of this surah to what precedes it is that Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the condition of the wretched and the blessed and mentioned the Greatest Terror, which is what is said on the Day of Resurrection. The polytheists of Makkah had denied the return (al-ma'ad) and denied it, because the punishment was delayed for them. This surah was revealed as a warning to them and a frightening, because of what it contains of the mention of the quake of the Hour and the severity of its terror, and the mention of what is prepared for those who deny it, and as an admonition to them concerning resurrection through their development in their creation, and through the stillness of the earth and its stirring after that with plants. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﹙O mankind﹚ is general. It has been said: the intended people are the people of Makkah. Allah, exalted is He, drew attention to the reason for taking heed, which is what the Hour leads to of its terrors. It is by omitting a modifier, meaning: ﴿Fear﴾ the punishment of ﴿your Lord﴾. The zalzalah (quake) is the disturbing movement, and it occurs at the first blast (of the Trumpet). It has been said: at the second. It has been said: at the saying of Allah, "O Adam, send forth the group for the Fire." The majority said: in this world, at the end of time, and it is followed by the rising of the sun from its west.

It is reported from al-Hasan: it is on the Day of Resurrection. It is reported from ʿAlqamah and al-Shaʿbi: at the rising of the sun from its west. It is attributed to the Hour because it is one of its portents. The verbal noun (al-masdar) is attributed to its subject, and the omitted object, which is the earth, is indicated by ﴿When the earth is shaken with its shaking﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1]. The attribution of the quake to "the Hour" is metaphorical (majaz). It is permissible to attribute it to the object, following the practice of extension in the adverbial complement (al-zarf), so that "the Hour" becomes the object. On these estimations there is a literal quake.

Al-Hasan said: the strongest quake is what occurs together with the establishment of the Hour. It has been said: the quake is a metaphor, and the intended meaning is the severity of the Hour and the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. The word "thing" (shay') here indicates its application to what does not exist, because the quake has not yet occurred. Whoever prohibits applying it to the non-existent says: He made the quake a "thing" because of the certainty of its occurrence and its coming into existence.

Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the most terrifying attributes in His saying ﴿you see it﴾ and the verse, so that they would look at that attribute with their insight and imagine it with their intellects, so that this would move them toward His piety, exalted is He, since there is no deliverance from those hardships except through piety. It is related that these two verses were revealed at night during the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited them, and he was not seen to weep more than on that night. When they woke in the morning, they did not remove the saddles from the animals, did not pitch the tents at the time of halting, and did not cook a pot; they were among the grieving weepers and the reflective.

The governing element (al-nasib) of ﴿the Day﴾ [in the verse] is ﴿will be forgetful﴾. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿you see it﴾ refers to the quake, because it is what is spoken of, and the existence of the nursing mother's forgetfulness and the pregnant woman's delivery indicates this. This is when the literal meaning is intended, which is the origin, and it would be in this world. It is reported from al-Hasan: ﴿every nursing mother will forget﴾ her nursling, not for weaning, ﴿and every pregnant one will deliver﴾ what is in her womb, not in completion.

A group said: the pronoun refers to (p. 350) the Hour, so the forgetting and the delivery are an expression of the severity of terror on that day, and there is no forgetting or delivery there, like their saying: "a day on which the youth grows gray." The word ﴿nursing mother﴾ (murdi'ah) is used instead of murdi' (nursing female, without the feminine ending) because it is intended as the act, not as a genealogical attribute, in the sense of "one who has the quality of nursing." As the poet said:

Like a nursing mother of other children, who has neglected her own children—this is the straying from the right course.

The apparent meaning is that what is in His saying ﴿of what she nursed﴾ means "that which" (alladhi), and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning "she nursed it." This is strengthened by the transitivity of "to lay down" (wada'a) to the object in His saying "her burden" and not to the verbal noun. It has been said: "ma" is a verbal noun, meaning "concerning her nursing."

Al-Zamakhshari said: the murdi'ah is the one who, at the time of nursing, puts her breast into the infant's mouth, while the murdi' is the one whose habit is to nurse even if she is not actually nursing at the time the description applies. So it is said "murdi'ah" to indicate that when this terror surprises her while she has put the suckling infant's breast in its mouth, she pulls it out of its mouth because of the consternation that overtakes her. Some Kufan grammarians restricted "murdi'ah" to the mother of the child and "murdi'" to the hired wet-nurse, and this is invalid by the poet's verse:

Like a nursing mother of other children, who has neglected
the house—so this is murdi'ah with the feminine ending, and she is not the mother of the one she nurses.

The saying of the Kufans that the description specific to the feminine does not need the feminine ending, because the ending is only introduced for distinction, is rejected by the Arabs' saying: murdi'ah, ha'idah (menstruating), and talaqah (divorced).

The majority read ﴿will be forgetful every﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and the ha', and raf' (nominative) on "every." Ibn Abi ʿAblah and al-Yamani read with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha', meaning ﴿causes to forget﴾ (tudhhilu): the quake or the Hour causes every [nursing mother] to forget, with the accusative. The word "hamal" with fatha means what is in a belly or on the top of a tree.

The majority read "and you see" (wa-tara) with an open ta' as the address to the singular. Zayd ibn ʿAli read with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ra', meaning "and the quake (or the Hour) makes you see." Al-Zaʿfarani and ʿAbbas in his choice read with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the ra', and raised "the people" and made the verb feminine according to the interpretation of the group. Abu Hurayrah, Abu Zurʿah ibn ʿAmr ibn Jarir, and Abu Nahik read likewise, except that they put "the people" in the accusative, so "see" (tara) took three objects. One of them is the concealed pronoun in "see," which is the second-person pronoun, the object that has not been named as subject. The second and third are ﴿the people drunk﴾: it affirmed that they are "drunk" by way of comparison, then it negated the reality of it, which is drunkenness from wine, because of the bewilderment they are in and the confusion of the intellect.

The majority read "drunk" (sukara) in both places on the pattern fu'ala, and the disagreement concerning fu'ala with a damma on the first letter was already mentioned: is it a plural or a collective noun?
