The majority view is that both verses, and the others that precede them, were revealed concerning al-Nadr, and that they were repeated for emphasis in censure, and because each one includes an addition not found in the other. It has been said about him that some ten-odd verses were revealed concerning him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He repeated this (verse) as a rebuke, as if he were saying: these examples are in the utmost clarity and explicitness, [yet] among people (wa-min al-nas) [there is one who], despite that, argues." So the waw here is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), whereas in the preceding verse the waw is the waw of coordination ('atf), coordinating the whole discourse with what came before it; the verse is in the sense of information, and here it is repeated for rebuke. End of quotation.

But it cannot be imagined that the waw in ﴿wa-min al-nas man yujadilu﴾ is a waw of circumstance. According to the clause he supposed before it, if it were stated explicitly, it could not be construed with "idh" (when), so it is not a circumstantial waw; rather it is a waw of coordination. It divides the forsaken into: one who argues ﴿about God without knowledge﴾, following a rebellious devil; one who argues ﴿without knowledge, guidance, or an illuminating Book﴾ and so on; and one who worships his Lord ﴿on an edge﴾. By "knowledge" is meant necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-daruri); by "guidance" is meant reasoning and reflection, since that leads to knowledge; and by "the illuminating Book" is meant revelation. That is, he argues without any one of these three.

﴿Thāniya ʿiṭfihi﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun concealed within (yujadilu). Ibn 'Abbas said: "arrogant." Mujahid said: "twisting his neck with ugliness." Al-Dahhak said: "lofty with his nose." Ibn Jurayj said: "turning away from the truth." Al-Hasan read thāniya ʿaṭfin, with a fatha on the ʿayn, meaning his tenderness and compassion (taʿattufuhu wa-taraḥḥumuhu). ﴿Li-yuḍilla﴾ is connected to (yujadilu). Mujahid, the people of Makka, and Abu 'Amr in one transmission read li-yaḍilla with a fatha on the yāʾ, meaning he himself goes astray. The majority read it with a ḍamma, li-yuḍilla, meaning he leads others astray [p. 355] (ghayrahu). It follows from his leading others astray that the punishment is multiplied, since he bears the burden of everyone who acts upon it. Since the outcome of his disputing is leading astray, it is as if it were its cause. Likewise, since he turns away from guidance and engages in argument for falsehood, he is as one who has left guidance for error.

Disgrace in this world is what befell him on the day of Badr: capture, killing, and defeat. Al-Nadr was indeed taken captive. It has been said that the disgrace was on the day of Badr at al-Safra'. As for ﴿al-ḥarīq﴾, it has been said to be one of the levels of Hell. It may also be an attributive construction, the noun being qualified by its adjective: "the punishment that burns," i.e., "the burning (muḥriq) punishment," like "al-samīʿ" in the sense of "the one who causes to hear."

Zayd ibn 'Ali read fa-uḥīquhu with the hamza of the first person. ﴿Dhālika﴾ refers to the disgrace and the causing to taste. The ways of construing ﴿dhālika﴾ permitted here are the same as those permitted in construing ﴿dhālika bi-anna Allāha huwa al-ḥaqq﴾ (that is, God is the Truth). The meaning of ﴿bi-mā qaddamat yadāka﴾ has been explained earlier: it means by your committing crimes, and by God's justice concerning you since you disobeyed Him. It is possible that wa-anna Allāha is a separate clause, not part of the causal phrase, and the sense is: "and the matter is that God..." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The word 'servants' (al-ʿabīd) is mentioned here in the sense of their destitution and lack of power, and therefore this form has come." End of quotation. He distinguishes between ʿabīd and ʿibād, and we have already refuted his distinction at the end of Āl ʿImrān in regard to the verse ﴿and indeed God is not unjust to the servants﴾, and we have explained here his phrase "bi-ẓallāmin" (unjust).

Concerning ﴿yaʿbudu Allāh﴾ (worships God): it was revealed concerning Bedouins of Aslam and Ghatafan who were slow to accept Islam and said: "We fear that Muhammad will not be helped, and then the bond between us and our allies among the Jews will be severed, and they will not protect us or shelter us." It was also said that it concerns Bedouins with no firm certainty, one of whom would embrace Islam and then, if his wealth increased, a male child was born to him, or some other good befell him, he would say: "This is a good religion," but if his circumstances reversed and he suffered misfortune, he would consider it a bad omen and apostatize, as happened with the 'Uranis. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, and others said this. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it concerns Shayba ibn Rabi'a, who embraced Islam before the Messenger (ﷺ) received revelation, and when revelation came to him he apostatized. It was also said that it concerns a Jew who embraced Islam and was then afflicted, so he considered Islam a bad omen and asked the Messenger (ﷺ) for its cancellation, and he said: "Islam is not cancelled," and then the verse was revealed. Al-Hasan said: it is the hypocrite who worships with his tongue without his heart. Ibn 'Isa said: "with weak certainty." Abu 'Ubayd said: ﴿ʿalā ḥarf﴾ means "on doubt." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "ḥarf" means on a deviation from the white creed, or on the brink of it, prepared to fall.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ʿalā ḥarf﴾ means "on an edge of the religion, not in its center or heart. This is a parable for their being in unrest and agitation in their religion, not in tranquility and calm, like one who stands on the edge of an army: if he senses victory and spoils, he stays and is at ease, but otherwise he flees and rushes off headlong." End of quotation.

His loss in this world is that he is afflicted in it with what grieves him, such as the loss of his wealth and the loss of his loved ones, and so he does not submit to the decree. His loss in the Hereafter is that he is deprived of the reward of the one who is patient, since he apostatized from Islam.

Mujahid, Humayd, al-A'raj, Ibn Muhaysin (through al-Za'faranani's transmission), Qa'nab, al-Ju'dari, and Ibn Miqsam read khāsira al-dunyā as an active participle (ism fa'il) in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It is also read khāsirun, as an active participle in the nominative, on the assumption of "and he is a loser." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The nominative is by way of subject (fā'iliyya), and the placing of the noun in place of the pronoun, and it is a good reading." End of quotation.

The majority read khasira as a past-tense verb. This is a new statement (isti'naf), and it may also be in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), without needing the particle qad, because the past tense has very frequently occurred as a circumstantial state in the language of the Arabs without qad, so this analogy is acceptable. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for "inqalaba ʿalā wajhihi" (turned back on his face), just as yuḍā'af was a substitute for yalqa (in the verse ﴿yalqa athāman﴾).

The explanation of ﴿al-ḍalāl al-baʿīd﴾ (the far-off error) has been given in the statement ﴿ḍalālan baʿīdan﴾ [al-Nisa': 60]. Here He negated harm and benefit, and affirmed them in the statement ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾, and that is due to the difference in what the terms refer to. The statement ﴿what can neither harm him nor benefit him﴾ refers to the idols and the images, and for this reason they are referred to with "mā" (what), which is not used for individual rational beings. The statement ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer﴾ refers to one who is worshipped by compulsion, and who demanded from his worshippers, namely those among the claimants to divinity such as Pharaoh and others of the kings of the Banu 'Ubayd, who were in the Maghrib and later ruled Egypt. They claimed divinity, and their palace in Egypt was circled, and they were proclaimed with what the Lord of the Worlds is proclaimed with, of glorification and sanctification. Although these may have some benefit for their worshippers in this worldly life, their harm is greater and nearer than their benefit, since in this world they are subjugated by the disbelievers and worship other than God, and in the Hereafter they are punished with everlasting punishment. For this reason the expression here is with "man," which is used for rational beings. On this view, the two clauses are God's report about the one who calls upon a god other than God.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: harm and benefit are negated of the idols and affirmed of them in the two verses, and this is a contradiction. I say: when the meaning is clear, this illusion disappears. God, exalted is He, rebuked the disbeliever for worshipping an inanimate object that has no power to harm or benefit, while he believes in it, in his ignorance and error, that it will benefit him. Then He said: on the Day of Resurrection this disbeliever will say, calling out and crying, when he sees his harm from the idols and his entry into the Fire because of worshipping them, and does not see the effect of the intercession he claimed for them: ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit; wretched is the patron, and wretched is the companion.﴾ And He repeated 'he calls upon' as if He had said: ﴿he calls upon besides God what neither harms him nor benefits him﴾, then said: ﴿whose harm﴾ by his being worshipped, ﴿is nearer than his benefit﴾ by his being an intercessor, ﴿wretched is the patron﴾." End of quotation.

So al-Zamakhshari made the one called upon in both verses the idols, and removed the contradiction by the difference of speakers: the first clause is God's statement, the report about the state of the idols; the second clause is the words of the idol-worshippers, who say this in the Hereafter, and God relates it about them, and that they affirmed harm by virtue of having worshipped them, and affirmed benefit by virtue of having believed them to be intercessors. So the one who negates there is not the one who affirms here, and the contradiction disappears according to his claim. What I say is that an idol has no benefit whatsoever, such that one could say ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾.

Some have answered those who claim that the two verses imply a contradiction by saying: they do not harm or benefit by themselves, but their worship attributes harm to them, like His statement ﴿My Lord, indeed they have led many of the people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], where He attributed the leading astray to them since they were the cause of error. So too here, the negation of harm from them is because they do not act, and then He attributed it to them because they are the cause of harm. Others said: in reality they neither harm nor benefit; He explained this in the first verse, and then affirmed for them harm and benefit in the second, by way of supposition: that is, even if we grant that they are harmful and beneficial, their harm would be greater than their benefit.

The grammarians have strained to give various analyses. They said: ﴿yadʿū﴾ may be connected to ﴿li-man ḍarruhu﴾ at first; if it has no connection, then there are the following possibilities.

First: it is an emphatic repetition by wording (tawkid lafzi) of the first "yadʿū," so it has no object of its own.

Second: it governs ﴿dhālika﴾ in the clause ﴿dhālika huwa al-ḍalāl﴾ (that is the error), and the object, which is "dhālika," is placed first and is made a relative noun in the sense of "alladhi." This was stated by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. This is not valid except according to the view of the Kufans, who allow the demonstrative to be a relative noun, whereas the Basrans do not allow that except with "dhā," on condition that it is preceded by the interrogative "mā" or "man."

Third: ﴿yadʿū﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial state, and ﴿dhālika﴾ is the subject, and it is a separating pronoun (fasl), or the subject is "dhālika" and the pronoun is deleted from ﴿yadʿū﴾, that is "yadʿūhu" (calls upon him), and he estimated it as "called upon." This is weak, because "yadʿūhu" cannot be estimated as "called upon," it can only be estimated as "calling"; if it were read in the passive, its estimate would be "called upon," following analogy. Al-Zajjaj said something similar.

If it is connected to ﴿li-man ḍarruhu﴾, then there are the following possibilities.

First: what al-Akhfash said, which is that ﴿yadʿū﴾ means "says," and ﴿man﴾ is a subject, a relative noun whose complement is the clause after it, which is ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾, and the predicate of the subject is omitted, its estimate being "a god and one of divine nature." The clause is in the position of the accusative, reported by ﴿yadʿū﴾ which means "says." It was said: this meaning is corrupt, because the disbeliever never believed that the idols' harm was nearer than their benefit. It was also said: in this view "labi'sa" (wretched is) is a new statement, not part of the report, because the disbelievers do not say of their idols "wretched is the patron."

Second: ﴿yadʿū﴾ means "names," and the omitted object at the end is the second object of "yusammā" (is named), its estimate being "a god." This is not complete except by estimating an added lām, that is "yadʿū li-man ḍarruhu" (calls upon for one whose harm...).

Third: ﴿yadʿū﴾ has been made analogous to verbs of the heart, because calling upon arises only from belief. The better view is that it is given the sense of "claims" (yazʿumu), and an object is estimated for "man," and the clause is in the position of the accusative as the object of ﴿yadʿū﴾. Al-Farisi pointed to this view.

The fourth view is that of al-Farra' (the grammarian), that the lam ("la-") entered a position where it does not belong, and that the original sense is "[He calls upon] one whose harm is nearer than his benefit." This is far-fetched, because what is within the relative clause (silah, the clause that completes a relative pronoun) cannot precede the relative pronoun itself (al-mawsul).

The fifth view is that the lam is an extra particle for emphasis, and "man" is the object of "yad'u." This is weak, because it is not one of the positions where the lam is added. Yet the reading of Abd Allah, "yad'u man darruhu" (without the lam), supports it. The most plausible explanation is that "yad'u" is an emphatic repetition of the first "yad'u." The lam in "la-man" is the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida'), and the predicate is the clause that forms a omitted oath, whose answer is ﴿لَبِئْسَ المَوْلى﴾ ("Wretched is the protector"). The apparent meaning of "yad'u" is calling out and seeking help. It has also been said that its meaning is distant. Here al-mawla means the helper, the close companion, the one who associates closely.

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the state of the one who worships Him "on an edge" and mocked his opinion, and threatened him with loss in the Hereafter, He followed this with the state of those who oppose them among the people of faith, and what He promised them of the sensory promise (al-wa'd al-hissi). Then He began to rebuke those first ones, as if He were saying: these worshippers "on an edge," anxiety has accompanied them, and they assumed that Allah will never help Muhammad ﷺ and his followers. We only commanded them to be patient and to await Our promise. Whoever thinks otherwise, let him extend a rope, and let him strangle himself, and see whether his rage is removed by that. Qatada said this meaning. This is in the manner of the well-known proverb, "Here is the mountain, so strangle yourself," which is said to one who wants of a matter what he cannot achieve.

On this view, the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to the Messenger ﷺ. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Kalbi, Muqatil, al-Dahhak, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi, and it was preferred by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. The meaning is that Allah will never help Muhammad, in this world by raising His word and making His religion manifest, and in the Hereafter by raising his rank and taking vengeance on those who denied him. Although the Messenger has no mention in the verse, the verse contains what indicates him, which is the mention of faith in His saying ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يُدْخِلُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ ("Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe"). Some Muslims held this opinion because of their intense rage against the polytheists, who were slow in what Allah had promised His Messenger of victory. Or they were bedouins who considered the Messenger's ascendancy slow, so they lagged behind in Islam.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to "man" (whoever), because it is what is mentioned, and the pronoun properly refers to what is mentioned. This is the view of Mujahid. Some who held this view took "naṣr" (help) here to mean provision (rizq), as they said: "ard mansurah," meaning a land that has been rained upon. The poet said:

*And you do not give a man beyond his right,*
*nor do you possess the portion you help.*

That is, you do not give to him. And it is said: a beggar from the Banu Bakr stopped by us and said, "Whoever helps me, may Allah help him." So the meaning is: whoever thinks that Allah will not provide for him, and so turns away from the religion of Muhammad because of this thought, as He described in His saying ﴿وإنْ أصابَتْهُ فِتْنَةٌ انْقَلَبَ عَلى وجْهِهِ﴾ ("And if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face"), then let him reach the utmost of distress, which is strangling. For that will not reach him except what has been decreed for him, and it will not make him provided with more than what has been apportioned to him.

On this view it is possible that "naṣr" retains its ordinary sense: whoever thought that Allah would not help him in this world and the Hereafter, and so is enraged at the absence of His help, let him extend a rope. The statement "then he is enraged" is supported by His saying ﴿هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ ما يَغِيظُ﴾ ("Will his scheming remove that which enrages him?"). The meaning of His saying ﴿فَلْيَمْدُدْ بِسَبَبٍ إلى السَّماءِ ثُمَّ لِيَقْطَعْ﴾ ("let him extend a rope to the sky, then cut it off") is: let him devise the greatest of stratagems to help Allah's help reach him, then let him cut the rope. ﴿فَلْيَنْظُرْ هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ﴾ ("then let him look: will his scheming remove that which enrages him?"). His scheming in bringing help to himself is the thing that enrages him, namely the absence of his help through the domination of his enemies over him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a statement in which something has been abbreviated, and the meaning is: Allah is the helper of His Messenger in this world and the Hereafter. So whoever among his envious and enemies thinks that Allah will do otherwise, and hopes for that, and is enraged that he will not attain his aim, then let him exhaust his capacity and expend his full effort in removing what enrages him, by doing what someone does when rage has reached its utmost limit, until he extends a rope to the sky of his house and strangles himself. ("Then let him look") meaning: let him picture in himself whether, if he does that, it will remove the help of Allah which enrages him. The strangling is called "cutting" (qat') because the one who strangles himself cuts off his breath by blocking its passages, and from this the panting breath is called qat'. His act is called a scheme (kayd) because he placed it in the position of scheming, since he could not do anything else, or as mockery, because he did not scheme against the one he envies; he only schemed against himself. The meaning is that there is nothing in his hand except what does not remove what enrages him.

It has been said: ("let him extend") with a rope "to the sky," meaning the canopy, and let him climb upon it, then let him cut off the revelation from descending upon him. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

It has been said: the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to the religion and Islam. Ibn Atiyya said: the clearest of the views on this verse is that it is a parable. "Naṣr" has its known meaning, "qat'" is strangling, and "sama'" (sky) is elevation in the air, a ceiling or a tree or the like. So reflect upon it. In ﴿ما يَغِيظُ﴾ ("that which enrages"), "ma" means "alladhi" (that which), and the returning pronoun is omitted, or it is a verbal noun (masdariyyah). Likewise, that is, and like that sending down, We sent down the whole Qur'an ﴿آياتٍ بَيِّناتٍ﴾ ("clear signs"), meaning there is no variation in the sending down of part of it or of all of it. The pronoun in "anzalnahu" refers to the Qur'an, and it was concealed because its reference is understood, as in His saying ﴿حَتّى تَوارَتْ بِالحِجابِ﴾ ("until it was hidden by the veil") [Sad 32]. The estimated meaning is: and the matter is ﴿أنَّ اللَّهَ يَهْدِي مَن يُرِيدُ﴾ ("that Allah guides whom He wills"), meaning He creates guidance in your heart. He wills its guidance, and there is no creator of guidance except Him.

[p. 354] ﴿Among people is one who argues about God without knowledge, without guidance, and without an illuminating Book, turning aside (in arrogance) to lead others astray from God's way. For him there is disgrace in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection We shall make him taste the punishment of the Blaze. That is for what your hands have sent ahead, and indeed God is not unjust to His servants.﴾ ﴿Among people is one who worships God on an edge: if good befalls him, he is content with it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss.﴾ ﴿He calls upon, besides God, what can neither harm him nor benefit him. That is the far-off error.﴾ ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. Wretched is the patron, and wretched is the companion.﴾ ﴿Indeed God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed God does what He wills.﴾ ﴿Whoever thinks that God will not help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope to the sky, then cut it off, and see whether his scheming removes what enrages him.﴾ ﴿Thus We have sent it down as clear signs, and indeed God guides whom He wills.﴾

The apparent view is that the one who argues in this verse is other than the one who argues in the verse before it. Muhammad ibn Ka'b reported that it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, while Ibn 'Abbas reported that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. It has also been said that the first verse concerns the blind followers (muqallidun) and this one concerns the blind followers as well. The majority view is that both verses, and the others that precede them, were revealed concerning al-Nadr, and that they were repeated for emphasis in censure, and because each one includes an addition not found in the other. It has been said about him that some ten-odd verses were revealed concerning him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He repeated this (verse) as a rebuke, as if he were saying: these examples are in the utmost clarity and explicitness, [yet] among people (wa-min al-nas) [there is one who], despite that, argues." So the waw here is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), whereas in the preceding verse the waw is the waw of coordination ('atf), coordinating the whole discourse with what came before it; the verse is in the sense of information, and here it is repeated for rebuke. End of quotation.

But it cannot be imagined that the waw in ﴿wa-min al-nas man yujadilu﴾ is a waw of circumstance. According to the clause he supposed before it, if it were stated explicitly, it could not be construed with "idh" (when), so it is not a circumstantial waw; rather it is a waw of coordination. It divides the forsaken into: one who argues ﴿about God without knowledge﴾, following a rebellious devil; one who argues ﴿without knowledge, guidance, or an illuminating Book﴾ and so on; and one who worships his Lord ﴿on an edge﴾. By "knowledge" is meant necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-daruri); by "guidance" is meant reasoning and reflection, since that leads to knowledge; and by "the illuminating Book" is meant revelation. That is, he argues without any one of these three.

﴿Thāniya ʿiṭfihi﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun concealed within (yujadilu). Ibn 'Abbas said: "arrogant." Mujahid said: "twisting his neck with ugliness." Al-Dahhak said: "lofty with his nose." Ibn Jurayj said: "turning away from the truth." Al-Hasan read thāniya ʿaṭfin, with a fatha on the ʿayn, meaning his tenderness and compassion (taʿattufuhu wa-taraḥḥumuhu). ﴿Li-yuḍilla﴾ is connected to (yujadilu). Mujahid, the people of Makka, and Abu 'Amr in one transmission read li-yaḍilla with a fatha on the yāʾ, meaning he himself goes astray. The majority read it with a ḍamma, li-yuḍilla, meaning he leads others astray [p. 355] (ghayrahu). It follows from his leading others astray that the punishment is multiplied, since he bears the burden of everyone who acts upon it. Since the outcome of his disputing is leading astray, it is as if it were its cause. Likewise, since he turns away from guidance and engages in argument for falsehood, he is as one who has left guidance for error.

Disgrace in this world is what befell him on the day of Badr: capture, killing, and defeat. Al-Nadr was indeed taken captive. It has been said that the disgrace was on the day of Badr at al-Safra'. As for ﴿al-ḥarīq﴾, it has been said to be one of the levels of Hell. It may also be an attributive construction, the noun being qualified by its adjective: "the punishment that burns," i.e., "the burning (muḥriq) punishment," like "al-samīʿ" in the sense of "the one who causes to hear."

Zayd ibn 'Ali read fa-uḥīquhu with the hamza of the first person. ﴿Dhālika﴾ refers to the disgrace and the causing to taste. The ways of construing ﴿dhālika﴾ permitted here are the same as those permitted in construing ﴿dhālika bi-anna Allāha huwa al-ḥaqq﴾ (that is, God is the Truth). The meaning of ﴿bi-mā qaddamat yadāka﴾ has been explained earlier: it means by your committing crimes, and by God's justice concerning you since you disobeyed Him. It is possible that wa-anna Allāha is a separate clause, not part of the causal phrase, and the sense is: "and the matter is that God..." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The word 'servants' (al-ʿabīd) is mentioned here in the sense of their destitution and lack of power, and therefore this form has come." End of quotation. He distinguishes between ʿabīd and ʿibād, and we have already refuted his distinction at the end of Āl ʿImrān in regard to the verse ﴿and indeed God is not unjust to the servants﴾, and we have explained here his phrase "bi-ẓallāmin" (unjust).

Concerning ﴿yaʿbudu Allāh﴾ (worships God): it was revealed concerning Bedouins of Aslam and Ghatafan who were slow to accept Islam and said: "We fear that Muhammad will not be helped, and then the bond between us and our allies among the Jews will be severed, and they will not protect us or shelter us." It was also said that it concerns Bedouins with no firm certainty, one of whom would embrace Islam and then, if his wealth increased, a male child was born to him, or some other good befell him, he would say: "This is a good religion," but if his circumstances reversed and he suffered misfortune, he would consider it a bad omen and apostatize, as happened with the 'Uranis. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, and others said this. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it concerns Shayba ibn Rabi'a, who embraced Islam before the Messenger (ﷺ) received revelation, and when revelation came to him he apostatized. It was also said that it concerns a Jew who embraced Islam and was then afflicted, so he considered Islam a bad omen and asked the Messenger (ﷺ) for its cancellation, and he said: "Islam is not cancelled," and then the verse was revealed. Al-Hasan said: it is the hypocrite who worships with his tongue without his heart. Ibn 'Isa said: "with weak certainty." Abu 'Ubayd said: ﴿ʿalā ḥarf﴾ means "on doubt." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "ḥarf" means on a deviation from the white creed, or on the brink of it, prepared to fall.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ʿalā ḥarf﴾ means "on an edge of the religion, not in its center or heart. This is a parable for their being in unrest and agitation in their religion, not in tranquility and calm, like one who stands on the edge of an army: if he senses victory and spoils, he stays and is at ease, but otherwise he flees and rushes off headlong." End of quotation.

His loss in this world is that he is afflicted in it with what grieves him, such as the loss of his wealth and the loss of his loved ones, and so he does not submit to the decree. His loss in the Hereafter is that he is deprived of the reward of the one who is patient, since he apostatized from Islam.

Mujahid, Humayd, al-A'raj, Ibn Muhaysin (through al-Za'faranani's transmission), Qa'nab, al-Ju'dari, and Ibn Miqsam read khāsira al-dunyā as an active participle (ism fa'il) in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It is also read khāsirun, as an active participle in the nominative, on the assumption of "and he is a loser." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The nominative is by way of subject (fā'iliyya), and the placing of the noun in place of the pronoun, and it is a good reading." End of quotation.

The majority read khasira as a past-tense verb. This is a new statement (isti'naf), and it may also be in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), without needing the particle qad, because the past tense has very frequently occurred as a circumstantial state in the language of the Arabs without qad, so this analogy is acceptable. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for "inqalaba ʿalā wajhihi" (turned back on his face), just as yuḍā'af was a substitute for yalqa (in the verse ﴿yalqa athāman﴾).

The explanation of ﴿al-ḍalāl al-baʿīd﴾ (the far-off error) has been given in the statement ﴿ḍalālan baʿīdan﴾ [al-Nisa': 60]. Here He negated harm and benefit, and affirmed them in the statement ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾, and that is due to the difference in what the terms refer to. The statement ﴿what can neither harm him nor benefit him﴾ refers to the idols and the images, and for this reason they are referred to with "mā" (what), which is not used for individual rational beings. The statement ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer﴾ refers to one who is worshipped by compulsion, and who demanded from his worshippers, namely those among the claimants to divinity such as Pharaoh and others of the kings of the Banu 'Ubayd, who were in the Maghrib and later ruled Egypt. They claimed divinity, and their palace in Egypt was circled, and they were proclaimed with what the Lord of the Worlds is proclaimed with, of glorification and sanctification. Although these may have some benefit for their worshippers in this worldly life, their harm is greater and nearer than their benefit, since in this world they are subjugated by the disbelievers and worship other than God, and in the Hereafter they are punished with everlasting punishment. For this reason the expression here is with "man," which is used for rational beings. On this view, the two clauses are God's report about the one who calls upon a god other than God.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: harm and benefit are negated of the idols and affirmed of them in the two verses, and this is a contradiction. I say: when the meaning is clear, this illusion disappears. God, exalted is He, rebuked the disbeliever for worshipping an inanimate object that has no power to harm or benefit, while he believes in it, in his ignorance and error, that it will benefit him. Then He said: on the Day of Resurrection this disbeliever will say, calling out and crying, when he sees his harm from the idols and his entry into the Fire because of worshipping them, and does not see the effect of the intercession he claimed for them: ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit; wretched is the patron, and wretched is the companion.﴾ And He repeated 'he calls upon' as if He had said: ﴿he calls upon besides God what neither harms him nor benefits him﴾, then said: ﴿whose harm﴾ by his being worshipped, ﴿is nearer than his benefit﴾ by his being an intercessor, ﴿wretched is the patron﴾." End of quotation.

So al-Zamakhshari made the one called upon in both verses the idols, and removed the contradiction by the difference of speakers: the first clause is God's statement, the report about the state of the idols; the second clause is the words of the idol-worshippers, who say this in the Hereafter, and God relates it about them, and that they affirmed harm by virtue of having worshipped them, and affirmed benefit by virtue of having believed them to be intercessors. So the one who negates there is not the one who affirms here, and the contradiction disappears according to his claim. What I say is that an idol has no benefit whatsoever, such that one could say ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾.

Some have answered those who claim that the two verses imply a contradiction by saying: they do not harm or benefit by themselves, but their worship attributes harm to them, like His statement ﴿My Lord, indeed they have led many of the people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], where He attributed the leading astray to them since they were the cause of error. So too here, the negation of harm from them is because they do not act, and then He attributed it to them because they are the cause of harm. Others said: in reality they neither harm nor benefit; He explained this in the first verse, and then affirmed for them harm and benefit in the second, by way of supposition: that is, even if we grant that they are harmful and beneficial, their harm would be greater than their benefit.

The grammarians have strained to give various analyses. They said: ﴿yadʿū﴾ may be connected to ﴿li-man ḍarruhu﴾ at first; if it has no connection, then there are the following possibilities.

First: it is an emphatic repetition by wording (tawkid lafzi) of the first "yadʿū," so it has no object of its own.

Second: it governs ﴿dhālika﴾ in the clause ﴿dhālika huwa al-ḍalāl﴾ (that is the error), and the object, which is "dhālika," is placed first and is made a relative noun in the sense of "alladhi." This was stated by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. This is not valid except according to the view of the Kufans, who allow the demonstrative to be a relative noun, whereas the Basrans do not allow that except with "dhā," on condition that it is preceded by the interrogative "mā" or "man."

Third: ﴿yadʿū﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial state, and ﴿dhālika﴾ is the subject, and it is a separating pronoun (fasl), or the subject is "dhālika" and the pronoun is deleted from ﴿yadʿū﴾, that is "yadʿūhu" (calls upon him), and he estimated it as "called upon." This is weak, because "yadʿūhu" cannot be estimated as "called upon," it can only be estimated as "calling"; if it were read in the passive, its estimate would be "called upon," following analogy. Al-Zajjaj said something similar.

If it is connected to ﴿li-man ḍarruhu﴾, then there are the following possibilities.

First: what al-Akhfash said, which is that ﴿yadʿū﴾ means "says," and ﴿man﴾ is a subject, a relative noun whose complement is the clause after it, which is ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾, and the predicate of the subject is omitted, its estimate being "a god and one of divine nature." The clause is in the position of the accusative, reported by ﴿yadʿū﴾ which means "says." It was said: this meaning is corrupt, because the disbeliever never believed that the idols' harm was nearer than their benefit. It was also said: in this view "labi'sa" (wretched is) is a new statement, not part of the report, because the disbelievers do not say of their idols "wretched is the patron."

Second: ﴿yadʿū﴾ means "names," and the omitted object at the end is the second object of "yusammā" (is named), its estimate being "a god." This is not complete except by estimating an added lām, that is "yadʿū li-man ḍarruhu" (calls upon for one whose harm...).

Third: ﴿yadʿū﴾ has been made analogous to verbs of the heart, because calling upon arises only from belief. The better view is that it is given the sense of "claims" (yazʿumu), and an object is estimated for "man," and the clause is in the position of the accusative as the object of ﴿yadʿū﴾. Al-Farisi pointed to this view.

The fourth view is that of al-Farra' (the grammarian), that the lam ("la-") entered a position where it does not belong, and that the original sense is "[He calls upon] one whose harm is nearer than his benefit." This is far-fetched, because what is within the relative clause (silah, the clause that completes a relative pronoun) cannot precede the relative pronoun itself (al-mawsul).

The fifth view is that the lam is an extra particle for emphasis, and "man" is the object of "yad'u." This is weak, because it is not one of the positions where the lam is added. Yet the reading of Abd Allah, "yad'u man darruhu" (without the lam), supports it. The most plausible explanation is that "yad'u" is an emphatic repetition of the first "yad'u." The lam in "la-man" is the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida'), and the predicate is the clause that forms a omitted oath, whose answer is ﴿لَبِئْسَ المَوْلى﴾ ("Wretched is the protector"). The apparent meaning of "yad'u" is calling out and seeking help. It has also been said that its meaning is distant. Here al-mawla means the helper, the close companion, the one who associates closely.

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the state of the one who worships Him "on an edge" and mocked his opinion, and threatened him with loss in the Hereafter, He followed this with the state of those who oppose them among the people of faith, and what He promised them of the sensory promise (al-wa'd al-hissi). Then He began to rebuke those first ones, as if He were saying: these worshippers "on an edge," anxiety has accompanied them, and they assumed that Allah will never help Muhammad ﷺ and his followers. We only commanded them to be patient and to await Our promise. Whoever thinks otherwise, let him extend a rope, and let him strangle himself, and see whether his rage is removed by that. Qatada said this meaning. This is in the manner of the well-known proverb, "Here is the mountain, so strangle yourself," which is said to one who wants of a matter what he cannot achieve.

On this view, the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to the Messenger ﷺ. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Kalbi, Muqatil, al-Dahhak, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi, and it was preferred by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. The meaning is that Allah will never help Muhammad, in this world by raising His word and making His religion manifest, and in the Hereafter by raising his rank and taking vengeance on those who denied him. Although the Messenger has no mention in the verse, the verse contains what indicates him, which is the mention of faith in His saying ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يُدْخِلُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ ("Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe"). Some Muslims held this opinion because of their intense rage against the polytheists, who were slow in what Allah had promised His Messenger of victory. Or they were bedouins who considered the Messenger's ascendancy slow, so they lagged behind in Islam.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to "man" (whoever), because it is what is mentioned, and the pronoun properly refers to what is mentioned. This is the view of Mujahid. Some who held this view took "naṣr" (help) here to mean provision (rizq), as they said: "ard mansurah," meaning a land that has been rained upon. The poet said:

*And you do not give a man beyond his right,*
*nor do you possess the portion you help.*

That is, you do not give to him. And it is said: a beggar from the Banu Bakr stopped by us and said, "Whoever helps me, may Allah help him." So the meaning is: whoever thinks that Allah will not provide for him, and so turns away from the religion of Muhammad because of this thought, as He described in His saying ﴿وإنْ أصابَتْهُ فِتْنَةٌ انْقَلَبَ عَلى وجْهِهِ﴾ ("And if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face"), then let him reach the utmost of distress, which is strangling. For that will not reach him except what has been decreed for him, and it will not make him provided with more than what has been apportioned to him.

On this view it is possible that "naṣr" retains its ordinary sense: whoever thought that Allah would not help him in this world and the Hereafter, and so is enraged at the absence of His help, let him extend a rope. The statement "then he is enraged" is supported by His saying ﴿هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ ما يَغِيظُ﴾ ("Will his scheming remove that which enrages him?"). The meaning of His saying ﴿فَلْيَمْدُدْ بِسَبَبٍ إلى السَّماءِ ثُمَّ لِيَقْطَعْ﴾ ("let him extend a rope to the sky, then cut it off") is: let him devise the greatest of stratagems to help Allah's help reach him, then let him cut the rope. ﴿فَلْيَنْظُرْ هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ﴾ ("then let him look: will his scheming remove that which enrages him?"). His scheming in bringing help to himself is the thing that enrages him, namely the absence of his help through the domination of his enemies over him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a statement in which something has been abbreviated, and the meaning is: Allah is the helper of His Messenger in this world and the Hereafter. So whoever among his envious and enemies thinks that Allah will do otherwise, and hopes for that, and is enraged that he will not attain his aim, then let him exhaust his capacity and expend his full effort in removing what enrages him, by doing what someone does when rage has reached its utmost limit, until he extends a rope to the sky of his house and strangles himself. ("Then let him look") meaning: let him picture in himself whether, if he does that, it will remove the help of Allah which enrages him. The strangling is called "cutting" (qat') because the one who strangles himself cuts off his breath by blocking its passages, and from this the panting breath is called qat'. His act is called a scheme (kayd) because he placed it in the position of scheming, since he could not do anything else, or as mockery, because he did not scheme against the one he envies; he only schemed against himself. The meaning is that there is nothing in his hand except what does not remove what enrages him.

It has been said: ("let him extend") with a rope "to the sky," meaning the canopy, and let him climb upon it, then let him cut off the revelation from descending upon him. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

It has been said: the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to the religion and Islam. Ibn Atiyya said: the clearest of the views on this verse is that it is a parable. "Naṣr" has its known meaning, "qat'" is strangling, and "sama'" (sky) is elevation in the air, a ceiling or a tree or the like. So reflect upon it. In ﴿ما يَغِيظُ﴾ ("that which enrages"), "ma" means "alladhi" (that which), and the returning pronoun is omitted, or it is a verbal noun (masdariyyah). Likewise, that is, and like that sending down, We sent down the whole Qur'an ﴿آياتٍ بَيِّناتٍ﴾ ("clear signs"), meaning there is no variation in the sending down of part of it or of all of it. The pronoun in "anzalnahu" refers to the Qur'an, and it was concealed because its reference is understood, as in His saying ﴿حَتّى تَوارَتْ بِالحِجابِ﴾ ("until it was hidden by the veil") [Sad 32]. The estimated meaning is: and the matter is ﴿أنَّ اللَّهَ يَهْدِي مَن يُرِيدُ﴾ ("that Allah guides whom He wills"), meaning He creates guidance in your heart. He wills its guidance, and there is no creator of guidance except Him.

[p. 354] ﴿Among people is one who argues about God without knowledge, without guidance, and without an illuminating Book, turning aside (in arrogance) to lead others astray from God's way. For him there is disgrace in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection We shall make him taste the punishment of the Blaze. That is for what your hands have sent ahead, and indeed God is not unjust to His servants.﴾ ﴿Among people is one who worships God on an edge: if good befalls him, he is content with it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss.﴾ ﴿He calls upon, besides God, what can neither harm him nor benefit him. That is the far-off error.﴾ ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. Wretched is the patron, and wretched is the companion.﴾ ﴿Indeed God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed God does what He wills.﴾ ﴿Whoever thinks that God will not help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope to the sky, then cut it off, and see whether his scheming removes what enrages him.﴾ ﴿Thus We have sent it down as clear signs, and indeed God guides whom He wills.﴾

The ways of construing ﴿dhālika﴾ permitted here are the same as those permitted in construing ﴿dhālika bi-anna Allāha huwa al-ḥaqq﴾ (that is, God is the Truth). The meaning of ﴿bi-mā qaddamat yadāka﴾ has been explained earlier: it means by your committing crimes, and by God's justice concerning you since you disobeyed Him. It is possible that wa-anna Allāha is a separate clause, not part of the causal phrase, and the sense is: "and the matter is that God..." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The word 'servants' (al-ʿabīd) is mentioned here in the sense of their destitution and lack of power, and therefore this form has come." End of quotation. He distinguishes between ʿabīd and ʿibād, and we have already refuted his distinction at the end of Āl ʿImrān in regard to the verse ﴿and indeed God is not unjust to the servants﴾, and we have explained here his phrase "bi-ẓallāmin" (unjust).

Concerning ﴿yaʿbudu Allāh﴾ (worships God): it was revealed concerning Bedouins of Aslam and Ghatafan who were slow to accept Islam and said: "We fear that Muhammad will not be helped, and then the bond between us and our allies among the Jews will be severed, and they will not protect us or shelter us." It was also said that it concerns Bedouins with no firm certainty, one of whom would embrace Islam and then, if his wealth increased, a male child was born to him, or some other good befell him, he would say: "This is a good religion," but if his circumstances reversed and he suffered misfortune, he would consider it a bad omen and apostatize, as happened with the 'Uranis. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, and others said this. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it concerns Shayba ibn Rabi'a, who embraced Islam before the Messenger (ﷺ) received revelation, and when revelation came to him he apostatized. It was also said that it concerns a Jew who embraced Islam and was then afflicted, so he considered Islam a bad omen and asked the Messenger (ﷺ) for its cancellation, and he said: "Islam is not cancelled," and then the verse was revealed. Al-Hasan said: it is the hypocrite who worships with his tongue without his heart. Ibn 'Isa said: "with weak certainty." Abu 'Ubayd said: ﴿ʿalā ḥarf﴾ means "on doubt." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "ḥarf" means on a deviation from the white creed, or on the brink of it, prepared to fall.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ʿalā ḥarf﴾ means "on an edge of the religion, not in its center or heart. This is a parable for their being in unrest and agitation in their religion, not in tranquility and calm, like one who stands on the edge of an army: if he senses victory and spoils, he stays and is at ease, but otherwise he flees and rushes off headlong." End of quotation.

His loss in this world is that he is afflicted in it with what grieves him, such as the loss of his wealth and the loss of his loved ones, and so he does not submit to the decree. His loss in the Hereafter is that he is deprived of the reward of the one who is patient, since he apostatized from Islam.

Mujahid, Humayd, al-A'raj, Ibn Muhaysin (through al-Za'faranani's transmission), Qa'nab, al-Ju'dari, and Ibn Miqsam read khāsira al-dunyā as an active participle (ism fa'il) in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It is also read khāsirun, as an active participle in the nominative, on the assumption of "and he is a loser." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The nominative is by way of subject (fā'iliyya), and the placing of the noun in place of the pronoun, and it is a good reading." End of quotation.

The majority read khasira as a past-tense verb. This is a new statement (isti'naf), and it may also be in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), without needing the particle qad, because the past tense has very frequently occurred as a circumstantial state in the language of the Arabs without qad, so this analogy is acceptable. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for "inqalaba ʿalā wajhihi" (turned back on his face), just as yuḍā'af was a substitute for yalqa (in the verse ﴿yalqa athāman﴾).

The explanation of ﴿al-ḍalāl al-baʿīd﴾ (the far-off error) has been given in the statement ﴿ḍalālan baʿīdan﴾ [al-Nisa': 60]. Here He negated harm and benefit, and affirmed them in the statement ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾, and that is due to the difference in what the terms refer to. The statement ﴿what can neither harm him nor benefit him﴾ refers to the idols and the images, and for this reason they are referred to with "mā" (what), which is not used for individual rational beings. The statement ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer﴾ refers to one who is worshipped by compulsion, and who demanded from his worshippers, namely those among the claimants to divinity such as Pharaoh and others of the kings of the Banu 'Ubayd, who were in the Maghrib and later ruled Egypt. They claimed divinity, and their palace in Egypt was circled, and they were proclaimed with what the Lord of the Worlds is proclaimed with, of glorification and sanctification. Although these may have some benefit for their worshippers in this worldly life, their harm is greater and nearer than their benefit, since in this world they are subjugated by the disbelievers and worship other than God, and in the Hereafter they are punished with everlasting punishment. For this reason the expression here is with "man," which is used for rational beings. On this view, the two clauses are God's report about the one who calls upon a god other than God.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: harm and benefit are negated of the idols and affirmed of them in the two verses, and this is a contradiction. I say: when the meaning is clear, this illusion disappears. God, exalted is He, rebuked the disbeliever for worshipping an inanimate object that has no power to harm or benefit, while he believes in it, in his ignorance and error, that it will benefit him. Then He said: on the Day of Resurrection this disbeliever will say, calling out and crying, when he sees his harm from the idols and his entry into the Fire because of worshipping them, and does not see the effect of the intercession he claimed for them: ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit; wretched is the patron, and wretched is the companion.﴾ And He repeated 'he calls upon' as if He had said: ﴿he calls upon besides God what neither harms him nor benefits him﴾, then said: ﴿whose harm﴾ by his being worshipped, ﴿is nearer than his benefit﴾ by his being an intercessor, ﴿wretched is the patron﴾." End of quotation.

So al-Zamakhshari made the one called upon in both verses the idols, and removed the contradiction by the difference of speakers: the first clause is God's statement, the report about the state of the idols; the second clause is the words of the idol-worshippers, who say this in the Hereafter, and God relates it about them, and that they affirmed harm by virtue of having worshipped them, and affirmed benefit by virtue of having believed them to be intercessors. So the one who negates there is not the one who affirms here, and the contradiction disappears according to his claim. What I say is that an idol has no benefit whatsoever, such that one could say ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾.

Some have answered those who claim that the two verses imply a contradiction by saying: they do not harm or benefit by themselves, but their worship attributes harm to them, like His statement ﴿My Lord, indeed they have led many of the people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], where He attributed the leading astray to them since they were the cause of error. So too here, the negation of harm from them is because they do not act, and then He attributed it to them because they are the cause of harm. Others said: in reality they neither harm nor benefit; He explained this in the first verse, and then affirmed for them harm and benefit in the second, by way of supposition: that is, even if we grant that they are harmful and beneficial, their harm would be greater than their benefit.

The grammarians have strained to give various analyses. They said: ﴿yadʿū﴾ may be connected to ﴿li-man ḍarruhu﴾ at first; if it has no connection, then there are the following possibilities.

First: it is an emphatic repetition by wording (tawkid lafzi) of the first "yadʿū," so it has no object of its own.

Second: it governs ﴿dhālika﴾ in the clause ﴿dhālika huwa al-ḍalāl﴾ (that is the error), and the object, which is "dhālika," is placed first and is made a relative noun in the sense of "alladhi." This was stated by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. This is not valid except according to the view of the Kufans, who allow the demonstrative to be a relative noun, whereas the Basrans do not allow that except with "dhā," on condition that it is preceded by the interrogative "mā" or "man."

Third: ﴿yadʿū﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial state, and ﴿dhālika﴾ is the subject, and it is a separating pronoun (fasl), or the subject is "dhālika" and the pronoun is deleted from ﴿yadʿū﴾, that is "yadʿūhu" (calls upon him), and he estimated it as "called upon." This is weak, because "yadʿūhu" cannot be estimated as "called upon," it can only be estimated as "calling"; if it were read in the passive, its estimate would be "called upon," following analogy. Al-Zajjaj said something similar.

If it is connected to ﴿li-man ḍarruhu﴾, then there are the following possibilities.

First: what al-Akhfash said, which is that ﴿yadʿū﴾ means "says," and ﴿man﴾ is a subject, a relative noun whose complement is the clause after it, which is ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾, and the predicate of the subject is omitted, its estimate being "a god and one of divine nature." The clause is in the position of the accusative, reported by ﴿yadʿū﴾ which means "says." It was said: this meaning is corrupt, because the disbeliever never believed that the idols' harm was nearer than their benefit. It was also said: in this view "labi'sa" (wretched is) is a new statement, not part of the report, because the disbelievers do not say of their idols "wretched is the patron."

Second: ﴿yadʿū﴾ means "names," and the omitted object at the end is the second object of "yusammā" (is named), its estimate being "a god." This is not complete except by estimating an added lām, that is "yadʿū li-man ḍarruhu" (calls upon for one whose harm...).

Third: ﴿yadʿū﴾ has been made analogous to verbs of the heart, because calling upon arises only from belief. The better view is that it is given the sense of "claims" (yazʿumu), and an object is estimated for "man," and the clause is in the position of the accusative as the object of ﴿yadʿū﴾. Al-Farisi pointed to this view.

The fourth view is that of al-Farra' (the grammarian), that the lam ("la-") entered a position where it does not belong, and that the original sense is "[He calls upon] one whose harm is nearer than his benefit." This is far-fetched, because what is within the relative clause (silah, the clause that completes a relative pronoun) cannot precede the relative pronoun itself (al-mawsul).

The fifth view is that the lam is an extra particle for emphasis, and "man" is the object of "yad'u." This is weak, because it is not one of the positions where the lam is added. Yet the reading of Abd Allah, "yad'u man darruhu" (without the lam), supports it. The most plausible explanation is that "yad'u" is an emphatic repetition of the first "yad'u." The lam in "la-man" is the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida'), and the predicate is the clause that forms a omitted oath, whose answer is ﴿لَبِئْسَ المَوْلى﴾ ("Wretched is the protector"). The apparent meaning of "yad'u" is calling out and seeking help. It has also been said that its meaning is distant. Here al-mawla means the helper, the close companion, the one who associates closely.

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the state of the one who worships Him "on an edge" and mocked his opinion, and threatened him with loss in the Hereafter, He followed this with the state of those who oppose them among the people of faith, and what He promised them of the sensory promise (al-wa'd al-hissi). Then He began to rebuke those first ones, as if He were saying: these worshippers "on an edge," anxiety has accompanied them, and they assumed that Allah will never help Muhammad ﷺ and his followers. We only commanded them to be patient and to await Our promise. Whoever thinks otherwise, let him extend a rope, and let him strangle himself, and see whether his rage is removed by that. Qatada said this meaning. This is in the manner of the well-known proverb, "Here is the mountain, so strangle yourself," which is said to one who wants of a matter what he cannot achieve.

On this view, the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to the Messenger ﷺ. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Kalbi, Muqatil, al-Dahhak, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi, and it was preferred by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. The meaning is that Allah will never help Muhammad, in this world by raising His word and making His religion manifest, and in the Hereafter by raising his rank and taking vengeance on those who denied him. Although the Messenger has no mention in the verse, the verse contains what indicates him, which is the mention of faith in His saying ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يُدْخِلُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ ("Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe"). Some Muslims held this opinion because of their intense rage against the polytheists, who were slow in what Allah had promised His Messenger of victory. Or they were bedouins who considered the Messenger's ascendancy slow, so they lagged behind in Islam.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to "man" (whoever), because it is what is mentioned, and the pronoun properly refers to what is mentioned. This is the view of Mujahid. Some who held this view took "naṣr" (help) here to mean provision (rizq), as they said: "ard mansurah," meaning a land that has been rained upon. The poet said:

*And you do not give a man beyond his right,*
*nor do you possess the portion you help.*

That is, you do not give to him. And it is said: a beggar from the Banu Bakr stopped by us and said, "Whoever helps me, may Allah help him." So the meaning is: whoever thinks that Allah will not provide for him, and so turns away from the religion of Muhammad because of this thought, as He described in His saying ﴿وإنْ أصابَتْهُ فِتْنَةٌ انْقَلَبَ عَلى وجْهِهِ﴾ ("And if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face"), then let him reach the utmost of distress, which is strangling. For that will not reach him except what has been decreed for him, and it will not make him provided with more than what has been apportioned to him.

On this view it is possible that "naṣr" retains its ordinary sense: whoever thought that Allah would not help him in this world and the Hereafter, and so is enraged at the absence of His help, let him extend a rope. The statement "then he is enraged" is supported by His saying ﴿هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ ما يَغِيظُ﴾ ("Will his scheming remove that which enrages him?"). The meaning of His saying ﴿فَلْيَمْدُدْ بِسَبَبٍ إلى السَّماءِ ثُمَّ لِيَقْطَعْ﴾ ("let him extend a rope to the sky, then cut it off") is: let him devise the greatest of stratagems to help Allah's help reach him, then let him cut the rope. ﴿فَلْيَنْظُرْ هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ﴾ ("then let him look: will his scheming remove that which enrages him?"). His scheming in bringing help to himself is the thing that enrages him, namely the absence of his help through the domination of his enemies over him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a statement in which something has been abbreviated, and the meaning is: Allah is the helper of His Messenger in this world and the Hereafter. So whoever among his envious and enemies thinks that Allah will do otherwise, and hopes for that, and is enraged that he will not attain his aim, then let him exhaust his capacity and expend his full effort in removing what enrages him, by doing what someone does when rage has reached its utmost limit, until he extends a rope to the sky of his house and strangles himself. ("Then let him look") meaning: let him picture in himself whether, if he does that, it will remove the help of Allah which enrages him. The strangling is called "cutting" (qat') because the one who strangles himself cuts off his breath by blocking its passages, and from this the panting breath is called qat'. His act is called a scheme (kayd) because he placed it in the position of scheming, since he could not do anything else, or as mockery, because he did not scheme against the one he envies; he only schemed against himself. The meaning is that there is nothing in his hand except what does not remove what enrages him.

It has been said: ("let him extend") with a rope "to the sky," meaning the canopy, and let him climb upon it, then let him cut off the revelation from descending upon him. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

It has been said: the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to the religion and Islam. Ibn Atiyya said: the clearest of the views on this verse is that it is a parable. "Naṣr" has its known meaning, "qat'" is strangling, and "sama'" (sky) is elevation in the air, a ceiling or a tree or the like. So reflect upon it. In ﴿ما يَغِيظُ﴾ ("that which enrages"), "ma" means "alladhi" (that which), and the returning pronoun is omitted, or it is a verbal noun (masdariyyah). Likewise, that is, and like that sending down, We sent down the whole Qur'an ﴿آياتٍ بَيِّناتٍ﴾ ("clear signs"), meaning there is no variation in the sending down of part of it or of all of it. The pronoun in "anzalnahu" refers to the Qur'an, and it was concealed because its reference is understood, as in His saying ﴿حَتّى تَوارَتْ بِالحِجابِ﴾ ("until it was hidden by the veil") [Sad 32]. The estimated meaning is: and the matter is ﴿أنَّ اللَّهَ يَهْدِي مَن يُرِيدُ﴾ ("that Allah guides whom He wills"), meaning He creates guidance in your heart. He wills its guidance, and there is no creator of guidance except Him.

[p. 354] ﴿Among people is one who argues about God without knowledge, without guidance, and without an illuminating Book, turning aside (in arrogance) to lead others astray from God's way. For him there is disgrace in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection We shall make him taste the punishment of the Blaze. That is for what your hands have sent ahead, and indeed God is not unjust to His servants.﴾ ﴿Among people is one who worships God on an edge: if good befalls him, he is content with it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss.﴾ ﴿He calls upon, besides God, what can neither harm him nor benefit him. That is the far-off error.﴾ ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. Wretched is the patron, and wretched is the companion.﴾ ﴿Indeed God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed God does what He wills.﴾ ﴿Whoever thinks that God will not help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope to the sky, then cut it off, and see whether his scheming removes what enrages him.﴾ ﴿Thus We have sent it down as clear signs, and indeed God guides whom He wills.﴾

The apparent view is that the one who argues in this verse is other than the one who argues in the verse before it. Muhammad ibn Ka'b reported that it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, while Ibn 'Abbas reported that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. It has also been said that the first verse concerns the blind followers (muqallidun) and this one concerns the blind followers as well. The majority view is that both verses, and the others that precede them, were revealed concerning al-Nadr, and that they were repeated for emphasis in censure, and because each one includes an addition not found in the other. It has been said about him that some ten-odd verses were revealed concerning him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He repeated this (verse) as a rebuke, as if he were saying: these examples are in the utmost clarity and explicitness, [yet] among people (wa-min al-nas) [there is one who], despite that, argues." So the waw here is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), whereas in the preceding verse the waw is the waw of coordination ('atf), coordinating the whole discourse with what came before it; the verse is in the sense of information, and here it is repeated for rebuke. End of quotation.

But it cannot be imagined that the waw in ﴿wa-min al-nas man yujadilu﴾ is a waw of circumstance. According to the clause he supposed before it, if it were stated explicitly, it could not be construed with "idh" (when), so it is not a circumstantial waw; rather it is a waw of coordination. It divides the forsaken into: one who argues ﴿about God without knowledge﴾, following a rebellious devil; one who argues ﴿without knowledge, guidance, or an illuminating Book﴾ and so on; and one who worships his Lord ﴿on an edge﴾. By "knowledge" is meant necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-daruri); by "guidance" is meant reasoning and reflection, since that leads to knowledge; and by "the illuminating Book" is meant revelation. That is, he argues without any one of these three.

﴿Thāniya ʿiṭfihi﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun concealed within (yujadilu). Ibn 'Abbas said: "arrogant." Mujahid said: "twisting his neck with ugliness." Al-Dahhak said: "lofty with his nose." Ibn Jurayj said: "turning away from the truth." Al-Hasan read thāniya ʿaṭfin, with a fatha on the ʿayn, meaning his tenderness and compassion (taʿattufuhu wa-taraḥḥumuhu). ﴿Li-yuḍilla﴾ is connected to (yujadilu). Mujahid, the people of Makka, and Abu 'Amr in one transmission read li-yaḍilla with a fatha on the yāʾ, meaning he himself goes astray. The majority read it with a ḍamma, li-yuḍilla, meaning he leads others astray [p. 355] (ghayrahu). It follows from his leading others astray that the punishment is multiplied, since he bears the burden of everyone who acts upon it. Since the outcome of his disputing is leading astray, it is as if it were its cause. Likewise, since he turns away from guidance and engages in argument for falsehood, he is as one who has left guidance for error.

Disgrace in this world is what befell him on the day of Badr: capture, killing, and defeat. Al-Nadr was indeed taken captive. It has been said that the disgrace was on the day of Badr at al-Safra'. As for ﴿al-ḥarīq﴾, it has been said to be one of the levels of Hell. It may also be an attributive construction, the noun being qualified by its adjective: "the punishment that burns," i.e., "the burning (muḥriq) punishment," like "al-samīʿ" in the sense of "the one who causes to hear."

Zayd ibn 'Ali read fa-uḥīquhu with the hamza of the first person. ﴿Dhālika﴾ refers to the disgrace and the causing to taste. The ways of construing ﴿dhālika﴾ permitted here are the same as those permitted in construing ﴿dhālika bi-anna Allāha huwa al-ḥaqq﴾ (that is, God is the Truth). The meaning of ﴿bi-mā qaddamat yadāka﴾ has been explained earlier: it means by your committing crimes, and by God's justice concerning you since you disobeyed Him. It is possible that wa-anna Allāha is a separate clause, not part of the causal phrase, and the sense is: "and the matter is that God..." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The word 'servants' (al-ʿabīd) is mentioned here in the sense of their destitution and lack of power, and therefore this form has come." End of quotation. He distinguishes between ʿabīd and ʿibād, and we have already refuted his distinction at the end of Āl ʿImrān in regard to the verse ﴿and indeed God is not unjust to the servants﴾, and we have explained here his phrase "bi-ẓallāmin" (unjust).

Concerning ﴿yaʿbudu Allāh﴾ (worships God): it was revealed concerning Bedouins of Aslam and Ghatafan who were slow to accept Islam and said: "We fear that Muhammad will not be helped, and then the bond between us and our allies among the Jews will be severed, and they will not protect us or shelter us." It was also said that it concerns a Jew who embraced Islam and was then afflicted, so he considered Islam a bad omen and asked the Messenger (ﷺ) for its cancellation, and he said: "Islam is not cancelled," and then the verse was revealed. Al-Hasan said: it is the hypocrite who worships with his tongue without his heart. Ibn 'Isa said: "with weak certainty." Abu 'Ubayd said: ﴿ʿalā ḥarf﴾ means "on doubt." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "ḥarf" means on a deviation from the white creed, or on the brink of it, prepared to fall.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ʿalā ḥarf﴾ means "on an edge of the religion, not in its center or heart. This is a parable for their being in unrest and agitation in their religion, not in tranquility and calm, like one who stands on the edge of an army: if he senses victory and spoils, he stays and is at ease, but otherwise he flees and rushes off headlong." End of quotation.

His loss in this world is that he is afflicted in it with what grieves him, such as the loss of his wealth and the loss of his loved ones, and so he does not submit to the decree. His loss in the Hereafter is that he is deprived of the reward of the one who is patient, since he apostatized from Islam.

Mujahid, Humayd, al-A'raj, Ibn Muhaysin (through al-Za'faranani's transmission), Qa'nab, al-Ju'dari, and Ibn Miqsam read khāsira al-dunyā as an active participle (ism fa'il) in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Al-Zamakhshari said: "The nominative is by way of subject (fā'iliyya), and the placing of the noun in place of the pronoun, and it is a good reading." End of quotation.
