Ibn Atiyya said: "*wa-kathir haqqa 'alayhi al-'adhab*" may be coordinated with what preceded it, meaning "and many [prostrate] though the punishment has become due upon them"; that is, prostrating unwillingly and against their will, either by their shadows or by their submission in times of hardship. Mujahid said something similar, and said: "Their prostration is by their shadow."

It was recited "*wa-kathir*" with *haqqan* (in truth), meaning the punishment has become due upon them truly. It was also recited "*huqqa*" with a *damma* on the *ha'*, and "*min*" is the object placed before "*yuhin*." Al-Jumhur recited "*min mukrim*" as an active participle (ism fa'il). Ibn Abi Ablah recited it with a *fatha* on the *ra'*, as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "*min ikram*" (from honoring).

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Whomever God humiliates, He has decreed for him wretchedness, because of what was foreknown in His knowledge of his disbelief or his deviance. So he remains humiliated, and for him there is no honorer, because He does what He wills of honor and humiliation, and He does not will of that except what is required by the deeds of the doers and the beliefs of the believers." End quote. In this there is a hint of Mu'tazilism (*dasisat al-i'tizal*).

When He mentioned the people of happiness and the people of wretchedness, He mentioned the disputes that took place among them concerning His religion, and so He said: "*hadhan*" (these two). Qays ibn 'Abbad and Hilal ibn Yasaf said: "It was revealed concerning the duelists on the day of Badr: Hamza, Ali, and 'Ubayda ibn al-Harith came forth, and 'Utba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabi'a, and al-Walid ibn 'Utba." It is related from Ali: "I will be the first to kneel on the Day of Resurrection for the dispute before the presence of God, the Exalted." Abu Dharr swore by this, and it occurs in the Sahih of al-Bukhari that the verse was about them.

Ibn Abbas said: "The reference is to the believers and the People of the Book, among whom a dispute occurred. The Jews said: 'We are older in religion than you,' so it was revealed." Mujahid, Ata ibn Abi Rabah, al-Hasan, Asim, and al-Kalbi said: "The reference is to the believers and the disbelievers in general." "*Khasm*" (adversary) is a verbal noun (masdar), and what is meant here is the group, which is why "*ikhtasamu*" (they disputed) came in the plural, in consideration of the meaning, since under each adversary are individuals. In a report from al-Kisa'i it is recited "*khisman*" with a *kasra* on the *kha'*. The meaning of "*fi rabbihim*" is "in the religion of their Lord." Ibn Abi Ablah recited "*ikhtasama*" (in the dual), taking into account the dual form of the word. Then He mentioned what He has prepared for the disbelievers.

Al-Za'farani, in his choice of reading, recited "*qutti'at*" with the *ta'* lightened, as if He, the Exalted, determines for them fires according to the measures of their bodies, enclosing them, just as clothing that is worn is cut. The apparent meaning is that these cut garments for them are of fire. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The garments are of molten copper, and there is nothing that, when heated, is more intensely hot than it. So the estimate is 'of copper heated by the fire.'" It has also been said: "The garments of fire" is a metaphor for the fire's encompassing them, just as a garment encompasses its wearer. Wahb said: "The people of the Fire will be clothed, and nakedness would be better for them, and they will live, and death would be better for them."

When He mentioned what is poured over their heads, since it is known that a garment is worn over the body and not the head, He therefore mentioned what reaches the head of punishment. It was related from Ibn Abbas: "If a single drop of the boiling water fell upon the mountains of the world, it would melt them." When He mentioned what punishes the body externally and what is poured over the head, He mentioned what reaches the inside of the one punished, which is the boiling water that melts what is in the belly of the intestines, and that melting reaches the outside, which is the skin, so it affects the exterior just as it affects the interior, as God, the Exalted, said: "*fa-qatta'a am'a'ahum*" (so He cut their intestines) [Muhammad: 15]. Al-Hasan and a group recited "*yusahharu*" with a *fatha* on the *sad* and a *shadda* on the *ha'*.

A hadith states: "Indeed the boiling water is poured over their heads, and it penetrates the skull until it reaches the inside, and it strips what is in the inside until it exits from their two feet. This is the *sahr* (melting), then it is returned as it was."

The apparent meaning is that "*wal-julud*" (and the skins) is coordinated with "*ma*" (what) in His saying "*yusharu bihi ma fi buṭunihim*" (by it what is in their bellies will be melted), and that the skins are melted just as the entrails are melted. It has also been said: the estimate is "and the skins are torn," because skins are not melted; they only gather together under the fire and shrink. This is like the saying of the poet:

*I fed them straw and cold water*

meaning "and I gave them water to drink."

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "*wa-lahum*" (and for them) refers to the disbelievers, and the *lam* indicates entitlement. It has been said that it means "*ʿalā*" (upon), as in His saying "*wa-lahumu al-la'na*" (and for them is the curse) [Ghafir: 52], meaning "upon them." It has also been said that the pronoun refers to what the meaning indicates, namely the angels of punishment (*al-zabaniya*). Some people, including al-Dahhak, said: "*al-maqami'*" are maces (*al-matariq*). It was said: they are whips of fire. A hadith states: "If one of them were placed upon the earth, and then the two weights (humans and jinn) gathered upon it, they would not be able to lift it from the earth."

"*Min ghamm*" (out of distress) is a substitute for "*minha*" (from them), an inclusive substitution (*badal al-ishtimal*), in which the preposition was repeated and the pronoun omitted, for the meaning is understood, meaning "*min ghammiha*" (out of its distress). It is possible that "*min*" indicates cause, meaning because of the distress that befalls them. The apparent meaning is that the return is conditioned on the desire to leave, so there must be an omitted element by which the meaning is sound: that is, from their places prepared for their punishment. "*Uʿidu fiha*" (they will be returned into it) means into those places. It has been said: "*uʿidu fiha*" means by the beating of the angels of punishment upon them with the maces. "*Wa-dhuqu*" (and taste) means and it will be said to them, "Taste."

When He mentioned what He has prepared of punishment for one of the two adversaries, He mentioned what He has prepared of reward for the other adversary. Al-Jumhur recited "*yuhallawna*" with a *damma* on the *ya'*, a *fatha* on the *ha'*, and a *shadda* on the *lam*. It has been said with a *damma* on the *ya'* and without the *shadda*, and this has the same meaning as the doubled form. Ibn Abbas recited "*yahlawna*" with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and the *lam*, and a *sukun* on the *ha'*, from their saying: "*haliya al-rajul*" and "*halit al-mar'a*," when the man or woman became one adorned with ornaments (*hilyy*), and the woman is "*dhat hilyy*" [one with ornaments], and the woman is "*halla*."

Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: "It is possible that it derives from '*haliya bi-'ayni*' (I was pleased with him/it) when you find it good, and then '*min*' would be extra, and the meaning would be 'they find the worn bracelets good in it.'" End quote. This is not sound, because he made "*haliya*" a transitive verb, and on that basis judged that "*min*" is extra in an obligatory position, which is not the view of the Basran grammarians. Also, according to this estimate, it would not be permissible, because it does not transmit an intransitive verb with this meaning. If it has this meaning, then "*min*" indicates cause, meaning "with the wearing of bracelets of gold they will be adorned, by the eyes of those who see them," that is, some of them will be adorned by the eyes of others.

Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: "It is also possible that '*min*' is from '*halaytu bihi*' when I obtained it. The meaning would be '*yuhallawna fiha*' [they will be adorned in it] with bracelets, so '*min*' would be a substitute for the *ba'* (with). The word *hilya* (ornament) derives from this. If you take it from *halaytu bihi*, it is *hilya*, and it is from the *ya'*. If you take it from *halia bi-'ayni*, it is from *halawa* (sweetness), from the *waw*." End quote. Among the meanings of "attaining" is their saying: "*lam yahlu fulan bi-ta'il*," meaning he did not attain anything.

The apparent meaning is that "*min*" in "*min asawira*" (of bracelets) is partitive, and "*min*" in "*min dhahab*" (of gold) indicates the beginning of the source, meaning they were made from gold.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The "min" in ﴿min asawira﴾ (of bracelets) is for specifying the kind (li-bayan al-jins), though it may also be partitive (lil-tab'id). The discussion of its counterpart in al-Kahf has already preceded.

Ibn 'Abbas read "min Aswara" with a fatha on the ra', without an alif or a ha'. By analogy, it should be triptote (yusrifuhu), since its form has been reduced and it becomes like Jandal; but he assumed the deleted element to be present, so he made it diptote (mana'ahu al-sarf).

'Asim, Nafi', al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Salam and Ya'qub read "(wa-lu'lu'an)" here and in Fatir with the accusative. Abu al-Fath interpreted it as governed by an implied verb, and al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "wa-yu'tawna ﴿lu'lu'an﴾" (and they are given pearls) [al-Insan: 19]. Whoever makes the "min" in ﴿min asawira﴾ superfluous may coordinate "(wa-lu'lu'an)" with the position of "(asawira)". It was also said that it is coordinated with the position of ﴿min asawira﴾, because it is estimated as "(yuhallawna)" [they are adorned] with ornaments ﴿min asawira﴾.

The rest of the Seven, and also al-Hasan, Talha, Ibn Thabit and al-A'mash, read it differently. The people of Makkah read "(wa-lu'lu'un)" in the genitive, coordinated with "(asawira)" or with "(dhahabin)", because a bracelet is made of gold and pearls, some of which is joined to others.

Al-Jahdari said: the alif is present after the waw in the Imam (the standard codex). Al-Asma'i said: there is no alif in it. Yahya reported from Abu Bakr the hamzing of the last and the substitution of the first, while al-Mu'alla ibn Mansur reported from him the opposite of that.

Al-Fayyad read "wa-luwliyyan": he changed the two hamzas into waws, so the second became a waw preceded by a damma, and it was treated as what was done in "adall", where the waw was changed into a ya' with a kasra before it. Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-laylIyyan": he substituted the two hamzas with two waws, then changed them into two ya's, making the first assimilate to the second. Talha read "wa-lulin" in the genitive, coordinated with what the hamzated word was coordinated with.

As for ﴿al-tayyibi min al-qawl﴾ (the good of speech): if the guidance is in this world, it is the statement "There is no god but Allah," and good utterances of remembrance and others; and "the path" is the way of Islam. If it is information about what happens to them in the Hereafter, it is their saying: "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us," and what resembles that of the dialogue of the people of Paradise; and "the path" is the way to Paradise. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is "There is no god but Allah" and "Praise be to Allah." Ibn Zayd added: "And Allah is greatest." From al-Suddi: the Qur'an.

Al-Mawardi reported: enjoining good and forbidding evil. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us." The apparent meaning is that "al-Hamid" (the Praiseworthy) is an attribute of Allah, Exalted is He. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that by "al-Hamid" he means the path itself, and that it was attributed to it in the manner of its attribution in His saying: "the abode of the Hereafter" (dar al-akhirah).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 22, verses 17–24 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associate others with God: indeed God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed God is Witness over all things.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the creatures, and many of mankind? And many have deserved the punishment. And whomever God humiliates, none can honor. Indeed God does what He wills.﴾ ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads.﴾ ﴿By it what is in their bellies will be melted, and the skins.﴾ ﴿And for them are maces of iron.﴾ ﴿Whenever they wish to leave it, out of distress, they will be returned into it, and [it will be said], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ ﴿Indeed God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾ ﴿And they have been guided to good speech, and guided to the path of the Praiseworthy.﴾

[p. 359] When He had mentioned earlier that God guides whomever He wills, He followed this with an explanation of who He guides and who He does not guide, because what precedes implies that whoever He does not will to guide, He does not guide. The affirmation of guidance for those He wills implies the negation of it for those He does not will. Those who associate others with God are the worshippers of idols and statues, and whoever worships other than God. Al-Zamakhshari said: "[The particle] inna (إنَّ) has been placed on each of the two parts of the sentence for the sake of emphasis. Similar to it is the verse of Jarir:

*Indeed the caliph—indeed God has clothed him in the garment of kingship, by which the endings are hoped for.*"

The apparent meaning of this is that he compared the line of poetry to the verse. Likewise al-Zajjaj paired it with the verse. However, it is not necessary that the line be like the verse, because the line may be understood as follows: the predicate of *inna al-khalifa* is his saying "*bihi turja al-khawatim*" (by it the endings are hoped for), and "*inna Allaha sarbalahu sirbala mulkin*" (indeed God has clothed him in the garment of kingship) is a parenthetical clause between the subject of *inna* and its predicate. This differs from the verse, for in the verse His saying "*inna Allaha yafsilu*" (indeed God will judge) is definite. The lengthy separation between them by the coordinated items made the placing of *inna* before the clause that serves as the predicate acceptable. The apparent meaning of "judging between them on the Day of Resurrection" is their arrival, the believers to Paradise and the disbelievers to Hellfire. The concluding phrase "*shahid*" (Witness) suits the judgment between the groups.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The judging is unrestricted, and it may include judging between them in all states and places, so He does not recompense them with one uniform recompense without distinction, nor gather them in one place." It has also been said: "*yafsilu baynahum*" means He decides between the believers and the disbelievers.

The apparent meaning of prostration here is an expression of submission to what God mentioned and compliance with what He wills. This meaning encompasses those who have reason and those who do not, and those who prostrate in the sense of obligation (*taklif*, religious accountability) and those who do not. He also coordinated with "whoever" those who are worshipped besides God. Thus, in "*al-samawat*" (the heavens) are the angels, who were worshipped; "the sun" was worshipped by Himyar; "the moon" was worshipped by Kinana, as said by Ibn Abbas; "al-Dabaran" by Tamim; "al-Shi'ra" by Lakhm and Quraysh; "al-Thurayya" by Tayy; "Utarid" by Asad; and "al-Murzim" by Rabi'a. And "*fi al-ard*" (on the earth) refers to those among mankind who were worshipped, and to the idols carved from "the mountains and the trees," and cows, and whatever animals were worshipped.

Al-Zuhri recited "*wal-dawabb*" with the *ba'* lightened. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: "There is no basis for this except that it is an escape from doubling the letter, like *zallat* and *qarana*."

There is no contradiction between His saying "*wa-man fi al-ard*" (and whoever is on the earth), which is general in its scope, and His saying "*wa-kathir min al-nas*" (and many of mankind), which is specific, because it is not necessary that "*wa-kathir*" be coordinated with what precedes it of the coordinated singular items that fall under "yasjudu" (prostrates), since it is permissible to supply "*yasjudu lahu*" (prostrates to Him) as "*kathir min al-nas*" (many of mankind) with the prostration of worship, which is indicated by the meaning, and not that the first "*yasjudu*" explains it, because the two usages differ. Whoever holds that it is permissible to combine polytheists with the literal and figurative senses permits coordinating "*wa-kathir min al-nas*" with the singular items before it, even if prostration differs in its attribution to what has reason and what does not. It is also permissible that it be in the nominative as the subject, with the predicate omitted, indicated by the contrast with "those" in the sentence that follows it. That is, "*wa-kathir min al-nas*" is rewarded.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that '*min al-nas*' be its predicate, meaning 'from among mankind' who are truly human, namely the righteous and the God-fearing. It is also permissible to exaggerate in multiplying those who deserve the punishment, so '*kathir*' is coordinated with '*kathir*,' and then He expressed them with '*haqqa 'alayhimu al-'adhab*' (the punishment has become due upon them), as if He had said: '*wa-kathir*' [and many]—'*wa-kathir min al-nas wa-kathir*' [and many of mankind and many]—upon whom the punishment [is due]." End quote. These two interpretations are weak.

If it is information about what happens to them in the Hereafter, it is their saying: "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us," and what resembles that of the dialogue of the people of Paradise; and "the path" is the way to Paradise. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is "There is no god but Allah" and "Praise be to Allah." Ibn Zayd added: "And Allah is greatest." From al-Suddi: the Qur'an.

Al-Mawardi reported: enjoining good and forbidding evil. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us." The apparent meaning is that "al-Hamid" (the Praiseworthy) is an attribute of Allah, Exalted is He. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that by "al-Hamid" he means the path itself, and that it was attributed to it in the manner of its attribution in His saying: "the abode of the Hereafter" (dar al-akhirah).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 22, verses 17–24 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associate others with God: indeed God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed God is Witness over all things.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the creatures, and many of mankind? And many have deserved the punishment. And whomever God humiliates, none can honor. Indeed God does what He wills.﴾ ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads.﴾ ﴿By it what is in their bellies will be melted, and the skins.﴾ ﴿And for them are maces of iron.﴾ ﴿Whenever they wish to leave it, out of distress, they will be returned into it, and [it will be said], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ ﴿Indeed God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾ ﴿And they have been guided to good speech, and guided to the path of the Praiseworthy.﴾

[p. 359] When He had mentioned earlier that God guides whomever He wills, He followed this with an explanation of who He guides and who He does not guide, because what precedes implies that whoever He does not will to guide, He does not guide. The affirmation of guidance for those He wills implies the negation of it for those He does not will. Those who associate others with God are the worshippers of idols and statues, and whoever worships other than God. Al-Zamakhshari said: "[The particle] inna (إنَّ) has been placed on each of the two parts of the sentence for the sake of emphasis. Similar to it is the verse of Jarir:

*Indeed the caliph—indeed God has clothed him in the garment of kingship, by which the endings are hoped for.*"

The apparent meaning of this is that he compared the line of poetry to the verse. Likewise al-Zajjaj paired it with the verse. However, it is not necessary that the line be like the verse, because the line may be understood as follows: the predicate of *inna al-khalifa* is his saying "*bihi turja al-khawatim*" (by it the endings are hoped for), and "*inna Allaha sarbalahu sirbala mulkin*" (indeed God has clothed him in the garment of kingship) is a parenthetical clause between the subject of *inna* and its predicate. This differs from the verse, for in the verse His saying "*inna Allaha yafsilu*" (indeed God will judge) is definite. The lengthy separation between them by the coordinated items made the placing of *inna* before the clause that serves as the predicate acceptable. The apparent meaning of "judging between them on the Day of Resurrection" is their arrival, the believers to Paradise and the disbelievers to Hellfire. The concluding phrase "*shahid*" (Witness) suits the judgment between the groups.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The judging is unrestricted, and it may include judging between them in all states and places, so He does not recompense them with one uniform recompense without distinction, nor gather them in one place." It has also been said: "*yafsilu baynahum*" means He decides between the believers and the disbelievers.

The apparent meaning of prostration here is an expression of submission to what God mentioned and compliance with what He wills. This meaning encompasses those who have reason and those who do not, and those who prostrate in the sense of obligation (*taklif*, religious accountability) and those who do not. He also coordinated with "whoever" those who are worshipped besides God. Thus, in "*al-samawat*" (the heavens) are the angels, who were worshipped; "the sun" was worshipped by Himyar; "the moon" was worshipped by Kinana, as said by Ibn Abbas; "al-Dabaran" by Tamim; "al-Shi'ra" by Lakhm and Quraysh; "al-Thurayya" by Tayy; "Utarid" by Asad; and "al-Murzim" by Rabi'a. And "*fi al-ard*" (on the earth) refers to those among mankind who were worshipped, and to the idols carved from "the mountains and the trees," and cows, and whatever animals were worshipped.

Al-Zuhri recited "*wal-dawabb*" with the *ba'* lightened. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: "There is no basis for this except that it is an escape from doubling the letter, like *zallat* and *qarana*."

There is no contradiction between His saying "*wa-man fi al-ard*" (and whoever is on the earth), which is general in its scope, and His saying "*wa-kathir min al-nas*" (and many of mankind), which is specific, because it is not necessary that "*wa-kathir*" be coordinated with what precedes it of the coordinated singular items that fall under "yasjudu" (prostrates), since it is permissible to supply "*yasjudu lahu*" (prostrates to Him) as "*kathir min al-nas*" (many of mankind) with the prostration of worship, which is indicated by the meaning, and not that the first "*yasjudu*" explains it, because the two usages differ. Whoever holds that it is permissible to combine polytheists with the literal and figurative senses permits coordinating "*wa-kathir min al-nas*" with the singular items before it, even if prostration differs in its attribution to what has reason and what does not. It is also permissible that it be in the nominative as the subject, with the predicate omitted, indicated by the contrast with "those" in the sentence that follows it. That is, "*wa-kathir min al-nas*" is rewarded.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that '*min al-nas*' be its predicate, meaning 'from among mankind' who are truly human, namely the righteous and the God-fearing. It is also permissible to exaggerate in multiplying those who deserve the punishment, so '*kathir*' is coordinated with '*kathir*,' and then He expressed them with '*haqqa 'alayhimu al-'adhab*' (the punishment has become due upon them), as if He had said: '*wa-kathir*' [and many]—'*wa-kathir min al-nas wa-kathir*' [and many of mankind and many]—upon whom the punishment [is due]." End quote. These two interpretations are weak.

Jana ibn Hubaysh recited "*wa-kabir haqqa*" with the *ba'*. Ibn Atiyya said: "*wa-kathir haqqa 'alayhi al-'adhab*" may be coordinated with what preceded it, meaning "and many [prostrate] though the punishment has become due upon them"; that is, prostrating unwillingly and against their will, either by their shadows or by their submission in times of hardship. Mujahid said something similar, and said: "Their prostration is by their shadow."

It was recited "*wa-kathir*" with *haqqan* (in truth), meaning the punishment has become due upon them truly. It was also recited "*huqqa*" with a *damma* on the *ha'*, and "*min*" is the object placed before "*yuhin*." Al-Jumhur recited "*min mukrim*" as an active participle (ism fa'il). Ibn Abi Ablah recited it with a *fatha* on the *ra'*, as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "*min ikram*" (from honoring).

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Whomever God humiliates, He has decreed for him wretchedness, because of what was foreknown in His knowledge of his disbelief or his deviance. So he remains humiliated, and for him there is no honorer, because He does what He wills of honor and humiliation, and He does not will of that except what is required by the deeds of the doers and the beliefs of the believers." End quote. In this there is a hint of Mu'tazilism (*dasisat al-i'tizal*).

When He mentioned the people of happiness and the people of wretchedness, He mentioned the disputes that took place among them concerning His religion, and so He said: "*hadhan*" (these two). Qays ibn 'Abbad and Hilal ibn Yasaf said: "It was revealed concerning the duelists on the day of Badr: Hamza, Ali, and 'Ubayda ibn al-Harith came forth, and 'Utba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabi'a, and al-Walid ibn 'Utba." It is related from Ali: "I will be the first to kneel on the Day of Resurrection for the dispute before the presence of God, the Exalted." Abu Dharr swore by this, and it occurs in the Sahih of al-Bukhari that the verse was about them.

Ibn Abbas said: "The reference is to the believers and the People of the Book, among whom a dispute occurred. The Jews said: 'We are older in religion than you,' so it was revealed." Mujahid, Ata ibn Abi Rabah, al-Hasan, Asim, and al-Kalbi said: "The reference is to the believers and the disbelievers in general." "*Khasm*" (adversary) is a verbal noun (masdar), and what is meant here is the group, which is why "*ikhtasamu*" (they disputed) came in the plural, in consideration of the meaning, since under each adversary are individuals. In a report from al-Kisa'i it is recited "*khisman*" with a *kasra* on the *kha'*. The meaning of "*fi rabbihim*" is "in the religion of their Lord." Ibn Abi Ablah recited "*ikhtasama*" (in the dual), taking into account the dual form of the word. Then He mentioned what He has prepared for the disbelievers.

Al-Za'farani, in his choice of reading, recited "*qutti'at*" with the *ta'* lightened, as if He, the Exalted, determines for them fires according to the measures of their bodies, enclosing them, just as clothing that is worn is cut. The apparent meaning is that these cut garments for them are of fire. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The garments are of molten copper, and there is nothing that, when heated, is more intensely hot than it. So the estimate is 'of copper heated by the fire.'" It has also been said: "The garments of fire" is a metaphor for the fire's encompassing them, just as a garment encompasses its wearer. Wahb said: "The people of the Fire will be clothed, and nakedness would be better for them, and they will live, and death would be better for them."

When He mentioned what is poured over their heads, since it is known that a garment is worn over the body and not the head, He therefore mentioned what reaches the head of punishment. It was related from Ibn Abbas: "If a single drop of the boiling water fell upon the mountains of the world, it would melt them." When He mentioned what punishes the body externally and what is poured over the head, He mentioned what reaches the inside of the one punished, which is the boiling water that melts what is in the belly of the intestines, and that melting reaches the outside, which is the skin, so it affects the exterior just as it affects the interior, as God, the Exalted, said: "*fa-qatta'a am'a'ahum*" (so He cut their intestines) [Muhammad: 15]. Al-Hasan and a group recited "*yusahharu*" with a *fatha* on the *sad* and a *shadda* on the *ha'*.

A hadith states: "Indeed the boiling water is poured over their heads, and it penetrates the skull until it reaches the inside, and it strips what is in the inside until it exits from their two feet. This is the *sahr* (melting), then it is returned as it was."

The apparent meaning is that "*wal-julud*" (and the skins) is coordinated with "*ma*" (what) in His saying "*yusharu bihi ma fi buṭunihim*" (by it what is in their bellies will be melted), and that the skins are melted just as the entrails are melted. It has also been said: the estimate is "and the skins are torn," because skins are not melted; they only gather together under the fire and shrink. This is like the saying of the poet:

*I fed them straw and cold water*

meaning "and I gave them water to drink."

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "*wa-lahum*" (and for them) refers to the disbelievers, and the *lam* indicates entitlement. It has been said that it means "*ʿalā*" (upon), as in His saying "*wa-lahumu al-la'na*" (and for them is the curse) [Ghafir: 52], meaning "upon them." It has also been said that the pronoun refers to what the meaning indicates, namely the angels of punishment (*al-zabaniya*). Some people, including al-Dahhak, said: "*al-maqami'*" are maces (*al-matariq*). It was said: they are whips of fire. A hadith states: "If one of them were placed upon the earth, and then the two weights (humans and jinn) gathered upon it, they would not be able to lift it from the earth."

"*Min ghamm*" (out of distress) is a substitute for "*minha*" (from them), an inclusive substitution (*badal al-ishtimal*), in which the preposition was repeated and the pronoun omitted, for the meaning is understood, meaning "*min ghammiha*" (out of its distress). It is possible that "*min*" indicates cause, meaning because of the distress that befalls them. The apparent meaning is that the return is conditioned on the desire to leave, so there must be an omitted element by which the meaning is sound: that is, from their places prepared for their punishment. "*Uʿidu fiha*" (they will be returned into it) means into those places. It has been said: "*uʿidu fiha*" means by the beating of the angels of punishment upon them with the maces. "*Wa-dhuqu*" (and taste) means and it will be said to them, "Taste."

When He mentioned what He has prepared of punishment for one of the two adversaries, He mentioned what He has prepared of reward for the other adversary. Al-Jumhur recited "*yuhallawna*" with a *damma* on the *ya'*, a *fatha* on the *ha'*, and a *shadda* on the *lam*. It has been said with a *damma* on the *ya'* and without the *shadda*, and this has the same meaning as the doubled form. Ibn Abbas recited "*yahlawna*" with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and the *lam*, and a *sukun* on the *ha'*, from their saying: "*haliya al-rajul*" and "*halit al-mar'a*," when the man or woman became one adorned with ornaments (*hilyy*), and the woman is "*dhat hilyy*" [one with ornaments], and the woman is "*halla*."

Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: "It is possible that it derives from '*haliya bi-'ayni*' (I was pleased with him/it) when you find it good, and then '*min*' would be extra, and the meaning would be 'they find the worn bracelets good in it.'" End quote. This is not sound, because he made "*haliya*" a transitive verb, and on that basis judged that "*min*" is extra in an obligatory position, which is not the view of the Basran grammarians. Also, according to this estimate, it would not be permissible, because it does not transmit an intransitive verb with this meaning. If it has this meaning, then "*min*" indicates cause, meaning "with the wearing of bracelets of gold they will be adorned, by the eyes of those who see them," that is, some of them will be adorned by the eyes of others.

Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: "It is also possible that '*min*' is from '*halaytu bihi*' when I obtained it. The meaning would be '*yuhallawna fiha*' [they will be adorned in it] with bracelets, so '*min*' would be a substitute for the *ba'* (with). The word *hilya* (ornament) derives from this. If you take it from *halaytu bihi*, it is *hilya*, and it is from the *ya'*. If you take it from *halia bi-'ayni*, it is from *halawa* (sweetness), from the *waw*." End quote. Among the meanings of "attaining" is their saying: "*lam yahlu fulan bi-ta'il*," meaning he did not attain anything.

It was related from Ibn Abbas: "If a single drop of the boiling water fell upon the mountains of the world, it would melt them." It has also been said: the estimate is "and the skins are torn," because skins are not melted; they only gather together under the fire and shrink. This is like the saying of the poet:

*I fed them straw and cold water*

meaning "and I gave them water to drink."

It has been said that it means "*ʿalā*" (upon), as in His saying "*wa-lahumu al-la'na*" (and for them is the curse) [Ghafir: 52], meaning "upon them." Some people, including al-Dahhak, said: "*al-maqami'*" are maces (*al-matariq*). It was said: they are whips of fire. A hadith states: "If one of them were placed upon the earth, and then the two weights (humans and jinn) gathered upon it, they would not be able to lift it from the earth."

It is possible that "*min*" indicates cause, meaning because of the distress that befalls them. The apparent meaning is that the return is conditioned on the desire to leave, so there must be an omitted element by which the meaning is sound: that is, from their places prepared for their punishment. "*Uʿidu fiha*" (they will be returned into it) means into those places. It has been said: "*uʿidu fiha*" means by the beating of the angels of punishment upon them with the maces. Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-laylIyyan": he substituted the two hamzas with two waws, then changed them into two ya's, making the first assimilate to the second. Talha read "wa-lulin" in the genitive, coordinated with what the hamzated word was coordinated with.

If it is information about what happens to them in the Hereafter, it is their saying: "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us," and what resembles that of the dialogue of the people of Paradise; and "the path" is the way to Paradise. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is "There is no god but Allah" and "Praise be to Allah." Ibn Zayd added: "And Allah is greatest." From al-Suddi: the Qur'an.

Al-Mawardi reported: enjoining good and forbidding evil. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us." The apparent meaning is that "al-Hamid" (the Praiseworthy) is an attribute of Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associate others with God: indeed God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed God is Witness over all things.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the creatures, and many of mankind? And many have deserved the punishment. And whomever God humiliates, none can honor. Indeed God does what He wills.﴾ ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads.﴾ ﴿By it what is in their bellies will be melted, and the skins.﴾ ﴿And for them are maces of iron.﴾ ﴿Whenever they wish to leave it, out of distress, they will be returned into it, and [it will be said], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ ﴿Indeed God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾ ﴿And they have been guided to good speech, and guided to the path of the Praiseworthy.﴾

[p. 359] When He had mentioned earlier that God guides whomever He wills, He followed this with an explanation of who He guides and who He does not guide, because what precedes implies that whoever He does not will to guide, He does not guide. The affirmation of guidance for those He wills implies the negation of it for those He does not will. Those who associate others with God are the worshippers of idols and statues, and whoever worships other than God. Al-Zamakhshari said: "[The particle] inna (إنَّ) has been placed on each of the two parts of the sentence for the sake of emphasis. Similar to it is the verse of Jarir:

*Indeed the caliph—indeed God has clothed him in the garment of kingship, by which the endings are hoped for.*"

The apparent meaning of this is that he compared the line of poetry to the verse. Likewise al-Zajjaj paired it with the verse. However, it is not necessary that the line be like the verse, because the line may be understood as follows: the predicate of *inna al-khalifa* is his saying "*bihi turja al-khawatim*" (by it the endings are hoped for), and "*inna Allaha sarbalahu sirbala mulkin*" (indeed God has clothed him in the garment of kingship) is a parenthetical clause between the subject of *inna* and its predicate. This differs from the verse, for in the verse His saying "*inna Allaha yafsilu*" (indeed God will judge) is definite. The lengthy separation between them by the coordinated items made the placing of *inna* before the clause that serves as the predicate acceptable. The apparent meaning of "judging between them on the Day of Resurrection" is their arrival, the believers to Paradise and the disbelievers to Hellfire. The concluding phrase "*shahid*" (Witness) suits the judgment between the groups.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The judging is unrestricted, and it may include judging between them in all states and places, so He does not recompense them with one uniform recompense without distinction, nor gather them in one place." It has also been said: "*yafsilu baynahum*" means He decides between the believers and the disbelievers.

The apparent meaning of prostration here is an expression of submission to what God mentioned and compliance with what He wills. This meaning encompasses those who have reason and those who do not, and those who prostrate in the sense of obligation (*taklif*, religious accountability) and those who do not. He also coordinated with "whoever" those who are worshipped besides God. Thus, in "*al-samawat*" (the heavens) are the angels, who were worshipped; "the sun" was worshipped by Himyar; "the moon" was worshipped by Kinana, as said by Ibn Abbas; "al-Dabaran" by Tamim; "al-Shi'ra" by Lakhm and Quraysh; "al-Thurayya" by Tayy; "Utarid" by Asad; and "al-Murzim" by Rabi'a. And "*fi al-ard*" (on the earth) refers to those among mankind who were worshipped, and to the idols carved from "the mountains and the trees," and cows, and whatever animals were worshipped.

Whoever holds that it is permissible to combine polytheists with the literal and figurative senses permits coordinating "*wa-kathir min al-nas*" with the singular items before it, even if prostration differs in its attribution to what has reason and what does not. It is also permissible that it be in the nominative as the subject, with the predicate omitted, indicated by the contrast with "those" in the sentence that follows it. That is, "*wa-kathir min al-nas*" is rewarded.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 22, verses 17–24 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associate others with God: indeed God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed God is Witness over all things.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the creatures, and many of mankind? And many have deserved the punishment. And whomever God humiliates, none can honor. Indeed God does what He wills.﴾ ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads.﴾ ﴿By it what is in their bellies will be melted, and the skins.﴾ ﴿And for them are maces of iron.﴾ ﴿Whenever they wish to leave it, out of distress, they will be returned into it, and [it will be said], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ ﴿Indeed God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾ ﴿And they have been guided to good speech, and guided to the path of the Praiseworthy.﴾

[p. 359] When He had mentioned earlier that God guides whomever He wills, He followed this with an explanation of who He guides and who He does not guide, because what precedes implies that whoever He does not will to guide, He does not guide. The affirmation of guidance for those He wills implies the negation of it for those He does not will. Those who associate others with God are the worshippers of idols and statues, and whoever worships other than God. Al-Zamakhshari said: "[The particle] inna (إنَّ) has been placed on each of the two parts of the sentence for the sake of emphasis. Similar to it is the verse of Jarir:

*Indeed the caliph—indeed God has clothed him in the garment of kingship, by which the endings are hoped for.*"

The apparent meaning of this is that he compared the line of poetry to the verse. Likewise al-Zajjaj paired it with the verse. However, it is not necessary that the line be like the verse, because the line may be understood as follows: the predicate of *inna al-khalifa* is his saying "*bihi turja al-khawatim*" (by it the endings are hoped for), and "*inna Allaha sarbalahu sirbala mulkin*" (indeed God has clothed him in the garment of kingship) is a parenthetical clause between the subject of *inna* and its predicate. This differs from the verse, for in the verse His saying "*inna Allaha yafsilu*" (indeed God will judge) is definite. The lengthy separation between them by the coordinated items made the placing of *inna* before the clause that serves as the predicate acceptable. The apparent meaning of "judging between them on the Day of Resurrection" is their arrival, the believers to Paradise and the disbelievers to Hellfire. The concluding phrase "*shahid*" (Witness) suits the judgment between the groups.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The judging is unrestricted, and it may include judging between them in all states and places, so He does not recompense them with one uniform recompense without distinction, nor gather them in one place." It has also been said: "*yafsilu baynahum*" means He decides between the believers and the disbelievers.

The apparent meaning of prostration here is an expression of submission to what God mentioned and compliance with what He wills. This meaning encompasses those who have reason and those who do not, and those who prostrate in the sense of obligation (*taklif*, religious accountability) and those who do not. He also coordinated with "whoever" those who are worshipped besides God. Thus, in "*al-samawat*" (the heavens) are the angels, who were worshipped; "the sun" was worshipped by Himyar; "the moon" was worshipped by Kinana, as said by Ibn Abbas; "al-Dabaran" by Tamim; "al-Shi'ra" by Lakhm and Quraysh; "al-Thurayya" by Tayy; "Utarid" by Asad; and "al-Murzim" by Rabi'a. And "*fi al-ard*" (on the earth) refers to those among mankind who were worshipped, and to the idols carved from "the mountains and the trees," and cows, and whatever animals were worshipped.

Al-Zuhri recited "*wal-dawabb*" with the *ba'* lightened. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: "There is no basis for this except that it is an escape from doubling the letter, like *zallat* and *qarana*."

There is no contradiction between His saying "*wa-man fi al-ard*" (and whoever is on the earth), which is general in its scope, and His saying "*wa-kathir min al-nas*" (and many of mankind), which is specific, because it is not necessary that "*wa-kathir*" be coordinated with what precedes it of the coordinated singular items that fall under "yasjudu" (prostrates), since it is permissible to supply "*yasjudu lahu*" (prostrates to Him) as "*kathir min al-nas*" (many of mankind) with the prostration of worship, which is indicated by the meaning, and not that the first "*yasjudu*" explains it, because the two usages differ. Whoever holds that it is permissible to combine polytheists with the literal and figurative senses permits coordinating "*wa-kathir min al-nas*" with the singular items before it, even if prostration differs in its attribution to what has reason and what does not. It is also permissible that it be in the nominative as the subject, with the predicate omitted, indicated by the contrast with "those" in the sentence that follows it. That is, "*wa-kathir min al-nas*" is rewarded.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that '*min al-nas*' be its predicate, meaning 'from among mankind' who are truly human, namely the righteous and the God-fearing. It is also permissible to exaggerate in multiplying those who deserve the punishment, so '*kathir*' is coordinated with '*kathir*,' and then He expressed them with '*haqqa 'alayhimu al-'adhab*' (the punishment has become due upon them), as if He had said: '*wa-kathir*' [and many]—'*wa-kathir min al-nas wa-kathir*' [and many of mankind and many]—upon whom the punishment [is due]." End quote. These two interpretations are weak.

Jana ibn Hubaysh recited "*wa-kabir haqqa*" with the *ba'*. Ibn Atiyya said: "*wa-kathir haqqa 'alayhi al-'adhab*" may be coordinated with what preceded it, meaning "and many [prostrate] though the punishment has become due upon them"; that is, prostrating unwillingly and against their will, either by their shadows or by their submission in times of hardship. Mujahid said something similar, and said: "Their prostration is by their shadow."

It was recited "*wa-kathir*" with *haqqan* (in truth), meaning the punishment has become due upon them truly. It was also recited "*huqqa*" with a *damma* on the *ha'*, and "*min*" is the object placed before "*yuhin*." Al-Jumhur recited "*min mukrim*" as an active participle (ism fa'il). Ibn Abi Ablah recited it with a *fatha* on the *ra'*, as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "*min ikram*" (from honoring).

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Whomever God humiliates, He has decreed for him wretchedness, because of what was foreknown in His knowledge of his disbelief or his deviance. So he remains humiliated, and for him there is no honorer, because He does what He wills of honor and humiliation, and He does not will of that except what is required by the deeds of the doers and the beliefs of the believers." End quote. In this there is a hint of Mu'tazilism (*dasisat al-i'tizal*).

When He mentioned the people of happiness and the people of wretchedness, He mentioned the disputes that took place among them concerning His religion, and so He said: "*hadhan*" (these two). Qays ibn 'Abbad and Hilal ibn Yasaf said: "It was revealed concerning the duelists on the day of Badr: Hamza, Ali, and 'Ubayda ibn al-Harith came forth, and 'Utba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabi'a, and al-Walid ibn 'Utba." It is related from Ali: "I will be the first to kneel on the Day of Resurrection for the dispute before the presence of God, the Exalted." Abu Dharr swore by this, and it occurs in the Sahih of al-Bukhari that the verse was about them.

Ibn Abbas said: "The reference is to the believers and the People of the Book, among whom a dispute occurred. The Jews said: 'We are older in religion than you,' so it was revealed." Mujahid, Ata ibn Abi Rabah, al-Hasan, Asim, and al-Kalbi said: "The reference is to the believers and the disbelievers in general." "*Khasm*" (adversary) is a verbal noun (masdar), and what is meant here is the group, which is why "*ikhtasamu*" (they disputed) came in the plural, in consideration of the meaning, since under each adversary are individuals. In a report from al-Kisa'i it is recited "*khisman*" with a *kasra* on the *kha'*. The meaning of "*fi rabbihim*" is "in the religion of their Lord." Ibn Abi Ablah recited "*ikhtasama*" (in the dual), taking into account the dual form of the word. Then He mentioned what He has prepared for the disbelievers.

Al-Za'farani, in his choice of reading, recited "*qutti'at*" with the *ta'* lightened, as if He, the Exalted, determines for them fires according to the measures of their bodies, enclosing them, just as clothing that is worn is cut. The apparent meaning is that these cut garments for them are of fire. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The garments are of molten copper, and there is nothing that, when heated, is more intensely hot than it. So the estimate is 'of copper heated by the fire.'" It has also been said: "The garments of fire" is a metaphor for the fire's encompassing them, just as a garment encompasses its wearer. Wahb said: "The people of the Fire will be clothed, and nakedness would be better for them, and they will live, and death would be better for them."

When He mentioned what is poured over their heads, since it is known that a garment is worn over the body and not the head, He therefore mentioned what reaches the head of punishment. It was related from Ibn Abbas: "If a single drop of the boiling water fell upon the mountains of the world, it would melt them." When He mentioned what punishes the body externally and what is poured over the head, He mentioned what reaches the inside of the one punished, which is the boiling water that melts what is in the belly of the intestines, and that melting reaches the outside, which is the skin, so it affects the exterior just as it affects the interior, as God, the Exalted, said: "*fa-qatta'a am'a'ahum*" (so He cut their intestines) [Muhammad: 15]. Al-Hasan and a group recited "*yusahharu*" with a *fatha* on the *sad* and a *shadda* on the *ha'*.

A hadith states: "Indeed the boiling water is poured over their heads, and it penetrates the skull until it reaches the inside, and it strips what is in the inside until it exits from their two feet. This is the *sahr* (melting), then it is returned as it was."

The apparent meaning is that "*wal-julud*" (and the skins) is coordinated with "*ma*" (what) in His saying "*yusharu bihi ma fi buṭunihim*" (by it what is in their bellies will be melted), and that the skins are melted just as the entrails are melted. It has also been said: the estimate is "and the skins are torn," because skins are not melted; they only gather together under the fire and shrink. This is like the saying of the poet:

*I fed them straw and cold water*

meaning "and I gave them water to drink."

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "*wa-lahum*" (and for them) refers to the disbelievers, and the *lam* indicates entitlement. It has been said that it means "*ʿalā*" (upon), as in His saying "*wa-lahumu al-la'na*" (and for them is the curse) [Ghafir: 52], meaning "upon them." It has also been said that the pronoun refers to what the meaning indicates, namely the angels of punishment (*al-zabaniya*). Some people, including al-Dahhak, said: "*al-maqami'*" are maces (*al-matariq*). It was said: they are whips of fire. A hadith states: "If one of them were placed upon the earth, and then the two weights (humans and jinn) gathered upon it, they would not be able to lift it from the earth."

"*Min ghamm*" (out of distress) is a substitute for "*minha*" (from them), an inclusive substitution (*badal al-ishtimal*), in which the preposition was repeated and the pronoun omitted, for the meaning is understood, meaning "*min ghammiha*" (out of its distress). It is possible that "*min*" indicates cause, meaning because of the distress that befalls them. The apparent meaning is that the return is conditioned on the desire to leave, so there must be an omitted element by which the meaning is sound: that is, from their places prepared for their punishment. "*Uʿidu fiha*" (they will be returned into it) means into those places. It has been said: "*uʿidu fiha*" means by the beating of the angels of punishment upon them with the maces. "*Wa-dhuqu*" (and taste) means and it will be said to them, "Taste."

When He mentioned what He has prepared of punishment for one of the two adversaries, He mentioned what He has prepared of reward for the other adversary. Al-Jumhur recited "*yuhallawna*" with a *damma* on the *ya'*, a *fatha* on the *ha'*, and a *shadda* on the *lam*. It has been said with a *damma* on the *ya'* and without the *shadda*, and this has the same meaning as the doubled form. Ibn Abbas recited "*yahlawna*" with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and the *lam*, and a *sukun* on the *ha'*, from their saying: "*haliya al-rajul*" and "*halit al-mar'a*," when the man or woman became one adorned with ornaments (*hilyy*), and the woman is "*dhat hilyy*" [one with ornaments], and the woman is "*halla*."

Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: "It is possible that it derives from '*haliya bi-'ayni*' (I was pleased with him/it) when you find it good, and then '*min*' would be extra, and the meaning would be 'they find the worn bracelets good in it.'" End quote. This is not sound, because he made "*haliya*" a transitive verb, and on that basis judged that "*min*" is extra in an obligatory position, which is not the view of the Basran grammarians. Also, according to this estimate, it would not be permissible, because it does not transmit an intransitive verb with this meaning. If it has this meaning, then "*min*" indicates cause, meaning "with the wearing of bracelets of gold they will be adorned, by the eyes of those who see them," that is, some of them will be adorned by the eyes of others.

Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: "It is also possible that '*min*' is from '*halaytu bihi*' when I obtained it. The meaning would be '*yuhallawna fiha*' [they will be adorned in it] with bracelets, so '*min*' would be a substitute for the *ba'* (with). The word *hilya* (ornament) derives from this. If you take it from *halaytu bihi*, it is *hilya*, and it is from the *ya'*. If you take it from *halia bi-'ayni*, it is from *halawa* (sweetness), from the *waw*." End quote. Among the meanings of "attaining" is their saying: "*lam yahlu fulan bi-ta'il*," meaning he did not attain anything.

Ibn 'Abbas read "min Aswara" with a fatha on the ra', without an alif or a ha'. By analogy, it should be triptote (yusrifuhu), since its form has been reduced and it becomes like Jandal; but he assumed the deleted element to be present, so he made it diptote (mana'ahu al-sarf).

It was also said that it is coordinated with the position of ﴿min asawira﴾, because it is estimated as "(yuhallawna)" [they are adorned] with ornaments ﴿min asawira﴾.

Qays ibn 'Abbad and Hilal ibn Yasaf said: "It was revealed concerning the duelists on the day of Badr: Hamza, Ali, and 'Ubayda ibn al-Harith came forth, and 'Utba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabi'a, and al-Walid ibn 'Utba." It is related from Ali: "I will be the first to kneel on the Day of Resurrection for the dispute before the presence of God, the Exalted." Abu Dharr swore by this, and it occurs in the Sahih of al-Bukhari that the verse was about them.

Ibn Abbas said: "The reference is to the believers and the People of the Book, among whom a dispute occurred. The Jews said: 'We are older in religion than you,' so it was revealed." Mujahid, Ata ibn Abi Rabah, al-Hasan, Asim, and al-Kalbi said: "The reference is to the believers and the disbelievers in general." "*Khasm*" (adversary) is a verbal noun (masdar), and what is meant here is the group, which is why "*ikhtasamu*" (they disputed) came in the plural, in consideration of the meaning, since under each adversary are individuals. In a report from al-Kisa'i it is recited "*khisman*" with a *kasra* on the *kha'*. The meaning of "*fi rabbihim*" is "in the religion of their Lord." Ibn Abi Ablah recited "*ikhtasama*" (in the dual), taking into account the dual form of the word. Then He mentioned what He has prepared for the disbelievers.

Al-Za'farani, in his choice of reading, recited "*qutti'at*" with the *ta'* lightened, as if He, the Exalted, determines for them fires according to the measures of their bodies, enclosing them, just as clothing that is worn is cut. The apparent meaning is that these cut garments for them are of fire. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The garments are of molten copper, and there is nothing that, when heated, is more intensely hot than it. So the estimate is 'of copper heated by the fire.'" It has also been said: "The garments of fire" is a metaphor for the fire's encompassing them, just as a garment encompasses its wearer. Wahb said: "The people of the Fire will be clothed, and nakedness would be better for them, and they will live, and death would be better for them."

When He mentioned what is poured over their heads, since it is known that a garment is worn over the body and not the head, He therefore mentioned what reaches the head of punishment. It was related from Ibn Abbas: "If a single drop of the boiling water fell upon the mountains of the world, it would melt them." When He mentioned what punishes the body externally and what is poured over the head, He mentioned what reaches the inside of the one punished, which is the boiling water that melts what is in the belly of the intestines, and that melting reaches the outside, which is the skin, so it affects the exterior just as it affects the interior, as God, the Exalted, said: "*fa-qatta'a am'a'ahum*" (so He cut their intestines) [Muhammad: 15]. Al-Hasan and a group recited "*yusahharu*" with a *fatha* on the *sad* and a *shadda* on the *ha'*.

A hadith states: "Indeed the boiling water is poured over their heads, and it penetrates the skull until it reaches the inside, and it strips what is in the inside until it exits from their two feet. This is the *sahr* (melting), then it is returned as it was."

The apparent meaning is that "*wal-julud*" (and the skins) is coordinated with "*ma*" (what) in His saying "*yusharu bihi ma fi buṭunihim*" (by it what is in their bellies will be melted), and that the skins are melted just as the entrails are melted. It has also been said: the estimate is "and the skins are torn," because skins are not melted; they only gather together under the fire and shrink. This is like the saying of the poet:

*I fed them straw and cold water*

meaning "and I gave them water to drink."

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "*wa-lahum*" (and for them) refers to the disbelievers, and the *lam* indicates entitlement. It has been said that it means "*ʿalā*" (upon), as in His saying "*wa-lahumu al-la'na*" (and for them is the curse) [Ghafir: 52], meaning "upon them." It has also been said that the pronoun refers to what the meaning indicates, namely the angels of punishment (*al-zabaniya*). Some people, including al-Dahhak, said: "*al-maqami'*" are maces (*al-matariq*). It was said: they are whips of fire. A hadith states: "If one of them were placed upon the earth, and then the two weights (humans and jinn) gathered upon it, they would not be able to lift it from the earth."

"*Min ghamm*" (out of distress) is a substitute for "*minha*" (from them), an inclusive substitution (*badal al-ishtimal*), in which the preposition was repeated and the pronoun omitted, for the meaning is understood, meaning "*min ghammiha*" (out of its distress). It is possible that "*min*" indicates cause, meaning because of the distress that befalls them. The apparent meaning is that the return is conditioned on the desire to leave, so there must be an omitted element by which the meaning is sound: that is, from their places prepared for their punishment. "*Uʿidu fiha*" (they will be returned into it) means into those places. It has been said: "*uʿidu fiha*" means by the beating of the angels of punishment upon them with the maces. "*Wa-dhuqu*" (and taste) means and it will be said to them, "Taste."

When He mentioned what He has prepared of punishment for one of the two adversaries, He mentioned what He has prepared of reward for the other adversary. Al-Jumhur recited "*yuhallawna*" with a *damma* on the *ya'*, a *fatha* on the *ha'*, and a *shadda* on the *lam*. It has been said with a *damma* on the *ya'* and without the *shadda*, and this has the same meaning as the doubled form. Ibn Abbas recited "*yahlawna*" with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and the *lam*, and a *sukun* on the *ha'*, from their saying: "*haliya al-rajul*" and "*halit al-mar'a*," when the man or woman became one adorned with ornaments (*hilyy*), and the woman is "*dhat hilyy*" [one with ornaments], and the woman is "*halla*."

Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: "It is possible that it derives from '*haliya bi-'ayni*' (I was pleased with him/it) when you find it good, and then '*min*' would be extra, and the meaning would be 'they find the worn bracelets good in it.'" End quote. This is not sound, because he made "*haliya*" a transitive verb, and on that basis judged that "*min*" is extra in an obligatory position, which is not the view of the Basran grammarians. Also, according to this estimate, it would not be permissible, because it does not transmit an intransitive verb with this meaning. If it has this meaning, then "*min*" indicates cause, meaning "with the wearing of bracelets of gold they will be adorned, by the eyes of those who see them," that is, some of them will be adorned by the eyes of others.

Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: "It is also possible that '*min*' is from '*halaytu bihi*' when I obtained it. The meaning would be '*yuhallawna fiha*' [they will be adorned in it] with bracelets, so '*min*' would be a substitute for the *ba'* (with). The word *hilya* (ornament) derives from this. If you take it from *halaytu bihi*, it is *hilya*, and it is from the *ya'*. If you take it from *halia bi-'ayni*, it is from *halawa* (sweetness), from the *waw*." End quote. Among the meanings of "attaining" is their saying: "*lam yahlu fulan bi-ta'il*," meaning he did not attain anything.

The apparent meaning is that "*min*" in "*min asawira*" (of bracelets) is partitive, and "*min*" in "*min dhahab*" (of gold) indicates the beginning of the source, meaning they were made from gold.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The "min" in ﴿min asawira﴾ (of bracelets) is for specifying the kind (li-bayan al-jins), though it may also be partitive (lil-tab'id). The discussion of its counterpart in al-Kahf has already preceded.

Ibn 'Abbas read "min Aswara" with a fatha on the ra', without an alif or a ha'. By analogy, it should be triptote (yusrifuhu), since its form has been reduced and it becomes like Jandal; but he assumed the deleted element to be present, so he made it diptote (mana'ahu al-sarf).

'Asim, Nafi', al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Salam and Ya'qub read "(wa-lu'lu'an)" here and in Fatir with the accusative. Abu al-Fath interpreted it as governed by an implied verb, and al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "wa-yu'tawna ﴿lu'lu'an﴾" (and they are given pearls) [al-Insan: 19]. Whoever makes the "min" in ﴿min asawira﴾ superfluous may coordinate "(wa-lu'lu'an)" with the position of "(asawira)". It was also said that it is coordinated with the position of ﴿min asawira﴾, because it is estimated as "(yuhallawna)" [they are adorned] with ornaments ﴿min asawira﴾.

The rest of the Seven, and also al-Hasan, Talha, Ibn Thabit and al-A'mash, read it differently. The people of Makkah read "(wa-lu'lu'un)" in the genitive, coordinated with "(asawira)" or with "(dhahabin)", because a bracelet is made of gold and pearls, some of which is joined to others.

Al-Jahdari said: the alif is present after the waw in the Imam (the standard codex). Al-Asma'i said: there is no alif in it. Yahya reported from Abu Bakr the hamzing of the last and the substitution of the first, while al-Mu'alla ibn Mansur reported from him the opposite of that.

Al-Fayyad read "wa-luwliyyan": he changed the two hamzas into waws, so the second became a waw preceded by a damma, and it was treated as what was done in "adall", where the waw was changed into a ya' with a kasra before it. Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-laylIyyan": he substituted the two hamzas with two waws, then changed them into two ya's, making the first assimilate to the second. Talha read "wa-lulin" in the genitive, coordinated with what the hamzated word was coordinated with.

As for ﴿al-tayyibi min al-qawl﴾ (the good of speech): if the guidance is in this world, it is the statement "There is no god but Allah," and good utterances of remembrance and others; and "the path" is the way of Islam. If it is information about what happens to them in the Hereafter, it is their saying: "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us," and what resembles that of the dialogue of the people of Paradise; and "the path" is the way to Paradise. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is "There is no god but Allah" and "Praise be to Allah." Ibn Zayd added: "And Allah is greatest." From al-Suddi: the Qur'an.

Al-Mawardi reported: enjoining good and forbidding evil. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us." The apparent meaning is that "al-Hamid" (the Praiseworthy) is an attribute of Allah, Exalted is He. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that by "al-Hamid" he means the path itself, and that it was attributed to it in the manner of its attribution in His saying: "the abode of the Hereafter" (dar al-akhirah).

(p-٣٦٢) Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar (others) from the way of God and from the Sacred Mosque, which We have made equal for the people, the resident in it and the visitor, and whoever intends in it deviation through wrongdoing, We shall make him taste a painful punishment. [Al-Hajj: 25] And when We settled Abraham at the site of the House, (saying): "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate it, those who stand (in prayer), and those who bow and prostrate." [Al-Hajj: 26] "And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, coming from every deep mountain pass, [Al-Hajj: 27] that they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of God on known days over the livestock He has provided for them. So eat from them and feed the miserable poor." [Al-Hajj: 28] "Then let them complete their untidiness, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the ancient House." [Al-Hajj: 29] "That (is so). And whoever honours the sacred rites of God, it is better for him with his Lord. And the livestock have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you. So avoid the abomination of idols and avoid the word of falsehood, [Al-Hajj: 30] being upright for God, not associating anything with Him. And whoever associates others with God, it is as if he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away, or the wind threw him into a distant place." [Al-Hajj: 31]

The imperfect verb (al-mudari') may be one in which no specific time of present or future is intended, so it then indicates continuity. Of this is ﴿and they bar (others) from the way of God﴾, like His saying ﴿those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of God﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 28]. It has also been said: it is an imperfect verb used with the meaning of the past, coordinated with (kafaru, "they disbelieved"). And it has been said: it is on the basis of an implied subject, i.e., "and they (are) barring." The predicate of inna (indeed) is omitted; Ibn 'Atiyya estimated it after (wal-bad, "and the visitor"): "they will lose or perish." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it after his saying (al-haram, "the Sacred"): "We shall make them taste ﴿a painful punishment﴾." It is not valid to estimate it after that, because alladhi (the relative pronoun "which") is an adjective of (al-Masjid al-Haram, "the Sacred Mosque"), so the place of the estimate is after (wal-bad). But al-Zamakhshari's estimate is better than Ibn 'Atiyya's, because the conditional sentence that follows indicates it verbally. Ibn 'Atiyya took it into account semantically, because whoever is made to taste the punishment loses and perishes.

It has been said: the wa (and) in (wa-yasuddun, "and they bar") is superfluous, and the predicate of inna is (yasuddun, "they bar"), its estimate being: "Indeed those who disbelieve bar..." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This corrupts the intended meaning." End.

The Basrans do not permit the superfluity of the wa; it is merely a Kufan view, which is disfavoured.

This verse was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was barred from the Sacred Mosque. That is because no collective barring of them is known prior to that, unless what is meant is their barring of individuals from among the people, which occurred at the beginning of the mission. The apparent meaning is the Mosque itself, and whoever is barred from reaching it has been barred from it. It has also been said: the entire Sanctuary (al-haram) is meant, because they barred him and his people from it, peace be upon him, so they stopped outside it. But He mentioned the principal objective of the Sanctuary, which is the important goal.

The majority of readers recite (sawa'un, "equal") with the nominative (raf'), so that the sentence consisting of subject and predicate is in the position of the second object. The better view is that al-'Akif and al-Badi are the subject, and (sawa'an, "equal"), (p-٣٦٣) the predicate, although the reverse has also been permitted. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The meaning of ﴿which We have made for the people﴾ is a qibla (direction of prayer) or a place of worship." End. He would not need this estimate unless he meant an explanation of the meaning rather than the grammatical analysis (i'rab), and then it is acceptable, because the sentence is in the position of the second object, so there is no need for this estimate.

Hafs and al-A'mash recite (sawa'an) with the accusative (nasb), and al-'Akif is raised by it, because it is a verbal noun (masdar) with the meaning of the active participle (musta-w, "one who is equal"). Among their speech: "I passed by a man, equal (sawa'an) to him and to nothing." If ja'ala (made) is transitive to two objects, then sawa'an is the second; if it is transitive to one, then sawa'an is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun (ha', "it").

A group, including al-A'mash in the transmission of al-Qat'i, recited (sawa'an) with the accusative and ﴿al-'akif fihi﴾ with the genitive (jarr). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "in coordination with 'the people' (al-nas)." End. He apparently means that it is an explanatory apposition ('atf al-bayan), the first possibility being that it is a substitute of detail (badal tafsil).

(Al-Badi) has been read both with and without the final vowel, both in pausal and continuous recitation, and with its retention in continuous recitation and omission in pause. Al-'Akif is the one who resides in it; al-Badi is the one who arrives at it. They agreed on equality in the Sacred Mosque itself, but differed concerning Mecca. Umar, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and a group held that the matter is the same regarding the houses of Mecca, that the arrival has the right to lodge wherever he finds (a place), and the owner of the dwelling must shelter him whether he wishes or not. al-Thawri held this view, and so it was in the early period. Ibn Sabit said: "Their houses had no doors until theft increased, and a man made a door, so Umar objected to him and said: 'Will you close a door in the face of the pilgrim to the House of God?' He said: 'I only intended to protect their goods from theft,' and he left it. Then the people made doors." This disagreement depends on the disagreement concerning the conquest of Mecca: was it by force (‘anwatan) or by treaty (sulhan)? This is a question discussed in jurisprudence (fiqh).

Al-ilhad is inclination away from the right course. The object of (yurid, "intends") — Abu 'Ubayda said it is (bi-ilhadin, "in deviation"), and the preposition (ba') is superfluous in the object. Al-A'sha said:

"Our spears have been guaranteed for the provision of our dependants."

That is, (rizq, "provision"). Likewise is the recitation of al-Hasan, in the accusative: ﴿and whoever intends (ilhadahu, "its deviation")﴾ bi-zulmin, i.e., (ilhadan fihi, "deviation in it"), so he has extended the usage. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is permissible for the estimate to be ﴿and whoever intends in it﴾ — the people — (bi-ilhadin). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿bi-ilhadin bi-zulmin﴾ are two synonymous circumstantial clauses (hal), and the object of (yurid) is omitted so as to encompass every possible object, as if He said: "and whoever intends in it, intending either one who swerves from the aim or one who is a wrongdoer, ﴿We shall make him taste a painful punishment﴾." It has been said: deviation in the Sanctuary is preventing people from its cultivation. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: hoarding (al-ihtikar). From 'Ata': a man's saying in a sale, "No, by God," and "Yes, by God." End.

The better view is that (yurid) should be taken as implying (yatalabbas, "to be involved in"), so that it takes the preposition (ba'). He made the consequence, which is (nudhiqhu, "We make him taste"), conditional upon the intention. Therefore, if one intends an evil deed and does not do it, he will not be held to account for it, except in Mecca. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and a group. Ibn Abbas said: deviation here is polytheism. He also said: it is making the forbidden lawful. Mujahid said: it is evil action in it. Ibn Umar said: "No, by God," and "Yes, by God," are among deviation. Habib ibn Abi Thabit said: hoarding in Mecca is deviation through wrongdoing. The better course is to take these sayings as examples rather than as exhaustive limitations, since the speech indicates generality. A group recited ﴿and whoever intends﴾ with a fatha on the ya' from (al-wurud, "arrival"), which al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' transmitted; its meaning is: whoever arrives with (ilhad) in wrongdoing.

When He, exalted, mentioned the state of the disbelievers and their barring from the Sacred Mosque, and threatened whoever intends in it deviation, He mentioned the state of their father Abraham, reproaching them for their taking a path other than his, through their disbelief in taking idols, and His bestowing favour on them by bringing the world (in its provision) to them. ﴿And when We settled﴾: i.e., remember when We settled (bawwa'na) — that is, We placed ﴿for Abraham the site of the House﴾ as a (mabā'a), i.e., a place of return to which he returns for its maintenance and worship. It has been said: the lam is superfluous, i.e., We settled Abraham at the site of the House, that is, We made it a place for him to return to, like His saying: ﴿We shall surely settle them in the lofty chambers of Paradise﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 58]. The poet said:

"How many a righteous companion of mine I settled, with my own hands, in a tomb."

It has been said: the object of (bawwa'na) is omitted, its estimate being "We settled the people," and the lam in (li-Ibrahim) is the lam of cause, i.e., for the sake of Abraham, as an honour to him and at his hands. The apparent view is that His saying ﴿that you do not associate anything with Me﴾ is addressed to Abraham, and likewise what follows of commands. It has been said: it is addressed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). (Anna, "that") is a lightened form of the heavy (anna), as Ibn 'Atiyya said. The original is that it should be followed by a verb of certainty or probability, as is its case when it is heavy, or by a particle of explanation. So said al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya, (p-٣٦٤) and its condition is that it be preceded by a sentence with the meaning of speech; but (bawwa'na, "We settled") does not have the meaning of speech. The better view in my opinion is that (an, "that") is the one that governs the imperfect verb, since it is followed by a conjugated verb, past, imperfect or imperative, and the prohibition is like the command.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how can the prohibition of associating and the command to purify the House be an explanation of the settling? I say: the settling was intended for the sake of worship, so it is as if it were said: "We made Abraham worship, and We said to him: ﴿Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House﴾ from idols, images and filth, so that they are not cast around it."

Ikrima and Abu Nahik recited (an yushrika, "that he associate") with the ya', in the sense that (an yaqula, "that he say") carries the meaning of the speech that was said to him. Abu Hatim said: in this recitation the kaf must be in the accusative, with the meaning of (an, "that"), ﴿do not associate﴾.

Al-qa'imun (those who stand) are those who pray; He mentioned the greatest of its pillars, namely standing, bowing and prostrating.

The majority recite ﴿wa-adhdhin﴾ (and proclaim) with the doubled dhal, meaning "call out." It is narrated that he climbed Abu Qubays and said: "O people, perform the pilgrimage to the House of your Lord." The statement of those who said it is addressed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) has preceded, and al-Hasan said: he was commanded to do this in the Farewell Pilgrimage. Al-Hasan, Ibn Muhaysin recited (wa-adhana, "and he proclaimed") with a long vowel and a light dhal. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this was distorted for Ibn Jinni, for he transmitted from them (wa-adhina), as a past verb, and parsed it on that basis as coordinated with (bawwa'na). End.

It is not a distortion; rather Abu 'Abd Allah al-Husayn ibn Khalawayh indeed transmitted it among the irregular readings (shawadhdh al-qira'at) in his compilation, and the author of al-Lawami', Abu al-Fadl al-Razi, transmitted it from al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin.
