The author of al-Lawami' said: it is coordinated with ﴿and when We settled﴾, so that there is a transposition in the speech, and (ya'tuka, "they will come to you") becomes jussive as an answer to the command which is ﴿and purify﴾. End. Ibn Abi Ishaq recited (bil-hijji, "for the pilgrimage") with a kasra on the ha' wherever it occurs, whereas the majority have a fatha. The majority recite (rijalan, "on foot") and Ibn Abi Ishaq with a damma on the ra' and light pronunciation; it is narrated likewise from Ikrima, al-Hasan and Abu Mijlaz, and it is a collective noun (ism jam'), like (zu'ar). It is narrated from them, and from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ja'far ibn Muhammad, with a damma on the ra' and a doubled jim. From Ikrima also: rujala on the pattern of nu'ama, with the feminine ending of the shortened alif; and likewise with a doubled jim from Ibn Abbas, Ata' and Ibn Hudayr. Rijal is the plural of rajil, like tajir and tujjar (merchant, merchants).

The majority recite (ya'tina, "they will come", feminine plural), so the apparent reference of the pronoun is to (kulli dhamirin, "every lean camel"), since the usual case is that vast lands cannot be reached on foot to Mecca, though the pronoun may also include (rijalan) and (kulli dhamirin) in the sense of groups and companies. ‘Abd Allah and his companions, al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited (ya'tuna, "they will come", masculine plural), giving precedence to the masculine rational plural at the beginning with (rijal, "men"), in preference of those who walk to the pilgrimage. Ibn Abbas said: "I do not regret anything that escaped me more than not having performed the pilgrimage on foot." The argument from His saying ﴿they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel﴾ that the obligation of pilgrimage falls on one who must travel by sea with no other route, because it is not mentioned in this verse, is weak, because Mecca is not on the sea; one reaches it by one of two means, walking or riding, and He mentioned what one reaches it by. Ibn Mas'ud recited (fajjin mu'ayyiq, "a deep pass"). Ibn Abbas and others said: among the benefits is commerce. Al-Baqir said: the reward. Mujahid and 'Ata' both said (both of these), and Ibn al-'Arabi preferred it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He made (manafi', "benefits") indefinite because He intended benefits specific to this worship, religious and worldly, which are not found in other acts of worship. It is narrated from Abu Hanifa that he used to rank the acts of worship before he performed the pilgrimage; when he performed it, he preferred the pilgrimage over all the acts of worship because of those distinctive features he witnessed. He referred to the slaughter and sacrifice by mentioning the name of God, because the people of Islam do not cease from mentioning His name when they slaughter or sacrifice. In this is an indication that the principal aim in what is done to draw near to God is that His name be mentioned. He has embellished the speech with a clear embellishment, in that He combined His saying ﴿that they may mention the name of God over it﴾ with His saying ﴿over what He has provided for them﴾. Had it been said "that they may slaughter" ﴿on known days over the livestock﴾, you would not see any of that beauty and splendour. End.

(p. 365) Those who held that the purpose of mentioning God's name is over the slaughter and sacrifice cited as evidence that slaughter may not take place at night and is not permitted then, based on His saying ﴿on known days﴾. This is the view of Malik and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y).

It was also said: the remembrance here means praising Him and extolling Him in gratitude for His provision. This is supported by the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Indeed they are days of eating, drinking, and remembrance of God's name."

The "known days" are the ten days, according to Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibrahim, Qatada and Abu Hanifa. The "counted days" are the three days of tashriq (the days after Eid al-Adha).

A group including Malik and his companions said: the "known days" are the Day of Sacrifice and the two days after it, and the "counted days" are the three days of tashriq. The Day of Sacrifice is thus known but not counted, the two days after it are both known and counted, and the fourth is counted but not known.

According to Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Anas, Abu Hurayra, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri, the days of sacrifice are the Day of Sacrifice and the two days after it. According to al-Hasan, Ata' and al-Shafi'i, they are the Day of Sacrifice and three days after it. According to al-Nakha'i, they are two days, and according to Ibn Sirin, one day, the Day of Sacrifice. From Abu Salama and Sulayman ibn Yasar: the sacrifice extends until the new moon of Muharram.

Ibn Atiyya said: It appears that the "known" and "counted" days mean all of those virtuous days together. The matter of slaughter and the matter of haste are not tied to a counted or known day. The purpose of His saying "known" and "counted" is to encourage attention to these days and to seize their virtue, meaning that they are not like other days. It is as if He said: they are distinguished, so seize them. End of quote.

The beast (bahima) is undetermined in every four-footed creature on land and sea, so it was specified by "livestock" (al-an'am), namely camels, cattle, sheep and goats. The disagreement over the meaning of ﴿the beast of livestock﴾ [al-Hajj: 34] has already been discussed at the beginning of al-Ma'ida. The apparent ruling is that eating from it and feeding others from it are obligatory. It was also said that both are recommended. It was also said that eating is recommended while feeding is obligatory.

The "distressed" (al-ba'is) is one who has been struck by hardship, meaning severe need.

The "tafath" (unkempt state) is what the muhrim does upon exiting ihram: trimming or shaving hair and removing its disarray and the like, including the five acts of fitra according to the hadith. Included in this is fulfilling all the rites of hajj, since one does not complete the tafath except after that. Ibn Umar said: the tafath is what is upon them of hajj. Also from him: all the rites. The "vows" here are what they vow of acts of righteousness during their pilgrimage. It was also said that the intended meaning is discharging what has become obligatory upon them, whether they vowed or did not vow.

Shu'ba, from Asim, read ﴿wal-yuwaffu﴾ with a shadda, while the majority read it without shadda. ﴿wal-yattawwafu﴾ refers to the tawaf al-ifada, which is the tawaf of visitation and one of the pillars of hajj, and with it the exit from ihram is completed. It was also said that it is the tawaf al-sadr, which is the tawaf al-wada' (farewell circumambulation). Al-Tabari said: there is no disagreement among the commentators that it is the tawaf al-ifada. Ibn Atiyya said: according to the order, it may also be the tawaf al-wada'. End of quote.

The "ancient" (al-atiq) means the old, according to al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. Or it means the one freed from tyrants, according to Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abi Najih and Qatada: how many tyrants marched against it and God destroyed them. Tubba' intended to demolish it, but he was struck with paralysis, so the righteous advised him to refrain from it and said: it has a Lord who protects it. So he left it, clothed it, and he was the first to clothe it. Abraha also targeted it and was struck by what struck him. As for al-Hajjaj, he did not intend to gain control over the House, but Ibn al-Zubayr took refuge in it, so he devised a way to remove him, and then rebuilt it. Or it means the one freed, whose site was never owned, according to Mujahid. Or it means the one freed from the flood, also according to Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr. Or it means the excellent, from their saying "ataq of horses" and "ataq of birds." Or it means the one in which the necks of sinners are freed from punishment. Ibn Atiyya said: this is rejected by morphology (tasrif, the science of word forms). End of quote. Morphology does not reject it, because he explained it as a matter of meaning. As for grammatical analysis (i'rab), "al-atiq" is a form (fa'il) in the sense of a form (muf'il), i.e., one who frees the necks of sinners. The freeing is attributed to it figuratively, since through visiting it and circumambulating it freeing occurs, and from its being one who frees it may be said: in it the necks of sinners are freed.

(Dhalika) is the predicate of an omitted subject. Ibn Atiyya estimated it as "your duty is that," or "the obligatory is that." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "the matter or the affair is that." He said: just as a writer begins a section of his book on some meaning, then when he wishes to move to another meaning he says: "This is so, and it was such."

It was also said: it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning "that" is the matter you have mentioned. It was also said it is in the accusative position, estimated as "comply with that."

A parallel to this eloquent demonstrative is the line of Zuhayr, who had earlier composed verses describing Harim:

"This! Not like one who falters in his speech
amid the generous when a speaker speaks."

He had described him before this with generosity and courage, then in this line he described him with eloquence. It is as if he said: this is his character, not like one who falters in his speech.

The sacred things (al-hurumat) are whatever is not lawful to violate. All the obligations, including the rites of hajj and others, are its sacred things. The apparent meaning is general over all obligations, but it may be restricted to what relates to hajj. Al-Kalbi said this and said: what He commanded of the rites. From Ibn Abbas: they are all the prohibitions of hajj: wrongful speech, disputation, intercourse and hunting. From Ibn Zayd: they are five: the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram), the Sacred Mosque, the Sacred House, the Sacred Month, and the forbidden thing until it becomes lawful.

The pronoun in ﴿fa-huwa﴾ refers to the verbal noun implied by His saying ﴿and whoever honours﴾, meaning: so the honouring ﴿is better for him with his Lord﴾, meaning nearness to Him and an increase in obedience to Him, for which He will reward him. The apparent meaning is that "khayr" here is not a comparative superlative.

And ﴿Lawful for you is the beast of livestock﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 1] is a refutation of what they used to forbid by their own opinion, such as the bahira and the sa'iba. By His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ He means what He stated in His Book as forbidden, and the meaning is the verse recited to you about its prohibition.

When He urged the honouring of God's sacred things and mentioned that honouring them is better for the one who honours them before God, He followed it with the command to avoid idols and false speech, because the oneness of God, the negation of partners from Him, and truthful speech are the greatest sacred things. These two were joined in one pairing because shirk falls under the category of falsehood, since the polytheist claims that the idol deserves worship. It is as if He said: ﴿so avoid﴾ worshipping ﴿the idols﴾, which are the head of falsehood, ﴿and avoid the word of falsehood﴾ entirely.

The "min" in ﴿min al-awthan﴾ is for specifying the genus (bayan al-jins), and according to them it is to be estimated as a relative clause, meaning the filth which is the idols. Whoever denies that "min" specifies the genus takes it to indicate the starting point (ibtida' al-ghaya). It is as if He forbade the filth in general and then specified for them its origin, from which it reaches them, since worship of idols encompasses every corruption and filth. According to the first view, the prohibition of the rest of the filths would be from another place than this.

Ibn Atiyya said: whoever says that "min" is partitive has inverted the meaning of the verse and corrupted it. End of quote.

Partitiveness is possible here, in that by "filth" one means the worship of idols. This has been related from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jurayj. It is as if He said: avoid from the idols the filth, which is worship, because what is forbidden of idols is only their worship. Do you not see that it is conceivable to use an idol in building or other things that the Law has not forbidden? So for the idol there are aspects, among them its worship, which is what is commanded to be avoided, and its worship is one of its aspects.

Since the word of falsehood equals disbelief, it was not joined to the filth by conjunction. Rather, it was singled out by repeating the governing verb, out of concern for avoiding it. In a hadith: "The testimony of falsehood was equated with shirk."

When He commanded avoiding the worship of idols and the word of falsehood, He struck an example for the polytheist, saying ﴿and whoever associates partners with God﴾ and so on. Al-Zamakhshari said: this comparison may be of the composite or the divided type. If it is a composite comparison, it is as if He said: whoever associates with God has destroyed himself with a destruction beyond which there is none, by depicting his state in the form of one who ﴿falls from the sky﴾ and is snatched away by ﴿the birds﴾, so that he is scattered into pieces in their crops, and ﴿the wind﴾ sweeps him away until it throws him into some distant abyss. If it is a divided comparison, then faith in its elevation is likened to the sky, the one who abandons faith and associates partners with God is likened to the one who falls from the sky, the desires that contend for his nest are likened to the birds that snatch, and the devil who casts him into the valley of misguidance is likened to the wind that carries away what it has swept into some destructive abyss. End of quote.

Nafi' read ﴿fa-takhtafuhu﴾ with a fatha on the kha' and a shadda on the ta', while the rest of the seven read it with a sukun on the kha' and a light ta'. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and al-A'mash read it with a kasra on the ta', kha', and a shadda on the ta'. From al-Hasan it is the same, except that he put a fatha on the ta' with a shadda. Al-A'mash also read ﴿takhuttuhu﴾ without a fa', with a sukun on the kha' and a light fatha on the ta'. Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read ﴿al-rayyah﴾ (the winds).

(p. 367)

(p-٣٦٢) Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar (others) from the way of God and from the Sacred Mosque, which We have made equal for the people, the resident in it and the visitor, and whoever intends in it deviation through wrongdoing, We shall make him taste a painful punishment. [Al-Hajj: 25] And when We settled Abraham at the site of the House, (saying): "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate it, those who stand (in prayer), and those who bow and prostrate." [Al-Hajj: 26] "And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, coming from every deep mountain pass, [Al-Hajj: 27] that they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of God on known days over the livestock He has provided for them. So eat from them and feed the miserable poor." [Al-Hajj: 28] "Then let them complete their untidiness, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the ancient House." [Al-Hajj: 29] "That (is so). And whoever honours the sacred rites of God, it is better for him with his Lord. And the livestock have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you. So avoid the abomination of idols and avoid the word of falsehood, [Al-Hajj: 30] being upright for God, not associating anything with Him. And whoever associates others with God, it is as if he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away, or the wind threw him into a distant place." [Al-Hajj: 31]

The imperfect verb (al-mudari') may be one in which no specific time of present or future is intended, so it then indicates continuity. Of this is ﴿and they bar (others) from the way of God﴾, like His saying ﴿those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of God﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 28]. It has also been said: it is an imperfect verb used with the meaning of the past, coordinated with (kafaru, "they disbelieved"). And it has been said: it is on the basis of an implied subject, i.e., "and they (are) barring." The predicate of inna (indeed) is omitted; Ibn 'Atiyya estimated it after (wal-bad, "and the visitor"): "they will lose or perish." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it after his saying (al-haram, "the Sacred"): "We shall make them taste ﴿a painful punishment﴾." It is not valid to estimate it after that, because alladhi (the relative pronoun "which") is an adjective of (al-Masjid al-Haram, "the Sacred Mosque"), so the place of the estimate is after (wal-bad). But al-Zamakhshari's estimate is better than Ibn 'Atiyya's, because the conditional sentence that follows indicates it verbally. Ibn 'Atiyya took it into account semantically, because whoever is made to taste the punishment loses and perishes.

It has been said: the wa (and) in (wa-yasuddun, "and they bar") is superfluous, and the predicate of inna is (yasuddun, "they bar"), its estimate being: "Indeed those who disbelieve bar..." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This corrupts the intended meaning." End.

The Basrans do not permit the superfluity of the wa; it is merely a Kufan view, which is disfavoured.

This verse was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was barred from the Sacred Mosque. That is because no collective barring of them is known prior to that, unless what is meant is their barring of individuals from among the people, which occurred at the beginning of the mission. The apparent meaning is the Mosque itself, and whoever is barred from reaching it has been barred from it. It has also been said: the entire Sanctuary (al-haram) is meant, because they barred him and his people from it, peace be upon him, so they stopped outside it. But He mentioned the principal objective of the Sanctuary, which is the important goal.

The majority of readers recite (sawa'un, "equal") with the nominative (raf'), so that the sentence consisting of subject and predicate is in the position of the second object. The better view is that al-'Akif and al-Badi are the subject, and (sawa'an, "equal"), (p-٣٦٣) the predicate, although the reverse has also been permitted. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The meaning of ﴿which We have made for the people﴾ is a qibla (direction of prayer) or a place of worship." End. He would not need this estimate unless he meant an explanation of the meaning rather than the grammatical analysis (i'rab), and then it is acceptable, because the sentence is in the position of the second object, so there is no need for this estimate.

Hafs and al-A'mash recite (sawa'an) with the accusative (nasb), and al-'Akif is raised by it, because it is a verbal noun (masdar) with the meaning of the active participle (musta-w, "one who is equal"). Among their speech: "I passed by a man, equal (sawa'an) to him and to nothing." If ja'ala (made) is transitive to two objects, then sawa'an is the second; if it is transitive to one, then sawa'an is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun (ha', "it").

A group, including al-A'mash in the transmission of al-Qat'i, recited (sawa'an) with the accusative and ﴿al-'akif fihi﴾ with the genitive (jarr). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "in coordination with 'the people' (al-nas)." End. He apparently means that it is an explanatory apposition ('atf al-bayan), the first possibility being that it is a substitute of detail (badal tafsil).

(Al-Badi) has been read both with and without the final vowel, both in pausal and continuous recitation, and with its retention in continuous recitation and omission in pause. Al-'Akif is the one who resides in it; al-Badi is the one who arrives at it. They agreed on equality in the Sacred Mosque itself, but differed concerning Mecca. Umar, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and a group held that the matter is the same regarding the houses of Mecca, that the arrival has the right to lodge wherever he finds (a place), and the owner of the dwelling must shelter him whether he wishes or not. al-Thawri held this view, and so it was in the early period. Ibn Sabit said: "Their houses had no doors until theft increased, and a man made a door, so Umar objected to him and said: 'Will you close a door in the face of the pilgrim to the House of God?' He said: 'I only intended to protect their goods from theft,' and he left it. Then the people made doors." This disagreement depends on the disagreement concerning the conquest of Mecca: was it by force (‘anwatan) or by treaty (sulhan)? This is a question discussed in jurisprudence (fiqh).

Al-ilhad is inclination away from the right course. The object of (yurid, "intends") — Abu 'Ubayda said it is (bi-ilhadin, "in deviation"), and the preposition (ba') is superfluous in the object. Al-A'sha said:

"Our spears have been guaranteed for the provision of our dependants."

That is, (rizq, "provision"). Likewise is the recitation of al-Hasan, in the accusative: ﴿and whoever intends (ilhadahu, "its deviation")﴾ bi-zulmin, i.e., (ilhadan fihi, "deviation in it"), so he has extended the usage. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is permissible for the estimate to be ﴿and whoever intends in it﴾ — the people — (bi-ilhadin). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿bi-ilhadin bi-zulmin﴾ are two synonymous circumstantial clauses (hal), and the object of (yurid) is omitted so as to encompass every possible object, as if He said: "and whoever intends in it, intending either one who swerves from the aim or one who is a wrongdoer, ﴿We shall make him taste a painful punishment﴾." It has been said: deviation in the Sanctuary is preventing people from its cultivation. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: hoarding (al-ihtikar). From 'Ata': a man's saying in a sale, "No, by God," and "Yes, by God." End.

The better view is that (yurid) should be taken as implying (yatalabbas, "to be involved in"), so that it takes the preposition (ba'). He made the consequence, which is (nudhiqhu, "We make him taste"), conditional upon the intention. Therefore, if one intends an evil deed and does not do it, he will not be held to account for it, except in Mecca. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and a group. Ibn Abbas said: deviation here is polytheism. He also said: it is making the forbidden lawful. Mujahid said: it is evil action in it. Ibn Umar said: "No, by God," and "Yes, by God," are among deviation. Habib ibn Abi Thabit said: hoarding in Mecca is deviation through wrongdoing. The better course is to take these sayings as examples rather than as exhaustive limitations, since the speech indicates generality. A group recited ﴿and whoever intends﴾ with a fatha on the ya' from (al-wurud, "arrival"), which al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' transmitted; its meaning is: whoever arrives with (ilhad) in wrongdoing.

When He, exalted, mentioned the state of the disbelievers and their barring from the Sacred Mosque, and threatened whoever intends in it deviation, He mentioned the state of their father Abraham, reproaching them for their taking a path other than his, through their disbelief in taking idols, and His bestowing favour on them by bringing the world (in its provision) to them. ﴿And when We settled﴾: i.e., remember when We settled (bawwa'na) — that is, We placed ﴿for Abraham the site of the House﴾ as a (mabā'a), i.e., a place of return to which he returns for its maintenance and worship. It has been said: the lam is superfluous, i.e., We settled Abraham at the site of the House, that is, We made it a place for him to return to, like His saying: ﴿We shall surely settle them in the lofty chambers of Paradise﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 58]. The poet said:

"How many a righteous companion of mine I settled, with my own hands, in a tomb."

It has been said: the object of (bawwa'na) is omitted, its estimate being "We settled the people," and the lam in (li-Ibrahim) is the lam of cause, i.e., for the sake of Abraham, as an honour to him and at his hands. The apparent view is that His saying ﴿that you do not associate anything with Me﴾ is addressed to Abraham, and likewise what follows of commands. It has been said: it is addressed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). (Anna, "that") is a lightened form of the heavy (anna), as Ibn 'Atiyya said. The original is that it should be followed by a verb of certainty or probability, as is its case when it is heavy, or by a particle of explanation. So said al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya, (p-٣٦٤) and its condition is that it be preceded by a sentence with the meaning of speech; but (bawwa'na, "We settled") does not have the meaning of speech. The better view in my opinion is that (an, "that") is the one that governs the imperfect verb, since it is followed by a conjugated verb, past, imperfect or imperative, and the prohibition is like the command.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how can the prohibition of associating and the command to purify the House be an explanation of the settling? I say: the settling was intended for the sake of worship, so it is as if it were said: "We made Abraham worship, and We said to him: ﴿Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House﴾ from idols, images and filth, so that they are not cast around it."

Ikrima and Abu Nahik recited (an yushrika, "that he associate") with the ya', in the sense that (an yaqula, "that he say") carries the meaning of the speech that was said to him. Abu Hatim said: in this recitation the kaf must be in the accusative, with the meaning of (an, "that"), ﴿do not associate﴾.

Al-qa'imun (those who stand) are those who pray; He mentioned the greatest of its pillars, namely standing, bowing and prostrating.

The majority recite ﴿wa-adhdhin﴾ (and proclaim) with the doubled dhal, meaning "call out." It is narrated that he climbed Abu Qubays and said: "O people, perform the pilgrimage to the House of your Lord." The statement of those who said it is addressed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) has preceded, and al-Hasan said: he was commanded to do this in the Farewell Pilgrimage. Al-Hasan, Ibn Muhaysin recited (wa-adhana, "and he proclaimed") with a long vowel and a light dhal. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this was distorted for Ibn Jinni, for he transmitted from them (wa-adhina), as a past verb, and parsed it on that basis as coordinated with (bawwa'na). End.

It is not a distortion; rather Abu 'Abd Allah al-Husayn ibn Khalawayh indeed transmitted it among the irregular readings (shawadhdh al-qira'at) in his compilation, and the author of al-Lawami', Abu al-Fadl al-Razi, transmitted it from al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin. The author of al-Lawami' said: it is coordinated with ﴿and when We settled﴾, so that there is a transposition in the speech, and (ya'tuka, "they will come to you") becomes jussive as an answer to the command which is ﴿and purify﴾. End. Ibn Abi Ishaq recited (bil-hijji, "for the pilgrimage") with a kasra on the ha' wherever it occurs, whereas the majority have a fatha. The majority recite (rijalan, "on foot") and Ibn Abi Ishaq with a damma on the ra' and light pronunciation; it is narrated likewise from Ikrima, al-Hasan and Abu Mijlaz, and it is a collective noun (ism jam'), like (zu'ar). It is narrated from them, and from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ja'far ibn Muhammad, with a damma on the ra' and a doubled jim. From Ikrima also: rujala on the pattern of nu'ama, with the feminine ending of the shortened alif; and likewise with a doubled jim from Ibn Abbas, Ata' and Ibn Hudayr. Rijal is the plural of rajil, like tajir and tujjar (merchant, merchants).

The majority recite (ya'tina, "they will come", feminine plural), so the apparent reference of the pronoun is to (kulli dhamirin, "every lean camel"), since the usual case is that vast lands cannot be reached on foot to Mecca, though the pronoun may also include (rijalan) and (kulli dhamirin) in the sense of groups and companies. ‘Abd Allah and his companions, al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited (ya'tuna, "they will come", masculine plural), giving precedence to the masculine rational plural at the beginning with (rijal, "men"), in preference of those who walk to the pilgrimage. Ibn Abbas said: "I do not regret anything that escaped me more than not having performed the pilgrimage on foot." The argument from His saying ﴿they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel﴾ that the obligation of pilgrimage falls on one who must travel by sea with no other route, because it is not mentioned in this verse, is weak, because Mecca is not on the sea; one reaches it by one of two means, walking or riding, and He mentioned what one reaches it by. Ibn Mas'ud recited (fajjin mu'ayyiq, "a deep pass"). Ibn Abbas and others said: among the benefits is commerce. Al-Baqir said: the reward. Mujahid and 'Ata' both said (both of these), and Ibn al-'Arabi preferred it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He made (manafi', "benefits") indefinite because He intended benefits specific to this worship, religious and worldly, which are not found in other acts of worship. It is narrated from Abu Hanifa that he used to rank the acts of worship before he performed the pilgrimage; when he performed it, he preferred the pilgrimage over all the acts of worship because of those distinctive features he witnessed. He referred to the slaughter and sacrifice by mentioning the name of God, because the people of Islam do not cease from mentioning His name when they slaughter or sacrifice. In this is an indication that the principal aim in what is done to draw near to God is that His name be mentioned. He has embellished the speech with a clear embellishment, in that He combined His saying ﴿that they may mention the name of God over it﴾ with His saying ﴿over what He has provided for them﴾. Had it been said "that they may slaughter" ﴿on known days over the livestock﴾, you would not see any of that beauty and splendour. End.

(p. 365) Those who held that the purpose of mentioning God's name is over the slaughter and sacrifice cited as evidence that slaughter may not take place at night and is not permitted then, based on His saying ﴿on known days﴾. This is the view of Malik and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y).

It was also said: the remembrance here means praising Him and extolling Him in gratitude for His provision. This is supported by the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Indeed they are days of eating, drinking, and remembrance of God's name."

The "known days" are the ten days, according to Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibrahim, Qatada and Abu Hanifa. The "counted days" are the three days of tashriq (the days after Eid al-Adha).

A group including Malik and his companions said: the "known days" are the Day of Sacrifice and the two days after it, and the "counted days" are the three days of tashriq. The Day of Sacrifice is thus known but not counted, the two days after it are both known and counted, and the fourth is counted but not known.

According to Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Anas, Abu Hurayra, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri, the days of sacrifice are the Day of Sacrifice and the two days after it. According to al-Hasan, Ata' and al-Shafi'i, they are the Day of Sacrifice and three days after it. According to al-Nakha'i, they are two days, and according to Ibn Sirin, one day, the Day of Sacrifice. From Abu Salama and Sulayman ibn Yasar: the sacrifice extends until the new moon of Muharram.

Ibn Atiyya said: It appears that the "known" and "counted" days mean all of those virtuous days together. The matter of slaughter and the matter of haste are not tied to a counted or known day. The purpose of His saying "known" and "counted" is to encourage attention to these days and to seize their virtue, meaning that they are not like other days. It is as if He said: they are distinguished, so seize them. End of quote.

The beast (bahima) is undetermined in every four-footed creature on land and sea, so it was specified by "livestock" (al-an'am), namely camels, cattle, sheep and goats. The disagreement over the meaning of ﴿the beast of livestock﴾ [al-Hajj: 34] has already been discussed at the beginning of al-Ma'ida. The apparent ruling is that eating from it and feeding others from it are obligatory. It was also said that both are recommended. It was also said that eating is recommended while feeding is obligatory.

The "distressed" (al-ba'is) is one who has been struck by hardship, meaning severe need.

The "tafath" (unkempt state) is what the muhrim does upon exiting ihram: trimming or shaving hair and removing its disarray and the like, including the five acts of fitra according to the hadith. Included in this is fulfilling all the rites of hajj, since one does not complete the tafath except after that. Ibn Umar said: the tafath is what is upon them of hajj. Also from him: all the rites. The "vows" here are what they vow of acts of righteousness during their pilgrimage. It was also said that the intended meaning is discharging what has become obligatory upon them, whether they vowed or did not vow.

Shu'ba, from Asim, read ﴿wal-yuwaffu﴾ with a shadda, while the majority read it without shadda. ﴿wal-yattawwafu﴾ refers to the tawaf al-ifada, which is the tawaf of visitation and one of the pillars of hajj, and with it the exit from ihram is completed. It was also said that it is the tawaf al-sadr, which is the tawaf al-wada' (farewell circumambulation). Al-Tabari said: there is no disagreement among the commentators that it is the tawaf al-ifada. Ibn Atiyya said: according to the order, it may also be the tawaf al-wada'. End of quote.

The "ancient" (al-atiq) means the old, according to al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. Or it means the one freed from tyrants, according to Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abi Najih and Qatada: how many tyrants marched against it and God destroyed them. Tubba' intended to demolish it, but he was struck with paralysis, so the righteous advised him to refrain from it and said: it has a Lord who protects it. So he left it, clothed it, and he was the first to clothe it. Abraha also targeted it and was struck by what struck him. As for al-Hajjaj, he did not intend to gain control over the House, but Ibn al-Zubayr took refuge in it, so he devised a way to remove him, and then rebuilt it. Or it means the one freed, whose site was never owned, according to Mujahid. Or it means the one freed from the flood, also according to Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr. Or it means the excellent, from their saying "ataq of horses" and "ataq of birds." Or it means the one in which the necks of sinners are freed from punishment. Ibn Atiyya said: this is rejected by morphology (tasrif, the science of word forms). End of quote. Morphology does not reject it, because he explained it as a matter of meaning. As for grammatical analysis (i'rab), "al-atiq" is a form (fa'il) in the sense of a form (muf'il), i.e., one who frees the necks of sinners. The freeing is attributed to it figuratively, since through visiting it and circumambulating it freeing occurs, and from its being one who frees it may be said: in it the necks of sinners are freed.

(Dhalika) is the predicate of an omitted subject. Ibn Atiyya estimated it as "your duty is that," or "the obligatory is that." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "the matter or the affair is that." He said: just as a writer begins a section of his book on some meaning, then when he wishes to move to another meaning he says: "This is so, and it was such."

It was also said: it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning "that" is the matter you have mentioned. It was also said it is in the accusative position, estimated as "comply with that."

A parallel to this eloquent demonstrative is the line of Zuhayr, who had earlier composed verses describing Harim:

"This! Not like one who falters in his speech
amid the generous when a speaker speaks."

He had described him before this with generosity and courage, then in this line he described him with eloquence. It is as if he said: this is his character, not like one who falters in his speech.

The sacred things (al-hurumat) are whatever is not lawful to violate. All the obligations, including the rites of hajj and others, are its sacred things. The apparent meaning is general over all obligations, but it may be restricted to what relates to hajj. Al-Kalbi said this and said: what He commanded of the rites. From Ibn Abbas: they are all the prohibitions of hajj: wrongful speech, disputation, intercourse and hunting. From Ibn Zayd: they are five: the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram), the Sacred Mosque, the Sacred House, the Sacred Month, and the forbidden thing until it becomes lawful.

The pronoun in ﴿fa-huwa﴾ refers to the verbal noun implied by His saying ﴿and whoever honours﴾, meaning: so the honouring ﴿is better for him with his Lord﴾, meaning nearness to Him and an increase in obedience to Him, for which He will reward him. The apparent meaning is that "khayr" here is not a comparative superlative.

And ﴿Lawful for you is the beast of livestock﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 1] is a refutation of what they used to forbid by their own opinion, such as the bahira and the sa'iba. By His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ He means what He stated in His Book as forbidden, and the meaning is the verse recited to you about its prohibition.

When He urged the honouring of God's sacred things and mentioned that honouring them is better for the one who honours them before God, He followed it with the command to avoid idols and false speech, because the oneness of God, the negation of partners from Him, and truthful speech are the greatest sacred things. These two were joined in one pairing because shirk falls under the category of falsehood, since the polytheist claims that the idol deserves worship. It is as if He said: ﴿so avoid﴾ worshipping ﴿the idols﴾, which are the head of falsehood, ﴿and avoid the word of falsehood﴾ entirely.

The "min" in ﴿min al-awthan﴾ is for specifying the genus (bayan al-jins), and according to them it is to be estimated as a relative clause, meaning the filth which is the idols. Whoever denies that "min" specifies the genus takes it to indicate the starting point (ibtida' al-ghaya). It is as if He forbade the filth in general and then specified for them its origin, from which it reaches them, since worship of idols encompasses every corruption and filth. According to the first view, the prohibition of the rest of the filths would be from another place than this.

Ibn Atiyya said: whoever says that "min" is partitive has inverted the meaning of the verse and corrupted it. End of quote.

Partitiveness is possible here, in that by "filth" one means the worship of idols. This has been related from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jurayj. It is as if He said: avoid from the idols the filth, which is worship, because what is forbidden of idols is only their worship. Do you not see that it is conceivable to use an idol in building or other things that the Law has not forbidden? So for the idol there are aspects, among them its worship, which is what is commanded to be avoided, and its worship is one of its aspects.

Since the word of falsehood equals disbelief, it was not joined to the filth by conjunction. Rather, it was singled out by repeating the governing verb, out of concern for avoiding it. In a hadith: "The testimony of falsehood was equated with shirk."

When He commanded avoiding the worship of idols and the word of falsehood, He struck an example for the polytheist, saying ﴿and whoever associates partners with God﴾ and so on. Al-Zamakhshari said: this comparison may be of the composite or the divided type. If it is a composite comparison, it is as if He said: whoever associates with God has destroyed himself with a destruction beyond which there is none, by depicting his state in the form of one who ﴿falls from the sky﴾ and is snatched away by ﴿the birds﴾, so that he is scattered into pieces in their crops, and ﴿the wind﴾ sweeps him away until it throws him into some distant abyss. If it is a divided comparison, then faith in its elevation is likened to the sky, the one who abandons faith and associates partners with God is likened to the one who falls from the sky, the desires that contend for his nest are likened to the birds that snatch, and the devil who casts him into the valley of misguidance is likened to the wind that carries away what it has swept into some destructive abyss. End of quote.

Nafi' read ﴿fa-takhtafuhu﴾ with a fatha on the kha' and a shadda on the ta', while the rest of the seven read it with a sukun on the kha' and a light ta'. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and al-A'mash read it with a kasra on the ta', kha', and a shadda on the ta'. From al-Hasan it is the same, except that he put a fatha on the ta' with a shadda. Al-A'mash also read ﴿takhuttuhu﴾ without a fa', with a sukun on the kha' and a light fatha on the ta'. Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read ﴿al-rayyah﴾ (the winds).

(p. 367)

(p-٣٦٢) Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar (others) from the way of God and from the Sacred Mosque, which We have made equal for the people, the resident in it and the visitor, and whoever intends in it deviation through wrongdoing, We shall make him taste a painful punishment. [Al-Hajj: 25] And when We settled Abraham at the site of the House, (saying): "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate it, those who stand (in prayer), and those who bow and prostrate." [Al-Hajj: 26] "And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, coming from every deep mountain pass, [Al-Hajj: 27] that they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of God on known days over the livestock He has provided for them. So eat from them and feed the miserable poor." [Al-Hajj: 28] "Then let them complete their untidiness, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the ancient House." [Al-Hajj: 29] "That (is so). And whoever honours the sacred rites of God, it is better for him with his Lord. And the livestock have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you. So avoid the abomination of idols and avoid the word of falsehood, [Al-Hajj: 30] being upright for God, not associating anything with Him. And whoever associates others with God, it is as if he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away, or the wind threw him into a distant place." [Al-Hajj: 31]

The imperfect verb (al-mudari') may be one in which no specific time of present or future is intended, so it then indicates continuity. Of this is ﴿and they bar (others) from the way of God﴾, like His saying ﴿those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of God﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 28]. It has also been said: it is an imperfect verb used with the meaning of the past, coordinated with (kafaru, "they disbelieved"). And it has been said: it is on the basis of an implied subject, i.e., "and they (are) barring." The predicate of inna (indeed) is omitted; Ibn 'Atiyya estimated it after (wal-bad, "and the visitor"): "they will lose or perish." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it after his saying (al-haram, "the Sacred"): "We shall make them taste ﴿a painful punishment﴾." It is not valid to estimate it after that, because alladhi (the relative pronoun "which") is an adjective of (al-Masjid al-Haram, "the Sacred Mosque"), so the place of the estimate is after (wal-bad). But al-Zamakhshari's estimate is better than Ibn 'Atiyya's, because the conditional sentence that follows indicates it verbally. Ibn 'Atiyya took it into account semantically, because whoever is made to taste the punishment loses and perishes.

It has been said: the wa (and) in (wa-yasuddun, "and they bar") is superfluous, and the predicate of inna is (yasuddun, "they bar"), its estimate being: "Indeed those who disbelieve bar..." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This corrupts the intended meaning." End.

The Basrans do not permit the superfluity of the wa; it is merely a Kufan view, which is disfavoured.

This verse was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was barred from the Sacred Mosque. That is because no collective barring of them is known prior to that, unless what is meant is their barring of individuals from among the people, which occurred at the beginning of the mission. The apparent meaning is the Mosque itself, and whoever is barred from reaching it has been barred from it. It has also been said: the entire Sanctuary (al-haram) is meant, because they barred him and his people from it, peace be upon him, so they stopped outside it. But He mentioned the principal objective of the Sanctuary, which is the important goal.

The majority of readers recite (sawa'un, "equal") with the nominative (raf'), so that the sentence consisting of subject and predicate is in the position of the second object. The better view is that al-'Akif and al-Badi are the subject, and (sawa'an, "equal"), (p-٣٦٣) the predicate, although the reverse has also been permitted. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The meaning of ﴿which We have made for the people﴾ is a qibla (direction of prayer) or a place of worship." End. He would not need this estimate unless he meant an explanation of the meaning rather than the grammatical analysis (i'rab), and then it is acceptable, because the sentence is in the position of the second object, so there is no need for this estimate.

Hafs and al-A'mash recite (sawa'an) with the accusative (nasb), and al-'Akif is raised by it, because it is a verbal noun (masdar) with the meaning of the active participle (musta-w, "one who is equal"). Among their speech: "I passed by a man, equal (sawa'an) to him and to nothing." If ja'ala (made) is transitive to two objects, then sawa'an is the second; if it is transitive to one, then sawa'an is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun (ha', "it").

A group, including al-A'mash in the transmission of al-Qat'i, recited (sawa'an) with the accusative and ﴿al-'akif fihi﴾ with the genitive (jarr). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "in coordination with 'the people' (al-nas)." End. He apparently means that it is an explanatory apposition ('atf al-bayan), the first possibility being that it is a substitute of detail (badal tafsil).

(Al-Badi) has been read both with and without the final vowel, both in pausal and continuous recitation, and with its retention in continuous recitation and omission in pause. Al-'Akif is the one who resides in it; al-Badi is the one who arrives at it. They agreed on equality in the Sacred Mosque itself, but differed concerning Mecca. Umar, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and a group held that the matter is the same regarding the houses of Mecca, that the arrival has the right to lodge wherever he finds (a place), and the owner of the dwelling must shelter him whether he wishes or not. al-Thawri held this view, and so it was in the early period. Ibn Sabit said: "Their houses had no doors until theft increased, and a man made a door, so Umar objected to him and said: 'Will you close a door in the face of the pilgrim to the House of God?' He said: 'I only intended to protect their goods from theft,' and he left it. Then the people made doors." This disagreement depends on the disagreement concerning the conquest of Mecca: was it by force (‘anwatan) or by treaty (sulhan)? This is a question discussed in jurisprudence (fiqh).

Al-ilhad is inclination away from the right course. The object of (yurid, "intends") — Abu 'Ubayda said it is (bi-ilhadin, "in deviation"), and the preposition (ba') is superfluous in the object. Al-A'sha said:

"Our spears have been guaranteed for the provision of our dependants."

That is, (rizq, "provision"). Likewise is the recitation of al-Hasan, in the accusative: ﴿and whoever intends (ilhadahu, "its deviation")﴾ bi-zulmin, i.e., (ilhadan fihi, "deviation in it"), so he has extended the usage. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is permissible for the estimate to be ﴿and whoever intends in it﴾ — the people — (bi-ilhadin). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿bi-ilhadin bi-zulmin﴾ are two synonymous circumstantial clauses (hal), and the object of (yurid) is omitted so as to encompass every possible object, as if He said: "and whoever intends in it, intending either one who swerves from the aim or one who is a wrongdoer, ﴿We shall make him taste a painful punishment﴾." It has been said: deviation in the Sanctuary is preventing people from its cultivation. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: hoarding (al-ihtikar). From 'Ata': a man's saying in a sale, "No, by God," and "Yes, by God." End.

The better view is that (yurid) should be taken as implying (yatalabbas, "to be involved in"), so that it takes the preposition (ba'). He made the consequence, which is (nudhiqhu, "We make him taste"), conditional upon the intention. Therefore, if one intends an evil deed and does not do it, he will not be held to account for it, except in Mecca. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and a group. Ibn Abbas said: deviation here is polytheism. He also said: it is making the forbidden lawful. Mujahid said: it is evil action in it. Ibn Umar said: "No, by God," and "Yes, by God," are among deviation. Habib ibn Abi Thabit said: hoarding in Mecca is deviation through wrongdoing. The better course is to take these sayings as examples rather than as exhaustive limitations, since the speech indicates generality. A group recited ﴿and whoever intends﴾ with a fatha on the ya' from (al-wurud, "arrival"), which al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' transmitted; its meaning is: whoever arrives with (ilhad) in wrongdoing.

When He, exalted, mentioned the state of the disbelievers and their barring from the Sacred Mosque, and threatened whoever intends in it deviation, He mentioned the state of their father Abraham, reproaching them for their taking a path other than his, through their disbelief in taking idols, and His bestowing favour on them by bringing the world (in its provision) to them. ﴿And when We settled﴾: i.e., remember when We settled (bawwa'na) — that is, We placed ﴿for Abraham the site of the House﴾ as a (mabā'a), i.e., a place of return to which he returns for its maintenance and worship. It has been said: the lam is superfluous, i.e., We settled Abraham at the site of the House, that is, We made it a place for him to return to, like His saying: ﴿We shall surely settle them in the lofty chambers of Paradise﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 58]. The poet said:

"How many a righteous companion of mine I settled, with my own hands, in a tomb."

It has been said: the object of (bawwa'na) is omitted, its estimate being "We settled the people," and the lam in (li-Ibrahim) is the lam of cause, i.e., for the sake of Abraham, as an honour to him and at his hands. The apparent view is that His saying ﴿that you do not associate anything with Me﴾ is addressed to Abraham, and likewise what follows of commands. It has been said: it is addressed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). (Anna, "that") is a lightened form of the heavy (anna), as Ibn 'Atiyya said. The original is that it should be followed by a verb of certainty or probability, as is its case when it is heavy, or by a particle of explanation. So said al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya, (p-٣٦٤) and its condition is that it be preceded by a sentence with the meaning of speech; but (bawwa'na, "We settled") does not have the meaning of speech. The better view in my opinion is that (an, "that") is the one that governs the imperfect verb, since it is followed by a conjugated verb, past, imperfect or imperative, and the prohibition is like the command.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how can the prohibition of associating and the command to purify the House be an explanation of the settling? I say: the settling was intended for the sake of worship, so it is as if it were said: "We made Abraham worship, and We said to him: ﴿Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House﴾ from idols, images and filth, so that they are not cast around it."

Ikrima and Abu Nahik recited (an yushrika, "that he associate") with the ya', in the sense that (an yaqula, "that he say") carries the meaning of the speech that was said to him. Abu Hatim said: in this recitation the kaf must be in the accusative, with the meaning of (an, "that"), ﴿do not associate﴾.

Al-qa'imun (those who stand) are those who pray; He mentioned the greatest of its pillars, namely standing, bowing and prostrating.

The majority recite ﴿wa-adhdhin﴾ (and proclaim) with the doubled dhal, meaning "call out." It is narrated that he climbed Abu Qubays and said: "O people, perform the pilgrimage to the House of your Lord." The statement of those who said it is addressed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) has preceded, and al-Hasan said: he was commanded to do this in the Farewell Pilgrimage. Al-Hasan, Ibn Muhaysin recited (wa-adhana, "and he proclaimed") with a long vowel and a light dhal. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this was distorted for Ibn Jinni, for he transmitted from them (wa-adhina), as a past verb, and parsed it on that basis as coordinated with (bawwa'na). End.

It is not a distortion; rather Abu 'Abd Allah al-Husayn ibn Khalawayh indeed transmitted it among the irregular readings (shawadhdh al-qira'at) in his compilation, and the author of al-Lawami', Abu al-Fadl al-Razi, transmitted it from al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin. The author of al-Lawami' said: it is coordinated with ﴿and when We settled﴾, so that there is a transposition in the speech, and (ya'tuka, "they will come to you") becomes jussive as an answer to the command which is ﴿and purify﴾. End. Ibn Abi Ishaq recited (bil-hijji, "for the pilgrimage") with a kasra on the ha' wherever it occurs, whereas the majority have a fatha. The majority recite (rijalan, "on foot") and Ibn Abi Ishaq with a damma on the ra' and light pronunciation; it is narrated likewise from Ikrima, al-Hasan and Abu Mijlaz, and it is a collective noun (ism jam'), like (zu'ar). It is narrated from them, and from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ja'far ibn Muhammad, with a damma on the ra' and a doubled jim. From Ikrima also: rujala on the pattern of nu'ama, with the feminine ending of the shortened alif; and likewise with a doubled jim from Ibn Abbas, Ata' and Ibn Hudayr. Rijal is the plural of rajil, like tajir and tujjar (merchant, merchants).

The majority recite (ya'tina, "they will come", feminine plural), so the apparent reference of the pronoun is to (kulli dhamirin, "every lean camel"), since the usual case is that vast lands cannot be reached on foot to Mecca, though the pronoun may also include (rijalan) and (kulli dhamirin) in the sense of groups and companies. ‘Abd Allah and his companions, al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited (ya'tuna, "they will come", masculine plural), giving precedence to the masculine rational plural at the beginning with (rijal, "men"), in preference of those who walk to the pilgrimage. Ibn Abbas said: "I do not regret anything that escaped me more than not having performed the pilgrimage on foot." The argument from His saying ﴿they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel﴾ that the obligation of pilgrimage falls on one who must travel by sea with no other route, because it is not mentioned in this verse, is weak, because Mecca is not on the sea; one reaches it by one of two means, walking or riding, and He mentioned what one reaches it by. Ibn Mas'ud recited (fajjin mu'ayyiq, "a deep pass"). Ibn Abbas and others said: among the benefits is commerce. Al-Baqir said: the reward. Mujahid and 'Ata' both said (both of these), and Ibn al-'Arabi preferred it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He made (manafi', "benefits") indefinite because He intended benefits specific to this worship, religious and worldly, which are not found in other acts of worship. It is narrated from Abu Hanifa that he used to rank the acts of worship before he performed the pilgrimage; when he performed it, he preferred the pilgrimage over all the acts of worship because of those distinctive features he witnessed. He referred to the slaughter and sacrifice by mentioning the name of God, because the people of Islam do not cease from mentioning His name when they slaughter or sacrifice. In this is an indication that the principal aim in what is done to draw near to God is that His name be mentioned. He has embellished the speech with a clear embellishment, in that He combined His saying ﴿that they may mention the name of God over it﴾ with His saying ﴿over what He has provided for them﴾. Had it been said "that they may slaughter" ﴿on known days over the livestock﴾, you would not see any of that beauty and splendour. End.

(p. 365) Those who held that the purpose of mentioning God's name is over the slaughter and sacrifice cited as evidence that slaughter may not take place at night and is not permitted then, based on His saying ﴿on known days﴾. This is the view of Malik and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y).

It was also said: the remembrance here means praising Him and extolling Him in gratitude for His provision. This is supported by the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Indeed they are days of eating, drinking, and remembrance of God's name."

The "known days" are the ten days, according to Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibrahim, Qatada and Abu Hanifa. The "counted days" are the three days of tashriq (the days after Eid al-Adha).

A group including Malik and his companions said: the "known days" are the Day of Sacrifice and the two days after it, and the "counted days" are the three days of tashriq. The Day of Sacrifice is thus known but not counted, the two days after it are both known and counted, and the fourth is counted but not known.

According to Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Anas, Abu Hurayra, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri, the days of sacrifice are the Day of Sacrifice and the two days after it. According to al-Hasan, Ata' and al-Shafi'i, they are the Day of Sacrifice and three days after it. According to al-Nakha'i, they are two days, and according to Ibn Sirin, one day, the Day of Sacrifice. From Abu Salama and Sulayman ibn Yasar: the sacrifice extends until the new moon of Muharram.

Ibn Atiyya said: It appears that the "known" and "counted" days mean all of those virtuous days together. The matter of slaughter and the matter of haste are not tied to a counted or known day. The purpose of His saying "known" and "counted" is to encourage attention to these days and to seize their virtue, meaning that they are not like other days. It is as if He said: they are distinguished, so seize them. End of quote.

The beast (bahima) is undetermined in every four-footed creature on land and sea, so it was specified by "livestock" (al-an'am), namely camels, cattle, sheep and goats. The disagreement over the meaning of ﴿the beast of livestock﴾ [al-Hajj: 34] has already been discussed at the beginning of al-Ma'ida. The apparent ruling is that eating from it and feeding others from it are obligatory. It was also said that both are recommended. It was also said that eating is recommended while feeding is obligatory.

The "distressed" (al-ba'is) is one who has been struck by hardship, meaning severe need.

The "tafath" (unkempt state) is what the muhrim does upon exiting ihram: trimming or shaving hair and removing its disarray and the like, including the five acts of fitra according to the hadith. Included in this is fulfilling all the rites of hajj, since one does not complete the tafath except after that. Ibn Umar said: the tafath is what is upon them of hajj. Also from him: all the rites. The "vows" here are what they vow of acts of righteousness during their pilgrimage. It was also said that the intended meaning is discharging what has become obligatory upon them, whether they vowed or did not vow.

Shu'ba, from Asim, read ﴿wal-yuwaffu﴾ with a shadda, while the majority read it without shadda. ﴿wal-yattawwafu﴾ refers to the tawaf al-ifada, which is the tawaf of visitation and one of the pillars of hajj, and with it the exit from ihram is completed. It was also said that it is the tawaf al-sadr, which is the tawaf al-wada' (farewell circumambulation). Al-Tabari said: there is no disagreement among the commentators that it is the tawaf al-ifada. Ibn Atiyya said: according to the order, it may also be the tawaf al-wada'. End of quote.

The "ancient" (al-atiq) means the old, according to al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. Or it means the one freed from tyrants, according to Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abi Najih and Qatada: how many tyrants marched against it and God destroyed them. Tubba' intended to demolish it, but he was struck with paralysis, so the righteous advised him to refrain from it and said: it has a Lord who protects it. So he left it, clothed it, and he was the first to clothe it. Abraha also targeted it and was struck by what struck him. As for al-Hajjaj, he did not intend to gain control over the House, but Ibn al-Zubayr took refuge in it, so he devised a way to remove him, and then rebuilt it. Or it means the one freed, whose site was never owned, according to Mujahid. Or it means the one freed from the flood, also according to Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr. Or it means the excellent, from their saying "ataq of horses" and "ataq of birds." Or it means the one in which the necks of sinners are freed from punishment. Ibn Atiyya said: this is rejected by morphology (tasrif, the science of word forms). End of quote. Morphology does not reject it, because he explained it as a matter of meaning. As for grammatical analysis (i'rab), "al-atiq" is a form (fa'il) in the sense of a form (muf'il), i.e., one who frees the necks of sinners. The freeing is attributed to it figuratively, since through visiting it and circumambulating it freeing occurs, and from its being one who frees it may be said: in it the necks of sinners are freed.

(Dhalika) is the predicate of an omitted subject. Ibn Atiyya estimated it as "your duty is that," or "the obligatory is that." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "the matter or the affair is that." He said: just as a writer begins a section of his book on some meaning, then when he wishes to move to another meaning he says: "This is so, and it was such."

It was also said: it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning "that" is the matter you have mentioned. It was also said it is in the accusative position, estimated as "comply with that."

A parallel to this eloquent demonstrative is the line of Zuhayr, who had earlier composed verses describing Harim:

"This! Not like one who falters in his speech
amid the generous when a speaker speaks."

He had described him before this with generosity and courage, then in this line he described him with eloquence. It is as if he said: this is his character, not like one who falters in his speech.

The sacred things (al-hurumat) are whatever is not lawful to violate. All the obligations, including the rites of hajj and others, are its sacred things. The apparent meaning is general over all obligations, but it may be restricted to what relates to hajj. Al-Kalbi said this and said: what He commanded of the rites. From Ibn Abbas: they are all the prohibitions of hajj: wrongful speech, disputation, intercourse and hunting. From Ibn Zayd: they are five: the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram), the Sacred Mosque, the Sacred House, the Sacred Month, and the forbidden thing until it becomes lawful.

The pronoun in ﴿fa-huwa﴾ refers to the verbal noun implied by His saying ﴿and whoever honours﴾, meaning: so the honouring ﴿is better for him with his Lord﴾, meaning nearness to Him and an increase in obedience to Him, for which He will reward him. The apparent meaning is that "khayr" here is not a comparative superlative.

And ﴿Lawful for you is the beast of livestock﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 1] is a refutation of what they used to forbid by their own opinion, such as the bahira and the sa'iba. By His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ He means what He stated in His Book as forbidden, and the meaning is the verse recited to you about its prohibition.

When He urged the honouring of God's sacred things and mentioned that honouring them is better for the one who honours them before God, He followed it with the command to avoid idols and false speech, because the oneness of God, the negation of partners from Him, and truthful speech are the greatest sacred things. These two were joined in one pairing because shirk falls under the category of falsehood, since the polytheist claims that the idol deserves worship. It is as if He said: ﴿so avoid﴾ worshipping ﴿the idols﴾, which are the head of falsehood, ﴿and avoid the word of falsehood﴾ entirely.

The "min" in ﴿min al-awthan﴾ is for specifying the genus (bayan al-jins), and according to them it is to be estimated as a relative clause, meaning the filth which is the idols. Whoever denies that "min" specifies the genus takes it to indicate the starting point (ibtida' al-ghaya). It is as if He forbade the filth in general and then specified for them its origin, from which it reaches them, since worship of idols encompasses every corruption and filth. According to the first view, the prohibition of the rest of the filths would be from another place than this.

Ibn Atiyya said: whoever says that "min" is partitive has inverted the meaning of the verse and corrupted it. End of quote.

Partitiveness is possible here, in that by "filth" one means the worship of idols. This has been related from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jurayj. It is as if He said: avoid from the idols the filth, which is worship, because what is forbidden of idols is only their worship. Do you not see that it is conceivable to use an idol in building or other things that the Law has not forbidden? So for the idol there are aspects, among them its worship, which is what is commanded to be avoided, and its worship is one of its aspects.

Since the word of falsehood equals disbelief, it was not joined to the filth by conjunction. Rather, it was singled out by repeating the governing verb, out of concern for avoiding it. In a hadith: "The testimony of falsehood was equated with shirk."

When He commanded avoiding the worship of idols and the word of falsehood, He struck an example for the polytheist, saying ﴿and whoever associates partners with God﴾ and so on. Al-Zamakhshari said: this comparison may be of the composite or the divided type. If it is a composite comparison, it is as if He said: whoever associates with God has destroyed himself with a destruction beyond which there is none, by depicting his state in the form of one who ﴿falls from the sky﴾ and is snatched away by ﴿the birds﴾, so that he is scattered into pieces in their crops, and ﴿the wind﴾ sweeps him away until it throws him into some distant abyss. If it is a divided comparison, then faith in its elevation is likened to the sky, the one who abandons faith and associates partners with God is likened to the one who falls from the sky, the desires that contend for his nest are likened to the birds that snatch, and the devil who casts him into the valley of misguidance is likened to the wind that carries away what it has swept into some destructive abyss. End of quote.

Nafi' read ﴿fa-takhtafuhu﴾ with a fatha on the kha' and a shadda on the ta', while the rest of the seven read it with a sukun on the kha' and a light ta'. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and al-A'mash read it with a kasra on the ta', kha', and a shadda on the ta'. From al-Hasan it is the same, except that he put a fatha on the ta' with a shadda. Al-A'mash also read ﴿takhuttuhu﴾ without a fa', with a sukun on the kha' and a light fatha on the ta'. Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read ﴿al-rayyah﴾ (the winds).

(p. 367)

(p-٣٦٢) Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar (others) from the way of God and from the Sacred Mosque, which We have made equal for the people, the resident in it and the visitor, and whoever intends in it deviation through wrongdoing, We shall make him taste a painful punishment. [Al-Hajj: 25] And when We settled Abraham at the site of the House, (saying): "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate it, those who stand (in prayer), and those who bow and prostrate." [Al-Hajj: 26] "And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, coming from every deep mountain pass, [Al-Hajj: 27] that they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of God on known days over the livestock He has provided for them. So eat from them and feed the miserable poor." [Al-Hajj: 28] "Then let them complete their untidiness, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the ancient House." [Al-Hajj: 29] "That (is so). And whoever honours the sacred rites of God, it is better for him with his Lord. And the livestock have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you. So avoid the abomination of idols and avoid the word of falsehood, [Al-Hajj: 30] being upright for God, not associating anything with Him. And whoever associates others with God, it is as if he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away, or the wind threw him into a distant place." [Al-Hajj: 31]

The imperfect verb (al-mudari') may be one in which no specific time of present or future is intended, so it then indicates continuity. Of this is ﴿and they bar (others) from the way of God﴾, like His saying ﴿those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of God﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 28]. It has also been said: it is an imperfect verb used with the meaning of the past, coordinated with (kafaru, "they disbelieved"). And it has been said: it is on the basis of an implied subject, i.e., "and they (are) barring." The predicate of inna (indeed) is omitted; Ibn 'Atiyya estimated it after (wal-bad, "and the visitor"): "they will lose or perish." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it after his saying (al-haram, "the Sacred"): "We shall make them taste ﴿a painful punishment﴾." It is not valid to estimate it after that, because alladhi (the relative pronoun "which") is an adjective of (al-Masjid al-Haram, "the Sacred Mosque"), so the place of the estimate is after (wal-bad). But al-Zamakhshari's estimate is better than Ibn 'Atiyya's, because the conditional sentence that follows indicates it verbally. Ibn 'Atiyya took it into account semantically, because whoever is made to taste the punishment loses and perishes.

It has been said: the wa (and) in (wa-yasuddun, "and they bar") is superfluous, and the predicate of inna is (yasuddun, "they bar"), its estimate being: "Indeed those who disbelieve bar..." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This corrupts the intended meaning." End.

The Basrans do not permit the superfluity of the wa; it is merely a Kufan view, which is disfavoured.

This verse was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was barred from the Sacred Mosque. That is because no collective barring of them is known prior to that, unless what is meant is their barring of individuals from among the people, which occurred at the beginning of the mission. The apparent meaning is the Mosque itself, and whoever is barred from reaching it has been barred from it. It has also been said: the entire Sanctuary (al-haram) is meant, because they barred him and his people from it, peace be upon him, so they stopped outside it. But He mentioned the principal objective of the Sanctuary, which is the important goal.

The majority of readers recite (sawa'un, "equal") with the nominative (raf'), so that the sentence consisting of subject and predicate is in the position of the second object. The better view is that al-'Akif and al-Badi are the subject, and (sawa'an, "equal"), (p-٣٦٣) the predicate, although the reverse has also been permitted. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The meaning of ﴿which We have made for the people﴾ is a qibla (direction of prayer) or a place of worship." End. He would not need this estimate unless he meant an explanation of the meaning rather than the grammatical analysis (i'rab), and then it is acceptable, because the sentence is in the position of the second object, so there is no need for this estimate.

Hafs and al-A'mash recite (sawa'an) with the accusative (nasb), and al-'Akif is raised by it, because it is a verbal noun (masdar) with the meaning of the active participle (musta-w, "one who is equal"). Among their speech: "I passed by a man, equal (sawa'an) to him and to nothing." If ja'ala (made) is transitive to two objects, then sawa'an is the second; if it is transitive to one, then sawa'an is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun (ha', "it").

A group, including al-A'mash in the transmission of al-Qat'i, recited (sawa'an) with the accusative and ﴿al-'akif fihi﴾ with the genitive (jarr). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "in coordination with 'the people' (al-nas)." End. He apparently means that it is an explanatory apposition ('atf al-bayan), the first possibility being that it is a substitute of detail (badal tafsil).

(Al-Badi) has been read both with and without the final vowel, both in pausal and continuous recitation, and with its retention in continuous recitation and omission in pause. Al-'Akif is the one who resides in it; al-Badi is the one who arrives at it. They agreed on equality in the Sacred Mosque itself, but differed concerning Mecca. Umar, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and a group held that the matter is the same regarding the houses of Mecca, that the arrival has the right to lodge wherever he finds (a place), and the owner of the dwelling must shelter him whether he wishes or not. al-Thawri held this view, and so it was in the early period. Ibn Sabit said: "Their houses had no doors until theft increased, and a man made a door, so Umar objected to him and said: 'Will you close a door in the face of the pilgrim to the House of God?' He said: 'I only intended to protect their goods from theft,' and he left it. Then the people made doors." This disagreement depends on the disagreement concerning the conquest of Mecca: was it by force (‘anwatan) or by treaty (sulhan)? This is a question discussed in jurisprudence (fiqh).

Al-ilhad is inclination away from the right course. The object of (yurid, "intends") — Abu 'Ubayda said it is (bi-ilhadin, "in deviation"), and the preposition (ba') is superfluous in the object. Al-A'sha said:

"Our spears have been guaranteed for the provision of our dependants."

That is, (rizq, "provision"). Likewise is the recitation of al-Hasan, in the accusative: ﴿and whoever intends (ilhadahu, "its deviation")﴾ bi-zulmin, i.e., (ilhadan fihi, "deviation in it"), so he has extended the usage. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is permissible for the estimate to be ﴿and whoever intends in it﴾ — the people — (bi-ilhadin). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿bi-ilhadin bi-zulmin﴾ are two synonymous circumstantial clauses (hal), and the object of (yurid) is omitted so as to encompass every possible object, as if He said: "and whoever intends in it, intending either one who swerves from the aim or one who is a wrongdoer, ﴿We shall make him taste a painful punishment﴾." It has been said: deviation in the Sanctuary is preventing people from its cultivation. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: hoarding (al-ihtikar). From 'Ata': a man's saying in a sale, "No, by God," and "Yes, by God." End.

The better view is that (yurid) should be taken as implying (yatalabbas, "to be involved in"), so that it takes the preposition (ba'). He made the consequence, which is (nudhiqhu, "We make him taste"), conditional upon the intention. Therefore, if one intends an evil deed and does not do it, he will not be held to account for it, except in Mecca. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and a group. Ibn Abbas said: deviation here is polytheism. He also said: it is making the forbidden lawful. Mujahid said: it is evil action in it. Ibn Umar said: "No, by God," and "Yes, by God," are among deviation. Habib ibn Abi Thabit said: hoarding in Mecca is deviation through wrongdoing. The better course is to take these sayings as examples rather than as exhaustive limitations, since the speech indicates generality. A group recited ﴿and whoever intends﴾ with a fatha on the ya' from (al-wurud, "arrival"), which al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' transmitted; its meaning is: whoever arrives with (ilhad) in wrongdoing.

When He, exalted, mentioned the state of the disbelievers and their barring from the Sacred Mosque, and threatened whoever intends in it deviation, He mentioned the state of their father Abraham, reproaching them for their taking a path other than his, through their disbelief in taking idols, and His bestowing favour on them by bringing the world (in its provision) to them. ﴿And when We settled﴾: i.e., remember when We settled (bawwa'na) — that is, We placed ﴿for Abraham the site of the House﴾ as a (mabā'a), i.e., a place of return to which he returns for its maintenance and worship. It has been said: the lam is superfluous, i.e., We settled Abraham at the site of the House, that is, We made it a place for him to return to, like His saying: ﴿We shall surely settle them in the lofty chambers of Paradise﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 58]. The poet said:

"How many a righteous companion of mine I settled, with my own hands, in a tomb."

It has been said: the object of (bawwa'na) is omitted, its estimate being "We settled the people," and the lam in (li-Ibrahim) is the lam of cause, i.e., for the sake of Abraham, as an honour to him and at his hands. The apparent view is that His saying ﴿that you do not associate anything with Me﴾ is addressed to Abraham, and likewise what follows of commands. It has been said: it is addressed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). (Anna, "that") is a lightened form of the heavy (anna), as Ibn 'Atiyya said. The original is that it should be followed by a verb of certainty or probability, as is its case when it is heavy, or by a particle of explanation. So said al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya, (p-٣٦٤) and its condition is that it be preceded by a sentence with the meaning of speech; but (bawwa'na, "We settled") does not have the meaning of speech. The better view in my opinion is that (an, "that") is the one that governs the imperfect verb, since it is followed by a conjugated verb, past, imperfect or imperative, and the prohibition is like the command.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how can the prohibition of associating and the command to purify the House be an explanation of the settling? I say: the settling was intended for the sake of worship, so it is as if it were said: "We made Abraham worship, and We said to him: ﴿Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House﴾ from idols, images and filth, so that they are not cast around it."

Ikrima and Abu Nahik recited (an yushrika, "that he associate") with the ya', in the sense that (an yaqula, "that he say") carries the meaning of the speech that was said to him. Abu Hatim said: in this recitation the kaf must be in the accusative, with the meaning of (an, "that"), ﴿do not associate﴾.

Al-qa'imun (those who stand) are those who pray; He mentioned the greatest of its pillars, namely standing, bowing and prostrating.

The majority recite ﴿wa-adhdhin﴾ (and proclaim) with the doubled dhal, meaning "call out." It is narrated that he climbed Abu Qubays and said: "O people, perform the pilgrimage to the House of your Lord." The statement of those who said it is addressed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) has preceded, and al-Hasan said: he was commanded to do this in the Farewell Pilgrimage. Al-Hasan, Ibn Muhaysin recited (wa-adhana, "and he proclaimed") with a long vowel and a light dhal. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this was distorted for Ibn Jinni, for he transmitted from them (wa-adhina), as a past verb, and parsed it on that basis as coordinated with (bawwa'na). End.
