Ibn 'Atiyya said: this was distorted for Ibn Jinni, for he transmitted from them (wa-adhina), as a past verb, and parsed it on that basis as coordinated with (bawwa'na). End.

It is not a distortion; rather Abu 'Abd Allah al-Husayn ibn Khalawayh indeed transmitted it among the irregular readings (shawadhdh al-qira'at) in his compilation, and the author of al-Lawami', Abu al-Fadl al-Razi, transmitted it from al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin. The author of al-Lawami' said: it is coordinated with ﴿and when We settled﴾, so that there is a transposition in the speech, and (ya'tuka, "they will come to you") becomes jussive as an answer to the command which is ﴿and purify﴾. End. Ibn Abi Ishaq recited (bil-hijji, "for the pilgrimage") with a kasra on the ha' wherever it occurs, whereas the majority have a fatha. The majority recite (rijalan, "on foot") and Ibn Abi Ishaq with a damma on the ra' and light pronunciation; it is narrated likewise from Ikrima, al-Hasan and Abu Mijlaz, and it is a collective noun (ism jam'), like (zu'ar). It is narrated from them, and from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ja'far ibn Muhammad, with a damma on the ra' and a doubled jim. From Ikrima also: rujala on the pattern of nu'ama, with the feminine ending of the shortened alif; and likewise with a doubled jim from Ibn Abbas, Ata' and Ibn Hudayr. Rijal is the plural of rajil, like tajir and tujjar (merchant, merchants).

The majority recite (ya'tina, "they will come", feminine plural), so the apparent reference of the pronoun is to (kulli dhamirin, "every lean camel"), since the usual case is that vast lands cannot be reached on foot to Mecca, though the pronoun may also include (rijalan) and (kulli dhamirin) in the sense of groups and companies. ‘Abd Allah and his companions, al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited (ya'tuna, "they will come", masculine plural), giving precedence to the masculine rational plural at the beginning with (rijal, "men"), in preference of those who walk to the pilgrimage. Ibn Abbas said: "I do not regret anything that escaped me more than not having performed the pilgrimage on foot." The argument from His saying ﴿they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel﴾ that the obligation of pilgrimage falls on one who must travel by sea with no other route, because it is not mentioned in this verse, is weak, because Mecca is not on the sea; one reaches it by one of two means, walking or riding, and He mentioned what one reaches it by. Ibn Mas'ud recited (fajjin mu'ayyiq, "a deep pass"). Ibn Abbas and others said: among the benefits is commerce. Al-Baqir said: the reward. Mujahid and 'Ata' both said (both of these), and Ibn al-'Arabi preferred it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He made (manafi', "benefits") indefinite because He intended benefits specific to this worship, religious and worldly, which are not found in other acts of worship. It is narrated from Abu Hanifa that he used to rank the acts of worship before he performed the pilgrimage; when he performed it, he preferred the pilgrimage over all the acts of worship because of those distinctive features he witnessed. He referred to the slaughter and sacrifice by mentioning the name of God, because the people of Islam do not cease from mentioning His name when they slaughter or sacrifice. In this is an indication that the principal aim in what is done to draw near to God is that His name be mentioned. He has embellished the speech with a clear embellishment, in that He combined His saying ﴿that they may mention the name of God over it﴾ with His saying ﴿over what He has provided for them﴾. Had it been said "that they may slaughter" ﴿on known days over the livestock﴾, you would not see any of that beauty and splendour. End.

(p. 365) Those who held that the purpose of mentioning God's name is over the slaughter and sacrifice cited as evidence that slaughter may not take place at night and is not permitted then, based on His saying ﴿on known days﴾. This is the view of Malik and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y).

It was also said: the remembrance here means praising Him and extolling Him in gratitude for His provision. This is supported by the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Indeed they are days of eating, drinking, and remembrance of God's name."

The "known days" are the ten days, according to Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibrahim, Qatada and Abu Hanifa. The "counted days" are the three days of tashriq (the days after Eid al-Adha).

A group including Malik and his companions said: the "known days" are the Day of Sacrifice and the two days after it, and the "counted days" are the three days of tashriq. The Day of Sacrifice is thus known but not counted, the two days after it are both known and counted, and the fourth is counted but not known.

According to Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Anas, Abu Hurayra, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri, the days of sacrifice are the Day of Sacrifice and the two days after it. According to al-Hasan, Ata' and al-Shafi'i, they are the Day of Sacrifice and three days after it. According to al-Nakha'i, they are two days, and according to Ibn Sirin, one day, the Day of Sacrifice. From Abu Salama and Sulayman ibn Yasar: the sacrifice extends until the new moon of Muharram.

Ibn Atiyya said: It appears that the "known" and "counted" days mean all of those virtuous days together. The matter of slaughter and the matter of haste are not tied to a counted or known day. The purpose of His saying "known" and "counted" is to encourage attention to these days and to seize their virtue, meaning that they are not like other days. It is as if He said: they are distinguished, so seize them. End of quote.

The beast (bahima) is undetermined in every four-footed creature on land and sea, so it was specified by "livestock" (al-an'am), namely camels, cattle, sheep and goats. The disagreement over the meaning of ﴿the beast of livestock﴾ [al-Hajj: 34] has already been discussed at the beginning of al-Ma'ida. The apparent ruling is that eating from it and feeding others from it are obligatory. It was also said that both are recommended. It was also said that eating is recommended while feeding is obligatory.

The "distressed" (al-ba'is) is one who has been struck by hardship, meaning severe need.

The "tafath" (unkempt state) is what the muhrim does upon exiting ihram: trimming or shaving hair and removing its disarray and the like, including the five acts of fitra according to the hadith. Included in this is fulfilling all the rites of hajj, since one does not complete the tafath except after that. Ibn Umar said: the tafath is what is upon them of hajj. Also from him: all the rites. The "vows" here are what they vow of acts of righteousness during their pilgrimage. It was also said that the intended meaning is discharging what has become obligatory upon them, whether they vowed or did not vow.

Shu'ba, from Asim, read ﴿wal-yuwaffu﴾ with a shadda, while the majority read it without shadda. ﴿wal-yattawwafu﴾ refers to the tawaf al-ifada, which is the tawaf of visitation and one of the pillars of hajj, and with it the exit from ihram is completed. It was also said that it is the tawaf al-sadr, which is the tawaf al-wada' (farewell circumambulation). Al-Tabari said: there is no disagreement among the commentators that it is the tawaf al-ifada. Ibn Atiyya said: according to the order, it may also be the tawaf al-wada'. End of quote.

The "ancient" (al-atiq) means the old, according to al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. Or it means the one freed from tyrants, according to Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abi Najih and Qatada: how many tyrants marched against it and God destroyed them. Tubba' intended to demolish it, but he was struck with paralysis, so the righteous advised him to refrain from it and said: it has a Lord who protects it. So he left it, clothed it, and he was the first to clothe it. Abraha also targeted it and was struck by what struck him. As for al-Hajjaj, he did not intend to gain control over the House, but Ibn al-Zubayr took refuge in it, so he devised a way to remove him, and then rebuilt it. Or it means the one freed, whose site was never owned, according to Mujahid. Or it means the one freed from the flood, also according to Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr. Or it means the excellent, from their saying "ataq of horses" and "ataq of birds." Or it means the one in which the necks of sinners are freed from punishment. Ibn Atiyya said: this is rejected by morphology (tasrif, the science of word forms). End of quote. Morphology does not reject it, because he explained it as a matter of meaning. As for grammatical analysis (i'rab), "al-atiq" is a form (fa'il) in the sense of a form (muf'il), i.e., one who frees the necks of sinners. The freeing is attributed to it figuratively, since through visiting it and circumambulating it freeing occurs, and from its being one who frees it may be said: in it the necks of sinners are freed.

(Dhalika) is the predicate of an omitted subject. Ibn Atiyya estimated it as "your duty is that," or "the obligatory is that." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "the matter or the affair is that." He said: just as a writer begins a section of his book on some meaning, then when he wishes to move to another meaning he says: "This is so, and it was such."

It was also said: it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning "that" is the matter you have mentioned. It was also said it is in the accusative position, estimated as "comply with that."

A parallel to this eloquent demonstrative is the line of Zuhayr, who had earlier composed verses describing Harim:

"This! Not like one who falters in his speech
amid the generous when a speaker speaks."

He had described him before this with generosity and courage, then in this line he described him with eloquence. It is as if he said: this is his character, not like one who falters in his speech.

The sacred things (al-hurumat) are whatever is not lawful to violate. All the obligations, including the rites of hajj and others, are its sacred things. The apparent meaning is general over all obligations, but it may be restricted to what relates to hajj. Al-Kalbi said this and said: what He commanded of the rites. From Ibn Abbas: they are all the prohibitions of hajj: wrongful speech, disputation, intercourse and hunting. From Ibn Zayd: they are five: the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram), the Sacred Mosque, the Sacred House, the Sacred Month, and the forbidden thing until it becomes lawful.

The pronoun in ﴿fa-huwa﴾ refers to the verbal noun implied by His saying ﴿and whoever honours﴾, meaning: so the honouring ﴿is better for him with his Lord﴾, meaning nearness to Him and an increase in obedience to Him, for which He will reward him. The apparent meaning is that "khayr" here is not a comparative superlative.

And ﴿Lawful for you is the beast of livestock﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 1] is a refutation of what they used to forbid by their own opinion, such as the bahira and the sa'iba. By His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ He means what He stated in His Book as forbidden, and the meaning is the verse recited to you about its prohibition.

When He urged the honouring of God's sacred things and mentioned that honouring them is better for the one who honours them before God, He followed it with the command to avoid idols and false speech, because the oneness of God, the negation of partners from Him, and truthful speech are the greatest sacred things. These two were joined in one pairing because shirk falls under the category of falsehood, since the polytheist claims that the idol deserves worship. It is as if He said: ﴿so avoid﴾ worshipping ﴿the idols﴾, which are the head of falsehood, ﴿and avoid the word of falsehood﴾ entirely.

The "min" in ﴿min al-awthan﴾ is for specifying the genus (bayan al-jins), and according to them it is to be estimated as a relative clause, meaning the filth which is the idols. Whoever denies that "min" specifies the genus takes it to indicate the starting point (ibtida' al-ghaya). It is as if He forbade the filth in general and then specified for them its origin, from which it reaches them, since worship of idols encompasses every corruption and filth. According to the first view, the prohibition of the rest of the filths would be from another place than this.

Ibn Atiyya said: whoever says that "min" is partitive has inverted the meaning of the verse and corrupted it. End of quote.

Partitiveness is possible here, in that by "filth" one means the worship of idols. This has been related from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jurayj. It is as if He said: avoid from the idols the filth, which is worship, because what is forbidden of idols is only their worship. Do you not see that it is conceivable to use an idol in building or other things that the Law has not forbidden? So for the idol there are aspects, among them its worship, which is what is commanded to be avoided, and its worship is one of its aspects.

Since the word of falsehood equals disbelief, it was not joined to the filth by conjunction. Rather, it was singled out by repeating the governing verb, out of concern for avoiding it. In a hadith: "The testimony of falsehood was equated with shirk."

When He commanded avoiding the worship of idols and the word of falsehood, He struck an example for the polytheist, saying ﴿and whoever associates partners with God﴾ and so on. Al-Zamakhshari said: this comparison may be of the composite or the divided type. If it is a composite comparison, it is as if He said: whoever associates with God has destroyed himself with a destruction beyond which there is none, by depicting his state in the form of one who ﴿falls from the sky﴾ and is snatched away by ﴿the birds﴾, so that he is scattered into pieces in their crops, and ﴿the wind﴾ sweeps him away until it throws him into some distant abyss. If it is a divided comparison, then faith in its elevation is likened to the sky, the one who abandons faith and associates partners with God is likened to the one who falls from the sky, the desires that contend for his nest are likened to the birds that snatch, and the devil who casts him into the valley of misguidance is likened to the wind that carries away what it has swept into some destructive abyss. End of quote.

Nafi' read ﴿fa-takhtafuhu﴾ with a fatha on the kha' and a shadda on the ta', while the rest of the seven read it with a sukun on the kha' and a light ta'. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and al-A'mash read it with a kasra on the ta', kha', and a shadda on the ta'. From al-Hasan it is the same, except that he put a fatha on the ta' with a shadda. Al-A'mash also read ﴿takhuttuhu﴾ without a fa', with a sukun on the kha' and a light fatha on the ta'. Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read ﴿al-rayyah﴾ (the winds).

(p. 367)

﴿That﴾ is parsed like the earlier ﴿that﴾. The tafsir (interpretation) of ﴿the rites of God﴾ has been given at the beginning of Surat al-Ma'idah. Here, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and a group said: they are the sacrificial camels (al-budn al-hada'a), and honouring them means fattening them, giving them special care, and paying generously for them. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the rites are six: al-Safa, al-Marwah, the camels, the stoning pillars (al-jimar), al-Mash'ar al-Haram, 'Arafah, and al-Rukn. Honouring them means completing what is done with them. Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, Malik and Ibn Zayd said: they are all the places of the Hajj and its markers: Mina, 'Arafah, Muzdalifah, al-Safa, al-Marwah, the House, and others. This is close to the view of Zayd ibn Aslam.

It has also been said: they are the laws of His religion, and honouring them means adhering to them. The benefits are the reward. The pronoun in ﴿in them﴾ in His saying ﴿for you in them are benefits﴾ refers to the rites, which are the laws. That is: for you, in adhering to them, are benefits ﴿until a specified term﴾, which is the end of the obligation, ﴿then their place of sacrifice is﴾ problematic under this interpretation. It was said: faith and turning towards Him in prayer; likewise the intention in Hajj and 'Umrah, that is, the place of what is specifically connected with the state of ihram, ﴿the Ancient House﴾. It was also said: the meaning is, ﴿then their reward is with the Lord of the Ancient House﴾. It was said: if it were said under this interpretation that the Ancient House is Paradise, they would not be far off. The pronoun in ﴿indeed it﴾ refers to the rites, with an omitted noun, that is, ﴿indeed the honouring of them﴾, or it refers to the honouring. He attributed piety to the hearts, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Piety is here," and he pointed to his chest.

It is related from 'Umar that he gave as a gift a noble she-camel, which was requested from him for three hundred dinars. He asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to let him sell it and buy with its price camels for sacrifice, but he forbade him from that and said: "Rather, give it as a gift." The Messenger himself (ﷺ) gave a hundred camels as sacrifice, among them a camel that had a gold nose-ring belonging to Abu Jahl in its nose. Ibn 'Umar used to drive the camels adorned with cloths, and he would give away their meat and their coverings in charity. He believed that obedience to God in drawing near to Him through them and sending them to His honoured House is a great matter that must be carried out and hastened. He mentioned ﴿the hearts﴾ because the hypocrite shows piety while his heart is empty of it, so he is not diligent in performing acts of worship; whereas the sincere person has the piety of God in his heart, so he strives to perform them in sincerity.

Al-Zamakhshari said: indeed the honouring of them is among the deeds of those with ﴿the piety of the hearts﴾, so these additional terms are omitted, and the meaning does not stand without their estimate, because there must be a returning pronoun from the conditional clause to ﴿whoever﴾ to connect it. The hearts are mentioned because they are the seats of piety; when it is firmly established and settled in them, its effect appears in the other limbs. End of quotation.

What he estimated lacks a returning pronoun to the conditional clause ﴿whoever﴾. Do you not see that his statement "indeed the honouring of them is among the deeds of the hearts" contains no pronoun referring back to ﴿whoever﴾ that links the consequent clause to the conditional clause whose particle is ﴿whoever﴾? The correction of what he said would be that the estimate be ﴿whatever honouring of them is from him﴾, so the pronoun in ﴿from him﴾ refers to ﴿whoever﴾, and thus the consequent is linked to the condition.

The reading ﴿the hearts﴾ is also recited in the nominative, as the agent of the verbal noun ﴿piety﴾. The pronoun in ﴿in them﴾ refers to the camels according to the majority view. The benefits are their milk, offspring, wool, and riding on their backs, ﴿until a specified term﴾, which is when one designates them and makes them obligatory as a sacrifice (hady), so that he has no benefit from them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas in the transmission of Miqsam, and by Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak. 'Ata' said: the benefits of the sacrificial animals, after they become obligatory and are named as sacrifice, are that they may be ridden and their milk drunk when there is need, ﴿until a specified term﴾, that is, until they are slaughtered. It was said: until they are marked, so they are not ridden except in case of necessity. Abu Razin related from Ibn 'Abbas: the specified term is leaving Makkah. And from Ibn 'Abbas, ﴿until a specified term﴾ means until the departure and moving from these rites to others. It was said: the term is the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari said: until they are slaughtered, their meat is given in charity and eaten from.

The ﴿then﴾ (thumma) indicates delay in time, and it is borrowed to indicate delay in actions. The meaning is that for you in the sacrificial animals there are many benefits in your worldly life and your religion, for God is worshipped only through religious benefits. He, exalted, said: ﴿You desire the goods of this world, but God desires the Hereafter﴾ [al-Anfal: 67]. The greatest of these benefits, and the furthest in reaching benefit, is ﴿their place of sacrifice is to the Ancient House﴾, that is, the obligation of slaughtering them, or the time of its obligation, ending at the House, as in His saying ﴿an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. The intended meaning is slaughtering them in the sacred precinct (haram), which has the ruling of the House, because the haram is the protected surroundings of the House. A similar broad usage is your saying: "We reached the city," when you only approached it and your journey connected to its boundaries. It was said: the rites in the verse mean all the rituals, and ﴿their place of sacrifice is to the Ancient House﴾ rejects that. End of quotation.

Al-Qaffal said: the voluntary offering, if it perishes before reaching Makkah, its place of sacrifice is the place where it perishes; when it reaches Mina, then that is its place, and all the paths of Makkah are its place. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿then﴾ is repeated to order the clauses, because the place of sacrifice comes before the term. The meaning of the speech, according to these two groups, namely those who say Mujahid's view and those who agree with him, and those who say 'Ata's view, is ﴿then their place of sacrifice﴾ is the place of slaughter. So He mentioned the House because it is the most honoured part of the sacred precinct, and it is what the offering and other things are intended for. The term is the return to Makkah for the Tawaf al-Ifadah, and His saying ﴿then their place of sacrifice﴾ is derived from the release of the one in ihram, meaning. Then He delayed all of this to the Tawaf al-Ifadah at the Ancient House, so the House, according to this interpretation, is meant in itself. This was said by Malik in al-Muwatta'. End of quotation.

The word al-mansak is a mafal form from nasaka, and it may be a place of worship (nusuk), that is, a place of rites. It may also be a verbal noun. It may mean a place of worship in general or worship itself. It may mean a specific rite, or a specific rite which is a place of slaughter or slaughter. Al-Zamakhshari took it to mean slaughter. It is said: God prescribed for every community that they should perform the nusuk for Him, that is, slaughter for His sake, in the manner of drawing near to Him. He made the reason for this that His name, may His names be sanctified, be mentioned over the rites. End of quotation.

The regular pattern of the mafal form, from verbs whose present tense is yaf'alu with a damma on the 'ayn, is mafal with a fatha on the 'ayn, for the verbal noun, the time and the place. Most readers recited it with a fatha. The two brothers (al-Akhawan), Ibn Sa'dan, Abu Hatim from Abu 'Amr, Yunus, Mahbub and 'Abd al-Warith, except al-Qasabi from him, read it with a kasra. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the kasra in this is anomalous (shadh), and analogy does not permit it. It is likely that al-Kisa'i heard it from the Arabs. Al-Azhari said: mansak and minsak are two dialects. Mujahid said: al-mansak is slaughter and the shedding of blood. It is said: nasaka when he slaughtered, and the sacrificed animal is nasikah, whose plural is nusuk. Al-Farra' said: al-mansak in the speech of the Arabs means what is customary in goodness and righteousness. Ibn 'Arafah said: mansakan, meaning a way of obedience to God. It is said: he followed the rites of his people when he went their way. Al-Farra' said: mansakan means a festival. Qatadah said: Hajj.

﴿That﴾ is parsed like the earlier ﴿that﴾. The tafsir (interpretation) of ﴿the rites of God﴾ has been given at the beginning of Surat al-Ma'idah. Here, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and a group said: they are the sacrificial camels (al-budn al-hada'a), and honouring them means fattening them, giving them special care, and paying generously for them. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the rites are six: al-Safa, al-Marwah, the camels, the stoning pillars (al-jimar), al-Mash'ar al-Haram, 'Arafah, and al-Rukn. Honouring them means completing what is done with them. Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, Malik and Ibn Zayd said: they are all the places of the Hajj and its markers: Mina, 'Arafah, Muzdalifah, al-Safa, al-Marwah, the House, and others. This is close to the view of Zayd ibn Aslam.

It has also been said: they are the laws of His religion, and honouring them means adhering to them. The benefits are the reward. The pronoun in ﴿in them﴾ in His saying ﴿for you in them are benefits﴾ refers to the rites, which are the laws. That is: for you, in adhering to them, are benefits ﴿until a specified term﴾, which is the end of the obligation, ﴿then their place of sacrifice is﴾ problematic under this interpretation. It was said: faith and turning towards Him in prayer; likewise the intention in Hajj and 'Umrah, that is, the place of what is specifically connected with the state of ihram, ﴿the Ancient House﴾. It was also said: the meaning is, ﴿then their reward is with the Lord of the Ancient House﴾. It was said: if it were said under this interpretation that the Ancient House is Paradise, they would not be far off. The pronoun in ﴿indeed it﴾ refers to the rites, with an omitted noun, that is, ﴿indeed the honouring of them﴾, or it refers to the honouring. He attributed piety to the hearts, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Piety is here," and he pointed to his chest.

It is related from 'Umar that he gave as a gift a noble she-camel, which was requested from him for three hundred dinars. He asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to let him sell it and buy with its price camels for sacrifice, but he forbade him from that and said: "Rather, give it as a gift." The Messenger himself (ﷺ) gave a hundred camels as sacrifice, among them a camel that had a gold nose-ring belonging to Abu Jahl in its nose. Ibn 'Umar used to drive the camels adorned with cloths, and he would give away their meat and their coverings in charity. He believed that obedience to God in drawing near to Him through them and sending them to His honoured House is a great matter that must be carried out and hastened. He mentioned ﴿the hearts﴾ because the hypocrite shows piety while his heart is empty of it, so he is not diligent in performing acts of worship; whereas the sincere person has the piety of God in his heart, so he strives to perform them in sincerity.

Al-Zamakhshari said: indeed the honouring of them is among the deeds of those with ﴿the piety of the hearts﴾, so these additional terms are omitted, and the meaning does not stand without their estimate, because there must be a returning pronoun from the conditional clause to ﴿whoever﴾ to connect it. The hearts are mentioned because they are the seats of piety; when it is firmly established and settled in them, its effect appears in the other limbs. End of quotation.

What he estimated lacks a returning pronoun to the conditional clause ﴿whoever﴾. Do you not see that his statement "indeed the honouring of them is among the deeds of the hearts" contains no pronoun referring back to ﴿whoever﴾ that links the consequent clause to the conditional clause whose particle is ﴿whoever﴾? The correction of what he said would be that the estimate be ﴿whatever honouring of them is from him﴾, so the pronoun in ﴿from him﴾ refers to ﴿whoever﴾, and thus the consequent is linked to the condition.

﴿لِيَذْكُرُوا اسْمَ اللَّهِ﴾ means: We commanded them to mention the name of God at their sacrificial slaughter, and that the slaughter be for Him, because He is the provider of that. Then he turned to those present and said: ﴿فَإلَهُكم إلَهٌ واحِدٌ فَلَهُ أسْلِمُوا﴾ ("Your God is one God, so submit to Him"), meaning: submit in obedience. Just as God is one, it is obligatory that the sacrifice be devoted to Him sincerely and not associated with anything else. The explanation of *al-ikhbat* (humble submission) has already passed. 'Amr ibn Aws said: "The *mukhbitun* (the humble) are those who do not wrong, and when they are wronged, they do not retaliate."

The majority read ﴿والمُقِيمِي الصَّلاةِ﴾ with a *khafd* (genitive) ending, through the *idafa* (genitive construction), and the nun was dropped on account of it. Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Hasan, and Abu 'Amr in one narration read (*al-salata*) with a *nasb* (accusative) ending, and the nun was dropped on account of it. Ibn Mas'ud, al-A'mash, and *al-muqimina* with the nun read (*al-salata*) with the accusative. al-Dahhak read: *wa-al-muqimu al-salata*.

The giving of good news to those who are characterized by humility fits here, because the rites of the Hajj, such as removing one's garments, stripping of stitched clothing, uncovering the head, and moving about in those dusty, enclosed places, and engaging in arduous acts whose meaning none knows except God Most High, indicate pure submission and extreme humility, in that a person departs from what is familiar to him into strange acts. For this reason He described them with humility, and with awe when God Most High is mentioned, and with patience over what afflicted them of hardships, and with establishing the prayers in places where none establish them except the faithful who have been chosen, and with spending from what He has provided them, and among it the offerings which they exaggerate in their value.

The majority read ﴿والبُدْنَ﴾ with a sukun on the *dal*. al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Shayba, and 'Isa read it with a *damma* on it, which is the original form. It was also narrated from Abu Ja'far and Nafi'. Ibn Abi Ishaq also read it with a *damma* on the *ya'* and the *dal*, and with a shadda on the nun. This may be a single noun patterned on *fu'ul* like *'utul*, or the shadda may be from the permissible doubling in pausal form, with the connected reading treated as if it were a pause. The majority read ﴿والبُدْنَ﴾ with the accusative under *al-ishtighal* (the verb-preoccupation construction), meaning: and We made (*al-budna*) [...]. It was also read in the nominative under *al-ibtida'* (nominal beginning), with (*lakum*) meaning *li-ajlikum* ("for your sake"), and ﴿مِن شَعائِرِ﴾ is in the position of the second object.

The meaning of ﴿مِن شَعائِرِ اللَّهِ﴾ is: from the markers of the Sharia which God has prescribed, and He attributed them to His name, Exalted, to magnify them. ﴿لَكم فِيها خَيْرٌ﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: benefit in this world and reward in the Hereafter. al-Suddi said: reward. al-Nakha'i said: whoever needs its back may ride it, and whoever needs its milk may drink it.

﴿عَلَيْها صَوافَّ﴾ means: upon their necks. Mujahid said: tied. Ibn 'Umar said: standing, with their forelegs bound with fetters. Ibn 'Isa said: lined up.

Mentioning God's name means saying at the time of the slaughter: "God is greatest, there is no god but God, and God is greatest. O God, from You and to You."

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Zayd ibn Aslam, Shaqiq, Sulayman al-Taymi, and al-A'raj read: *sawafiyyu*, plural of *safiya*. 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read the *ya'* with tanwin. al-Zamakhshari said: the tanwin is a substitute for a letter at pause. End of quotation.

The better view is that it is according to the dialect of those who make diptote words take tanwin, especially the plural of the final form. For this reason some said that *al-sarf* (taking tanwin) is common in the plural, to the point that some claimed it was the most frequent usage. Meaning: pure, exclusively for the face of God Most High, associating nothing with Him in them, as the pre-Islamic people used to associate.

al-Hasan also read *sawaff* like *'awarr*, which is according to those who say *fakasartu ghara lahmihi* ("I broke the flesh's bone"), meaning *'aryan* ("bare"), and the saying: *a'ti al-qaws bariyaha* ("give the bow to its carver").

'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baqir, Qatada, Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, al-Kalbi, and al-A'mash, in a variant from him, read *sawafin* with a nun. *Al-safina* from the camels is one that rests on the tip of one foot after becoming settled on three legs, and it is most commonly used of horses.

﴿فَإذا وجَبَتْ جُنُوبُها﴾ is an expression for their falling to the ground after being slaughtered. Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Mujahid, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, and al-Kalbi said: *al-qani'* is the one who asks, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who approaches without asking. A group reversed this.

al-Tabari reported from Ibn 'Abbas: *al-qani'* is the one who is content with what is given to him, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who approaches without asking. He also reported from him: *al-qani'* is the one who abstains, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who asks. From Mujahid: *al-qani'* is the neighbor, even if he is wealthy. Qatada said: *al-qani'* is from contentment, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who approaches for asking. It was also said: *al-mu'tarr* is the visiting friend.

Abu Raja' read *al-qanʿ* without an alif, meaning *al-qani'*, dropping the alif as in *al-hadhar* and *al-hadhir*. al-Hasan read *wal-mu'tarri* as an active participle from *i'tara*. 'Amr and Isma'il read *wal-mu'tarr* with a kasra on the *ra'* without a *ya'*; this is the transmission of Ibn Khalawayh. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi in *Kitab al-Lawami'* said: Abu Raja', in a variant from him, and Ibn 'Ubayd read *wal-mu'tari* in the pattern *mufta'al*. From Ibn 'Abbas through the narration of al-Muqri': *wal-mu'tarr*, meaning *al-mu'tari*, but he dropped the *ya'* for lightness, being satisfied with the kasra in its place. The same came from Abu Raja'.

Ibn Mas'ud said: the offering is in three parts. Ja'far ibn Muhammad said: I feed the one who is content and the one who approaches, one third; the wretched poor, one third; and my family, one third. Ibn al-Musayyib said: the owner of the offering has no share of it except a quarter. All of this is by way of recommendation, not obligation, as Ibn 'Atiyya said.

﴿كَذَلِكَ سَخَّرَها لَكم﴾ means: in the same manner He subjected them to you. ﴿سَخَّرْناها لَكُمْ﴾ means: you take them compliant, so you tie them and restrain them with their legs bound, and you stab them in their chests. God Most High bestowed this favor upon them. Were it not for God's subjecting them, you would not have been able to, and they would not be less powerful than some of the wild beasts which are smaller in body and weaker in strength. The camels that have endured are sufficient as a witness and a lesson.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: just as We commanded you concerning them with all of this, We subjected them to you. ﴿لَنْ يَنالَ اللَّهَ لُحُومُها ولا دِماؤُها﴾ Mujahid said: the Muslims wanted to do what the polytheists did, slaughtering and cutting the flesh placed around the Ka'ba, and splashing the Ka'ba around with blood, seeking nearness to God, so this verse was revealed. Ibn 'Abbas reported something close to this. The meaning is: the flesh given in charity and the blood spilled in slaughter will not reach God's pleasure. The intended meaning is the owners of the flesh and blood. The meaning is: the sacrificers and those who draw near will not please their Lord except by observing the intention, sincerity, and caution with the conditions of piety in the lawfulness of what they offer and other Sharia safeguards and commands of scrupulousness. If they do not observe that, the sacrifice and nearness will not avail them, even if it be abundant. Al-Zamakhshari said this, and it is hyperbole in wording.

Malik ibn Dinar, al-A'raj, Ibn Ya'mar, al-Zuhri, Ishaq al-Kufi from 'Asim, al-Za'farani, and Ya'qub read it. Ibn Khalawayh said: *tanalhu al-taqwa* with the *ta'* [feminine]: Yahya ibn Ya'mar and al-Jahdari. Zayd ibn 'Ali read *luhumuha wa-la dimauha* with the accusative, and *wa-lakin yanaluhu* with a *damma* on the *ya'*.

He repeated the mention of the blessing of subjection. al-Zamakhshari said: so that you may thank God for His guidance to you, by making known His religion and the rites of His Hajj, by declaring His greatness and proclaiming His oneness. He abridged the speech by including the sense of thanks in the magnifying and giving it the same transitivity.

Indeed, God defends those who believe. Indeed, God does not love every treacherous ingrate. (22:38)

Permission has been given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged; and indeed God is capable of giving them victory. (22:39)

They are those who were expelled from their homes without right, only because they said, "Our Lord is God." Had God not repelled some people by means of others, monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in which the name of God is much mentioned would have been demolished. God will surely help those who help Him; indeed God is Powerful, Mighty. (22:40)

They are those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And to God belongs the outcome of all matters. (22:41)

If they deny you, the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud have denied before them, (22:42)

and the people of Abraham and the people of Lot, (22:43)

and the companions of Madyan. And Moses was denied, but I gave the disbelievers respite, then I seized them. So how was My rejection! (22:44)

How many a town We destroyed while it was wrongdoing; it lies in ruins over its roofs, and [how many] an abandoned well and a lofty palace! (22:45)

Will they not travel through the land so that they may have hearts with which to understand or ears with which to hear? For indeed, it is not eyes that go blind, but hearts that are in the breasts that go blind. (22:46)

They ask you to hasten the punishment, but God will not fail His promise. Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count. (22:47)

And how many a town I gave respite while it was wrongdoing; then I seized it, and to Me is the destination. (22:48)

Say, "O mankind, I am only a clear warner to you." (22:49)

So those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and noble provision. (22:50)

But those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, they are the companions of the Blazing Fire. (22:51)

We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he spoke a wish, Satan threw [something] into his wish. But God abolishes what Satan throws in, then God establishes His verses; and God is Knowing, Wise. (22:52)

That He may make what Satan throws in a trial for those in whose hearts is disease and whose hearts are hardened. Indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme dissension. (22:53)

And that those who were given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, so they believe in it and their hearts humble before Him. Indeed, God is the Guide of those who believe to a straight path. (22:54)

And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them suddenly or there comes to them the punishment of a barren day. (22:55)

Sovereignty that Day belongs to God; He will judge between them. So those who believed and did righteous deeds will be in Gardens of Bliss. (22:56)

But those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, for them is a humiliating punishment. (22:57)

And those who emigrated in the way of God and then were killed or died, God will surely provide for them a good provision; and indeed, God is the best of providers. (22:58)

He will surely admit them to an entrance that they will be pleased with; and indeed, God is Knowing, Forbearing. (22:59)

That [is so]. And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with and then is wronged again, God will surely support him; indeed, God is Pardoning, Forgiving. (22:60)

That is because God causes the night to enter the day and causes the day to enter the night, and because God is Hearing, Seeing. (22:61)

That is because God is the Truth, and what they invoke other than Him is falsehood, and because God is the Most High, the Great. (22:62)

Have you not considered that God sends down water from the sky, and the earth becomes green? Indeed, God is Subtle, Acquainted. (22:63)

To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth; and indeed, God is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy. (22:64)

Have you not considered that God has subjected to you what is on the earth and the ship that sails through the sea by His command, and He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission? Indeed, God is Kind and Merciful to the people. (22:65)

And it is He who gave you life, then will cause you to die, then will give you life [again]. Indeed, mankind is ungrateful. (22:66)

For every community We have appointed rites which they perform, so let them not dispute with you in the matter; and invite to your Lord, for you are surely on a straight guidance. (22:67)

And if they argue with you, say, "God is most knowing of what you do." (22:68)

God will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which you used to differ. (22:69)

Do you not know that God knows what is in the heaven and the earth? Indeed, that is in a Book; indeed, that is easy for God. (22:70)

And they worship other than God that for which He has sent down no authority and of which they have no knowledge. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers. (22:71)

And when Our clear verses are recited to them, you can recognize denial on the faces of those who disbelieve; they almost attack those who recite Our verses to them. Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that? The Fire, which God has promised those who disbelieve; and wretched is the destination." (22:72)

O mankind, a parable has been presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those you invoke other than God will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it. And if the fly should snatch away from them anything, they could not rescue it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought. (22:73)

They have not appraised God with His true appraisal. Indeed, God is Powerful, Mighty. (22:74)

God selects messengers from the angels and from mankind; indeed, God is Hearing, Seeing. (22:75)

He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and to God are returned all matters. (22:76)

O you who believe, bow, prostrate, worship your Lord, and do good that you may succeed. (22:77)

And strive for God with the striving due to Him. He has chosen you and has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty; [it is] the religion of your father Abraham. He named you "Muslims" before, and in this [Revelation], that the Messenger may be a witness over you and you may be witnesses over the people. So establish prayer, give zakat, and hold fast to God; He is your Protector, and what an excellent Protector and what an excellent Helper! (22:78)

Al-Hadm (demolition): known; it is the tearing down of what has been built. A poet said:

"Every house, however long its occupancy, upon its supports is bound to be demolished."

Al-Sawma'a (the monastic cell, i.e., the place of worship): its form is fa'wala; it is a tall, isolated structure with a sharp top. Al-asma' among men means one of sharp speech. Before Islam it was specific to Christian monks and to the Sabians' worshippers, as stated by Qatada; then it came to be used for the minaret of Muslims. Al-bi'a (churches): the churches of the Christians, singular bai'a. It was also said: the synagogues of the Jews. Al-bi'r (well): from "ba'rat," meaning she dug; it is feminine on the pattern fi'l in the sense of maf'ul, though it may be masculine in the sense of qalib (a dug well). Ta'til al-shay' (rendering a thing idle): nullifying its benefits. Al-'uqm (barrenness): abstention from childbearing. It is said: a barren woman ('aqim) and a barren man who cannot father children; the plural is 'uqm. Its root is cutting; hence "a king who is 'aqim," meaning he cuts off the kinship ties by killing. And al-'aqim is the one whose childbearing has been cut off. Abu 'Ubayd said: al-'uqm means blocking; it is said: a woman whose womb is ma'quma, i.e., her womb is blocked. Al-sat'w: subjugation. Ibn 'Isa said: al-sat'wa is displaying what terrifies for the sake of intimidation. Al-dhubab: the known creature; its plural is dhubab with kasra or damma on the dhal, and dhabb; al-midhabba is what flies are driven away with; dhubab al-sayf is its tip; al-'ayn is its pupil; and the teeth of camels. Salabtu al-shay': I snatched it quickly. Istanqadha: istaf'ala used in the sense of af'ala, i.e., anqadha, like aballa and istaballa.

* *

[p. 373]

It is narrated that when the believers became numerous in Mecca, the disbelievers harmed them, and some of them emigrated to the land of Abyssinia. Some believers in Mecca wanted to kill whichever disbelievers they could reach, and to resort to deception and treachery. Then [verses] were revealed up to His saying "ungrateful." In them is a promise of defense and a prohibition of betrayal. He singled out the believers for defense and support, and He gave the reason: that He does not love their enemies, the treacherous ones who betray God and the Messenger, the disbelievers who reject His blessings. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He mentioned a number of things done during the Hajj, and the polytheists had prevented the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the year of al-Hudaybiyya and harmed those among the believers who were in Mecca, God revealed these verses, giving good news to the believers of His defense of them, indicating their support, His permission for them to fight, and their establishment in the land by returning them to their homes and the conquest of Mecca; and that the outcome of all matters returns to God the Exalted. God the Exalted said: "And the final outcome is for the righteous" (7:128).

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, and Nafi' read "yudafi'u" and "wa-law la difa'u Allah." Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read "yadfa'u" and "wa-law la daf'u." The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir read "yudafi'u" and "wa-law la daf'u." The form fa'ala here has the meaning of the unaugmented verb, as in jawadtu and juztu. Al-Akhfash said: daf'a is more common than dafa'a. Al-Zahrawi related that difa' is the verbal noun of dafa'a, like hasaba hisaban. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "yudafi'u" is preferable, because some people have appeared to the believers who push them back and harm them, so their resistance comes, and their pushing back becomes a defense on their behalf. End.

That is, the form fa'ala is for the mutual sharing of the agent and the patient in wording, with sharing in meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: whoever reads "yudafi'u" means that it intensifies the defense on their behalf, as one who contends in opposition does, because the action of one who contends comes out stronger and more emphatic. End.

He, the Exalted, did not mention what He repels from them, so that it would be more majestic, greater, and more general. When the believers emigrated to Medina, God gave them permission to fight.

Nafi', 'Asim, and Abu 'Amr read the hamza of "udhina" with a damma, and the rest of the seven read it with a fatha. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs read "yuqatalun" with a fatha on the ta', and the rest read it with a kasra. The object of the permission is omitted, i.e., "in fighting," indicated by "yuqatilun." And He gave the reason for the permission: "because they were wronged." They used to come to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with bruised and wounded wounds, and he would tell them: "Be patient, for I have not been commanded to fight," until he emigrated. This is (p. 374) the first verse in which permission to fight was given, after being forbidden in about seventy-some verses. It was said: it was revealed concerning a people who went out as emigrants, and the polytheists of Mecca confronted them, so He gave them permission to fight them.

"And indeed God is capable of giving them victory": a promise of victory and an announcement of His defending them.

"Those who were expelled": in a genitive position as a qualifier of "those," or a substitute, or in an accusative position with "a'ni," or in a nominative position by supposing "hum." "Illa an yaqulu" (except that they say) is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), since "yaqulu" is in an accusative position, and as it is disjunctive, the governing verb cannot be directed at it; it is thus assumed to be equivalent to "lakinna" (but) in meaning, because if you said: "those who were expelled from their homes except that they say, 'Our Lord is God,'" it would not be correct. In contrast, with "there is no one in the house except a donkey," the exception is disjunctive but the governing verb can be directed at it, so you say: "there is in the house only a donkey." This allows both the accusative and the nominative: the accusative for the Hijazis and the nominative for the Tamim. But with a construction like this, the Arabs agree on the accusative. Abu Ishaq allowed the genitive here as a substitute, and al-Zamakhshari followed him, saying: "an yaqulu" is in a genitive position as a substitute for "haqq" (right), meaning "without any cause other than monotheism, which should be the cause of acknowledgment and empowerment, not the cause of expulsion and punishment." A similar example is: "Do you resent us except that we believed?" (5:59). End.

[p. 375]

What he (al-Zamakhshari) permitted as a *badal* (substitute, or appositive) is not permissible, because a *badal* occurs only when it is preceded by a negation, a prohibition, or an interrogative with the meaning of negation, as in: *ma qama ahadun illa Zaydun* (no one stood except Zayd), *wa la yadribu ahadun illa Zaydun* (and no one strikes except Zayd), and *wa hal yadribu ahadun illa Zaydun* (and does anyone strike except Zayd?). But when the sentence is affirmative or imperative, the *badal* is not permissible. One does not say *qama al-qawmu illa Zaydun* ("the people stood except Zayd") with *illa Zaydun* as a *badal*, nor *la yadribu al-qawma illa Zaydun* ("he does not strike the people except Zayd") as a *badal*, because a *badal* occurs only where the governing element (*al-'amil*) exercises its influence over it. If you said *qama illa Zaydun* or *liyadrib illa 'Umaru*, it would not be permissible. And if you said outside the Qur'an, *akhraja al-nasa min diyarihim illa bi-an yaqulu la ilaha illa Allah*, it would not be a meaningful sentence. This is the case when one imagines that *illa an yaqulu* ("except that they say") is in a position of *jarr* (genitive) as a *badal* for the noun not annexed to *haqq* ("truth"). As for it being a *badal* for *haqq*, as the author (al-Zamakhshari) explicitly states, this is utterly corrupt, because it would necessitate that the *badal* follows *ghayr* (the word "other"), so the construction would become *bi-ghayri an yaqulu* ("other than that they say"), and this is not valid. Even if *illa* were interpreted as *bi-ghayr* (in the sense of "other than"), as is done in the negation of *ma marartu bi-ahadin illa Zaydin*, making it a *badal*, it would still not be valid, because the construction would become *bi-ghayri ghayri qawlihim Rabbuna Allah* ("other than the other than their saying 'Our Lord is Allah'"), so you would be annexing *ghayr* to *ghayr* when they are identical, and thus it would become *bi-ghayri ghayrin*. In *ma marartu bi-ahadin illa Zaydin*, it is valid to say *ma marartu bi-ghayri Zaydin* ("I did not pass by other than Zayd"). Furthermore, when al-Zamakhshari illustrated the *badal*, he interpreted it as *bi-ghayri muwajjibin siwa al-tawhid* ("by other than an affirming [cause] besides monotheism"), and this is an illustration of the *sifa* (qualifying adjunct, attribute); he made *illa* to mean *siwa* ("besides"). This is valid for the *sifa*, so he confused the chapter of the *sifa* with the chapter of the *badal*. It is permissible for you to say *marartu bi-l-qawmi illa Zaydin* as a *sifa* (attributive qualifier), not as a *badal*.

﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others﴾ (the verse). In it there is an exhortation to fight, the fighting that had been permitted previously. He (Exalted is He) had established this custom in past nations, by which the affair would be organized, the laws would be upheld, the places of worship would be protected from demolition, and their adherents from killing and dispersal. It is as though, when He said ﴿Permission has been given to those who are fought against﴾, it was said: then let the believers fight. Without fighting, the truth would be overcome in every nation. Consider the coming of His saying ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Baqarah: 251], following the fighting of Talut against Jalut, and Dawud (David) killed Jalut. He (Exalted is He) informed us that were it not for that repelling, the earth would be corrupted. So it is likewise here.

Ali ibn Abi Talib said: "And were it not for Allah's repelling the disbelievers through the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) from the Followers and those after them." Al-Zamakhshari took Ali's statement, found it good, and expanded upon it, saying: "Allah's repelling some people by means of others is His making them manifest, and empowering the believers among them over the disbelievers through striving (mujahadah). Were it not for that, the polytheists would have overpowered the adherents of the different religions in their times, and would have demolished their places of worship. They would not have left churches (biya') for the Christians, nor their monks' cells (sawami'), nor synagogues (salawat) for the Jews, nor mosques for the Muslims, and the polytheists would have prevailed over the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) against the Muslims and against the People of the Book who were under their protection, and they would have demolished the places of worship of both groups." End of quote.

Mujahid said: "﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling﴾ the oppression of a people by the testimony of upright witnesses and the like." Others said: He repels the oppression of oppressors by the justice of rulers. A group said: He repels punishment by the supplication of the righteous. Qutrub said: by retaliation (qisas) against lives. It was also said: by the prophets against the believers. Al-Hasan said: were it not for the security of Islam, the places of worship of the People of the *dhimma* (protected non-Muslims) would have been ruined. The meaning of repelling by fighting is more fitting for the verse and more effective in repelling corruption.

The two Harams (the readers of Makkah and Madinah), Ayyub, Qatadah, Talhah, Za'idah (on the authority of al-A'mash), and al-Za'farani read *lahudimat* (with the verb in the form with single emphasis, *lahudimat*), while the rest of the Seven and a group read it with doubled emphasis (*lahuddimat*). Since the places are many, it was appropriate to use the intensive form, because of the multiplicity of places, so the demolition is repeated for their multiplicity. The majority read *wa-salawatun* as the plural of *salat* (prayer, here in the sense of Jewish places of prayer). Ja'far ibn Muhammad read *wa-sulawatun* with a *damma* on the *sad* and the *lam*. Ibn Khalawayh reported from him *silwatun* with a sukun on the *lam* and a kasra on the *sad*. It is also reported from al-Juhdari and al-Juhdari *sulawatun* with a *damma* on the *sad* and a *fatha* on the *lam*. It is reported from al-Kalbi and Abu al-'Aliyah with a *fatha* on the *sad* and sukun on the *lam*: *salwatun*. And from al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf and al-Juhdari also: *wa-sulutun*, meaning Christian places of worship, with two *dammas* without an *alif*. Mujahid likewise, except that he read it with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and an *alif* after it. Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi read *wa-sulusun* with two *dammas* without an *alif* and with a *tha'* dotted with three dots. Likewise it came from Abu Raja', al-Juhdari, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Mujahid, except that there is an *alif* after the *tha'*. Ikrimah read: *wa-silwithan* with a kasra on the *sad*, sukun on the *lam*, a kasra on the following *waw*, followed by a *ya'*, followed by a *tha'* dotted with three dots, followed by an *alif*. Al-Juhdari also read *sulwathun* with a *damma* on the *sad*, sukun on the *lam*, an open *waw* followed by an *alif*, followed by a *tha'* with three dots. Ibn Mujahid reported that it was read likewise, except with a kasra on the *sad*. Ibn Khalawayh and Ibn 'Atiyyah reported from al-Hajjaj and al-Juhdari *sulubun* with a *ba'* with one dot, on the pattern of *ku'ub* (plural of *ka'b*), the plural of *salib* (cross), like *zarif* and *zurif*, and *asinah* and *asun*. This is an anomalous plural, namely the plural of *fa'il* on the pattern *fu'ul*. These are thirteen readings, and the one with the *tha'* dotted with three dots (the Arabic letter *tha'*) is the other.

It was said: They are the synagogues of the Jews, and the word is Syriac, which entered the language of the Arabs. It was also said: it is Hebrew. The reading of the majority should be understood as referring to the prayers known in the religions. As for the other forms, in which the Arabs played with the pronunciation through distortion and alteration, one should look at what the word means in the language from which it was transmitted, and interpret it accordingly. Harun reported from Abu 'Amr *wa-salawatu* like the reading of the community, except that he does not give the *ta'* tanwin, as if he made it the name of a place like the places mentioned before it, and as if it were a proper name, so he withheld its declension because of its status as a proper noun and its foreignness. Thus the readings were completed at fourteen readings. The most evident point regarding the enumeration of these places is that it is according to the beliefs of the nations: the *sawami'* are for the monks; it was said they are for the Sabians; the *biya'* are for the Christians; the *salawat* are for the Jews; and the *masajid* are for the Muslims. This was said by Khusayf. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The most evident view is that by them He intended emphasis in mentioning places of worship. These names are shared by the nations in their referents, except *biy'ah*, which is specific to the Christians in the customary usage of the language. The meanings of these names pertain to the nations that have a scripture from ancient times. He did not mention the Magians or the polytheists in this verse, because they have nothing that would require protecting it, and the mention of God is found only among the people of the revealed laws. End of quote.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in His saying *yudhkaru fiha* ("in which the name is mentioned") refers to all the places together. This was also said by al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Thus *yudhkaru* is a descriptive qualifier (*sifah*) of the *masajid* (mosques). If we take *al-salawat* to refer to the acts that the adherents of the religious laws perform in prayer, then this would either be by omitting a genitive phrase, meaning "and the places of prayers" (*wa-mawadi'u salawatin*), or by implicitly including in *lahuddimat* the meaning of *u'attilat* ("were left idle"), so that the idleness becomes a common term shared between the places and the acts. The mention of the mosques last is either because of the antiquity of the others and the recency of these, or because of a transition from the more noble to the most noble.

God swore by an oath that He would surely help those who help Him, that is, He helps His religion and His allies. His help (Exalted is He) is for His allies to triumph over their enemies, by the sword and by argument. In this there is an exhortation to fight. Then He informed us that He is powerful to help them and is *'Aziz* (Mighty), who cannot be overcome.

The apparent view is that the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) of ﴿those who, if We establish them in the land﴾ may be the same as the analysis of ﴿those who were expelled﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a *badal* for *man yansuruhu* ("the one who helps Him"). The *tamkin* (establishment) is authority and the execution of command over creation. The apparent view is that it describes those permitted to fight, namely the emigrants (*muhajirun*). In it there is a report of the unseen, concerning what their conduct would be if He established them in the land and extended for them in this world, and how they would carry out the matter of religion. It is related from 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him: "By Allah, this is praise before trial," meaning that Allah praised them before they had produced the good that they produced. They said: In it is evidence for the soundness of the affair of the Rightly-Guided Caliphs, because Allah (Exalted is He) did not make establishment and the execution of command together with just conduct to be for others among the emigrants; there is no share in that for the Ansar or the *tulaqa'* (those freed at the conquest of Makkah). In the verse He took a covenant upon whoever Allah establishes, that he should do what the verse ordains upon establishment. It was said: it was revealed concerning the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). From al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliyah: they are his community (peace be upon him). From Ikrimah: they are the people of the five daily prayers, which is close to what came before. Ibn Abi Najih said: they are the rulers. Al-Dahhak said: it is a condition that Allah imposed upon whoever He grants sovereignty.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the emigrants, the Ansar, and the Followers.

﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of affairs﴾: a threat to the one who opposes what is ordained upon establishment. ﴿And if they deny you﴾ (the verse): in it is consolation to the Messenger concerning the denial by the earlier nations mentioned for their prophets, and a warning to Quraysh, since He compared them to the nations that denied and were punished. He attributed the verb with the feminine marker because He meant the community and the tribe. He made the verb passive in ﴿and Musa was denied﴾ to indicate that his people did not deny him, but rather the Copts denied him. ﴿Then I gave the disbelievers respite﴾, that is, I granted them a delay and postponed punishment from them, though I knew what they did. In His saying ﴿Then I gave the disbelievers respite﴾ there is the ordering of respite upon the attribute of disbelief. Likewise, Allah gave Quraysh respite, then seized them at the Battle of Badr, at the conquest of Makkah, and at other times. The seizing is a metaphor for punishment and destruction. *Al-nakir* (denial, rejection) is a verbal noun, like *al-nadhir*, here meant as a verbal noun. The meaning is: how was My denunciation of them, and the transformation of their good state into an evil one, their life into destruction, and their inhabited places into ruin? This is an interrogative that carries the sense of wonder, as though it were said: how terrible was My denunciation of them. Overall it is a warning to Quraysh. ﴿Fa-ka'ayyin﴾ is for multiplicity, and it is possible that it is in the nominative position as a subject, and in the accusative position by the construction of *ishtighal* (the verb being governed by a pronoun suffix that is elided and the noun is topicalized).

Abu 'Amr and a group read *ahlaktuha* with the first-person singular *ta'* (I destroyed it), while the majority read it with the royal *nun* (we destroyed it). ﴿While she was wrongdoing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*). ﴿So it lies in ruins upon its foundations﴾: the explanation of this sentence was given in al-Baqarah in His saying ﴿or like the one who passed by a town﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the grammatical position of the two clauses, i.e. ﴿while she is wrongdoing, so she is in ruins﴾? I say: the first is in the accusative position as a circumstantial element, and the second has no position because it is conjoined to *ahlaknaha* (We destroyed it), and this verb has no position." End of quote.

What he said is not good, because the most preferable analysis of *fa-ka'ayyin* is that it is an inceptive (*mubtada'*) noun, and the predicate is the clause *ahlaknaha* (We destroyed it), so it is in the nominative position; and what is conjoined to the predicate is a predicate, so the words *fa-hiya khawiyah* ("so it lies in ruins") are in the nominative position. However, al-Zamakhshari's view is supported on the less common analysis, namely that *fa-ka'ayyin* is in the accusative by the construction of *ishtighal* with an implied verb, so the clause *ahlaknaha* is the explanatory clause for that verb. In this case, this explanatory clause has no position, and what is conjoined to it has no position either.

Al-Jahdari, al-Hasan, and a group read *mu'attalatin* with a lightened form, as it is said: *'uttilat al-bi'r* and *a'taltuha*, so *fa-'atalat*, with a *fatha* on the *ta'*. And *'atilat al-mar'ah min al-hulyi* (the woman was without ornaments) with a kasra on the *ta'*. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of *mu'attalah* (abandoned) is that it is inhabited: water is in it, and the implements for drawing water are with it, except that it has been left idle, that is, abandoned, and no water is drawn from it because its people have perished. *Al-mashid* is the one plastered with gypsum, or the one whose construction is elevated. The meaning is: how many towns did We destroy, and how many wells did We leave idle, cut off from their drawers, and ﴿and a lofty palace﴾, which We emptied of its residents. The rest is omitted because the word *mu'attalah* indicates it. End of quote.

(وبِئْرٍ) (وقَصْرٍ) are conjoined (ma'tufani) to ﴿مِن قَرْيَةٍ﴾ (from a town). (ومِن قَرْيَةٍ) is a specifying noun (tamyiz) for (كَأيِّنْ) (ka'ayyin, "how many"). (وكَأيِّنْ) requires multiplicity (al-taksir), so this indicates that by "a well" and "a palace" no specific one is meant. Although destruction does occur to a specific thing, that is in terms of actual occurrence, not in terms of the implication of the wording. It should be that (وبِئْرٍ) (وقَصْرٍ), insofar as they are conjoined to ﴿مِن قَرْيَةٍ﴾, carry the sense: "I destroyed them both just as I destroyed the town," reported about (كَأيِّنْ), which is the town in meaning. The intended meaning is the people of the town, the well, and the palace. To take ﴿وبِئْرٍ مُعَطَّلَةٍ وقَصْرٍ مَشِيدٍ﴾ as conjoined to (عُرُوشِها) (its roofs) is ignorance of eloquence (jahl bil-fasaha). He described the palace as (مَشِيدٌ) (mashid) and not as (مُشَيَّدٌ) (mushayyad), as in His saying ﴿فِي بُرُوجٍ مُشَيَّدَةٍ﴾ [an-Nisa': 78], because that is a plural form, which suits multiplicity there, whereas this is singular. Also, (مُشَيَّدٌ) would be the end of a verse (fasilat ayah) for rhyme.

Some exegetes have specified this well. From Ibn 'Abbas it is reported that it belonged to the people of 'Adan in Yemen, and it is ar-Rass. From Ka'b al-Ahbar it is reported that the palace was built by 'Ad the second, who is Mundhir ibn 'Ad ibn Iram ibn 'Ad. From ad-Dahhak and others: the well is in Hadramawt, in the land of ash-Shihr, and the palace overlooks the summit of a mountain that cannot be climbed, while the well is at its foot; the wind does not leave anything that falls into it. It is narrated that Salih, peace be upon him, descended there with four thousand men who had believed in him, and Allah saved them from the punishment. It is in Hadramawt, and it was named so because Salih, when he arrived there, died, and there is a town near the well named Hadur, which the people of Salih built, and they appointed over themselves Jalis ibn Julas. They remained there for a time, then they disbelieved and worshipped an idol, and they sent to them Hanzalah ibn Safwan, and it is said: his name was Shurayh ibn Safwan, as a prophet, and they killed him in the market, so Allah destroyed them to the last one and left their well idle and ruined their palace. From Imam Abu al-Qasim al-Ansari that he said: "I saw the grave of Salih in ash-Sham in a town called 'Akka, so how could it be in Hadramawt?"

[p. 371]

Indeed, God defends those who believe. Indeed, God does not love every treacherous ingrate. (22:38)

Permission has been given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged; and indeed God is capable of giving them victory. (22:39)

They are those who were expelled from their homes without right, only because they said, "Our Lord is God." Had God not repelled some people by means of others, monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in which the name of God is much mentioned would have been demolished. God will surely help those who help Him; indeed God is Powerful, Mighty. (22:40)

They are those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And to God belongs the outcome of all matters. (22:41)

If they deny you, the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud have denied before them, (22:42)

and the people of Abraham and the people of Lot, (22:43)

and the companions of Madyan. And Moses was denied, but I gave the disbelievers respite, then I seized them. So how was My rejection! (22:44)

How many a town We destroyed while it was wrongdoing; it lies in ruins over its roofs, and [how many] an abandoned well and a lofty palace! (22:45)

Will they not travel through the land so that they may have hearts with which to understand or ears with which to hear? For indeed, it is not eyes that go blind, but hearts that are in the breasts that go blind. (22:46)

They ask you to hasten the punishment, but God will not fail His promise. Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count. (22:47)

And how many a town I gave respite while it was wrongdoing; then I seized it, and to Me is the destination. (22:48)

Say, "O mankind, I am only a clear warner to you." (22:49)

So those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and noble provision. (22:50)

But those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, they are the companions of the Blazing Fire. (22:51)

We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he spoke a wish, Satan threw [something] into his wish. But God abolishes what Satan throws in, then God establishes His verses; and God is Knowing, Wise. (22:52)

That He may make what Satan throws in a trial for those in whose hearts is disease and whose hearts are hardened. Indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme dissension. (22:53)

And that those who were given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, so they believe in it and their hearts humble before Him. Indeed, God is the Guide of those who believe to a straight path. (22:54)

And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them suddenly or there comes to them the punishment of a barren day. (22:55)

Sovereignty that Day belongs to God; He will judge between them. So those who believed and did righteous deeds will be in Gardens of Bliss. (22:56)

But those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, for them is a humiliating punishment. (22:57)

And those who emigrated in the way of God and then were killed or died, God will surely provide for them a good provision; and indeed, God is the best of providers. (22:58)

He will surely admit them to an entrance that they will be pleased with; and indeed, God is Knowing, Forbearing. (22:59)

That [is so]. And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with and then is wronged again, God will surely support him; indeed, God is Pardoning, Forgiving. (22:60)

That is because God causes the night to enter the day and causes the day to enter the night, and because God is Hearing, Seeing. (22:61)

That is because God is the Truth, and what they invoke other than Him is falsehood, and because God is the Most High, the Great. (22:62)

Have you not considered that God sends down water from the sky, and the earth becomes green? Indeed, God is Subtle, Acquainted. (22:63)

To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth; and indeed, God is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy. (22:64)

Have you not considered that God has subjected to you what is on the earth and the ship that sails through the sea by His command, and He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission? Indeed, God is Kind and Merciful to the people. (22:65)

And it is He who gave you life, then will cause you to die, then will give you life [again]. Indeed, mankind is ungrateful. (22:66)

For every community We have appointed rites which they perform, so let them not dispute with you in the matter; and invite to your Lord, for you are surely on a straight guidance. (22:67)

And if they argue with you, say, "God is most knowing of what you do." (22:68)

God will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which you used to differ. (22:69)

Do you not know that God knows what is in the heaven and the earth? Indeed, that is in a Book; indeed, that is easy for God. (22:70)

And they worship other than God that for which He has sent down no authority and of which they have no knowledge. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers. (22:71)

And when Our clear verses are recited to them, you can recognize denial on the faces of those who disbelieve; they almost attack those who recite Our verses to them. Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that? The Fire, which God has promised those who disbelieve; and wretched is the destination." (22:72)

O mankind, a parable has been presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those you invoke other than God will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it. And if the fly should snatch away from them anything, they could not rescue it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought. (22:73)

They have not appraised God with His true appraisal. Indeed, God is Powerful, Mighty. (22:74)

God selects messengers from the angels and from mankind; indeed, God is Hearing, Seeing. (22:75)

He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and to God are returned all matters. (22:76)

O you who believe, bow, prostrate, worship your Lord, and do good that you may succeed. (22:77)

And strive for God with the striving due to Him. He has chosen you and has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty; [it is] the religion of your father Abraham. He named you "Muslims" before, and in this [Revelation], that the Messenger may be a witness over you and you may be witnesses over the people. So establish prayer, give zakat, and hold fast to God; He is your Protector, and what an excellent Protector and what an excellent Helper! (22:78)

Al-Hadm (demolition): known; it is the tearing down of what has been built. A poet said:

"Every house, however long its occupancy, upon its supports is bound to be demolished."

Al-Sawma'a (the monastic cell, i.e., the place of worship): its form is fa'wala; it is a tall, isolated structure with a sharp top. Al-asma' among men means one of sharp speech. Before Islam it was specific to Christian monks and to the Sabians' worshippers, as stated by Qatada; then it came to be used for the minaret of Muslims. Al-bi'a (churches): the churches of the Christians, singular bai'a. It was also said: the synagogues of the Jews. Al-bi'r (well): from "ba'rat," meaning she dug; it is feminine on the pattern fi'l in the sense of maf'ul, though it may be masculine in the sense of qalib (a dug well). Ta'til al-shay' (rendering a thing idle): nullifying its benefits. Al-'uqm (barrenness): abstention from childbearing. It is said: a barren woman ('aqim) and a barren man who cannot father children; the plural is 'uqm. Its root is cutting; hence "a king who is 'aqim," meaning he cuts off the kinship ties by killing. And al-'aqim is the one whose childbearing has been cut off. Abu 'Ubayd said: al-'uqm means blocking; it is said: a woman whose womb is ma'quma, i.e., her womb is blocked. Al-sat'w: subjugation. Ibn 'Isa said: al-sat'wa is displaying what terrifies for the sake of intimidation. Al-dhubab: the known creature; its plural is dhubab with kasra or damma on the dhal, and dhabb; al-midhabba is what flies are driven away with; dhubab al-sayf is its tip; al-'ayn is its pupil; and the teeth of camels. Salabtu al-shay': I snatched it quickly. Istanqadha: istaf'ala used in the sense of af'ala, i.e., anqadha, like aballa and istaballa.

* *

[p. 373]

It is narrated that when the believers became numerous in Mecca, the disbelievers harmed them, and some of them emigrated to the land of Abyssinia. Some believers in Mecca wanted to kill whichever disbelievers they could reach, and to resort to deception and treachery. Then [verses] were revealed up to His saying "ungrateful." In them is a promise of defense and a prohibition of betrayal. He singled out the believers for defense and support, and He gave the reason: that He does not love their enemies, the treacherous ones who betray God and the Messenger, the disbelievers who reject His blessings. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He mentioned a number of things done during the Hajj, and the polytheists had prevented the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the year of al-Hudaybiyya and harmed those among the believers who were in Mecca, God revealed these verses, giving good news to the believers of His defense of them, indicating their support, His permission for them to fight, and their establishment in the land by returning them to their homes and the conquest of Mecca; and that the outcome of all matters returns to God the Exalted. God the Exalted said: "And the final outcome is for the righteous" (7:128).

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, and Nafi' read "yudafi'u" and "wa-law la difa'u Allah." Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read "yadfa'u" and "wa-law la daf'u." The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir read "yudafi'u" and "wa-law la daf'u." The form fa'ala here has the meaning of the unaugmented verb, as in jawadtu and juztu. Al-Akhfash said: daf'a is more common than dafa'a. Al-Zahrawi related that difa' is the verbal noun of dafa'a, like hasaba hisaban. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "yudafi'u" is preferable, because some people have appeared to the believers who push them back and harm them, so their resistance comes, and their pushing back becomes a defense on their behalf. End.

That is, the form fa'ala is for the mutual sharing of the agent and the patient in wording, with sharing in meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: whoever reads "yudafi'u" means that it intensifies the defense on their behalf, as one who contends in opposition does, because the action of one who contends comes out stronger and more emphatic. End.

He, the Exalted, did not mention what He repels from them, so that it would be more majestic, greater, and more general. When the believers emigrated to Medina, God gave them permission to fight.

Nafi', 'Asim, and Abu 'Amr read the hamza of "udhina" with a damma, and the rest of the seven read it with a fatha. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs read "yuqatalun" with a fatha on the ta', and the rest read it with a kasra. The object of the permission is omitted, i.e., "in fighting," indicated by "yuqatilun." And He gave the reason for the permission: "because they were wronged." They used to come to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with bruised and wounded wounds, and he would tell them: "Be patient, for I have not been commanded to fight," until he emigrated. This is (p. 374) the first verse in which permission to fight was given, after being forbidden in about seventy-some verses. It was said: it was revealed concerning a people who went out as emigrants, and the polytheists of Mecca confronted them, so He gave them permission to fight them.

"And indeed God is capable of giving them victory": a promise of victory and an announcement of His defending them.
