﴿Have they not travelled through the land, so that they might have hearts with which to understand, or ears with which to hear? For indeed it is not the eyes that go blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind.﴾ ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment, but Allah will not fail His promise. Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.﴾ ﴿How many a town I gave respite while it was wrongdoing, then I seized it, and to Me is the destination.﴾ ﴿Say: O people, I am only for you a clear warner.﴾ ﴿So those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness and generous provision.﴾ ﴿And those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, those are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾

When Allah mentioned those who denied the messengers among the earlier nations, and the Arabs had some knowledge of their circumstances, which they transmitted, since they knew their lands and often passed by many of their sites, He said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land?﴾ This may be an exhortation to travel, so that they witness the places where the disbelievers fell and take heed. Or it may mean that they had travelled and witnessed these things but did not take heed, so they were treated as if they had never travelled and had never seen.

Mubashshir ibn 'Ubayd read ﴿fa-yakūna﴾ with a ya' (the third person), while the majority read ﴿fa-takūna﴾ with a ta'. The verb ﴿fa-takūna﴾ is in the subjunctive as an answer to the interrogative, as stated by Ibn 'Atiyya, and as an answer to the affirmative (taqrīr), as stated by al-Ḥawfī. It was also said to be an answer to the negation. The view of the Basrans (grammarians of Basra) is that the subjunctive is governed by an implied ﴿an﴾, and a verbal noun is formed from it and the verb, which is coordinated with an assumed verbal noun (p. 378). The view of the Kufans (grammarians of Kufa) is that it is in the subjunctive by way of ṣarf (deflection), since the meaning of the speech is a statement; they deflected it from the jussive, by coordinating it with ﴿yasīrū﴾, and returned it to its sibling, the jussive, which is the subjunctive. This is what ṣarf means to them. The view of al-Jarmī is that the subjunctive is governed by the fā' itself. Attributing intellect (ʿaql) to the heart indicates that it is its locus, and it cannot be denied that the brain has a connection with the heart, which entails that intellect is corrupted when the brain is corrupted.

The complement of ﴿they understand by them﴾ is omitted; the meaning is: by means of them they understand what befell the earlier nations when they denied their prophets, and they understand what tawhid (the oneness of God) makes obligatory. Likewise the object of ﴿they hear﴾ is omitted: they hear the reports of those nations, or what it is obligatory to hear of the revelation.

The pronoun in ﴿fa-innahā﴾ is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣa), and the feminine form is appropriate here, favoured by the fact that the pronoun is directly followed by a verb bearing the feminine marker, namely the ta' in ﴿lā ta'mā﴾. The masculine is also permissible in speech, and ʿAbd Allāh read ﴿fa-innahu lā ta'mā﴾.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It may be an ambiguous pronoun (ḍamīr mubham) explained by ﴿al-abṣār﴾ (the eyes), and in ﴿ta'mā﴾ it refers back to it. End of quotation.

What he mentioned is not permissible, because the thing explained by what follows must be one of a restricted set of cases, and this is not one of them. It occurs in the chapter of rubba (how many), of ni'ma and bi'sa (the verbs of praise and blame), in the chapter of operation (al-a'māl), in the chapter of substitution (al-badal), and in the chapter of the subject and predicate (al-mubtada' wa'l-khabar), with disagreement about these four according to what is established in their respective chapters. In these five, the pronoun is explained by a singular noun, or it is the pronoun of the matter, and it may be explained by a clause, with disagreement about that too. What al-Zamakhsharī mentioned is not one of these six, so it must be discarded.

The meaning is that their eyes are sound and there is no blindness in them; blindness is only in their hearts. It is known that eyes may go blind, but what is negated here is not true blindness. It is rather the fruit of sight, namely its leading to reflection upon what sight perceives. But that depends on intellect, whose locus is the heart. The hearts are described as ﴿those within the breasts﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is hyperbole, like His saying ﴿they say with their mouths﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:167), and like when you say "I looked at it with my own eye."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: What is commonly known and believed is that blindness in its true sense is the place of sight, namely that the pupil is struck by something that extinguishes its light. Using it for the heart is a metaphor and a figure of speech. When the speech affirms what is contrary to the common belief, attributing blindness literally to the hearts and negating it from the eyes, this depiction requires additional specification and further definition, to establish that the locus of blindness is the hearts and not the eyes. This is like when you say: "Sharpness is not for the sword, but for your tongue which is between your jaws." Your phrase "which is between your jaws" confirms what you attributed to the tongue, and establishes that the locus of sharpness is precisely that, and nothing else. It is as if you said: I did not deny sharpness from the sword and affirm it for your tongue by slip or inadvertence on my part; rather, I intended this deliberately and specifically. End of quotation.

His saying "but I intended it by it exactly, deliberately" separates the pronoun (fa-ṣl al-ḍamīr), and this is not a place for its separation. The correct form is "but I intended it by it" (wa-lākin ta'ammadtuhu bihi), as you say "the sword, I struck you with it," not "I struck with it you." Separating it in a place where it should be attached is an un-Arabic usage (ʿujma).

Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī said: I have another view: the heart may be used as a metonym for thought and deliberation, as in His saying ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾ (Qāf 50:37). Among some people the locus of thought is the brain, so Allah made clear that its locus is the chest.

The pronoun in ﴿they ask you to hasten﴾ refers to the Quraysh. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to warn them of Allah's vengeance and threatened them with it in this world and in the Hereafter, but they did not believe it and considered its occurrence far-fetched. So their hastening was in the manner of mockery, saying that what you threaten us with will not happen and that there is no resurrection.

In His saying ﴿Allah will not fail His promise﴾, the meaning is that this is certain to occur, but its occurrence has a term that it will not exceed. He attributed the promise to Himself because His messenger (ﷺ) is the one who reports it from Allah, the Exalted.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: He denied their hastening for the threatened punishment, whether immediate or delayed, as if He said: why do they hasten it? As though they assume they will escape it, but escape is only conceivable for one whose promise may be broken. Allah, mighty and exalted, does not break His promise. What He has promised He will bring upon them, even after some time, and He, glory be to Him, is forbearing and does not hasten. End of quotation.

In his saying "escape is only conceivable for one whose promise may be broken," there is a concealed insinuation of the Mu'tazilite doctrine (i'tizāl). The Mu'tazila are a theological school that holds that God's promises and threats are bound by what is rationally just.

It was said: ﴿Allah will not fail His promise﴾ refers to respite and delay, and they differed about this comparison. It was said: it concerns number, i.e., a day with Allah is a thousand years of your counting. In the sound hadith: "The poor among the believers will enter Paradise before the rich by half a day, and that is five hundred years." So the meaning is: although the respite may be long, it is only within part of a day of Allah's days.

It was said: the comparison is in the length and severity of the punishment, i.e., ﴿a day﴾ of the days of Allah's punishment, because of the severity of the punishment in it and its length, ﴿is like a thousand years﴾ of your counting, since days of sorrow feel long and days of joy feel short. So that one day is like a thousand years of years of punishment. The meaning is that if they knew the state of the Hereafter, they would not hasten it. This view is close to that of Abū Muslim.

It was said: the comparison is relative to His knowledge, His power, and the execution of what He wills, ﴿like a thousand years﴾. He limited it to a thousand years, although the day with Him has no limit in number, because a thousand is the highest number before repetition begins. This view does not fit the context unless it means that He is the Capable whom nothing can overcome. If they did not find a day's respite strange, then they should not find a thousand years' respite strange either.

Ibn 'Abbās said: He meant one of the days in which Allah created the heavens and the earth. Ibn 'Īsā said: the punishment of a thousand years will be gathered for them in one day, and the people of Paradise will have the joy of a thousand years in one day.

Al-Farrā' said: the verse includes the punishment of this world and of the Hereafter, and the punishment of this world is what is meant: ﴿Allah will not fail His promise﴾ to send punishment upon you in this world, ﴿and indeed a day﴾ of the days of your punishment in the Hereafter ﴿is like a thousand years﴾ of the years of this world. So how can you hasten the punishment?

Al-Zajjāj said: Allah has graciously granted them respite. The meaning is that the day and the thousand years are equal in His power, between what they hasten and its postponement.

Al-Akhawān (Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī) and Ibn Kathīr read ﴿ya'uddūn﴾ with the ya' of the third person, and the rest of the seven read ﴿ta'uddūn﴾ with the ta' of address. The first ﴿fa-ka'ayyin﴾ was joined with the fā', and this second one with the wāw.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The first occurrence came as a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿fa-kayfa kāna nakīr﴾ (then how was My denial?). As for this one, its ruling is that of the two preceding sentences joined by the wāw, namely His saying ﴿Allah will not fail His promise, and indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years﴾. The repetition of ﴿ka'ayyin﴾ (how many) concerning the towns serves to convey a meaning other than that of the first. The first mentioned towns that He destroyed without respite or delay, but rather destruction followed warning. In this verse, since Allah had given Quraysh respite until they hastened the punishment, He brought destruction after respite, to alert them that although He grants them respite and gives them time, their punishment is inevitable, so they should not rejoice at the postponement of punishment from them.

Then He commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to say to the people of Makkah: ﴿O people, I am only for you a clear warner﴾, i.e., from Allah's punishment, making clear to you what you fear, or one whose warning is unambiguous and free of any confusion. He mentioned warning without good tidings, though the division that follows requires both, because the discourse is addressed to the polytheists. ﴿O people﴾ is a call to them, and they are the ones spoken about in ﴿Have they not travelled﴾, and the ones reported as hastening the punishment.

The believers are mentioned here, with what Allah has prepared for them of reward, so that the polytheists would be enraged, and to incite them to attain this lofty rank in which their success lies. He restricted the warning (by the phrase ﴿innamā﴾, "only") because the meaning is: it is not for me to hasten your punishment or to delay it from you; I am only warning you of it.

Al-Kirmānī said: the estimated wording is "a bringer of good news and a warner," so one was omitted, and the division is included within the words that are spoken.

Al-Sa'y is seeking and striving toward something. One says: so-and-so strove (sa'ā) regarding so-and-so's affair, and this may be for reform or for corruption, and it is sometimes used for evil. One says: sa'ā bi-fulān sa'āyah, meaning he schemed against him and plotted to bring harm upon him. Their striving for corruption against Allah's signs consisted in their disparaging them, calling them sorcery, poetry, and the fables of the ancients, and discouraging people from believing in them.

Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr, al-Jaḥdarī, Abū al-Simmāl and al-Za'farānī read ﴿mu'ajjizīna﴾ with the doubled letter here, and in the two places in Sabaʾ (34:5, 34:38). Al-Jaḥdarī added the doubling throughout the Qur'an, i.e., ﴿mu'ajjizīna﴾ meaning ﴿muthabbiṭīna﴾ (discouraging people). The remaining seven read it with an alif (﴿mu'ājizīna﴾).

It was said that ﴿mu'ājizīna﴾ means opponents. As for ﴿mu'ajjizīna﴾ with doubling, it means discouraging people from Islam, and one says ﴿muthabbiṭīna﴾.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: ʿājazahu means "he outstripped him," because each of the two is seeking to make the other unable to catch up with him. If one outstrips the other, it is said a'jazahu and 'ajjazahu. So the meaning is "outstripping" or "competing," in their assumption and calculation, hoping that their scheme against Islam would succeed for them. End of quotation.

The explanation of the other of these two sentences, which were mentioned in the division, has already preceded.

For indeed it is not the eyes that go blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind.﴾ ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment, but Allah will not fail His promise. Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.﴾ ﴿How many a town I gave respite while it was wrongdoing, then I seized it, and to Me is the destination.﴾ ﴿Say: O people, I am only for you a clear warner.﴾ ﴿So those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness and generous provision.﴾ ﴿And those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, those are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾

When Allah mentioned those who denied the messengers among the earlier nations, and the Arabs had some knowledge of their circumstances, which they transmitted, since they knew their lands and often passed by many of their sites, He said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land?﴾ This may be an exhortation to travel, so that they witness the places where the disbelievers fell and take heed. Or it may mean that they had travelled and witnessed these things but did not take heed, so they were treated as if they had never travelled and had never seen.

Mubashshir ibn 'Ubayd read ﴿fa-yakūna﴾ with a ya' (the third person), while the majority read ﴿fa-takūna﴾ with a ta'. The verb ﴿fa-takūna﴾ is in the subjunctive as an answer to the interrogative, as stated by Ibn 'Atiyya, and as an answer to the affirmative (taqrīr), as stated by al-Ḥawfī. It was also said to be an answer to the negation. The view of the Basrans (grammarians of Basra) is that the subjunctive is governed by an implied ﴿an﴾, and a verbal noun is formed from it and the verb, which is coordinated with an assumed verbal noun (p. 378). The view of the Kufans (grammarians of Kufa) is that it is in the subjunctive by way of ṣarf (deflection), since the meaning of the speech is a statement; they deflected it from the jussive, by coordinating it with ﴿yasīrū﴾, and returned it to its sibling, the jussive, which is the subjunctive. This is what ṣarf means to them. The view of al-Jarmī is that the subjunctive is governed by the fā' itself. Attributing intellect (ʿaql) to the heart indicates that it is its locus, and it cannot be denied that the brain has a connection with the heart, which entails that intellect is corrupted when the brain is corrupted.

The complement of ﴿they understand by them﴾ is omitted; the meaning is: by means of them they understand what befell the earlier nations when they denied their prophets, and they understand what tawhid (the oneness of God) makes obligatory. Likewise the object of ﴿they hear﴾ is omitted: they hear the reports of those nations, or what it is obligatory to hear of the revelation.

The pronoun in ﴿fa-innahā﴾ is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣa), and the feminine form is appropriate here, favoured by the fact that the pronoun is directly followed by a verb bearing the feminine marker, namely the ta' in ﴿lā ta'mā﴾. The masculine is also permissible in speech, and ʿAbd Allāh read ﴿fa-innahu lā ta'mā﴾.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It may be an ambiguous pronoun (ḍamīr mubham) explained by ﴿al-abṣār﴾ (the eyes), and in ﴿ta'mā﴾ it refers back to it. End of quotation.

What he mentioned is not permissible, because the thing explained by what follows must be one of a restricted set of cases, and this is not one of them. It occurs in the chapter of rubba (how many), of ni'ma and bi'sa (the verbs of praise and blame), in the chapter of operation (al-a'māl), in the chapter of substitution (al-badal), and in the chapter of the subject and predicate (al-mubtada' wa'l-khabar), with disagreement about these four according to what is established in their respective chapters. In these five, the pronoun is explained by a singular noun, or it is the pronoun of the matter, and it may be explained by a clause, with disagreement about that too. What al-Zamakhsharī mentioned is not one of these six, so it must be discarded.

The meaning is that their eyes are sound and there is no blindness in them; blindness is only in their hearts. It is known that eyes may go blind, but what is negated here is not true blindness. It is rather the fruit of sight, namely its leading to reflection upon what sight perceives. But that depends on intellect, whose locus is the heart. The hearts are described as ﴿those within the breasts﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is hyperbole, like His saying ﴿they say with their mouths﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:167), and like when you say "I looked at it with my own eye."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: What is commonly known and believed is that blindness in its true sense is the place of sight, namely that the pupil is struck by something that extinguishes its light. Using it for the heart is a metaphor and a figure of speech. When the speech affirms what is contrary to the common belief, attributing blindness literally to the hearts and negating it from the eyes, this depiction requires additional specification and further definition, to establish that the locus of blindness is the hearts and not the eyes. This is like when you say: "Sharpness is not for the sword, but for your tongue which is between your jaws." Your phrase "which is between your jaws" confirms what you attributed to the tongue, and establishes that the locus of sharpness is precisely that, and nothing else. It is as if you said: I did not deny sharpness from the sword and affirm it for your tongue by slip or inadvertence on my part; rather, I intended this deliberately and specifically. End of quotation.

His saying "but I intended it by it exactly, deliberately" separates the pronoun (fa-ṣl al-ḍamīr), and this is not a place for its separation. The correct form is "but I intended it by it" (wa-lākin ta'ammadtuhu bihi), as you say "the sword, I struck you with it," not "I struck with it you." Separating it in a place where it should be attached is an un-Arabic usage (ʿujma).

Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī said: I have another view: the heart may be used as a metonym for thought and deliberation, as in His saying ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾ (Qāf 50:37). Among some people the locus of thought is the brain, so Allah made clear that its locus is the chest.

The pronoun in ﴿they ask you to hasten﴾ refers to the Quraysh. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to warn them of Allah's vengeance and threatened them with it in this world and in the Hereafter, but they did not believe it and considered its occurrence far-fetched. So their hastening was in the manner of mockery, saying that what you threaten us with will not happen and that there is no resurrection.

In His saying ﴿Allah will not fail His promise﴾, the meaning is that this is certain to occur, but its occurrence has a term that it will not exceed. He attributed the promise to Himself because His messenger (ﷺ) is the one who reports it from Allah, the Exalted.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: He denied their hastening for the threatened punishment, whether immediate or delayed, as if He said: why do they hasten it? As though they assume they will escape it, but escape is only conceivable for one whose promise may be broken. Allah, mighty and exalted, does not break His promise. What He has promised He will bring upon them, even after some time, and He, glory be to Him, is forbearing and does not hasten. End of quotation.

In his saying "escape is only conceivable for one whose promise may be broken," there is a concealed insinuation of the Mu'tazilite doctrine (i'tizāl). The Mu'tazila are a theological school that holds that God's promises and threats are bound by what is rationally just.

It was said: ﴿Allah will not fail His promise﴾ refers to respite and delay, and they differed about this comparison. It was said: it concerns number, i.e., a day with Allah is a thousand years of your counting. In the sound hadith: "The poor among the believers will enter Paradise before the rich by half a day, and that is five hundred years." So the meaning is: although the respite may be long, it is only within part of a day of Allah's days.

It was said: the comparison is in the length and severity of the punishment, i.e., ﴿a day﴾ of the days of Allah's punishment, because of the severity of the punishment in it and its length, ﴿is like a thousand years﴾ of your counting, since days of sorrow feel long and days of joy feel short. So that one day is like a thousand years of years of punishment. The meaning is that if they knew the state of the Hereafter, they would not hasten it. This view is close to that of Abū Muslim.

It was said: the comparison is relative to His knowledge, His power, and the execution of what He wills, ﴿like a thousand years﴾. He limited it to a thousand years, although the day with Him has no limit in number, because a thousand is the highest number before repetition begins. This view does not fit the context unless it means that He is the Capable whom nothing can overcome. If they did not find a day's respite strange, then they should not find a thousand years' respite strange either.

Ibn 'Abbās said: He meant one of the days in which Allah created the heavens and the earth. Ibn 'Īsā said: the punishment of a thousand years will be gathered for them in one day, and the people of Paradise will have the joy of a thousand years in one day.

Al-Farrā' said: the verse includes the punishment of this world and of the Hereafter, and the punishment of this world is what is meant: ﴿Allah will not fail His promise﴾ to send punishment upon you in this world, ﴿and indeed a day﴾ of the days of your punishment in the Hereafter ﴿is like a thousand years﴾ of the years of this world. So how can you hasten the punishment?

Al-Zajjāj said: Allah has graciously granted them respite. The meaning is that the day and the thousand years are equal in His power, between what they hasten and its postponement.

Al-Akhawān (Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī) and Ibn Kathīr read ﴿ya'uddūn﴾ with the ya' of the third person, and the rest of the seven read ﴿ta'uddūn﴾ with the ta' of address. The first ﴿fa-ka'ayyin﴾ was joined with the fā', and this second one with the wāw.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The first occurrence came as a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿fa-kayfa kāna nakīr﴾ (then how was My denial?). As for this one, its ruling is that of the two preceding sentences joined by the wāw, namely His saying ﴿Allah will not fail His promise, and indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years﴾. The repetition of ﴿ka'ayyin﴾ (how many) concerning the towns serves to convey a meaning other than that of the first. The first mentioned towns that He destroyed without respite or delay, but rather destruction followed warning. In this verse, since Allah had given Quraysh respite until they hastened the punishment, He brought destruction after respite, to alert them that although He grants them respite and gives them time, their punishment is inevitable, so they should not rejoice at the postponement of punishment from them.

Then He commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to say to the people of Makkah: ﴿O people, I am only for you a clear warner﴾, i.e., from Allah's punishment, making clear to you what you fear, or one whose warning is unambiguous and free of any confusion. He mentioned warning without good tidings, though the division that follows requires both, because the discourse is addressed to the polytheists. ﴿O people﴾ is a call to them, and they are the ones spoken about in ﴿Have they not travelled﴾, and the ones reported as hastening the punishment.

The believers are mentioned here, with what Allah has prepared for them of reward, so that the polytheists would be enraged, and to incite them to attain this lofty rank in which their success lies. He restricted the warning (by the phrase ﴿innamā﴾, "only") because the meaning is: it is not for me to hasten your punishment or to delay it from you; I am only warning you of it.

Al-Kirmānī said: the estimated wording is "a bringer of good news and a warner," so one was omitted, and the division is included within the words that are spoken.

Al-Sa'y is seeking and striving toward something. One says: so-and-so strove (sa'ā) regarding so-and-so's affair, and this may be for reform or for corruption, and it is sometimes used for evil. One says: sa'ā bi-fulān sa'āyah, meaning he schemed against him and plotted to bring harm upon him. Their striving for corruption against Allah's signs consisted in their disparaging them, calling them sorcery, poetry, and the fables of the ancients, and discouraging people from believing in them.

It was said that ﴿mu'ājizīna﴾ means opponents. As for ﴿mu'ajjizīna﴾ with doubling, it means discouraging people from Islam, and one says ﴿muthabbiṭīna﴾.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: ʿājazahu means "he outstripped him," because each of the two is seeking to make the other unable to catch up with him. Al-Jaḥdarī added the doubling throughout the Qur'an, i.e., ﴿mu'ajjizīna﴾ meaning ﴿muthabbiṭīna﴾ (discouraging people). The remaining seven read it with an alif (﴿mu'ājizīna﴾).

Ibn al-Zubayr read ﴿mu'jizīna﴾ with a sukūn on the 'ayn and a lightened zāy, from a'jaznī, meaning "he outstripped me and escaped me." The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: but here it means ﴿mu'ājizīna﴾, i.e., supposing that they can defeat us, because they think they will not be raised again.

It was said that ﴿mu'ājizīna﴾ means opponents. As for ﴿mu'ajjizīna﴾ with doubling, it means discouraging people from Islam, and one says ﴿muthabbiṭīna﴾.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: ʿājazahu means "he outstripped him," because each of the two is seeking to make the other unable to catch up with him. If one outstrips the other, it is said a'jazahu and 'ajjazahu. So the meaning is "outstripping" or "competing," in their assumption and calculation, hoping that their scheme against Islam would succeed for them. End of quotation.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: ﴿mu'ajjizīna﴾ means attributing incapacity (ʿajz) to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), just as you say "I declared so-and-so a sinner (fassaqtu)" when you attribute sin to him.

The explanation of the other of these two sentences, which were mentioned in the division, has already preceded.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 22, verses 52–62 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Never did We send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he wished, Satan cast into his wish. But God abolishes what Satan casts, then God establishes His signs. God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿That He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease and whose hearts are hardened. Indeed the wrongdoers are in a far-off schism.﴾ ﴿And that those given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, so that they believe in it and their hearts humble themselves before it. Indeed God guides those who believe to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them suddenly or there comes to them the punishment of a barren day.﴾ ﴿The dominion on that day belongs to God; He judges between them. As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ ﴿And as for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, they will have a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿And those who emigrated in the way of God and were then killed or died, God will surely provide for them a goodly provision. Indeed God is the best of providers.﴾ ﴿He will surely admit them to an entrance they will be pleased with. Indeed God is All-Knowing, Forbearing.﴾ ﴿That is so. And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with, and then is wronged again, God will surely help him. Indeed God is Pardoning, Forgiving.﴾ ﴿That is so, because God causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and because God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿That is so, because God is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood, and because God is the Most High, the Most Great.﴾

When God mentioned that He defends those who believe [p. 381], and that He permitted the believers to fight, and that they had been expelled from their homes, and when He mentioned the consolation of His messenger ﷺ by the denial of those nations before him toward their prophets, and what their affair came to in destruction after denial and after being given respite, He commanded him to call the people and inform them that he is a warner to them, after they had hastened for the punishment, and that it is not for him to bring the punishment forward or delay it. He, exalted is He, mentioned to him a second consolation in regard to the messengers and prophets who passed before him: that they were eager for the faith of their peoples, wishing for it and striving toward it. None of them was without Satan opposing him by adorning disbelief for his people, spreading it among them and casting it into their souls. Likewise the Prophet ﷺ was among the most eager of people for the guidance of his people, and among them were devils such as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who cast doubts to his people and to those who came to him, by which they sought to hinder them from Islam. For this reason there came before this verse: ﴿And those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them﴾ [al-Hajj: 51], and their striving was by casting doubts into the hearts of those whom they sought to win over. He attributed this to Satan because he is the one who misleads and who moves the devils of mankind to lead astray, as he said: ﴿I will surely mislead them﴾. It was also said that "the Satan" here is a genus, meant to include the devils of mankind. The pronoun in ﴿his wish﴾ refers to "Satan," i.e., in the wish of his own self, meaning because of the wish of his own self. The object of ﴿cast﴾ is omitted for understanding; it is evil and disbelief, and the opposition of that to the messenger or prophet, because Satan does not cast good. The meaning of ﴿then God abolishes what Satan casts﴾ is that He removes those doubts little by little until people become Muslims, as He said: ﴿And you see people entering the religion of God in multitudes﴾ [al-Nasr: 2]. And ﴿God establishes His signs﴾ means His miracles, which He shows firmly established, with no confusion in them. ﴿That He may make what Satan casts﴾ of those doubts and deceptive speech ﴿a trial﴾ for the one with a diseased heart and the hardened one. ﴿And that those given knowledge﴾ may know that what the messenger and the prophet wished for, of the guidance and faith of his people, is the truth. This verse does not attribute anything to the Messenger of God ﷺ; it only includes the state of those messengers and prophets before him when they wished.

The commentators, in their books, including Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari, and those before and after them, mentioned what it is not permissible to occur from ordinary believers attributed to the infallible one, may God's blessings be upon him. They went at length on this, with question and answer, and it is a story about which the Imam Muhammad ibn Ishaq, compiler of the Prophetic biography, was asked. He said: "This is from the fabrications of the heretics," and he wrote a book on this [p. 382]. The Imam, the hadith master Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn al-Husayn al-Bayhaqi, said: "This story is not established in terms of transmission." He said something to the effect that its narrators are criticized, and that nothing of what they mentioned is in the Sahih collections or in the hadith compilations, so it must be discarded; for this reason I kept my book free of mentioning it. How strange it is to transmit this when they recite in the Book of God: ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [al-Najm: 1], ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2], ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ [al-Najm: 3], ﴿It is but a revelation revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 4]. God, exalted is He, also said, commanding His Prophet: ﴿Say: It is not for me to change it on my own accord; I follow only what is revealed to me﴾ [Yunus: 15]. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Had he fabricated against Us some sayings﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44], the verse onward. He said: ﴿Had We not made you firm, you would nearly have inclined toward them﴾ [al-Isra: 74], the verse onward; so firmness has occurred and the near-inclination is negated. He said: ﴿Thus that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]. He said: ﴿We will make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6]. These are texts that testify to his infallibility. As for the rational argument, it is not possible for that to occur, because permitting it leads to permitting it in all rulings and the law, so there would be no assurance against alteration and change in them, and the impossibility of that is known.

Let us return to explaining some words of the verse, now that we have established what meaning appeared to us in it. His saying ﴿from before you﴾: the ﴿from﴾ here indicates the starting point. The ﴿from﴾ in ﴿from a messenger﴾ is extra and conveys the comprehensiveness of the genus. The conjunction of ﴿nor a prophet﴾ to ﴿a messenger﴾ is evidence of difference. We have already discussed their two meanings earlier, so there is no need to repeat it here. After ﴿illa﴾ (except) there came a clause whose apparent form is a condition, namely ﴿when he wished, Satan cast﴾. Al-Hawfi said this, and they stated that after it, in negation, a present-tense verb follows that does not require a condition; you say: "Zayd is not but he does such-and-such," and "I did not see Zayd but he does such-and-such." And a past-tense verb follows only on the condition that a verb precedes it, as in His saying: ﴿And no messenger came to them but they mocked him﴾ [al-Hijr: 11], or the past verb is accompanied by ﴿qad﴾, as in: "Zayd is not but he has indeed stood." What came after ﴿illa﴾ in the verse is a conditional clause, and it was not followed by a past verb accompanied by ﴿qad﴾, nor one free of it. If what they stated is correct, it is interpreted as: ﴿when﴾ is used purely as a temporal adverb with no conditional force, and it separates ﴿illa﴾ from the verb ﴿cast﴾, which is a permissible separation. Thus ﴿illa qad﴾ is followed by a past verb in estimation, and its condition is met, namely that a verb precedes ﴿illa﴾, which is ﴿And We did not send﴾. The pronoun in ﴿wished﴾ returned singular. They mentioned that when the conjunction is with ﴿waw﴾, the pronoun returns agreeing with both conjoined elements, and this is a conjunction with ﴿waw﴾; what came not agreeing they interpreted as ellipsis. So the interpretation of this is: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger﴾ ﴿except when he wished, Satan cast into his wish﴾ ﴿nor a prophet except when he wished, Satan cast into his wish﴾. So the first was omitted because the second indicates it. ﴿Tamanna﴾ (wished) is the form ﴿tafa''ala﴾ from ﴿al-munya﴾.

Abu Muslim said: "Tamanni is the end of estimation, and from it comes al-munya, the death of a person at the time God has decreed; and 'manna Allahu laka' means 'God decreed for you.'" The narrators of the language said: "al-umniyya means recitation," and they argued with the verse of Hassan, and this returns to the original root, for the reciter estimates the letters and mentions them one by one. End of quotation. The verse of Hassan:

He wished the Book of God, the first night and its last; he met the death-doom of the decreed fates.

Another said:

He wished the Book of God the first night ... as Dawud wished the Zabur, at a steady pace.

Some commentators understood His saying ﴿when he wished﴾ as ﴿recited﴾, and ﴿in his wish﴾ as ﴿in his recitation﴾. The clause after ﴿illa﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: ﴿And We did not send him﴾ except [while], and this is his state. It was also said that the clause is in the position of a descriptive clause, which is al-Zamakhshari's view in such constructions as: "I did not pass by anyone except that Zayd is better than him." The correct view is that the clause is circumstantial, not descriptive, because it accepts the ﴿waw﴾ of circumstance. The ﴿lam﴾ in ﴿that He may make﴾ is connected to ﴿yahkumu﴾ (He judges), as al-Hawfi said. Ibn 'Atiyya said: connected to ﴿yansakhu﴾ (abolishes). Others said: connected to ﴿alqa﴾ (casts). The apparent view is that it is the ﴿lam﴾ of causation. It was also said it is the ﴿lam﴾ of consequence. The ﴿ma﴾ in ﴿what Satan casts﴾: the apparent view is that it means ﴿alladhi﴾ (that which), and it was permitted that it be verbal-source (masdariyya).

Al-fitna means testing and trial. Those ﴿in whose hearts is a disease﴾ are generally the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari said: the hypocrites and the doubters. ﴿And the hardened of heart﴾ are the elite of the disbelievers, the obstinate, such as Abu Jahl, al-Nadr, and Utba. Al-Zamakhshari said: [p. 383] the polytheists, the deniers. ﴿Indeed the wrongdoers﴾: he means these hypocrites and polytheists; the original would be ﴿indeed they﴾, but he placed the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, passing judgment on them as wrongdoers. Al-shiqaq means opposition, i.e., in a split other than the split of righteousness; describing it as ﴿far-off﴾ is an intensification of its extremity and that their return from it is not to be hoped for.

The pronoun in ﴿that it﴾: Ibn 'Atiyya said it refers to the Qur'an. ﴿Those given knowledge﴾ [al-Mujadila: 11] are the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ. The pronoun to which it refers has already been mentioned in our earlier discussion of the verse. ﴿So their hearts humble themselves﴾ means they become humble and submissive, unlike the one in whose heart is a disease and whose heart has hardened. Al-Jumhur read ﴿la-hadi alladhina amanu﴾ with the genitive construction, while Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿lahadin﴾ with tanwin.

Al-mirya means doubt. The pronoun in ﴿about it﴾ is said to refer to the Qur'an; it was said to refer to the Messenger; and it was said to refer to what Satan cast. When he first mentioned the state of the disbelievers and then the state of the believers, he returned to explaining the state of the disbelievers. The apparent view is that ﴿the Hour﴾ is the Day of Resurrection. It was said: ﴿the barren day﴾ is the Day of Badr. It was said: it is the moment of their death or their killing in this world, like the Day of Badr, and the barren day is the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the barren day is the Day of Badr, and the day of battle was described as barren because the children of women are killed in it, so they become as if they were barren women who did not bear; or because the fighters are called "sons of war," and when they are killed the day of war is described as barren, figuratively. It was also said: it is the day that has no good in it; one says "a barren wind" when it does not bring rain nor fertilize trees. It was said: there is no equal to it in the magnitude of its matter, because the angels fought in it. From al-Dahhak: it is the Day of Resurrection, and the intended meaning of "the Hour" is its preliminaries. It is permissible that "the Hour" and "a barren day" both mean the Day of Resurrection, as though it said: ﴿until the Hour comes upon them﴾ or ﴿its punishment comes upon them﴾, so ﴿a barren day﴾ was placed in the position of the pronoun. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The Day of Resurrection, or the day of annihilation, was called barren because there is no night after it nor day, whereas all days are successive results, one following another, and the last day has become barren. This is a metaphor. The whole of this verse is a threat. End of quotation. ﴿Until﴾ (hatta) marks the endpoint of the continuation of their doubt, so the meaning is: ﴿until the Hour comes upon them﴾ (or ﴿the punishment of a barren day﴾), at which point their doubt will vanish and they will witness the matter with their own eyes.

The tanwin in ﴿on that day﴾ is the tanwin of replacement (iwad), and the clause for which this tanwin is a replacement is what was omitted after the endpoint, i.e., ﴿the dominion﴾ belongs to the day when their doubt ceases. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it first as "the day they believe," which is necessarily implied by the cessation of doubt, for when doubt ceases they believe; and he estimated it secondly as we have estimated, which is the better view. The apparent view is that this day is the Day of Resurrection, in that there is no dominion in it for any of the kings of this world, as God said: ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾ [Ghafir: 16]. The following division supports this. Whoever says it is the Day of Badr or the like considers that God's decree alone is carried out, everything else is nullified, and His judgment passes on whomever He wills to punish; and the division would then be a report built upon their state on that barren day, in terms of faith and disbelief. The wordings of the division and their meanings are clear and need no explanation. He contrasted bliss with punishment and described the punishment as humiliating, for emphasis.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 22, verse 52–62 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And those who emigrated﴾ — the verse. This begins another meaning. When Uthman ibn Maz'un and Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Asad died, some people said: "Whoever among the emigrants was killed is better than the one who died of his own natural death." So it was revealed, placing them on an equal footing in that Allah will provide them with ﴿a goodly provision﴾. The apparent sense of ﴿And those who emigrated﴾ is generality. Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning groups who left Mecca for Medina for the hijrah, and the polytheists pursued them and fought them. It is related that groups of the Companions said: "O Prophet of Allah, we know what good Allah has given to those who were killed. We strive alongside you as they strove. So what is ours if we die with you?" Then Allah revealed these two verses.

Al-Zamakhshari said: When the emigration in the way of Allah brought them together, He equated them in the promise, so that He gives whoever among them died the same as He gives whoever was killed, as a bounty and a kindness from Him. And Allah is All-Knowing of the degrees of those who act and the ranks of their deservingness, Forbearing toward the negligence of the negligent among them, by His grace and generosity. End.

In his saying "and the ranks of their deservingness" there is the subtle Mu'tazilite notion (dasisat al-i'tizal). Equality in the promise of provision does not indicate preference in the amount given, and there is no equality (in rank); if there is preference, it is from another proof. The apparent teaching of the Shari'ah is that the one who was killed is superior. It has been said: the one killed and the one who dies in the way of Allah are both martyrs.

The goodly provision may be intended to mean the provision of the martyrs in the barzakh, and it may be that it is after the Day of Resurrection in Paradise, which is its bliss. Al-Kalbi said: it is the spoils of war. Al-Asamm said: it is knowledge and understanding, like the saying of Shu'ayb: ﴿and He has provided me from Himself with goodly provision﴾ [Hud: 88]. These two opinions are weak, because He made the goodly provision a reward for their being killed in the way of Allah or dying after their emigration, and after that the provision is not in this world. The apparent meaning is that ﴿the best of providers﴾ is an elative (af'al al-tafdil), and the superiority is that He is singularly able to provide by means that no one other than Him can command, and that He is the origin of provision, whereas others provide only by what they have of provision from Allah.

When He mentioned provision, He mentioned the dwelling, saying ﴿He will surely admit them to an admission they will be pleased with﴾, which is Paradise. They are pleased with it, meaning they choose it, since in it is their contentment, as He said ﴿they will not desire a change from it﴾ [al-Kahf: 108]. The disagreement in the recitation regarding the vowelling of the mim, with a damma or a fatha, has been mentioned in al-Nisa'. The better view is that by the madkhal (admission) is meant the place of entering or the place of causing entry, and it may be a verbal noun.

﴿That, and whoever retaliates﴾ — the verse. It has been said: it was revealed concerning a group of believers whom disbelievers met in the sacred months; the believers refused to fight them, and the polytheists insisted on fighting. When they fought, the believers exerted themselves, and Allah gave them victory. Its connection to what precedes is clear: when He mentioned the reward of the one who emigrated and was killed or died in the way of Allah, He informed that He does not abandon their support in this world against whoever transgresses against them. Ibn Jurayj said: the verse concerns the polytheists who transgressed against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and expelled him, and the estimate is "the matter is that."

Al-Zamakhshari said: naming the beginning by its recompense is because it is connected to it, in that it is a cause and that is an effect of it, just as they pair a like with a like and an opposite with an opposite, for the connection. If you ask: how does the mention of "the Pardoner, the Forgiving" fit this place? I say: the one who retaliates is sent by Allah, glorified and exalted, to correct the neglect of punishment, while pardon of the offender is by way of tanzih (purification/commendation), not prohibition, and it is recommended and merits praise from Allah if one prefers what is recommended and takes the path of tanzih. When he did not prefer that, and retaliated and punished, and did not heed the saying ﴿So whoever pardons and makes amends, his reward is upon Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 40], ﴿and that you pardon is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], ﴿and whoever is patient and forgives, that is indeed of the steadfast matters﴾ [al-Shura: 43], ﴿Indeed Allah is Pardoning, Forgiving﴾, meaning He does not blame him for leaving what He sent him to, and He guarantees his victory in his second assault after his neglect of pardon, and his vengeance upon the transgressor against him. It is also permissible that He guarantees him victory over the transgressor, while turning away with that from what was better for him of pardon. The mention of these two attributes hints at this, or by mentioning pardon and forgiveness indicates that He is able to punish, because one is described as pardoning only if he is capable of that limit; that is, that victory is by means of His being capable.

Among the signs of His far-reaching power is that ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾ and ﴿the day into the night﴾, or by reason of His being the Creator of night and day and their Director. Nothing that takes place in them at the hands of His servants of good and evil, transgression and retaliation, is hidden from Him. And He is (All-Hearing) of what they say, (All-Seeing) of what they do. The explanation of this "entering" was mentioned earlier at the beginning of Al 'Imran.

(That) — that attribute of creating night and day, encompassing what occurs within them and perceiving every saying and deed — is because (Allah) is the Truth, the established Divinity, and because everything called god besides Him is false in its claim, and because there is nothing exalted above Him in rank or greater in sovereignty. The majority read (wa-anna ma) with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra. Al-Akhawan, Abu Amr and Hafs read (yad'una) here and in Luqman with the third-person ya. The rest of the seven read it with the second-person ta. Both forms have the verb in the active voice. Mujahid, al-Yamani and Musa al-Uswari read (yud'a) with ya in the passive voice, and the waw refers to "ma," which is by its meaning. The apparent referent of "ma" is their idols. It has been said: the devils. The better view is generality, covering everything called upon besides Allah, Exalted.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 22, verses 52–62 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Never did We send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he wished, Satan cast into his wish. But God abolishes what Satan casts, then God establishes His signs. God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿That He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease and whose hearts are hardened. Indeed the wrongdoers are in a far-off schism.﴾ ﴿And that those given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, so that they believe in it and their hearts humble themselves before it. Indeed God guides those who believe to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them suddenly or there comes to them the punishment of a barren day.﴾ ﴿The dominion on that day belongs to God; He judges between them. As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ ﴿And as for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, they will have a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿And those who emigrated in the way of God and were then killed or died, God will surely provide for them a goodly provision. Indeed God is the best of providers.﴾ ﴿He will surely admit them to an entrance they will be pleased with. Indeed God is All-Knowing, Forbearing.﴾ ﴿That is so. And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with, and then is wronged again, God will surely help him. Indeed God is Pardoning, Forgiving.﴾ ﴿That is so, because God causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and because God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿That is so, because God is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood, and because God is the Most High, the Most Great.﴾

When God mentioned that He defends those who believe [p. 381], and that He permitted the believers to fight, and that they had been expelled from their homes, and when He mentioned the consolation of His messenger ﷺ by the denial of those nations before him toward their prophets, and what their affair came to in destruction after denial and after being given respite, He commanded him to call the people and inform them that he is a warner to them, after they had hastened for the punishment, and that it is not for him to bring the punishment forward or delay it. He, exalted is He, mentioned to him a second consolation in regard to the messengers and prophets who passed before him: that they were eager for the faith of their peoples, wishing for it and striving toward it. None of them was without Satan opposing him by adorning disbelief for his people, spreading it among them and casting it into their souls. Likewise the Prophet ﷺ was among the most eager of people for the guidance of his people, and among them were devils such as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who cast doubts to his people and to those who came to him, by which they sought to hinder them from Islam. For this reason there came before this verse: ﴿And those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them﴾ [al-Hajj: 51], and their striving was by casting doubts into the hearts of those whom they sought to win over. He attributed this to Satan because he is the one who misleads and who moves the devils of mankind to lead astray, as he said: ﴿I will surely mislead them﴾. It was also said that "the Satan" here is a genus, meant to include the devils of mankind. The pronoun in ﴿his wish﴾ refers to "Satan," i.e., in the wish of his own self, meaning because of the wish of his own self. The object of ﴿cast﴾ is omitted for understanding; it is evil and disbelief, and the opposition of that to the messenger or prophet, because Satan does not cast good. The meaning of ﴿then God abolishes what Satan casts﴾ is that He removes those doubts little by little until people become Muslims, as He said: ﴿And you see people entering the religion of God in multitudes﴾ [al-Nasr: 2]. And ﴿God establishes His signs﴾ means His miracles, which He shows firmly established, with no confusion in them. ﴿That He may make what Satan casts﴾ of those doubts and deceptive speech ﴿a trial﴾ for the one with a diseased heart and the hardened one. ﴿And that those given knowledge﴾ may know that what the messenger and the prophet wished for, of the guidance and faith of his people, is the truth. This verse does not attribute anything to the Messenger of God ﷺ; it only includes the state of those messengers and prophets before him when they wished.

The commentators, in their books, including Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari, and those before and after them, mentioned what it is not permissible to occur from ordinary believers attributed to the infallible one, may God's blessings be upon him. They went at length on this, with question and answer, and it is a story about which the Imam Muhammad ibn Ishaq, compiler of the Prophetic biography, was asked. He said: "This is from the fabrications of the heretics," and he wrote a book on this [p. 382]. The Imam, the hadith master Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn al-Husayn al-Bayhaqi, said: "This story is not established in terms of transmission." He said something to the effect that its narrators are criticized, and that nothing of what they mentioned is in the Sahih collections or in the hadith compilations, so it must be discarded; for this reason I kept my book free of mentioning it. How strange it is to transmit this when they recite in the Book of God: ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [al-Najm: 1], ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2], ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ [al-Najm: 3], ﴿It is but a revelation revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 4]. God, exalted is He, also said, commanding His Prophet: ﴿Say: It is not for me to change it on my own accord; I follow only what is revealed to me﴾ [Yunus: 15]. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Had he fabricated against Us some sayings﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44], the verse onward. He said: ﴿Had We not made you firm, you would nearly have inclined toward them﴾ [al-Isra: 74], the verse onward; so firmness has occurred and the near-inclination is negated. He said: ﴿Thus that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]. He said: ﴿We will make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6]. These are texts that testify to his infallibility. As for the rational argument, it is not possible for that to occur, because permitting it leads to permitting it in all rulings and the law, so there would be no assurance against alteration and change in them, and the impossibility of that is known.

Let us return to explaining some words of the verse, now that we have established what meaning appeared to us in it. His saying ﴿from before you﴾: the ﴿from﴾ here indicates the starting point. The ﴿from﴾ in ﴿from a messenger﴾ is extra and conveys the comprehensiveness of the genus. The conjunction of ﴿nor a prophet﴾ to ﴿a messenger﴾ is evidence of difference. We have already discussed their two meanings earlier, so there is no need to repeat it here. After ﴿illa﴾ (except) there came a clause whose apparent form is a condition, namely ﴿when he wished, Satan cast﴾. Al-Hawfi said this, and they stated that after it, in negation, a present-tense verb follows that does not require a condition; you say: "Zayd is not but he does such-and-such," and "I did not see Zayd but he does such-and-such." And a past-tense verb follows only on the condition that a verb precedes it, as in His saying: ﴿And no messenger came to them but they mocked him﴾ [al-Hijr: 11], or the past verb is accompanied by ﴿qad﴾, as in: "Zayd is not but he has indeed stood." What came after ﴿illa﴾ in the verse is a conditional clause, and it was not followed by a past verb accompanied by ﴿qad﴾, nor one free of it. If what they stated is correct, it is interpreted as: ﴿when﴾ is used purely as a temporal adverb with no conditional force, and it separates ﴿illa﴾ from the verb ﴿cast﴾, which is a permissible separation. Thus ﴿illa qad﴾ is followed by a past verb in estimation, and its condition is met, namely that a verb precedes ﴿illa﴾, which is ﴿And We did not send﴾. The pronoun in ﴿wished﴾ returned singular. They mentioned that when the conjunction is with ﴿waw﴾, the pronoun returns agreeing with both conjoined elements, and this is a conjunction with ﴿waw﴾; what came not agreeing they interpreted as ellipsis. So the interpretation of this is: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger﴾ ﴿except when he wished, Satan cast into his wish﴾ ﴿nor a prophet except when he wished, Satan cast into his wish﴾. So the first was omitted because the second indicates it. ﴿Tamanna﴾ (wished) is the form ﴿tafa''ala﴾ from ﴿al-munya﴾.

Abu Muslim said: "Tamanni is the end of estimation, and from it comes al-munya, the death of a person at the time God has decreed; and 'manna Allahu laka' means 'God decreed for you.'" The narrators of the language said: "al-umniyya means recitation," and they argued with the verse of Hassan, and this returns to the original root, for the reciter estimates the letters and mentions them one by one. End of quotation. The verse of Hassan:

He wished the Book of God, the first night and its last; he met the death-doom of the decreed fates.

Another said:

He wished the Book of God the first night ... as Dawud wished the Zabur, at a steady pace.

Some commentators understood His saying ﴿when he wished﴾ as ﴿recited﴾, and ﴿in his wish﴾ as ﴿in his recitation﴾. The clause after ﴿illa﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: ﴿And We did not send him﴾ except [while], and this is his state. It was also said that the clause is in the position of a descriptive clause, which is al-Zamakhshari's view in such constructions as: "I did not pass by anyone except that Zayd is better than him." The correct view is that the clause is circumstantial, not descriptive, because it accepts the ﴿waw﴾ of circumstance. The ﴿lam﴾ in ﴿that He may make﴾ is connected to ﴿yahkumu﴾ (He judges), as al-Hawfi said. Ibn 'Atiyya said: connected to ﴿yansakhu﴾ (abolishes). Others said: connected to ﴿alqa﴾ (casts). The apparent view is that it is the ﴿lam﴾ of causation. It was also said it is the ﴿lam﴾ of consequence. The ﴿ma﴾ in ﴿what Satan casts﴾: the apparent view is that it means ﴿alladhi﴾ (that which), and it was permitted that it be verbal-source (masdariyya).

Al-fitna means testing and trial. Those ﴿in whose hearts is a disease﴾ are generally the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari said: the hypocrites and the doubters. ﴿And the hardened of heart﴾ are the elite of the disbelievers, the obstinate, such as Abu Jahl, al-Nadr, and Utba. Al-Zamakhshari said: [p. 383] the polytheists, the deniers. ﴿Indeed the wrongdoers﴾: he means these hypocrites and polytheists; the original would be ﴿indeed they﴾, but he placed the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, passing judgment on them as wrongdoers. Al-shiqaq means opposition, i.e., in a split other than the split of righteousness; describing it as ﴿far-off﴾ is an intensification of its extremity and that their return from it is not to be hoped for.

The pronoun in ﴿that it﴾: Ibn 'Atiyya said it refers to the Qur'an. ﴿Those given knowledge﴾ [al-Mujadila: 11] are the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ. The pronoun to which it refers has already been mentioned in our earlier discussion of the verse. ﴿So their hearts humble themselves﴾ means they become humble and submissive, unlike the one in whose heart is a disease and whose heart has hardened. Al-Jumhur read ﴿la-hadi alladhina amanu﴾ with the genitive construction, while Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿lahadin﴾ with tanwin.

Al-mirya means doubt. The pronoun in ﴿about it﴾ is said to refer to the Qur'an; it was said to refer to the Messenger; and it was said to refer to what Satan cast. When he first mentioned the state of the disbelievers and then the state of the believers, he returned to explaining the state of the disbelievers. The apparent view is that ﴿the Hour﴾ is the Day of Resurrection. It was said: ﴿the barren day﴾ is the Day of Badr. It was said: it is the moment of their death or their killing in this world, like the Day of Badr, and the barren day is the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the barren day is the Day of Badr, and the day of battle was described as barren because the children of women are killed in it, so they become as if they were barren women who did not bear; or because the fighters are called "sons of war," and when they are killed the day of war is described as barren, figuratively. It was also said: it is the day that has no good in it; one says "a barren wind" when it does not bring rain nor fertilize trees. It was said: there is no equal to it in the magnitude of its matter, because the angels fought in it. From al-Dahhak: it is the Day of Resurrection, and the intended meaning of "the Hour" is its preliminaries. It is permissible that "the Hour" and "a barren day" both mean the Day of Resurrection, as though it said: ﴿until the Hour comes upon them﴾ or ﴿its punishment comes upon them﴾, so ﴿a barren day﴾ was placed in the position of the pronoun. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The Day of Resurrection, or the day of annihilation, was called barren because there is no night after it nor day, whereas all days are successive results, one following another, and the last day has become barren. This is a metaphor. The whole of this verse is a threat. End of quotation. ﴿Until﴾ (hatta) marks the endpoint of the continuation of their doubt, so the meaning is: ﴿until the Hour comes upon them﴾ (or ﴿the punishment of a barren day﴾), at which point their doubt will vanish and they will witness the matter with their own eyes.

The tanwin in ﴿on that day﴾ is the tanwin of replacement (iwad), and the clause for which this tanwin is a replacement is what was omitted after the endpoint, i.e., ﴿the dominion﴾ belongs to the day when their doubt ceases. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it first as "the day they believe," which is necessarily implied by the cessation of doubt, for when doubt ceases they believe; and he estimated it secondly as we have estimated, which is the better view. The apparent view is that this day is the Day of Resurrection, in that there is no dominion in it for any of the kings of this world, as God said: ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾ [Ghafir: 16]. The following division supports this. Whoever says it is the Day of Badr or the like considers that God's decree alone is carried out, everything else is nullified, and His judgment passes on whomever He wills to punish; and the division would then be a report built upon their state on that barren day, in terms of faith and disbelief. The wordings of the division and their meanings are clear and need no explanation. He contrasted bliss with punishment and described the punishment as humiliating, for emphasis.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 22, verse 52–62 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And those who emigrated﴾ — the verse. This begins another meaning. When Uthman ibn Maz'un and Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Asad died, some people said: "Whoever among the emigrants was killed is better than the one who died of his own natural death." So it was revealed, placing them on an equal footing in that Allah will provide them with ﴿a goodly provision﴾. The apparent sense of ﴿And those who emigrated﴾ is generality. Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning groups who left Mecca for Medina for the hijrah, and the polytheists pursued them and fought them. It is related that groups of the Companions said: "O Prophet of Allah, we know what good Allah has given to those who were killed. We strive alongside you as they strove. So what is ours if we die with you?" Then Allah revealed these two verses.

Al-Zamakhshari said: When the emigration in the way of Allah brought them together, He equated them in the promise, so that He gives whoever among them died the same as He gives whoever was killed, as a bounty and a kindness from Him. And Allah is All-Knowing of the degrees of those who act and the ranks of their deservingness, Forbearing toward the negligence of the negligent among them, by His grace and generosity. End.

In his saying "and the ranks of their deservingness" there is the subtle Mu'tazilite notion (dasisat al-i'tizal). Equality in the promise of provision does not indicate preference in the amount given, and there is no equality (in rank); if there is preference, it is from another proof. The apparent teaching of the Shari'ah is that the one who was killed is superior. It has been said: the one killed and the one who dies in the way of Allah are both martyrs.

The goodly provision may be intended to mean the provision of the martyrs in the barzakh, and it may be that it is after the Day of Resurrection in Paradise, which is its bliss. Al-Kalbi said: it is the spoils of war. Al-Asamm said: it is knowledge and understanding, like the saying of Shu'ayb: ﴿and He has provided me from Himself with goodly provision﴾ [Hud: 88]. These two opinions are weak, because He made the goodly provision a reward for their being killed in the way of Allah or dying after their emigration, and after that the provision is not in this world. The apparent meaning is that ﴿the best of providers﴾ is an elative (af'al al-tafdil), and the superiority is that He is singularly able to provide by means that no one other than Him can command, and that He is the origin of provision, whereas others provide only by what they have of provision from Allah.

When He mentioned provision, He mentioned the dwelling, saying ﴿He will surely admit them to an admission they will be pleased with﴾, which is Paradise. They are pleased with it, meaning they choose it, since in it is their contentment, as He said ﴿they will not desire a change from it﴾ [al-Kahf: 108]. The disagreement in the recitation regarding the vowelling of the mim, with a damma or a fatha, has been mentioned in al-Nisa'. The better view is that by the madkhal (admission) is meant the place of entering or the place of causing entry, and it may be a verbal noun.

﴿That, and whoever retaliates﴾ — the verse. It has been said: it was revealed concerning a group of believers whom disbelievers met in the sacred months; the believers refused to fight them, and the polytheists insisted on fighting. When they fought, the believers exerted themselves, and Allah gave them victory. Its connection to what precedes is clear: when He mentioned the reward of the one who emigrated and was killed or died in the way of Allah, He informed that He does not abandon their support in this world against whoever transgresses against them. Ibn Jurayj said: the verse concerns the polytheists who transgressed against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and expelled him, and the estimate is "the matter is that."

Al-Zamakhshari said: naming the beginning by its recompense is because it is connected to it, in that it is a cause and that is an effect of it, just as they pair a like with a like and an opposite with an opposite, for the connection. If you ask: how does the mention of "the Pardoner, the Forgiving" fit this place? I say: the one who retaliates is sent by Allah, glorified and exalted, to correct the neglect of punishment, while pardon of the offender is by way of tanzih (purification/commendation), not prohibition, and it is recommended and merits praise from Allah if one prefers what is recommended and takes the path of tanzih. When he did not prefer that, and retaliated and punished, and did not heed the saying ﴿So whoever pardons and makes amends, his reward is upon Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 40], ﴿and that you pardon is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], ﴿and whoever is patient and forgives, that is indeed of the steadfast matters﴾ [al-Shura: 43], ﴿Indeed Allah is Pardoning, Forgiving﴾, meaning He does not blame him for leaving what He sent him to, and He guarantees his victory in his second assault after his neglect of pardon, and his vengeance upon the transgressor against him. It is also permissible that He guarantees him victory over the transgressor, while turning away with that from what was better for him of pardon. The mention of these two attributes hints at this, or by mentioning pardon and forgiveness indicates that He is able to punish, because one is described as pardoning only if he is capable of that limit; that is, that victory is by means of His being capable.

Among the signs of His far-reaching power is that ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾ and ﴿the day into the night﴾, or by reason of His being the Creator of night and day and their Director. Nothing that takes place in them at the hands of His servants of good and evil, transgression and retaliation, is hidden from Him. And He is (All-Hearing) of what they say, (All-Seeing) of what they do. The explanation of this "entering" was mentioned earlier at the beginning of Al 'Imran.

(That) — that attribute of creating night and day, encompassing what occurs within them and perceiving every saying and deed — is because (Allah) is the Truth, the established Divinity, and because everything called god besides Him is false in its claim, and because there is nothing exalted above Him in rank or greater in sovereignty. The majority read (wa-anna ma) with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra. Al-Akhawan, Abu Amr and Hafs read (yad'una) here and in Luqman with the third-person ya. The rest of the seven read it with the second-person ta. Both forms have the verb in the active voice. Mujahid, al-Yamani and Musa al-Uswari read (yud'a) with ya in the passive voice, and the waw refers to "ma," which is by its meaning. The apparent referent of "ma" is their idols. It has been said: the devils. The better view is generality, covering everything called upon besides Allah, Exalted.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 22, verses 52–62 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Never did We send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he wished, Satan cast into his wish. But God abolishes what Satan casts, then God establishes His signs. God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿That He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease and whose hearts are hardened. Indeed the wrongdoers are in a far-off schism.﴾ ﴿And that those given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, so that they believe in it and their hearts humble themselves before it. Indeed God guides those who believe to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them suddenly or there comes to them the punishment of a barren day.﴾ ﴿The dominion on that day belongs to God; He judges between them. As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ ﴿And as for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, they will have a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿And those who emigrated in the way of God and were then killed or died, God will surely provide for them a goodly provision. Indeed God is the best of providers.﴾ ﴿He will surely admit them to an entrance they will be pleased with. Indeed God is All-Knowing, Forbearing.﴾ ﴿That is so. And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with, and then is wronged again, God will surely help him. Indeed God is Pardoning, Forgiving.﴾ ﴿That is so, because God causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and because God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿That is so, because God is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood, and because God is the Most High, the Most Great.﴾

When God mentioned that He defends those who believe [p. 381], and that He permitted the believers to fight, and that they had been expelled from their homes, and when He mentioned the consolation of His messenger ﷺ by the denial of those nations before him toward their prophets, and what their affair came to in destruction after denial and after being given respite, He commanded him to call the people and inform them that he is a warner to them, after they had hastened for the punishment, and that it is not for him to bring the punishment forward or delay it. He, exalted is He, mentioned to him a second consolation in regard to the messengers and prophets who passed before him: that they were eager for the faith of their peoples, wishing for it and striving toward it. None of them was without Satan opposing him by adorning disbelief for his people, spreading it among them and casting it into their souls. Likewise the Prophet ﷺ was among the most eager of people for the guidance of his people, and among them were devils such as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who cast doubts to his people and to those who came to him, by which they sought to hinder them from Islam. For this reason there came before this verse: ﴿And those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them﴾ [al-Hajj: 51], and their striving was by casting doubts into the hearts of those whom they sought to win over. He attributed this to Satan because he is the one who misleads and who moves the devils of mankind to lead astray, as he said: ﴿I will surely mislead them﴾. It was also said that "the Satan" here is a genus, meant to include the devils of mankind. The pronoun in ﴿his wish﴾ refers to "Satan," i.e., in the wish of his own self, meaning because of the wish of his own self. The object of ﴿cast﴾ is omitted for understanding; it is evil and disbelief, and the opposition of that to the messenger or prophet, because Satan does not cast good. The meaning of ﴿then God abolishes what Satan casts﴾ is that He removes those doubts little by little until people become Muslims, as He said: ﴿And you see people entering the religion of God in multitudes﴾ [al-Nasr: 2]. And ﴿God establishes His signs﴾ means His miracles, which He shows firmly established, with no confusion in them. ﴿That He may make what Satan casts﴾ of those doubts and deceptive speech ﴿a trial﴾ for the one with a diseased heart and the hardened one. ﴿And that those given knowledge﴾ may know that what the messenger and the prophet wished for, of the guidance and faith of his people, is the truth. This verse does not attribute anything to the Messenger of God ﷺ; it only includes the state of those messengers and prophets before him when they wished.

The commentators, in their books, including Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari, and those before and after them, mentioned what it is not permissible to occur from ordinary believers attributed to the infallible one, may God's blessings be upon him. They went at length on this, with question and answer, and it is a story about which the Imam Muhammad ibn Ishaq, compiler of the Prophetic biography, was asked. He said: "This is from the fabrications of the heretics," and he wrote a book on this [p. 382]. The Imam, the hadith master Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn al-Husayn al-Bayhaqi, said: "This story is not established in terms of transmission." He said something to the effect that its narrators are criticized, and that nothing of what they mentioned is in the Sahih collections or in the hadith compilations, so it must be discarded; for this reason I kept my book free of mentioning it. How strange it is to transmit this when they recite in the Book of God: ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [al-Najm: 1], ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2], ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ [al-Najm: 3], ﴿It is but a revelation revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 4]. God, exalted is He, also said, commanding His Prophet: ﴿Say: It is not for me to change it on my own accord; I follow only what is revealed to me﴾ [Yunus: 15]. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Had he fabricated against Us some sayings﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44], the verse onward.
