The pronoun in ﴿that it﴾: Ibn 'Atiyya said it refers to the Qur'an. ﴿Those given knowledge﴾ [al-Mujadila: 11] are the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ. The pronoun to which it refers has already been mentioned in our earlier discussion of the verse. ﴿So their hearts humble themselves﴾ means they become humble and submissive, unlike the one in whose heart is a disease and whose heart has hardened. Al-Jumhur read ﴿la-hadi alladhina amanu﴾ with the genitive construction, while Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿lahadin﴾ with tanwin.

Al-mirya means doubt. The pronoun in ﴿about it﴾ is said to refer to the Qur'an; it was said to refer to the Messenger; and it was said to refer to what Satan cast. When he first mentioned the state of the disbelievers and then the state of the believers, he returned to explaining the state of the disbelievers. The apparent view is that ﴿the Hour﴾ is the Day of Resurrection. It was said: ﴿the barren day﴾ is the Day of Badr. It was said: it is the moment of their death or their killing in this world, like the Day of Badr, and the barren day is the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the barren day is the Day of Badr, and the day of battle was described as barren because the children of women are killed in it, so they become as if they were barren women who did not bear; or because the fighters are called "sons of war," and when they are killed the day of war is described as barren, figuratively. It was also said: it is the day that has no good in it; one says "a barren wind" when it does not bring rain nor fertilize trees. It was said: there is no equal to it in the magnitude of its matter, because the angels fought in it. From al-Dahhak: it is the Day of Resurrection, and the intended meaning of "the Hour" is its preliminaries. It is permissible that "the Hour" and "a barren day" both mean the Day of Resurrection, as though it said: ﴿until the Hour comes upon them﴾ or ﴿its punishment comes upon them﴾, so ﴿a barren day﴾ was placed in the position of the pronoun. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The Day of Resurrection, or the day of annihilation, was called barren because there is no night after it nor day, whereas all days are successive results, one following another, and the last day has become barren. This is a metaphor. The whole of this verse is a threat. End of quotation. ﴿Until﴾ (hatta) marks the endpoint of the continuation of their doubt, so the meaning is: ﴿until the Hour comes upon them﴾ (or ﴿the punishment of a barren day﴾), at which point their doubt will vanish and they will witness the matter with their own eyes.

The tanwin in ﴿on that day﴾ is the tanwin of replacement (iwad), and the clause for which this tanwin is a replacement is what was omitted after the endpoint, i.e., ﴿the dominion﴾ belongs to the day when their doubt ceases. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it first as "the day they believe," which is necessarily implied by the cessation of doubt, for when doubt ceases they believe; and he estimated it secondly as we have estimated, which is the better view. The apparent view is that this day is the Day of Resurrection, in that there is no dominion in it for any of the kings of this world, as God said: ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾ [Ghafir: 16]. The following division supports this. Whoever says it is the Day of Badr or the like considers that God's decree alone is carried out, everything else is nullified, and His judgment passes on whomever He wills to punish; and the division would then be a report built upon their state on that barren day, in terms of faith and disbelief. The wordings of the division and their meanings are clear and need no explanation. He contrasted bliss with punishment and described the punishment as humiliating, for emphasis.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 22, verse 52–62 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And those who emigrated﴾ — the verse. This begins another meaning. When Uthman ibn Maz'un and Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Asad died, some people said: "Whoever among the emigrants was killed is better than the one who died of his own natural death." So it was revealed, placing them on an equal footing in that Allah will provide them with ﴿a goodly provision﴾. The apparent sense of ﴿And those who emigrated﴾ is generality. Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning groups who left Mecca for Medina for the hijrah, and the polytheists pursued them and fought them. It is related that groups of the Companions said: "O Prophet of Allah, we know what good Allah has given to those who were killed. We strive alongside you as they strove. So what is ours if we die with you?" Then Allah revealed these two verses.

Al-Zamakhshari said: When the emigration in the way of Allah brought them together, He equated them in the promise, so that He gives whoever among them died the same as He gives whoever was killed, as a bounty and a kindness from Him. And Allah is All-Knowing of the degrees of those who act and the ranks of their deservingness, Forbearing toward the negligence of the negligent among them, by His grace and generosity. End.

In his saying "and the ranks of their deservingness" there is the subtle Mu'tazilite notion (dasisat al-i'tizal). Equality in the promise of provision does not indicate preference in the amount given, and there is no equality (in rank); if there is preference, it is from another proof. The apparent teaching of the Shari'ah is that the one who was killed is superior. It has been said: the one killed and the one who dies in the way of Allah are both martyrs.

The goodly provision may be intended to mean the provision of the martyrs in the barzakh, and it may be that it is after the Day of Resurrection in Paradise, which is its bliss. Al-Kalbi said: it is the spoils of war. Al-Asamm said: it is knowledge and understanding, like the saying of Shu'ayb: ﴿and He has provided me from Himself with goodly provision﴾ [Hud: 88]. These two opinions are weak, because He made the goodly provision a reward for their being killed in the way of Allah or dying after their emigration, and after that the provision is not in this world. The apparent meaning is that ﴿the best of providers﴾ is an elative (af'al al-tafdil), and the superiority is that He is singularly able to provide by means that no one other than Him can command, and that He is the origin of provision, whereas others provide only by what they have of provision from Allah.

When He mentioned provision, He mentioned the dwelling, saying ﴿He will surely admit them to an admission they will be pleased with﴾, which is Paradise. They are pleased with it, meaning they choose it, since in it is their contentment, as He said ﴿they will not desire a change from it﴾ [al-Kahf: 108]. The disagreement in the recitation regarding the vowelling of the mim, with a damma or a fatha, has been mentioned in al-Nisa'. The better view is that by the madkhal (admission) is meant the place of entering or the place of causing entry, and it may be a verbal noun.

﴿That, and whoever retaliates﴾ — the verse. It has been said: it was revealed concerning a group of believers whom disbelievers met in the sacred months; the believers refused to fight them, and the polytheists insisted on fighting. When they fought, the believers exerted themselves, and Allah gave them victory. Its connection to what precedes is clear: when He mentioned the reward of the one who emigrated and was killed or died in the way of Allah, He informed that He does not abandon their support in this world against whoever transgresses against them. Ibn Jurayj said: the verse concerns the polytheists who transgressed against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and expelled him, and the estimate is "the matter is that."

Al-Zamakhshari said: naming the beginning by its recompense is because it is connected to it, in that it is a cause and that is an effect of it, just as they pair a like with a like and an opposite with an opposite, for the connection. If you ask: how does the mention of "the Pardoner, the Forgiving" fit this place? I say: the one who retaliates is sent by Allah, glorified and exalted, to correct the neglect of punishment, while pardon of the offender is by way of tanzih (purification/commendation), not prohibition, and it is recommended and merits praise from Allah if one prefers what is recommended and takes the path of tanzih. When he did not prefer that, and retaliated and punished, and did not heed the saying ﴿So whoever pardons and makes amends, his reward is upon Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 40], ﴿and that you pardon is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], ﴿and whoever is patient and forgives, that is indeed of the steadfast matters﴾ [al-Shura: 43], ﴿Indeed Allah is Pardoning, Forgiving﴾, meaning He does not blame him for leaving what He sent him to, and He guarantees his victory in his second assault after his neglect of pardon, and his vengeance upon the transgressor against him. It is also permissible that He guarantees him victory over the transgressor, while turning away with that from what was better for him of pardon. The mention of these two attributes hints at this, or by mentioning pardon and forgiveness indicates that He is able to punish, because one is described as pardoning only if he is capable of that limit; that is, that victory is by means of His being capable.

Among the signs of His far-reaching power is that ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾ and ﴿the day into the night﴾, or by reason of His being the Creator of night and day and their Director. Nothing that takes place in them at the hands of His servants of good and evil, transgression and retaliation, is hidden from Him. And He is (All-Hearing) of what they say, (All-Seeing) of what they do. The explanation of this "entering" was mentioned earlier at the beginning of Al 'Imran.

(That) — that attribute of creating night and day, encompassing what occurs within them and perceiving every saying and deed — is because (Allah) is the Truth, the established Divinity, and because everything called god besides Him is false in its claim, and because there is nothing exalted above Him in rank or greater in sovereignty. The majority read (wa-anna ma) with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra. Al-Akhawan, Abu Amr and Hafs read (yad'una) here and in Luqman with the third-person ya. The rest of the seven read it with the second-person ta. Both forms have the verb in the active voice. Mujahid, al-Yamani and Musa al-Uswari read (yud'a) with ya in the passive voice, and the waw refers to "ma," which is by its meaning. The apparent referent of "ma" is their idols. It has been said: the devils. The better view is generality, covering everything called upon besides Allah, Exalted.

[p. 385] When God mentioned the signs of His overwhelming power in the alternation of night and day, which are two observable matters (the coming of darkness and of light), He also mentioned what is observable in the upper and lower worlds: the descent of rain, the growth of the earth, the sending down of rain, and the greening of the earth, which are visible. Attributing the sending down to God is grasped by reason. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: Although the water is visible, God's being the one who sends it down from the sky is not visible. If this is established, then the verse must be taken as referring to knowledge, because when sight is not accompanied by knowledge, it is as if it had not occurred.

al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "Why was it not said 'fa-asbahat' (so it became)? And why was it turned to the present tense form?" I answer: For a subtle purpose in it, which is to convey that the effect of the rain remains over time after time, as you say, "So-and-so bestowed favour upon me in such-and-such a year, so I spend my evenings and mornings thankful to him." Had you said, "I rejoiced and I spent my mornings," it would not have occupied that position.

If you ask, "Why was it put in the nominative and not the accusative as an answer to the interrogative?" I answer: If it were in the accusative, it would give the opposite of the purpose, because its meaning is affirming the greening, and by the accusative it would turn into negating the greening. An example of this is that you say to your companion, "Do you not see that I have bestowed favour upon you, so that you would be thankful?" If you put it in the accusative, you are negating his thankfulness and doubting his neglect; but if you put it in the nominative, you are affirming his thankfulness. This and similar matters are those that one who is characterized by knowledge in the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis of case endings) and the honouring of its people should desire.

Ibn Atiyya said: His words "fa-tusbihu al-ardu" (so the earth becomes) are in the position of His words "fa-tadha" (so it becomes bright) or "tasir" (it becomes), an expression of the earth's haste to react to the descent of the water and its continuing in that state habitually. The phrase "fa-tusbihu" in terms of the verse is a predicate (khabar), and the fa' is conjunctive, not a response, because its being a response to "a-lam tara" (have you not seen) is semantically corrupt. End of quote. Neither he nor al-Zamakhshari explained how the accusative would negate the greening, nor why the meaning would be corrupt.

Sibawayh said: I asked him, meaning al-Khalil, about "a-lam tara anna Allaha anzala min al-sama'ima'an fa-tusbihu al-ardu mukhdarratan" (Do you not see that God sent down water from the sky, so the earth becomes green?). He said: This is obligatory and is an alert, as if you had said, "Do you listen? God sent down water from the sky, so such-and-such occurred." Ibn Kharuf said: His saying "he said: this is obligatory," and his saying "so such-and-such occurred," means that both are past tense. He explained the statement by "atasma'u" (do you listen?) to show that it is not connected to the interrogative, because the force of the interrogative in it is weak. In the Eastern (copy) instead of "atasma'u" there occurs "intabih" (pay attention). End of quote. "Fi al-Sharqiyya" means in the Eastern copy of Sibawayh's book.

Some commentators on the book said: "fa-tusbihu" cannot be put in the accusative, because the statement is obligatory. Do you not see that the meaning is "that God sent down", so the earth is in this state? al-Farra' said: "a-lam tara" is a statement of fact, as when you say in speech, "Know that God does such-and-such, so such-and-such occurs." End of quote.

He says: The accusative as an answer to the interrogative is prevented here because when negation is preceded by the interrogative, although it may imply affirmation in some speech, it is treated in the answer as pure negation. Do you not see His words: "Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes" (7:172)? Likewise, in the answer with fa', when you answer a negation, it has two meanings, in each of which the answer is negated. So if you say, "You do not come to us, so you speak to us" in the accusative, the meaning is "You do not come to us speaking; you only come and do not speak," or it may mean "You do not come, so how do you speak?" Speaking is negated in both cases. Affirmation by means of the interrogative particle is like pure negation in the answer: it affirms what the hamza precedes, and the answer is negated. From what we have established follows the affirmation of seeing and the negation of greening, which is contrary to the purpose. Also, the answer to the interrogative forms, together with the preceding interrogative, a condition and a conditional result. So His poet's words:

"Have you not asked, so the traces will inform you?"

imply: "If you ask, the traces will inform you." Here it cannot be implied that "if you see the descent of rain, the earth becomes green," because its greening is not consequent upon your knowledge or your seeing; it is consequent upon the descent. He expressed it in the present tense because it depicts the state in which the earth is, and the condition that clothes the earth, whereas the past tense indicates that the thing has ended. This is like the words of Jahdar ibn Ma'awanah al-Ukli, describing his state at the hardest moment in an incident that befell him with al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf:

"He rises with two eyes; you would think in them,
when the gleam of a lamp moves across them, [a fire]"

"When I descended upon a fortress, lion-hearted and lowering his head,
to the champion of the foe, I snatched the spirits of the enemy"

"So I charge and attack while he crouches on his rump,
then when he returns, I turn back on my tracks"

"And I knew that if I refused to meet him in combat,
I would not escape al-Hajjaj"

So his words "fa-akirru" (so I charge) depict the state that clothed him. The apparent meaning is that the greening of the earth follows the descent of rain, and this is found only in Mecca and Tihama, as Ikrimah said; he took "tusbihu" in its literal sense, meaning "it becomes [green] by the morning of the night of rain." He held that in places other than Mecca and Tihama the greening is delayed. Ibn Atiyya said: I have witnessed this in the far Sus region, where rain fell at night after a drought, and by morning that sandy land, which the winds had scattered, had turned green with sparse vegetation. End of quote.

If we take "fa-tusbihu" to mean "fa-tasir" (so it becomes), it does not follow that the greening occurs in the morning. If the greening is delayed after the descent of rain, then there are omitted clauses in the sense: "so it stirs and swells, and so it becomes green." His exalted words clarify this: "And when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and puts forth [growth]" (22:5). It was read "mukhdarratan" in the pattern of "muf'alatan," and "musbi'atan," meaning possessing greenness. He singled out "tusbihu" from the other times of the day because seeing agreeable things at the beginning of the day is more delightful and joyful to the beholder.

"Inna Allaha latif" (God is subtle): that is, in bringing forth plants from the earth by the water He sent down. "Khabir" (All-Aware): of what comes from that plant of grain and other things. It was said: "Khabir" in the sense of subtle arrangement; "Khabir" in the sense of abundant craftsmanship; and it was said: "Khabir" with the measures of the interests of His servants, so He acts in proportion to that without excess or deficiency. Ibn Abbas said: "Latif" with the provisions of His servants; "Khabir" with what is in their hearts of despair. al-Kalbi said: "Latif" in His acts; "Khabir" with the deeds of His creation. al-Zamakhshari said: "Latif" whose knowledge or grace reaches every thing; "Khabir" with the interests and benefits of creation. Ibn Atiyya said: "al-Latif" is the one who arranges affairs with gentleness. "Ma fi al-ardi" (what is in the earth) includes animals, minerals, and provisions.

The majority read "wa-al-fulka" in the accusative. Ibn Miqsam and al-Kisa'i (from al-Hasan) read it with a damma on the lam. It is in the accusative by conjunction with "ma" (what), and it is singled out, though it is included in the general "ma," to draw attention to the strangeness of its subjection and the abundance of its benefits, and this is the apparent meaning. It was permitted that it be conjoined to the divine name (Allah) with the implied "anna" (that), "wa-anna al-fulka," which is a distant grammatical construction far from eloquence. "Tajri" is a circumstantial clause (hal) according to the apparent parsing, and in the genitive position according to the second parsing. al-Sulami, al-A'raj, Talhah, Abu Haywah and al-Za'faarani read "al-fulku" with a damma on the kaf, as a subject and predicate. Whoever permits conjunction to the position of the noun after "inna" permits it here, and then "tajri" is a circumstantial clause. The apparent view is that "an" (that) is in the accusative position as a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), meaning: and it prevents the sky from falling upon the earth. It was said it is an object of purpose, which the Basrans estimate as "karahata an taqa'" (lest it fall), and the Kufans as "li-'an la taqa'" (so that it does not fall). His words "illa bi-idhnihi" (except by His permission) mean on the Day of Resurrection, as if the folding of the sky is part of this condition for its occurrence. It is permissible that this is a threat to them: that if He permits its falling in pieces upon you, it will fall, as in their saying: "Or cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed" (17:92). "Illa bi-idhnihi" is connected to "an taqa'" (to fall), meaning "except by His permission, so it falls." Ibn Atiyya said: It is possible that His words "illa bi-idhnihi" refer to the holding, because the statement implies without pillars or the like, so it is as if He meant: except by His permission, in it, He holds it. End of quote.

If it were as Ibn Atiyya said, the construction would be "bi-idhnihi" without the exception particle, that is, the estimate would be: "and He holds the sky by His permission."

"Wa-huwa alladhi ahyakum" (It is He who gave you life): that is, after you were lifeless, dust, a drop, a clot, and a lump of flesh. This is the first death mentioned in His words: "How do you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life?" (2:28). "Al-insan" (the human): Ibn Abbas said: he is the disbeliever. He also said: he is al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Asad, Abu Jahl, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf. This is by way of example. "La-kafur" (truly ungrateful): truly ungrateful to the blessings of God, worshipping other than the One who bestowed these blessings and others upon him.

"Li-kulli ummatin ja'alna mansakan" (For every community We have made a rite): it is narrated that it was revealed because of the disputation of the disbelievers, Budayl ibn Warqa' and Bishr ibn Sufyan al-Khuza'i and others, about slaughtering and their saying to the believers: "You eat what you have slaughtered, and you do not eat what God has killed," so it was revealed because of this dispute. Ibn Atiyya said: "hum nasikuhu" (they are performers of it) indicates that "mansak" is a verbal noun; had the place been intended, it would have said "hum nasikuna fihi" (they perform it therein). End of quote. What he said is not necessarily fixed, since the object of an active participle may be extended just as the object of a verb is extended. So this is a place where the extension applies, and it is treated as the direct object by extension. Of the extension in the adverb of place is His poet's words:

"And a watering place I drink from, its pool,
neither stagnant water nor harmful"

"Mashrab" (watering place) is the place of drinking, and the pronoun refers to it; its original form was "ashrabu fihi" (I drink from it), then it was extended so that the verb reached its pronoun. Of the extension is "Sira bi-Zaydin farsakhan" (Zayd was journeyed a parasang). It was read "fa-la yunaziununnaka" with a light nun, meaning: hold firm to your religion with a steadfastness that they do not hope to draw you away from it. Similar is "wa-la yasuddanaka 'an ayati Allah" (and let them not turn you away from the signs of God) (28:87). This prohibition to them regarding disputation is from the kind of "la araynnaka huhuna" (I will not see you here), and the meaning is: they must not dispute with you, so they dispute with you. Abu Mijlaz read "fa-la yunaza'unnaka" from "al-naz'" (pulling), meaning: they will not pull you away, so that they carry you from your religion to their religions, from "naza'tuhu min kadha" (I pulled him from such-and-such). "Al-amr" here is the religion, and what you brought; and according to the narration about the occasion of revelation, "fi al-amri" means "in the slaughter." "La-'ala hudan" (surely upon guidance): that is, right guidance. "Wa-li-kulli ummatin" [22:34] came with "wa" (and), but here it is "li-kulli ummatin" without "wa," because that verse came together with what is close to it and suitable to it of verses concerning the rites of sacrifice, so it was conjoined to its siblings; but this one came with verses far from its meaning, so it found no conjunction. This is what al-Zamakhshari said.

"Wa-in jadaluka" (And if they dispute with you): a verse of conciliation (muwada'a) abrogated by the verse of the sword. That is, if they refuse, out of their obstinacy, anything but disputation after your effort that there should be no contention between you and them, then repel them by saying that God knows best your deeds and their ugliness and what they deserve for them of recompense. This is a threat and a warning, but with gentleness and mildness. "Allahu yahkumu baynakum" (God will judge between you): an address from God to believers and disbelievers, that is, He will separate you by reward and punishment, and it is a consolation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for what he encountered from them.

[p. 385] When God mentioned the signs of His overwhelming power in the alternation of night and day, which are two observable matters (the coming of darkness and of light), He also mentioned what is observable in the upper and lower worlds: the descent of rain, the growth of the earth, the sending down of rain, and the greening of the earth, which are visible. He singled out "tusbihu" from the other times of the day because seeing agreeable things at the beginning of the day is more delightful and joyful to the beholder.

"Inna Allaha latif" (God is subtle): that is, in bringing forth plants from the earth by the water He sent down. "Khabir" (All-Aware): of what comes from that plant of grain and other things. It was said: "Khabir" in the sense of subtle arrangement; "Khabir" in the sense of abundant craftsmanship; and it was said: "Khabir" with the measures of the interests of His servants, so He acts in proportion to that without excess or deficiency. Ibn Abbas said: "Latif" with the provisions of His servants; "Khabir" with what is in their hearts of despair. al-Kalbi said: "Latif" in His acts; "Khabir" with the deeds of His creation. al-Zamakhshari said: "Latif" whose knowledge or grace reaches every thing; "Khabir" with the interests and benefits of creation. Ibn Atiyya said: "al-Latif" is the one who arranges affairs with gentleness. "Ma fi al-ardi" (what is in the earth) includes animals, minerals, and provisions.

The majority read "wa-al-fulka" in the accusative. Ibn Miqsam and al-Kisa'i (from al-Hasan) read it with a damma on the lam. It is in the accusative by conjunction with "ma" (what), and it is singled out, though it is included in the general "ma," to draw attention to the strangeness of its subjection and the abundance of its benefits, and this is the apparent meaning. It was permitted that it be conjoined to the divine name (Allah) with the implied "anna" (that), "wa-anna al-fulka," which is a distant grammatical construction far from eloquence. "Tajri" is a circumstantial clause (hal) according to the apparent parsing, and in the genitive position according to the second parsing. al-Sulami, al-A'raj, Talhah, Abu Haywah and al-Za'faarani read "al-fulku" with a damma on the kaf, as a subject and predicate. Whoever permits conjunction to the position of the noun after "inna" permits it here, and then "tajri" is a circumstantial clause. The apparent view is that "an" (that) is in the accusative position as a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), meaning: and it prevents the sky from falling upon the earth. It was said it is an object of purpose, which the Basrans estimate as "karahata an taqa'" (lest it fall), and the Kufans as "li-'an la taqa'" (so that it does not fall). His words "illa bi-idhnihi" (except by His permission) mean on the Day of Resurrection, as if the folding of the sky is part of this condition for its occurrence. It is permissible that this is a threat to them: that if He permits its falling in pieces upon you, it will fall, as in their saying: "Or cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed" (17:92). "Illa bi-idhnihi" is connected to "an taqa'" (to fall), meaning "except by His permission, so it falls." Ibn Atiyya said: It is possible that His words "illa bi-idhnihi" refer to the holding, because the statement implies without pillars or the like, so it is as if He meant: except by His permission, in it, He holds it. End of quote.

If it were as Ibn Atiyya said, the construction would be "bi-idhnihi" without the exception particle, that is, the estimate would be: "and He holds the sky by His permission."

End of quote. What he said is not necessarily fixed, since the object of an active participle may be extended just as the object of a verb is extended. So this is a place where the extension applies, and it is treated as the direct object by extension. Of the extension in the adverb of place is His poet's words:

"And a watering place I drink from, its pool,
neither stagnant water nor harmful"

"Mashrab" (watering place) is the place of drinking, and the pronoun refers to it; its original form was "ashrabu fihi" (I drink from it), then it was extended so that the verb reached its pronoun. Of the extension is "Sira bi-Zaydin farsakhan" (Zayd was journeyed a parasang). It was read "fa-la yunaziununnaka" with a light nun, meaning: hold firm to your religion with a steadfastness that they do not hope to draw you away from it. Similar is "wa-la yasuddanaka 'an ayati Allah" (and let them not turn you away from the signs of God) (28:87). This prohibition to them regarding disputation is from the kind of "la araynnaka huhuna" (I will not see you here), and the meaning is: they must not dispute with you, so they dispute with you. Abu Mijlaz read "fa-la yunaza'unnaka" from "al-naz'" (pulling), meaning: they will not pull you away, so that they carry you from your religion to their religions, from "naza'tuhu min kadha" (I pulled him from such-and-such). "Al-amr" here is the religion, and what you brought; and according to the narration about the occasion of revelation, "fi al-amri" means "in the slaughter." "La-'ala hudan" (surely upon guidance): that is, right guidance. "Wa-li-kulli ummatin" [22:34] came with "wa" (and), but here it is "li-kulli ummatin" without "wa," because that verse came together with what is close to it and suitable to it of verses concerning the rites of sacrifice, so it was conjoined to its siblings; but this one came with verses far from its meaning, so it found no conjunction. This is what al-Zamakhshari said.

This is a threat and a warning, but with gentleness and mildness. "Allahu yahkumu baynakum" (God will judge between you): an address from God to believers and disbelievers, that is, He will separate you by reward and punishment, and it is a consolation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for what he encountered from them.

[p. 385] When God mentioned the signs of His overwhelming power in the alternation of night and day, which are two observable matters (the coming of darkness and of light), He also mentioned what is observable in the upper and lower worlds: the descent of rain, the growth of the earth, the sending down of rain, and the greening of the earth, which are visible. Attributing the sending down to God is grasped by reason. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: Although the water is visible, God's being the one who sends it down from the sky is not visible. If this is established, then the verse must be taken as referring to knowledge, because when sight is not accompanied by knowledge, it is as if it had not occurred.

al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "Why was it not said 'fa-asbahat' (so it became)? And why was it turned to the present tense form?" I answer: For a subtle purpose in it, which is to convey that the effect of the rain remains over time after time, as you say, "So-and-so bestowed favour upon me in such-and-such a year, so I spend my evenings and mornings thankful to him." Had you said, "I rejoiced and I spent my mornings," it would not have occupied that position.

If you ask, "Why was it put in the nominative and not the accusative as an answer to the interrogative?" I answer: If it were in the accusative, it would give the opposite of the purpose, because its meaning is affirming the greening, and by the accusative it would turn into negating the greening. An example of this is that you say to your companion, "Do you not see that I have bestowed favour upon you, so that you would be thankful?" If you put it in the accusative, you are negating his thankfulness and doubting his neglect; but if you put it in the nominative, you are affirming his thankfulness. This and similar matters are those that one who is characterized by knowledge in the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis of case endings) and the honouring of its people should desire.

The phrase "fa-tusbihu" in terms of the verse is a predicate (khabar), and the fa' is conjunctive, not a response, because its being a response to "a-lam tara" (have you not seen) is semantically corrupt. End of quote. Neither he nor al-Zamakhshari explained how the accusative would negate the greening, nor why the meaning would be corrupt.

Sibawayh said: I asked him, meaning al-Khalil, about "a-lam tara anna Allaha anzala min al-sama'ima'an fa-tusbihu al-ardu mukhdarratan" (Do you not see that God sent down water from the sky, so the earth becomes green?). He said: This is obligatory and is an alert, as if you had said, "Do you listen? God sent down water from the sky, so such-and-such occurred." Ibn Kharuf said: His saying "he said: this is obligatory," and his saying "so such-and-such occurred," means that both are past tense. He explained the statement by "atasma'u" (do you listen?) to show that it is not connected to the interrogative, because the force of the interrogative in it is weak. In the Eastern (copy) instead of "atasma'u" there occurs "intabih" (pay attention). End of quote. "Fi al-Sharqiyya" means in the Eastern copy of Sibawayh's book.

Some commentators on the book said: "fa-tusbihu" cannot be put in the accusative, because the statement is obligatory. Do you not see that the meaning is "that God sent down", so the earth is in this state? al-Farra' said: "a-lam tara" is a statement of fact, as when you say in speech, "Know that God does such-and-such, so such-and-such occurs." End of quote.

He says: The accusative as an answer to the interrogative is prevented here because when negation is preceded by the interrogative, although it may imply affirmation in some speech, it is treated in the answer as pure negation. Do you not see His words: "Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes" (7:172)? Likewise, in the answer with fa', when you answer a negation, it has two meanings, in each of which the answer is negated. So if you say, "You do not come to us, so you speak to us" in the accusative, the meaning is "You do not come to us speaking; you only come and do not speak," or it may mean "You do not come, so how do you speak?" Speaking is negated in both cases. Affirmation by means of the interrogative particle is like pure negation in the answer: it affirms what the hamza precedes, and the answer is negated. From what we have established follows the affirmation of seeing and the negation of greening, which is contrary to the purpose. Also, the answer to the interrogative forms, together with the preceding interrogative, a condition and a conditional result. So His poet's words:

"Have you not asked, so the traces will inform you?"

imply: "If you ask, the traces will inform you." Here it cannot be implied that "if you see the descent of rain, the earth becomes green," because its greening is not consequent upon your knowledge or your seeing; it is consequent upon the descent. "He rises with two eyes; you would think in them,
when the gleam of a lamp moves across them, [a fire]"

"When I descended upon a fortress, lion-hearted and lowering his head,
to the champion of the foe, I snatched the spirits of the enemy"

"So I charge and attack while he crouches on his rump,
then when he returns, I turn back on my tracks"

"And I knew that if I refused to meet him in combat,
I would not escape al-Hajjaj"

Ibn Atiyya said: I have witnessed this in the far Sus region, where rain fell at night after a drought, and by morning that sandy land, which the winds had scattered, had turned green with sparse vegetation. End of quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 22, verses 70–72:

﴿Do you not know that Allah knows what is in the heaven and the earth? Indeed, that is in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.﴾ ﴿And they worship besides Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and that of which they have no knowledge. And for the wrongdoers there will be no helper.﴾ ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, clear as they are, you recognize in the faces of those who disbelieve the denial. They nearly assault those who recite to them Our verses. Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that? The Fire, which Allah has promised to those who disbelieve. And wretched is the destination."﴾

When the separation between the disbelievers and the believers on the Day of Resurrection had been mentioned, Allah, exalted is He, followed it by stating that He has knowledge of all ﴿what is in the heaven and the earth﴾, so your deeds are not hidden from Him. And ﴿indeed, that is in a Book﴾. It was said: it is the Mother of the Book (Umm al-Kitab), which Allah wrote before He created the heavens and the earth, recording in it what will occur until the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: the Book is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). The demonstrative in His saying ﴿indeed, that is easy for Allah﴾ was said to refer to the previous judgment; the apparent meaning is that it refers to the encompassing of all creatures under His knowledge and comprehensiveness. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is known among the scholars of God that He knows everything that happens in the heavens and the earth, and He has written it on the Tablet before it occurs. Encompassing that, recording it and preserving it is easy, because the Knowing Essence is not hindered and cannot be prevented from being related to a known object." End of quote. In his saying "because the Knowing Essence" there is a trace of Mu'tazilite doctrine (dasisat al-i'tizal), for it is among their creed to deny the attributes, so He is Knowing by His essence, and knowledge is not attributed to Him in their view.

﴿And they worship besides Allah that for which He has sent down no authority﴾, i.e., no proof or divine evidence from revelation and scripture, ﴿and of which they have no knowledge﴾, i.e., no rational evidence, whether necessary or otherwise.

﴿And for the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who transgress the limit in worshipping what cannot be worshipped, ﴿there will be no helper (nasir)﴾ who supports them in what they have gone to, or when the punishment descends upon them.

﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾, i.e., recited by the Messenger or others, ﴿Our verses﴾ clear in rejecting their gods and calling them to the oneness of Allah and His worship, ﴿you recognize in the faces of those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., those who concealed and covered over the truth, though it is clear and manifest, ﴿the denial.﴾ The noun al-munkar is a verbal noun meaning denial (al-inkar). He pointed to the cause that necessitates the denial, which is disbelief, and the apparent noun took the place of the pronoun, as if it were said: "you recognize in their faces," but He drew attention to the cause that makes the denial appear in their faces. Al-munkar means displeasure, scowling, sullenness, glowering, and aggression, all of which indicate evil belief and corruption of inner disposition, because joy and sorrow, whose seat is the heart, appear in the face.

﴿They nearly assault﴾, i.e., they are in this state all their lives, so they are almost always close to doing that, though there has occurred from them an assault upon some of the Companions at rare times. Ibn 'Abbas said: "yasatun" means they stretch out their hands against them. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: they fall upon them. Al-Dahhak said: they seize them forcefully with the hand. The meaning is one.

Isa ibn Umar read yu'raf (passive) for al-munkar. The phrase "Say" (qul) is followed by: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that?" This is a threat and rebuke, and the demonstrative refers to their rage against those who recite and their assault upon them, or to the displeasure and sullenness that befell them because of what was recited to them. The majority read al-Nar (the Fire) in the nominative, by supposing an implied subject, as if a speaker says: "What is it?" and the answer is: "The Fire," i.e., the Fire of Hell. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that al-Nar be the subject and "wa'adaha" the predicate, and that "wa'adaha" be a circumstantial clause in the first reading, and that it be a new independent clause of information, and it was permitted that it be a predicate after a predicate, and that is in the first reading. It is narrated that they said: "Muhammad and his Companions are the worst of creation," so Allah said: "Say to them, O Muhammad, ﴿Shall I inform you of something worse﴾ than those you have mentioned by your claim, the people of the Fire; they are the worst of Allah's creation." Ibn Abi 'Abla and Ibrahim ibn Yusuf from al-A'sha and Zayd ibn 'Ali read al-Nara in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari said: "by way of specification (al-ikhtisas)." Whoever permitted the nominative as the subject would by analogy permit the accusative as an instance of al-ishtighal (the verb being occupied with a pronoun). Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ibrahim ibn Nuh from Qutayba read al-Nari in the genitive as an apposition (badal) to "sharr." The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "wa'adaha" is the first object, meaning that Allah promised the Fire to the disbelievers that it would feed on them, as you see in her saying: "Is there any more?" It is also possible that the pronoun is the second object and "alladhina kafaru" is the first, as He said: ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell﴾ [al-Tawba: 68].

This is a threat and rebuke, and the demonstrative refers to their rage against those who recite and their assault upon them, or to the displeasure and sullenness that befell them because of what was recited to them. The majority read al-Nar (the Fire) in the nominative, by supposing an implied subject, as if a speaker says: "What is it?" and the answer is: "The Fire," i.e., the Fire of Hell. And for the wrongdoers there will be no helper.﴾ ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, clear as they are, you recognize in the faces of those who disbelieve the denial. They nearly assault those who recite to them Our verses. Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that? The Fire, which Allah has promised to those who disbelieve. And wretched is the destination."﴾

It was also said: the Book is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). The demonstrative in His saying ﴿indeed, that is easy for Allah﴾ was said to refer to the previous judgment; the apparent meaning is that it refers to the encompassing of all creatures under His knowledge and comprehensiveness. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is known among the scholars of God that He knows everything that happens in the heavens and the earth, and He has written it on the Tablet before it occurs. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 22, verse 73–78:

﴿O mankind, a parable is presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those whom you invoke besides Allah will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for that. And if the fly should snatch away from them something, they could not retrieve it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought.﴾ ﴿They have not appraised Allah with His true appraisal. Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty.﴾ ﴿Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing.﴾ ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and to Allah are returned all matters.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, bow and prostrate and worship your Lord and do good that you may succeed.﴾ ﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him. He has chosen you and has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty – the religion of your father Abraham. He named you "Muslims" before [this] and in this [Revelation], that the Messenger may be a witness over you and you may be witnesses over the people. So establish prayer, give zakah, and hold fast to Allah. He is your Protector – how excellent a Protector and how excellent a Helper!﴾.

(p-390) When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that the disbelievers worship what has no proof of its worthiness of worship, neither from revelation nor from reason, and abandon the worship of Him who created them, He mentioned the condition of what they worship: the incapacity to create the smallest of things, rather even to retrieve from it what that smallest thing had taken. In this there is great ridicule of them, since they worship one with this attribute. This is by His saying ﴿Indeed, those whom you invoke﴾ with the second-person ta' of address. It was said: it is an address to the believers, and Allah wanted to clarify to them the error of the disbelievers, so "tad'un" (you invoke) would be an address to others, the disbelievers who worship other than Allah. It was also said: the address is general, encompassing whoever considers the matter of worshipping other than Allah, for the ugliness of that becomes apparent to him. "Ḍuriba" (a parable was presented) is in the passive voice, and the apparent view is that the one who presents the parable is Allah, exalted is He; He presented a parable for what is worshipped besides Him, meaning He explained a likeness to you and to your deities. It was also said: the one who presents the parable is the disbelievers, who made their idols and images a parable for Allah, exalted is He. Meaning: listen, you people, to the condition of this parable and similar to it. This is what al-Akhfash said; he said: there is no "mathal" (parable) here, rather the meaning is that the disbelievers made a parable for Allah. It was also said: it is a "mathal" in meaning, because "a parable was presented" concerning one who worships idols with one who worships what does not create a fly.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: what he has brought is not a parable, so how did he name it a parable? I say: he has named the attribute, or the wondrous story that is received with approval and astonishment, a parable, likening it to some of the well-known proverbs because it is approved and astonishing to them. End.

The majority read "tad'un" with the ta'. Al-Hasan, Ya'qub, Harun, al-Khufaf, and Mahbub from Abu 'Amr read it with the ya', and both are in the active voice. Al-Yamani and Musa al-Aswari read it with a ya' from below, in the passive voice. Al-Zamakhshari said: "lan" (never) is a sister of "lā" in negating the future, except that it negates it with emphasis, and its emphasis here is the indication that the creation of a fly by them is impossible and incompatible with their states, as if he said: it is impossible that they create. End. This statement of his about "lan" is the one reported from him, that "lan" is for negation in perpetuity. Do you not see that he explained it as impossibility? Other grammarians make "lan" like "lā" in negation. Do you not see His saying ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17], how negation came with "lā"? This is the correct view, and the proof for it is mentioned in grammar. Allah began with the negation of their bringing into existence and creating the least of created things, since bringing into existence is an attribute of His, exalted is He, established and exclusive, in which no one shares with Him. He followed it with the matter that reached them to the extreme of incapacity: the snatching away by the fly and their failure to rescue anything of what it snatches from them. The fly was numerous among the Arabs, and they used to anoint their idols with kinds of perfume, so the fly would take that away. From Ibn 'Abbas: they used to smear them with saffron and their heads with honey, and close them in, so the fly would enter through the openings and eat it. The position of "wa-law ijtama'ū lahu" (even if they gathered together for that): al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, as if he said: impossible that they create the fly, with the condition that they all gather together to create it and cooperate upon it. End.

We have already discussed the like of this "wa-law" before, and it was established that the "wāw" in it is for conjunction upon an omitted circumstance, as if it was said: ﴿they will never create a fly﴾ in every state, even in this state which would require that they create because of their gathering, yet it is not within their power.

﴿Weak are the seeker and the sought.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: the idol and the fly; meaning, it is fitting that the fly should be the seeker of what was taken from their perfume, according to the known disdain of animals. It was said: "the sought" is the gods and "the seeker" is the fly. The weakness of the gods is that they have no defense, and the weakness of the fly is in snatching what is upon the gods. Al-Dahhak said: the worshipper and the worshipped; the weakness of the worshipper is in seeking benefit from other than its proper source, and the weakness of the worshipped is in conveying that to its worshipper. Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying ﴿Weak are the seeker and the sought﴾ is like an equalization between them and the fly in weakness; but if you examine, you will find the seeker weaker and weaker, because the fly is an animal while they are inanimate; the fly is the victor and they are the vanquished. The apparent meaning is that it is a report of the weakness of the seeker and the sought. ﴿They have not appraised Allah with His true appraisal﴾: meaning they did not know Him with His true knowledge, in that they worshipped one who is stripped of His attributes, and named him with His name, and did not befit their Creator for worship. Then He concluded with two attributes contrary to the attributes of their deities: strength and dominance. ﴿Allah chooses﴾ to the end of the verse. It was revealed because of the saying of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira (p-391): ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ [Sad: 8], to the end of the verse, and they denied that the Messenger could be a human being. So Allah refuted them by stating that His messengers are angels and humans. Then He mentioned that He is Knowing of the states of those who are responsible, nothing of them being hidden from Him, and to Him is the return of all matters.

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that He had chosen messengers from among humans to the creation, He commanded them to establish what the messengers brought of obligations, namely prayer. It was said: when people first embraced Islam, they would prostrate without bowing and bow without prostrating, so they were commanded that their prayer be with bowing and prostration. They agreed on the legislation of prostration at the end of the verse ﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate...﴾ [al-Hajj: 18]. As for this verse, the school of Malik and Abu Hanifa is that no prostration is made in it, and the school of al-Shafi'i and Ahmad is that prostration is made in it. Thus said 'Umar, his son 'Abd Allah, 'Uthman, Abu al-Darda', Abu Musa, and Ibn 'Abbas. ﴿And worship your Lord﴾: meaning, single Him out with worship. ﴿And do good﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: maintaining ties of kinship and noble character. It appears in this order that they were first commanded with prayer, which is a kind of worship; second, with worship, which is a kind of doing good; and third, with doing good, which is more general than worship. Thus He began with the specific, then the general, then the more general.

﴿And strive for Allah﴾: a command to striving in the religion of Allah and exalting His word, encompassing the striving against disbelievers and innovators, and the striving against the self. It was said: it is a command to striving against disbelievers specifically. ﴿With the striving due to Him﴾: meaning exhaust your effort and capacity in that. He attributed the striving to Him, exalted is He, since it is specific to Allah in that it is done for His sake and for His purpose, so the attribution is by the least connection. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible to expand the adverb, as in his saying: "wa-yawma shahadnāhu Sulaymān wa-'Āmirā" (and the day we witnessed it, Sulaym and 'Amir). He means by the adverb the prepositional phrase: as if the original was "ḥaqqa jihādin fīhi," then it was expanded by deleting the preposition and attributing "jihād" to the pronoun. ﴿Ḥaqqa jihādihi﴾ belongs to the pattern of "huwa ḥaqqu ʿālimin" and "jiddu ʿālimin," meaning: truly knowledgeable and very knowledgeable. From Mujahid and al-Kalbi: it is abrogated by His saying ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16].

﴿He has chosen you﴾: meaning He selected you to bear His obligations. In His saying "huwa" (He) there is exaltation and specification, meaning He Himself, not another. ﴿From difficulty﴾: from constriction; rather it is the upright, tolerant religion, with no severity of the Children of Israel in it; rather repentance, expiations, and concessions were legislated in it. ﴿The religion of your father﴾ is in the accusative by an omitted verb. Ibn 'Atiyya estimated it as "make it the religion of ..." Al-Zamakhshari said: he put the religion in the accusative by the content of what precedes it, as if it was said: "widen your religion with the widening of the religion of your father," then he deleted the annexed noun and put the annexed-to noun in its place; or by specification, meaning "I mean by the religion the religion of your father," like His saying "al-ḥamdu lillāhi al-ḥamīd." Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' said: "follow the religion of Abraham." Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative by estimating the deletion of the "kāf" (like): as if it was said: the word "your father," by annexation to his father, the Messenger, and the Messenger's community is in the status of his children, so he became a father to his community through this intermediacy. It was also said: since most of them are from his offspring, like the Messenger and his kin and all the Arabs, the majority was sought and so it was annexed to them. His saying "religion" "of Abraham" came in regard to the worship of Allah and abandoning idols, which is what the preceding verses were directed toward; so this does not indicate following him in the details of the laws.

The apparent view is that the pronoun in ﴿He named you﴾ refers to Abraham, as he is the nearest mentioned. Every prophet has a granted supplication, and Abraham supplicated, saying: ﴿Our Lord, and make us submissive to You and from our descendants a Muslim community submissive to You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128]; Allah answered him and made it the community of Muhammad (peace be upon him). This is said by Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan. It was also said: "huwa" refers to Allah, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak. From Ibn 'Abbas: Allah ﴿named you Muslims before﴾, meaning in all the Books; "and in this" meaning the Qur'an. The indication that the pronoun is for Allah is the reading of Ubayy: "Allah named you." Ibn 'Atiyya said: this expression, meaning His saying "and in this," weakens the view of one who says the pronoun refers to Abraham, and it is not directed except by estimating an omitted, resumed clause in the speech. End. The estimate of the omission is: "you were named Muslims in this Qur'an," and the meaning is that He preferred you over the nations and named you by this name.

﴿That the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾: that he has conveyed to you, ﴿and you may be witnesses over the people﴾: that the messengers have conveyed to them. Since He has specified you with this honor and preference, worship Him, trust in Him, and do not seek (p-392) help and guardianship except from Him, for He is the best Protector and Helper.

From Qatadah: this community was given what no one was given except a prophet. It was said to the Prophet: "You are a witness over your community." It was said to him: "There is no difficulty upon you." It was said to him: "Ask, and you will be given." It was said to this community: ﴿and you may be witnesses over the people﴾; it was said to them: ﴿He has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty﴾; it was said to them: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. ﴿And hold fast﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: ask your Lord to protect you from everything you dislike. Al-Hasan said: hold fast to the religion of Allah.

Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty.﴾ ﴿Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing.﴾ ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and to Allah are returned all matters.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, bow and prostrate and worship your Lord and do good that you may succeed.﴾ ﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him. He has chosen you and has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty – the religion of your father Abraham. He named you "Muslims" before [this] and in this [Revelation], that the Messenger may be a witness over you and you may be witnesses over the people. So establish prayer, give zakah, and hold fast to Allah. He is your Protector – how excellent a Protector and how excellent a Helper!﴾.

Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing.﴾ ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and to Allah are returned all matters.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, bow and prostrate and worship your Lord and do good that you may succeed.﴾ ﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him. Every prophet has a granted supplication, and Abraham supplicated, saying: ﴿Our Lord, and make us submissive to You and from our descendants a Muslim community submissive to You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128]; Allah answered him and made it the community of Muhammad (peace be upon him). This is said by Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan. It was also said: "huwa" refers to Allah, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak. From Ibn 'Abbas: Allah ﴿named you Muslims before﴾, meaning in all the Books; "and in this" meaning the Qur'an. The indication that the pronoun is for Allah is the reading of Ubayy: "Allah named you." Ibn 'Atiyya said: this expression, meaning His saying "and in this," weakens the view of one who says the pronoun refers to Abraham, and it is not directed except by estimating an omitted, resumed clause in the speech. End. The estimate of the omission is: "you were named Muslims in this Qur'an," and the meaning is that He preferred you over the nations and named you by this name.

﴿That the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾: that he has conveyed to you, ﴿and you may be witnesses over the people﴾: that the messengers have conveyed to them. Since He has specified you with this honor and preference, worship Him, trust in Him, and do not seek (p-392) help and guardianship except from Him, for He is the best Protector and Helper.

From Qatadah: this community was given what no one was given except a prophet. It was said to the Prophet: "You are a witness over your community." It was said to him: "There is no difficulty upon you." It was said to him: "Ask, and you will be given." It was said to this community: ﴿and you may be witnesses over the people﴾; it was said to them: ﴿He has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty﴾; it was said to them: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. ﴿And hold fast﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: ask your Lord to protect you from everything you dislike. Al-Hasan said: hold fast to the religion of Allah.
